pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring crop, or in late summer for autumn. Can also transplant -- kale handles it well.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Great container crop. 3-5 gallon pot. Dwarf varieties (Dwarf Blue Curled) work especially well.

varieties.note_seasoned: Red Russian is the most tender and least bitter -- best choice for raw salads.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.fridge_seasoned: Up to 1 week -- don't wash until ready to use. Store dry.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 2-3 minutes, dry, freeze. Excellent for smoothies.
storage.notes_seasoned: Kale continues to sweeten in cold storage -- like refrigerator "aging."

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body_seasoned: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text_seasoned: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text_seasoned: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text_seasoned: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text_seasoned: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 1-2 lbs of leaves per plant over the season, more with regular harvesting
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A kale plant can produce for months if harvested correctly
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Kale is one of the most rewarding crops to grow. Pick it small for salads, larger for cooking.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 4 weeks from spring through midsummer. Like collards, kale is cut-and-come-again from the outer leaves -- one plant can produce for months. The most important succession is the late-summer sowing for autumn: kale planted 8-10 weeks before your first frost date will be at peak harvest when temperatures drop, and the flavor improves dramatically after frost. Don't skip this one.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool season crops such as spinach, leaf lettuce, peas, onions, and root crops can germinate at minimum soil temperatures of 35-40 degrees F. (MSU Extension) Sow seeds in the spring as soon as the soil is workable. Direct sow when soil consistently reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost in most zones. (UMN Extension)

crops.description_seasoned: Cold-hardy superfood that actually tastes better after frost. One of the most productive crops per square foot. Can harvest outer leaves all season.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick outer leaves when 8-10 inches. Younger leaves are more tender. Kale sweetens after light frost. Never take more than 1/3 of the plant at once.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Firm, fertile soil is key -- brassicas hate loose or acidic soil. Test pH and lime if below 6.5 (clubroot thrives in acidic conditions). Firm the soil by walking over it before planting -- transplants should feel solid, not loose. Dig in compost the previous autumn for spring planting.

pests.name: Leafminers
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pale winding tunnels or blotchy translucent patches between the upper and lower leaf surfaces. Affected tissue turns brown and the leaf is unusable even though the rest of the plant looks healthy.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spinach leafminer (Pegomya hyoscyami) and vegetable leafminer larvae feed inside the leaf. Beets and Swiss chard host the same pest, so nearby plantings spread the problem.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Contact insecticides do not reach larvae inside the leaf. Remove and destroy infested leaves as soon as trails appear. Check 2-3 times a week in spring.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest -- the adult fly cannot lay eggs through it. Rotate away from beets, chard, and last year's spinach location. Till in old crop residue.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small green or gray soft-bodied insects on undersides of leaves. Leaves curl and yellow. Sticky honeydew may develop into sooty mold.
pests.cause_seasoned: Green peach aphid (Myzus persicae) is the primary species on spinach; cotton-melon aphid also occurs. Green peach aphid also vectors several spinach viruses, so even small populations can cause disproportionate damage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with water. Insecticidal soap or neem oil on leaf undersides. Ladybugs and lacewings provide effective control on unprotected crops.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Floating row cover excludes aphids and their virus transmission. Control weeds nearby, which host aphids in the off-season. Avoid excess nitrogen.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large irregular holes chewed in leaves, often starting at the leaf margin. Silvery slime trails visible on leaves and soil in early morning. Damage worst in cool damp weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several slug and snail species feed at night, hiding in mulch and debris during the day. Spinach's tender low-growing leaves are especially exposed.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Iron phosphate bait (labeled for vegetable gardens and safe around pets) scattered thinly around beds. Hand-pick at night with a flashlight. Beer traps set at soil level.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up leaf debris and boards where slugs hide. Water in the morning so soil surface dries by evening. Copper tape around raised beds deters crossings.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow or pale green irregular patches on the upper leaf surface. Undersides show a fuzzy gray-violet mold in humid conditions. Badly infected leaves yellow entirely and collapse.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora effusa (formerly P. farinosa f. sp. spinaciae), an oomycete. Favored by cool wet weather with long leaf-wetness periods. Overwinters on crop residue and seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected leaves at first sign. No effective organic fungicide cure once established.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant downy-mildew-resistant varieties -- resistance is widely available and is the single best control. Water at soil level, not overhead. Space plants for airflow. Rotate away from spinach for 2-3 years.

diseases.name: White rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small white blister-like pustules on undersides of leaves, sometimes with yellow spots on the upper surface above each cluster. Heavily infected plants weaken and collapse.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Albugo occidentalis, an oomycete. Favored by cool humid nights (optimum 54°F germination) and mild days. Overwinters as thick-walled oospores in soil. TAMU lists white rust as the major disease of spinach in parts of the South.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove infected plants. Copper-based fungicide labeled for spinach may slow spread if applied early.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant white-rust-resistant varieties; most modern varieties with white-rust resistance also carry Fusarium resistance. Rotate out of spinach for 3+ years. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Numerous small circular spots with pale tan to off-white centers and reddish-purple margins. Spots may coalesce and cause extensive leaf loss. Heavy pressure in late summer.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Cercospora beticola fungus, the same pathogen that causes Cercospora leaf spot on beets and Swiss chard. Favored by warm temperatures (75-85°F), high humidity, and long nighttime leaf wetness.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Copper or biological fungicides (Bacillus subtilis products) applied preventively during humid stretches.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate out of beets, chard, and spinach for 2-3 years. Control weeds in the Chenopodium family (lambsquarters, pigweed) that host the pathogen. Drip-irrigate rather than overhead.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants yellow and wilt starting with older lower leaves. Roots turn black. Stunted plants fail to head up. Worse on heavy soils and during warm weather stretches, which shorten the cool-season spinach window.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. spinaciae, a soil-borne fungus. Can persist in soil for years. Beets and Swiss chard can host the pathogen without showing symptoms, spreading it silently.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective cure once plants are symptomatic. Remove and destroy infected plants.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties (most white-rust-resistant varieties are also Fusarium-resistant). Long rotations out of spinach, beets, and chard. Avoid waterlogged soils.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2-3 days -- spinach bolts in dry heat

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost. Cold-tolerant -- sow very early. Poor transplant candidate.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container crop -- shallow roots. Even window boxes work. 6-8 inches deep minimum.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 2 minutes, squeeze dry, freeze. Excellent.
storage.notes_seasoned: Spinach wilts fast -- harvest and use promptly, or freeze.

bolting.triggers: Heat, long days -- very day-length sensitive
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Plant very early (can handle frost). Choose slow-bolt varieties (Bloomsdale, Tyee). Autumn plantings last much longer. Shade cloth in spring heat.
bolting.note_seasoned: Spinach is the most difficult to keep from bolting in warm weather -- succession sow and accept the short season.

varieties.note_seasoned: Tyee is the most bolt-resistant variety available -- significantly extends the harvest window in spring.

thinning.method: Snip at soil level. Thinnings are edible.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Spinach germinates in clusters -- each seed capsule contains multiple seeds. Thin promptly for best yield.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beet family (same diseases)
rotation.good_after: Legumes (fix nitrogen that leafy crops need)
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate leafy greens to avoid leaf miner buildup.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body_seasoned: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text_seasoned: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text_seasoned: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text_seasoned: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text_seasoned: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 4-6 oz per plant before bolting
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Spinach is a quick crop -- harvest everything within the window
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Spinach bolts fast in heat. Plan for a spring and a fall sowing rather than one long crop.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 2 weeks in spring until temperatures consistently reach 75°F, then pause and restart in late August for a fall crop. Spinach bolts fast in heat and is genuinely pointless to sow mid-summer in most zones. The fall succession is often better than spring -- cooler nights and shorter days keep it sweet longer. Count back from your first fall frost to time your last sowing.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool season crops such as spinach, leaf lettuce, peas, onions, and root crops can germinate at minimum soil temperatures of 35-40 degrees F. (MSU Extension) Sow seeds in the spring as soon as the soil is workable. Direct sow when soil consistently reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost in most zones. (UMN Extension)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: For a fall crop of cool-season leafy greens, sow seed about 2 to 3 months before the average first fall frost date. UMN lettuce guidance specifies 'about three months'; shorter-cycle greens (arugula, bok choy) can be sown closer to 2 months out. (UMN Extension)

crops.description_seasoned: One of the fastest crops to harvest. Cold-hardy and can be direct sown as soon as ground can be worked. Bolts in heat -- time plantings for cool weather.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick outer leaves continuously. Harvest entire plant once it shows signs of bolting (central stem elongates).

crops.name: Carrot

soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Deep, loose, sandy loam -- no rocks or clumps

3.notes: Direct sow as soon as ground is workable. Thin to 3 inches apart or you'll get all tops, no roots.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct seed cool-season root vegetables (carrots, beets, radishes, turnips) when soil reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost. (UMN Extension) Roots do not transplant -- their long taproots develop early and transplanting damages and misdirects root growth. In Minnesota, start planting carrots beginning April 15. (UMN Extension)

uscrn_validation.zone_coverage_note_seasoned: station-years 28 below 30 confidence threshold; verdict uses available data but should not be auto-applied

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant a fall crop when summer heat subsides, approximately 2-3 months before first fall frost. Fall-matured roots are sweeter due to cool-weather sugar accumulation. Autumn-matured carrots from a late sowing are noticeably sweeter. (Crop succession guidance, UMN, Iowa State Extension)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct seed cool-season root vegetables (carrots, beets, radishes, turnips) when soil reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost. harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant a fall crop when summer heat subsides, approximately 2-3 months before first fall frost. harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool-season root crops develop off flavors, bitterness, or toughness when forced to mature in summer heat. Carrots become bitter above approximately 80 degrees F; radishes bolt and become woody; turnips become tough. (UMN Extension; UGA Circular 943; Clemson HGIC)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end for spring crop: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

harvest_end.label: secondary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool-season root crops tolerate light frost. Beets, carrots, radishes, and turnips can be left in the ground past first frost and stored in place in cold zones with mulch protection. (UMN Extension; Iowa State Extension; Cornell Extension)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Fall harvest window extends to approximately first_frost + 14d for most; parsnips extend much further.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Avoid high nitrogen -- it produces forked, hairy roots. A low-nitrogen feed worked into soil before sowing is ideal.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Rosemary
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Deters carrot fly with strong scent

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, Insects 2018, 9(4):112). Chives-with-carrots for carrot fly deterrence is specifically described by Mississippi State University Extension ('Chives tend to repel aphids, but the chives also repel rust flies in carrots'). Utah State University Extension's 'Carrot Rust Fly' management page does NOT endorse allium interplanting as a primary control -- it lists timely harvest, delayed planting, crop rotation, crop residue removal, and row covers as the recommended tactics. The carrot-fly-by-allium mechanism is plausible (both aphids and carrot rust fly locate hosts by scent), but the extension protocol rigor is lower than the extension-documented controls. The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's published aphid or carrot pest guidelines.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural shading is a real microclimate effect. Mechanism established; specific pairing benefits depend on conditions.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Rust-red tunnels and channels inside roots. Foliage yellows and wilts. Larvae (small white maggots) visible in roots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Psila rosae. Female flies attracted by carrot scent to lay eggs near roots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure once roots infested. Use fine mesh netting 60cm high as barrier -- flies are low-fliers.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow under fine insect mesh. Sow alongside chives or rosemary to mask scent. Avoid thinning on still evenings when smell is strongest.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Willow-carrot aphids curl leaf tips and reduce vigor. Leaves distorted. Can transmit viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cavariella aegopodii. Arrives from willow trees in spring.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insecticidal soap or neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow under insect mesh. Avoid planting near willow trees.

diseases.name: Cavity spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Oval gray/brown sunken cavities on carrot roots. First appears as small lesions that enlarge.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pythium violae soil pathogen. Favored by compacted, poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No chemical control. Improve soil structure with organic matter.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Deep, well-drained, stone-free soil. Avoid waterlogging. Crop rotation.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 3-4 days during germination, weekly once established
watering.method_seasoned: Gentle overhead or drip -- a strong stream washes seeds out of loose seedbed during germination

start_method.notes_seasoned: Always direct sow -- carrots do not transplant. Sow thinly, firm soil well, and keep moist until germination (can take 2-3 weeks).

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works in deep containers (12+ inches). Choose short varieties (Chantenay, Danvers, Paris Market). 3-gallon minimum.

varieties.note_seasoned: Chantenay is the best choice for heavy or rocky soil -- short and blunt rather than long and thin.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Carrots, parsnips, parsley, cilantro, dill, celery -- share carrot fly and Apiaceae diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Avoid planting carrots where parsnips (or vice versa) grew last year -- same pest pressures.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 4-6 weeks -- remove tops first (tops draw moisture from root)
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch and freeze for cooking
storage.notes_seasoned: Carrots store best in damp sand in a cool place. Can be left in ground through mild frosts. Store away from apples, pears, and bananas -- ethylene from those fruits triggers isocoumarin formation in carrots, producing a bitter taste within days.

thinning.when: Thin when seedlings are 1 inch tall
thinning.method: Snip with scissors rather than pulling -- pulling disturbs neighbors. Thin again to 3-4 inches when 3 inches tall. Thinning is critical -- crowded carrots produce a mass of small forked roots.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Thin on a still evening and firm soil around remaining plants to prevent carrot fly detecting the scent.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body_seasoned: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body_seasoned: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Root check-in
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text_seasoned: These crops are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the taproot and produces forked or stunted roots. Sow seeds shallowly (1/4 to 1/2 inch deep) and keep soil surface consistently moist for the 1 to 3 week germination window.
Carrot and parsnip seed is short-lived -- use fresh seed each year. Parsnip especially can take up to 3 weeks to germinate; do not give up early.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded roots stay small and forked. Pull weaker seedlings rather than transplanting them.
Mulch lightly between rows once seedlings are established to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the row -- hoeing damages shallow seedling roots.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently. Uneven moisture causes carrot and parsnip roots to split as they swell during a wet period after dry conditions.
These crops feed lightly. Side-dress with compost mid-season if growth slows; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush leafy tops at the expense of roots.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips after the first frost for best flavor -- this is not folklore; the cold genuinely converts starch to sugar in the root. Parsnip especially needs frost exposure to develop its characteristic sweetness.

Loosen soil with a fork before pulling -- yanking by the tops snaps the root, especially on long carrots and parsnips. Cut tops off within an inch of the crown for storage; tops left on draw moisture out of the root.

storage.text_seasoned: Store carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips in layers of damp sand or sawdust in a cool location (32 to 40 degrees) at high humidity. Properly stored, these crops keep 4 to 6 months.

In zones with mild winters, you can leave the roots in the ground and harvest as needed -- mulch heavily over the row before the ground freezes. This is often easier than indoor storage and preserves quality longer.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One carrot per plant -- a 3-foot row gives you around 30-40 carrots
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Carrots mature roughly all at once -- plan storage
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Homegrown carrots taste nothing like shop-bought ones. They are sweeter, more flavorful, and worth every bit of effort.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops actively benefit from light to moderate frost -- it improves flavor by converting root starch to sugar. Damage from frost is rare and usually only happens to exposed leaf tops on a hard freeze; the roots are insulated by soil and survive even harsh winter conditions in many zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time harvest to follow the first frost rather than precede it. In zones with mild winters, leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch and harvest as needed through winter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Carrot rust fly (carrot, parsnip) is the headline pest -- larvae tunnel through roots leaving rusty trails. Cabbage maggot (turnip, sometimes beetroot) does similar damage to brassica roots. Leaf spot diseases and powdery mildew can hit foliage but rarely affect the root harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest blocks both carrot rust fly and cabbage maggot -- this is the most effective home-garden defense. Rotate root crops to a new bed each year. Avoid planting carrot or parsnip after parsley or celery (same family, same pest).

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Uneven watering -- a dry spell followed by heavy water -- causes roots to split as they swell rapidly. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, soft black tissue, and crown collapse. Beetroot and turnip handle wet soil better than carrot and parsnip, both of which need excellent drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture rather than letting soil dry out and then soaking it. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed for carrot and parsnip especially. Mulch helps stabilize moisture.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought-stressed root crops produce small, fibrous roots with concentrated and often unpleasantly strong flavor. Parsnips become woody at the core; carrots become bitter; turnips become sharp; beetroot becomes earthy and tough.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply and consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Mulch between rows to retain moisture. In hot weather, root crops appreciate light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Carrot, parsnip, and beetroot seeds need 1 to 3 weeks of consistent surface moisture to germinate. The most common reason for failed sowings is the soil surface drying out during germination -- not poor seed or bad soil. Parsnip seed in particular loses viability fast and old seed simply does not come up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into pre-moistened soil and cover with a board or burlap until the first seedlings emerge -- this keeps the surface consistently moist without daily watering. Use fresh parsnip seed each year. Pre-sprout difficult seed on damp paper towels indoors before sowing if needed.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from early spring through midsummer. Carrots are slow to germinate (10-21 days) so keep the seedbed moist until sprouts appear. The key succession insight for carrots is that they store well in the ground -- you can leave a mature batch in place while a new one grows. But succession avoids having all your carrots mature in August heat, when they develop off flavors. Autumn-matured carrots from a late sowing are noticeably sweeter.

crops.description_seasoned: Slow to germinate but rewarding. Loose, deep soil is the key -- rocky or clay soil causes forked, stunted roots. Raised beds work well.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Shoulder of carrot visible at soil level and ½ inch across. Green tops should be vibrant. Loosen soil first, then pull. Frost improves sweetness.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Carrots need deep, light, stone-free soil to 12 inches. Remove all stones and break up clods. Never use fresh manure -- it causes forking and hairy roots. A light dressing of sand helps drainage. Firm the surface after sowing -- loose seedbed causes problems.

crops.name: Basil

3.notes: Start indoors 4 weeks before last frost. Cold kills basil instantly -- wait until nights are reliably above 50°F.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.source_quote_seasoned: Sow basil seeds directly into the ground after the danger of frost has passed. (UMN Extension, 'Growing basil in home gardens')
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Basil is a warm-weather herb that cannot tolerate frost. Plant after last frost when soil has warmed to about 70 degrees F, typically 2 weeks after last frost. For an earlier start, seeds can be started indoors 4 weeks before last frost and transplanted out.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Japanese beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Skeletonized leaves with only veins remaining. Metallic green beetles visible on plants in summer.
pests.cause_seasoned: Popillia japonica. Adults feed on foliage July-August.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick beetles into soapy water in the morning when sluggish. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers during peak beetle season. Milky spore disease treatment targets larvae in lawn.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of one or more stems, yellow leaves, streaking on stems. Plants die rapidly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. basilici soil fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants immediately.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified disease-free seed. Rotate basil crops. Improve soil drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing leaves with fuzzy gray-purple coating on leaf undersides. Spreads rapidly in humid conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora belbahrii. A major basil disease, especially indoors.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Do not wet foliage. Space plants well. Grow in full sun. Choose resistant varieties.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2-3 days -- wilts dramatically but recovers quickly
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level -- wet leaves cause disease

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 4-6 weeks before last frost. Very cold-sensitive -- do not transplant until night temps stay above 50°F. Harden off over 7-10 days.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: One of the best herbs for containers. Single large pot or window box. Keep in full sun and water regularly.

varieties.note_seasoned: Genovese is the standard for pesto and Italian cooking. Spicy Globe stays compact and is ideal for containers.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: On counter in a glass of water like flowers -- 1-2 weeks
storage.fridge_seasoned: Avoid -- basil turns black in cold
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blend with olive oil and freeze in ice cube trays. Excellent for winter cooking.
storage.notes_seasoned: Never refrigerate fresh basil. Counter-top vase method is the best storage.

bolting.prevention_seasoned: Pinch flower heads off immediately and consistently. Keep harvesting tips. Do not allow any flowers to set seed.
bolting.note_seasoned: Basil that flowers drops leaf quality but doesn't become inedible. Aggressive pinching extends harvest by weeks.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other herbs in the mint family
rotation.good_after: Tomatoes, peppers -- classic pairing and compatible rotation
rotation.note_seasoned: Basil grown near tomatoes for companion benefit can follow tomatoes the next year.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting / Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Central flower stem shooting up. Leaves becoming smaller and flavor intensifying or turning bitter depending on the herb.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove flower stems immediately on basil to extend harvest. For cilantro and dill, flowering is part of the lifecycle -- collect seeds for cooking or sowing.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start your basil indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Basil is frost-tender and loves warmth. Start seeds indoors 3-4 weeks before last frost. Keep at 70°F+ -- basil sown in cold conditions germinates poorly and grows slowly.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start pinching your basil
notifications.body_seasoned: Begin pinching out the growing tips as soon as you have 4-6 sets of leaves. This is the most important technique for growing productive basil -- it forces bushy side growth instead of a single tall stem. Pinch every 2-3 weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove basil flowers immediately
notifications.body_seasoned: Pinch out any flower buds the moment you see them. Basil that flowers shifts all its energy to seed production and the leaves become smaller and less flavorful. Be diligent about this through summer.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest all basil before first frost
notifications.body_seasoned: Basil blackens and dies at the first frost. Harvest everything now. Make pesto, freeze leaves in olive oil ice cube trays, or dry stems for winter. Nothing from the basil plant should be left to frost.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text_seasoned: These herbs are direct-sown or started indoors. Basil needs warm soil (70 degrees) for germination; dill and cilantro tolerate cooler soil (55 to 60 degrees) and actually germinate better in cool weather.
Sow shallowly -- 1/4 inch deep -- and keep soil surface moist. Cilantro and dill can be sown in succession every 2 to 3 weeks for continuous harvest, since both bolt fast.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded plants bolt faster and produce less leaf. Pinch basil tops at 6 inches to encourage branching.
These herbs all benefit from light afternoon shade in hot summer climates. Cilantro especially bolts within weeks of warm weather hitting.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch basil regularly to prevent flowering -- once basil flowers, leaf production slows and flavor changes. Removing flower buds extends the productive harvest by weeks.
Water consistently. Wilted plants recover but the stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill. Mulch to stabilize soil moisture.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by snipping outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. For basil, cut whole stems above a leaf pair to encourage two new shoots from each cut.
Cilantro is harvested as leaves OR seed (coriander). Same plant, same cycle: harvest leaves while plant is leafy, let it bolt, harvest dry seeds from the spent flower heads.

bolting.text_seasoned: Bolting (going to flower) signals the end of useful leaf production for these herbs. Basil bolts in heat or after flowering; dill and cilantro bolt fast in any warm weather.

Once bolting starts, decide: pinch flowers to extend leaf harvest by 1 to 2 weeks (basil), or let the plant flower and self-seed for next year (dill, cilantro). Bolted cilantro is often the original planting and reseeds prolifically.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous harvest of leaves all summer from one plant
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Basil from your own garden, still warm from the sun, is one of the great simple pleasures of growing food.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Basil is killed outright by light frost -- it is the most frost-sensitive culinary herb. Dill and cilantro are hardier; both tolerate light frost and cilantro actually grows better in cool weather. Basil also suffers chill damage (leaf blackening) below 50 degrees even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to plant basil until soil is reliably 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. For dill and cilantro, sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring -- they prefer cool conditions. Have row cover ready for cold nights with basil; in the fall, harvest basil heavily before the first cold snap because the plants will not recover.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids cluster on tender new growth across all three. Basil downy mildew is the headline disease (yellowing and gray fuzz on leaf undersides) and has spread aggressively in recent years. Dill and cilantro may attract carrot family pests (carrot rust fly larvae, leaf miner). Powdery mildew occasionally hits all three in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose downy-mildew-resistant basil varieties -- Rutgers Devotion DMR, Prospera, and similar bred for resistance. Space plants well for airflow. Hose off aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Rotate herb-bed location each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three herbs need well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Basil is especially sensitive to wet conditions and may collapse suddenly from Pythium or Fusarium in poorly-drained sites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Use containers with drainage holes for indoor or balcony herbs. Water at the base, not overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings. Avoid heavy clay sites for basil especially.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill -- often by weeks -- and produces small, tough basil leaves with concentrated bitter flavor. Wilted herbs recover with watering but the stress shortens the productive cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently, especially in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. For cilantro and dill, succession-plant every 2 to 3 weeks rather than relying on one planting through the season -- this gives you continuous harvest even as individual plantings bolt.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs need 6 hours of direct sun minimum for full flavor and growth. In partial shade, plants grow tall, leggy, and pale, with weaker flavor. Cilantro is a partial exception -- it tolerates partial shade in hot zones, where light shade actually slows bolting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun in cool climates. In hot climates (zone 8 and warmer), cilantro and parsley tolerate and even prefer light afternoon shade. Basil and dill want full sun even in heat. For indoor growing, herbs need a sunny south-facing window or supplemental grow lights.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from last frost through midsummer. Basil bolts quickly in heat -- flowering stems become bitter and the plant redirects energy from leaves to seeds. Pinching flowers delays this but doesn't stop it. A fresh succession planting every 3 weeks means you always have young, leafy plants at peak flavor. If you're growing for pesto, succession means you can harvest entire plants rather than carefully pinching to delay bolt.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heavy feeder -- add generous compost at planting. Avoid excess nitrogen once flowering or you'll get lots of leaf and few fruit.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Trap crop for aphids, attracts predators

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause_seasoned: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

watering.method_seasoned: At soil level -- wet leaves cause powdery mildew

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost. Zucchini grows so fast that starting indoors offers little advantage. If starting indoors, use biodegradable pots -- 3 weeks before last frost maximum.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Possible in large containers (10+ gallons) but not ideal -- plants are large and thirsty. Raised beds are much better.

varieties.note_seasoned: Patio Star and Bush Baby are excellent if space is limited -- compact plants, full yield.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Slice or grate, blanch 2 minutes, freeze. Good for baking.
storage.notes_seasoned: Small zucchini store much better than large ones.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large seed leaves pushing up fast -- squash germinates quickly in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow seeds on their edge to prevent rotting. Keep soil warm and moist.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large, hairy true leaves developing rapidly. Squash grows fast once it gets going.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give them space from the start -- squash plants get very large and do not like competition.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A strong central crown with multiple large leaves. Bush varieties stay compact; vining types will start to sprawl.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: If growing winter squash, direct the vines in the direction you want them to go now -- once established they are harder to redirect.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Growing well and in the right spot?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large orange-yellow flowers. Male flowers come first on long straight stems. Female flowers have a swollen base -- the future squash.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning if you are not seeing good fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowers open? Any tiny squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Summer squash: harvest small and often at 6-8 inches. Winter squash: wait until skin is hard and stem is dry and corky.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Summer squash picked small tastes better and keeps production going. Winter squash left on the vine longer develops better flavor and storage life.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production on summer squash. Winter squash stems drying and corking -- the cue to harvest before frost.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cure winter squash at room temperature for 10-14 days before storing -- it hardens the skin and sweetens the flesh. Summer squash plants can be composted after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Season done? Worth noting what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your squash
notifications.body_seasoned: Squash goes in a week after last frost, once the soil has had time to warm properly. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest plant. They grow fast -- you will see real progress within a week.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your squash flowers -- pollination time
notifications.body_seasoned: Your squash should be flowering now. If you see flowers but no fruit forming, check whether you have both male and female flowers open at the same time. Female flowers have a small swollen base. Hand-pollinate in the morning if bees are scarce.

notifications.title_seasoned: Summer squash ready -- pick small and often
notifications.body_seasoned: Your courgettes or summer squash should be ready. Pick them at 6-8 inches -- they taste better small and the plant produces far more when you harvest regularly. A forgotten courgette turns into a marrow overnight.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your squash plants
notifications.body_seasoned: Summer squash especially needs checking every few days -- they grow incredibly fast and a missed harvest sets back the whole plant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect your squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Squash is frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Winter squash still on the vine must be harvested before a hard frost -- even one frosty night can damage stored winter squash.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Powdery mildew risk for your squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Squash is very susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good spacing and airflow. If you see white powdery patches on leaves, remove affected leaves and spray with a dilute baking soda solution.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Your squash needs deep watering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Squash plants have large leaves and need a lot of water in dry conditions. Water deeply at the base -- not the leaves -- twice a week in drought conditions. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow squash seeds on their side, not flat. The root emerges from the pointed end and finds its way down more easily.
Squash germinates fast in warm soil -- sometimes in 4-5 days. In cold soil it rots. Wait for genuine warmth (60°F+ minimum, 70°F+ ideal).

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin ruthlessly to one plant per spot. Squash planted too close together become a tangled mass that is prone to mildew and difficult to harvest.
Do not start squash indoors too early -- 3-4 weeks maximum. They outgrow their pots quickly and transplant shock is real.

established.text_seasoned: Leave enough room -- a zucchini plant can easily cover 4-6 square feet. A butternut squash vine can run 6-10 feet. Plan for this before planting.
A thick layer of mulch around squash plants suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and keeps the fruit clean if it rests on the ground.

flowering.text_seasoned: Male flowers come before female flowers -- this is normal and not something to worry about. Female flowers (with the swollen base behind the petals) follow within a week or two.
Early morning is when squash flowers are most receptive. If you are hand-pollinating, do it between 7-10am while flowers are fully open.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick zucchini and yellow summer squash young -- 6 to 8 inches is the sweet spot for tender flesh and best flavor. At full marrow size the seeds are tough and the skin gets bitter.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Summer squash plants stop setting new fruit if mature ones are left on the vine; constant picking keeps the plant producing.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Summer squash do not store. Use, freeze (grated, blanched), or give them away within a week of picking. Refrigerate at 45-50°F at most -- below 40°F they get pitted and chilled.
When production slows in late summer, pull the plant rather than nursing it. Powdery mildew sets in by then on most varieties; clear the bed and replant for fall greens or cover crop.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 10-20 lbs over the season -- zucchini is one of the most productive vegetables you can grow
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: At peak, one healthy zucchini plant produces 1-2 fruits every 2-3 days
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Zucchini is famously easy and productive. You will likely have more than you can eat -- plan to give some away.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow a second batch 4 weeks after the first. One zucchini plant will produce more than most families can eat -- the reason for succession isn't quantity but quality. Younger plants produce more vigorously and with less disease pressure. Powdery mildew and squash vine borers typically hit older plants hard; a second generation sidesteps this. Two plants per succession, not a full bed.
