pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly -- avoid watering during flowering to prevent blossom drop

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow only after last frost -- beans hate transplanting. Plant 1 inch deep in warm soil (60°F+).

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Bush varieties work well in 5-gallon containers. Pole beans need a large pot with a trellis.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note_seasoned: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent
storage.notes_seasoned: Best eaten fresh. Frozen green beans are nearly as good as fresh for cooking.

recommended: Purple Queen (purple pod, turns green when cooked)
varieties.note_seasoned: Provider is the most reliable variety for difficult conditions -- very early, tolerates cool and warm soils.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body_seasoned: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title_seasoned: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body_seasoned: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text_seasoned: Beans are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the brittle taproot. Wait until soil is 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better) before sowing; cold soil rots seed before it germinates.

Sow 1 to 2 inches deep, 2 to 4 inches apart in rows. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria at sowing if the bed has not grown beans recently -- this boosts the nitrogen-fixing nodulation that beans depend on.

seedling.text_seasoned: Beans germinate fast in warm soil -- typically 7 to 10 days. Seedlings are vulnerable to slugs and bean leaf beetles in their first weeks; check daily.

Thin bush beans to 4 to 6 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Pole beans need a trellis or pole structure in place at this stage -- they grow fast and resent late-installed support.

established.text_seasoned: Do not fertilize beans with nitrogen. Beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- this is when water stress most reduces yield. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds.

flowering.text_seasoned: Beans are self-pollinating and do not need pollinators. Flowers open and self-pollinate within hours; fruit set is fast.
Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during flowering -- both populations spike in this window. Check undersides of leaves daily.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick beans young and often -- bush and pole beans ready when pods snap cleanly and the seeds inside are still small. Edamame ready when pods are plump and fill 80 to 90 percent with bright green beans, before yellowing.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Beans left on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Edamame is harvested whole-pod, not shelled in the field.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: After harvest, cut bean plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen for the bed.
Rotate beans to a new bed each year. Bean diseases (anthracnose, halo blight, bean rust) survive in soil and infect next year's planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Half a pound per plant over the season -- plant generously
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Bush beans produce in a flush -- all at once over 2-3 weeks, then done
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Bush beans are fast and reliable. Succession sow every 3 weeks for a continuous harvest.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Beans are warm-season tender annuals -- killed outright by light frost at any stage. Cold soil at sowing (below 60 degrees) rots seed; cool conditions during early growth produce stunted plants that never fully recover. Late summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to sow until soil is reliably 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better). In short-season zones, choose early-maturing bush varieties and use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring frosts. For fall harvests, time the planting so harvest finishes before first expected frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mexican bean beetle (yellow with black spots, similar to ladybug but a pest) is the dominant bean pest east of the Rockies -- larvae skeletonize leaves. Bean leaf beetle damages seedlings and pods. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Halo blight (water-soaked spots with yellow halo) and bean rust are the headline diseases. For edamame specifically, soybean aphid and Japanese beetle are also common.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For Mexican bean beetle, hand-pick adults and crush yellow egg masses on leaf undersides; in heavy infestations, parasitic wasp release works for organic gardeners. Rotate to a new bed each year. Avoid working bean plants when foliage is wet -- this spreads halo blight and bean rust. Choose disease-resistant varieties for the next planting.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Beans are also susceptible to white mold (Sclerotinia) in cool wet conditions, which produces fluffy white growth at the soil line and kills plants quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water in the morning so foliage dries before evening. Space plants for airflow. For white mold, rotate at least 3 years between bean plantings in any one bed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the leading cause of poor bean harvests. Plants drop flowers under water stress and produce small empty or partially-filled pods. Edamame is especially demanding of consistent water during the pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal because it provides consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower and produce well. In partial shade plants grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few pods. Tall pole beans can shade their own lower leaves if not pinched at the top of the support.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. For pole beans, pinch the growing tip when vines reach the top of the support to prevent excessive top growth and improve light penetration to lower flowering nodes.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from last frost through midsummer. Bush beans produce in a single flush over 2-3 weeks then decline -- succession is essential for a continuous harvest. Each sowing is a distinct new crop rather than a continuous one. Stop new sowings with enough growing season remaining before first frost: count back 60-70 days from your first expected frost date to find your last safe sowing date.

direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bush and pole bean seeds 1-2 weeks after last frost once soil has warmed to at least 60 degrees F (65 degrees F preferred). (UMN)

crops.description_seasoned: One of the easiest crops to grow from direct sow. Fast-maturing, productive, and great for beginners. Succession sow every 2-3 weeks for continuous harvest.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when pods snap cleanly and are pencil thin. Seeds inside should barely be visible as bumps. Check daily -- over-mature beans signal the plant to stop producing.

crops.name: Sugar Snap Peas

3.notes: Direct sow as soon as ground can be worked. Peas love cold soil -- don't wait for warm weather.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Most pea varieties need about 60 days of growth before harvest and stop producing once temperatures rise above 85 degrees F. (UMN Extension) Young pea plants can survive light frost and will grow at any temperature above 40 degrees F. Good growing temperatures are between 55 and 65 degrees F. Plant pea seeds as soon as the ground has thawed and the soil is workable. (UMN)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall peas can be direct seeded once soil temperatures drop below 75 degrees F -- typically 2-3 months before first frost. Peas tolerate light frosts once established; winter-hardy varieties survive dips to 20 degrees F with mulch or row cover. (Cornell, UMD)

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

watering.method_seasoned: At soil level or overhead early in day

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost -- peas prefer cool soil. Soak seeds overnight for faster germination.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works in deep containers with trellis. 5-gallon minimum. Dwarf varieties are best.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note_seasoned: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 2 minutes, freeze -- good
storage.notes_seasoned: Fresh is much better -- eat as soon as possible after harvest.

varieties.note_seasoned: Cascadia is the best for small gardens -- compact 30-inch vines need no staking and produce heavily.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body_seasoned: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title_seasoned: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body_seasoned: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text_seasoned: Peas are direct-sown 4 to 6 weeks before last frost -- they actually prefer cool soil (40 to 60 degrees) and germinate poorly above 75. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing for spring harvest works well.
Sow 1 to 1.5 inches deep, 2 inches apart. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria if the bed has not grown peas recently. Soak seeds overnight before sowing in cool soil to speed germination.

seedling.text_seasoned: Peas germinate in 7 to 14 days in cool soil. Seedlings tolerate light frost and even brief snow once established -- they are remarkably cold-hardy.
Install trellis or netting at sowing or as soon as seedlings emerge. Peas climb by tendrils and need something to grab. Even bush peas benefit from low brushwood support.

established.text_seasoned: Do not fertilize with nitrogen. Peas fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; extra N produces leafy plants with poor pod production.
Water consistently. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast -- mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and keep roots cool.

flowering.text_seasoned: Peas are self-pollinating; flowers do not need insect pollinators. Cool weather during flowering produces the most flowers and highest yields.
Watch for pea aphids on flower clusters and tender new growth. Powdery mildew often shows up as flowering peaks, especially in still humid conditions.

harvest.text_seasoned: Snow peas: pick when pods are flat and the peas inside are barely visible bumps. Sugar snap peas: pick when pods are plump and crisp but before peas inside become starchy. Both are best picked young and often.
Harvest every 1 to 2 days during peak production. Peas left on the plant signal it to stop producing new flowers; daily picking can extend the harvest by weeks.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Peas finish abruptly when daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees -- plants yellow, stop flowering, and decline. This is the natural cycle, not a problem.
Cut spent plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil for the nitrogen contribution. The freed-up bed is well-suited to a fall planting of cool-season crops or warm-season transplants.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A generous handful of pods per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Sugar snaps produce over several weeks in cool weather -- harvest daily at peak
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Fresh sugar snap peas eaten straight from the vine are one of the greatest garden rewards. They taste nothing like shop-bought.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peas are unusual among annuals in being killed by HEAT, not cold. Young plants tolerate light frost and even brief snow; mature plants flower through cool spring weather but stop and decline once daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees. The end of pea season is heat, not cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow as early as possible -- 4 to 6 weeks before last frost in most zones. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing gives a long cool-season harvest. Choose heat-tolerant varieties (Wando, Sugar Sprint) for warmer zones. Plan succession plantings so harvest finishes before the heat hits.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pea aphid (the headline pea pest) clusters on flower buds and tender new growth, weakening plants and reducing pod set. Pea weevil larvae bore into developing peas. Pea leaf miner damages leaves but rarely affects yield substantially. Powdery mildew is the headline disease, especially in cool humid conditions or as plants approach the heat-stress end of their cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off pea aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Choose powdery-mildew-resistant varieties (most modern peas have some resistance). Space plants for airflow and avoid overhead watering. Rotate peas to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot and yellowing of inner leaves. Peas in heavy clay or low-lying spots are especially vulnerable. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew and ascochyta blight.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Use raised beds in heavy or wet sites. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill produces small empty pods or partially-filled pods. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast; a few hot dry days during the critical flowering window can substantially reduce yield even on otherwise healthy plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and keep roots cool. Drip irrigation works well for peas because it keeps foliage dry while providing consistent water.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peas need 6 hours of sun minimum, though they tolerate light shade better than beans. In deep shade, plants grow leggy with sparse flowers and reduced yield. Crowded planting can shade lower flowering nodes on tall pole peas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun in cool climates; light afternoon shade is fine in warmer zones and may extend the bloom cycle by reducing heat stress. Space plants for airflow and light penetration. Trellis tall varieties properly so vines spread out rather than tangling.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 2-3 weeks from early spring until temperatures consistently exceed 70°F. Peas hate heat and will stop producing and die when summer arrives -- don't fight it. The goal is to have multiple batches maturing through the cool spring window rather than one big planting that's all done at once. In zones 7+ you can also sow in autumn for a fall crop. Pause all sowings in summer.

crops.description_seasoned: Eat the whole pod -- sweetest straight off the vine. Cool-season crop that thrives in spring and fall. Provide a trellis and they'll climb happily.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pods are plump and round, seeds visible. Pod should snap cleanly. Sweet and crunchy. Don't wait until pods yellow.

crops.name: Broccoli

3.notes: Spring planting only. Start indoors 5 weeks before transplanting. Harvest before summer heat causes bolting.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Heading brassica seedlings start best at normal room temperatures (60-70 degrees F) under bright overhead light; no heating mat is needed. (UMN Extension)

start_indoors.label: secondary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: For fall heading-brassica transplants, start seeds indoors 4 to 6 weeks before the fall transplant date -- typically June in cold zones (Z3-Z5) or August in warm zones (Z7-Z9). (UGA Circular 1258 Fall Vegetable Gardening; UGA Calendar) Keep seedlings in a partially shaded spot to avoid heat stress during summer indoor growing. (UGA fall gardening)

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote_seasoned: Five to seven-week-old transplants are set out four weeks prior to the last frost date in spring. (UMD Extension)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: For spring plantings, start seeds indoors in early to mid-April. (UMN Extension)
plant_out.design_note_seasoned: Hardened brassica transplants tolerate light frost once established; plant_out = last_frost - 28d captures this biology across most zones.

plant_out.label: secondary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall brassica transplants are set out about 30-45 days before the expected first frost so plants mature in cooling weather. (UMD Extension; UGA Circular 1258) Fall broccoli often produces higher yields than spring plantings in the mid-Atlantic region. For a fall crop, start seeds indoors or out in early to late July. (UMD Extension; UMN Extension, broccoli and cauliflower)

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest spring brassica crop before sustained heat causes bolting or head deterioration. Heading brassicas shift to reproductive phase and heads become unusable once temperatures climb. (UMN Extension; UMD Extension; UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar)

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heavy nitrogen feeder for leaf development. Switch to balanced feed once heads begin to form to avoid loose, leafy heads.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 6-8 weeks before transplant date. Harden off over 5-7 days. For fall crop, direct sow in midsummer.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Possible but challenging -- broccoli is large. 5-gallon minimum, one plant per pot.

varieties.note_seasoned: Di Cicco produces smaller central heads but many side shoots over a long season -- great yield.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

bolting.triggers: Heat, transplant shock, wide temperature swings
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Transplant carefully. Avoid temperature swings during head formation. Choose heat-tolerant varieties for summer crops.
bolting.note_seasoned: Bolted broccoli (flowers opening) is still edible but quality drops. Harvest immediately when any yellowing appears.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 3-5 days in a loosely wrapped bag -- don't seal tight, it needs airflow
storage.freezer_seasoned: Cut to florets, blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent, nearly as good as fresh
storage.notes_seasoned: Yellowing comes from senescence, ethylene exposure, and warm storage -- not moisture. Store cold (32-40°F) and humid in the crisper drawer; avoid storing near apples, bananas, or other ethylene-producing fruit. Use as soon as possible after harvest.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Round seed leaves pushing up cleanly. Brassicas germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist at 60-70°F. Brassicas do not need heat -- they prefer cool germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- slightly waxy and blue-green in color.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch for damping off -- good airflow and not overwatering prevents it. Thin to one plant per cell.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sturdy plants with multiple leaf sets, ready to go outside.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off well before transplanting. Net immediately after planting to protect from cabbage white butterflies -- do not delay on this.

growth_stages.name: Head Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Central head beginning to form. On broccoli, a tight green dome. On cauliflower, a white curd appearing in the center.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: For cauliflower, tie the outer leaves over the developing curd to blanch it and keep it white. Do this as soon as the curd is visible.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Broccoli: tight green head before any yellow flowers open. Cauliflower: firm white curd at full size. Cabbage: firm, dense head that does not give when squeezed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest broccoli with a long stem cut -- side shoots will continue producing for weeks. Cauliflower and cabbage are once-and-done harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvest time -- how did it look?

growth_stages.name: Side Shoots
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Broccoli only -- smaller side shoots developing from the stem after the main head is cut.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep harvesting side shoots regularly. A well-managed broccoli plant can produce for weeks after the main head is gone.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Getting side shoots from your broccoli?

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your brassicas indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage need 6-8 weeks indoors before transplanting. Start now -- they grow slowly at first but reward the patience. Cool temperatures suit them perfectly.

notifications.title_seasoned: Brassicas outside -- net them immediately
notifications.body_seasoned: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves within hours of planting. Cover with fine mesh netting immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Caterpillar damage can devastate an unprotected crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cauliflower curd forming -- time to blanch
notifications.body_seasoned: Tie a few outer leaves loosely over the developing curd now to protect it from light. This keeps the cauliflower white and tender. Check every few days -- once the curd is visible it develops quickly.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your broccoli heads
notifications.body_seasoned: Broccoli heads that are ready to harvest look like tight green domes with no yellow showing. Once you see any flower buds opening it is past its best. Cut with a long stem and watch for side shoots to develop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start a fall brassica crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Brassicas do well as a fall crop and often taste better -- frost sweetens cabbage and broccoli. Start seeds now for a crop that matures in the cooler autumn months.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your brassicas getting on?
notifications.body_seasoned: Check under the netting for caterpillar damage -- they can strip a plant surprisingly fast. Also look at the developing head for any signs of bolting or discoloration.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress -- brassicas may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained high temperatures cause broccoli and cauliflower to bolt -- heads open into flowers before they are full size. Harvest anything that looks close to ready before the heat peaks.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for clubroot and downy mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions favor several brassica diseases. Ensure good spacing and airflow. Check leaves for yellowing or powdery patches and remove affected material promptly.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Late frost -- protect young brassicas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Established brassicas handle frost well, but young transplants need protection for the first few weeks. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text_seasoned: Brassicas are reliable germinators in cool conditions -- 60-70°F is ideal. They do not need heat mats.
Sow into cells or modules rather than trays -- brassicas develop long tap roots and resent root disturbance.

seedling.text_seasoned: Grow brassica seedlings in the coolest, brightest spot you have. Warmth makes them soft and leggy.
Feed with a dilute liquid feed once the first true leaves appear. Brassicas are hungry plants from the start.

established.text_seasoned: Net immediately after transplanting. Cabbage white butterflies find brassicas within hours and lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides. Check the netting is secure all around -- one gap and caterpillars will find it.
Plant deeply -- broccoli forms roots along the buried stem like tomatoes and is more stable and drought-resistant for it.

head_forming.text_seasoned: Watch the central head daily once it starts forming. The window between a tight, dense, perfectly-domed head and one that has begun to open into yellow flower buds is short -- often just 3-5 days in warm weather.
Steady moisture during head formation produces firmer, larger heads. Drought stress at this stage is the most common cause of small or loose heads.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut the main head with a long stem -- 6-8 inches. The remaining stem will produce side shoots over the following weeks. Harvest while the head is tight and green; once you see any yellow flower buds opening, the head is past its best.
Broccoli sugars convert quickly after harvest. For the best flavor, cut just before cooking; refrigerate immediately if not eating within a few hours.

side_shoots.text_seasoned: Broccoli side shoots are sweeter and more tender than the main head. Keep the plant well watered and fed to encourage continuous production -- a single plant can yield for weeks after the main cut.
Some broccoli varieties are bred specifically for side shoot production. Purple sprouting broccoli is the best example -- it overwinters and produces all spring.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One large central head plus weeks of side shoots
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Side shoots can be harvested every 1-2 weeks for 4-6 weeks after the main head
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Broccoli is one of the most satisfying crops -- a large green head you grew yourself is genuinely impressive.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Established brassicas handle frost well -- it actually sweetens them. But young transplants in their first 2-3 weeks are more vulnerable. A hard freeze can damage or kill recently transplanted seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover new transplants with fleece for the first 2-3 weeks after planting if frost is possible. Once established they are among the hardiest vegetables you can grow.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves and the caterpillars can strip a plant in days. This is by far the most common reason brassicas fail. If you did not net, this is almost certainly what happened.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Net immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Fine mesh netting secured all the way around is the single most important thing you can do for brassicas. Check netting for gaps weekly.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brassicas in waterlogged soil develop root problems. Clubroot -- a soil-borne disease -- causes swollen, distorted roots and wilting. Once present in soil it persists for many years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage before planting. If clubroot is suspected, rotate brassicas to a new bed and do not grow them in the affected soil for 4-5 years. Liming to raise soil pH above 7 discourages clubroot.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brassicas need consistent moisture to develop good heads. Drought stress causes premature flowering in broccoli and cauliflower, and split heads in cabbage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently and mulch around plants to retain moisture. A dry spell during head formation is the most damaging period.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cauliflower is the most demanding -- it needs consistent temperatures and care to form a good curd. Broccoli heads opening into yellow flowers usually means the temperature swung too warm. Both benefit from 6+ hours of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cauliflower in particular needs a consistent, cool growing environment. Autumn sowings often perform better than spring ones in warmer zones. Shade cloth can help in warm spells.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Start a spring crop and a separate late-summer crop for autumn harvest -- two distinct plantings rather than rolling succession. Spring broccoli planted after last frost and autumn broccoli started 10-12 weeks before first frost are your two windows. In between, broccoli struggles with bolting in summer heat. The autumn crop is often superior -- cool nights produce tighter, sweeter heads. Don't skip starting seeds for the autumn batch in July.

crops.description_seasoned: Harvest the central head before flowers open, then enjoy weeks of side shoots. Temperature-sensitive -- needs cool weather for heading. Medium difficulty but very rewarding.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when head is tight and dark green with no yellowing. Beads should still be closed. Size alone doesn't indicate readiness -- a large loose head is past peak.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Firm, fertile, slightly alkaline soil. Lime if pH below 6.5. Brassicas follow well after legumes (peas and beans fix nitrogen that feeds leafy brassicas). Firm the soil well before planting -- loose soil produces loose-headed broccoli.

crops.name: Garlic

3.notes: Plant before ground freezes. Mulch heavily after planting. Hardneck varieties like Rocambole do best in Zone 3.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: The standard UMN recommendation is to plant garlic cloves one to two weeks after first frost -- typically late September in northern Minnesota, early October in southern Minnesota. (UMN Extension) Planting too early risks shoot emergence above soil before winter; too late means roots don't develop before ground freezes. Plant garlic cloves in the fall, usually one or two weeks after the first killing frost. Cover with 3-4 inches of leaf or straw mulch after planting. (UMN)

harvest_start.label: primary

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Depending on variety and climate zone, harvest garlic between late June and late July. Garlic planted in September produces the biggest bulbs the following July. (UMN Extension)

pests.name: Onion fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt and die. White maggots at the base of bulb eating roots and inner leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia antiqua fly. Lays eggs near onion seedlings in spring.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insect mesh over bed. Remove and destroy affected plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow under fine mesh. Rotate alliums every 3 years. Interplant with carrots -- mutual pest confusion.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silver streaking and speckling on leaves. Stunted growth. Tiny yellow-brown insects visible.
pests.cause_seasoned: Thrips tabaci. Worse in hot dry summers.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Neem oil spray. Insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reflective mulch. Adequate watering in dry weather.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants yellow and die. White fluffy growth at base with small black seed-like sclerotia. Roots and base rotted.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Sclerotium cepivorum soil fungus. Persists in soil for 20+ years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove all plant material. Do not replant alliums in infected soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Strict crop rotation. Buy allium seed sets from reputable sources.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaves. Leaves yellow and collapse. Worst in wet cool springs.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora destructor fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants for airflow. Rotate crops.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly spring-early summer, stop in June

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant individual cloves in autumn (Sept-Nov). Plant pointy end up, 2 inches deep. No hardening off needed.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works well in containers -- 6-8 inches deep minimum. One clove per 4 inches of space.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Onions, garlic, leeks, shallots -- share white rot and onion fly
rotation.note_seasoned: White rot can persist indefinitely in soil -- strict rotation is essential once present.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 3-6 months in cool dry place with good airflow
storage.fridge_seasoned: Not ideal for whole bulbs -- cold can trigger sprouting in the 40-60°F range. Once peeled or chopped, refrigerate.
storage.freezer_seasoned: Peel and freeze whole cloves, or make garlic paste and freeze in cubes
storage.notes_seasoned: Cured properly, garlic stores for months. Braiding improves airflow.

varieties.note_seasoned: Music is the most reliable hardneck for northern gardens -- large cloves, strong flavor, good disease resistance.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cloves, sets, or seeds in the ground. No visible growth yet.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant garlic and onion sets pointed end up, just below the surface. For leeks, sow seeds in modules and transplant as pencil-thin seedlings.

growth_stages.name: Early Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green shoots pushing up from sets or cloves. Slow growth initially -- alliums establish roots first.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep weed-free -- alliums are poor competitors with weeds, especially in early growth.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong upright leaves, healthy green color. Onions and garlic developing the bulb underground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop feeding garlic and onions with nitrogen once the bulb starts forming -- it encourages leafy growth at the expense of the bulb.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: For garlic: scapes curling upward on hardneck varieties. For onions: leaves beginning to yellow from the tips and fall over.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest garlic scapes when curled -- they are delicious and removing them redirects energy to the bulb. For onions, bending down any remaining upright leaves once half have fallen speeds final ripening.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seeing scapes on garlic, or leaves beginning to fall?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Garlic: leaves 2/3 brown. Onions: all leaves yellow and fallen. Leeks: any size -- harvest young for mild flavor.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Lift carefully with a fork to avoid bruising. Cure in a warm, airy spot for 2-4 weeks before storing -- this is essential for long storage life.

growth_stages.name: Curing and Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Skin papery and tight, neck dry and closed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hang or lay in a single layer in good airflow, out of direct rain, for 2-4 weeks. Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store well.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your garlic
notifications.body_seasoned: Garlic is planted in autumn and overwinters in the ground -- it needs a cold period to develop properly. Plant cloves now, pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart. You will not see much happen until spring, and that is exactly right.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your onion sets
notifications.body_seasoned: Onion sets can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost. Plant pointed end up with just the tip showing at the surface. They establish quickly and are more reliable than growing from seed.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest your garlic scapes
notifications.body_seasoned: Hardneck garlic sends up curled green shoots called scapes in early summer. Cut them off now -- they are delicious in stir fries and pestos, and removing them directs energy back into the bulb for a larger harvest.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your garlic for harvest readiness
notifications.body_seasoned: When two thirds of the leaves have turned brown, your garlic is ready. Do not wait for all leaves to die -- the outer wrapper deteriorates. Lift carefully with a fork, do not pull by the stem, and handle gently to avoid bruising.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cure your alliums properly -- it is worth it
notifications.body_seasoned: Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store through winter. Hang or lay them in a single layer in a warm, airy space out of rain for 3-4 weeks. The necks should be completely dry before storage. This step makes the difference between 3-month storage and 6-month storage.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for rust on your alliums
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid conditions. It weakens the plant but rarely kills it. Remove badly affected leaves and ensure good airflow. Rotate alliums to a different bed next year.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Keep curing alliums dry
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain on curing garlic and onions undoes the drying process and encourages rot. Make sure they are under cover -- a shed, garage, or covered porch is ideal.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant garlic in your best, most fertile bed. It is in the ground for 9 months -- give it good conditions from the start.
Save the largest cloves from each bulb for planting and eat the small ones. Larger cloves produce larger bulbs.

early_growth.text_seasoned: Keep allium beds completely weed-free. Onions and garlic have poor, shallow root systems and are easily out-competed. Even small weeds reduce yields significantly.
No need to water garlic in autumn and winter -- rainfall is usually sufficient. Begin watering in spring if it is dry.

established.text_seasoned: Stop feeding with nitrogen once bulbs start to form. High nitrogen at this stage produces soft, poorly-stored bulbs with thick necks.
Leeks can be earthed up as they grow to blanch the lower stem -- this gives you a longer white shaft and milder flavor.

bulb_forming.text_seasoned: When onion leaves begin to yellow and fall over, stop watering. The plant is telling you it is finishing -- let it dry down naturally.
Do not bend onion tops manually until at least half the leaves have yellowed on their own. Bending them too early exposes the neck to disease.

harvest.text_seasoned: Lift rather than pull. A garden fork under the bulb loosens the roots and prevents the stem tearing -- which exposes the bulb to rot during curing.
Harvest on a dry day and leave on top of the soil for a few hours before bringing in. The sun begins the drying process.

curing.text_seasoned: Curing is the most important step most gardeners skip. 3-4 weeks in warm, airy conditions transforms a perishable vegetable into one that stores for 6-9 months.
Braid garlic and onions for storage if you have enough -- it looks beautiful and is functional. Store in a cool, dry, dark place.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One full bulb per clove planted
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Garlic is a single harvest -- one bulb per planting
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Homegrown garlic is incomparably better than shop-bought. The flavor is more complex and the satisfaction of a string of cured bulbs is real.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Established alliums are among the hardiest vegetables and handle frost well. Garlic overwintering in the ground is designed for frost. Young onion seedlings are more vulnerable to late hard freezes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Protect young onion sets if a hard freeze threatens in the first few weeks after planting. Established plants need no protection from ordinary frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid summers -- it weakens but rarely kills the plant. White rot is more serious: a soil-borne fungus that causes bulbs to rot at the base. Once white rot is in soil it persists for decades.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rotate alliums to a new bed every year. White rot cannot be eliminated from infected soil -- grow alliums elsewhere if you see it. Rust is largely cosmetic -- harvest early and the bulbs are usually fine.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Garlic and onion bulbs rot in waterlogged soil, especially during curing. Rain on curing alliums reverses the drying process and causes neck rot -- one of the most common storage failures.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Ensure excellent drainage. Cure garlic and onions under cover -- a shed or garage with good airflow. Even a few hours of rain on curing bulbs can significantly reduce storage life.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Alliums that experience drought stress during bulb development produce small, tight bulbs. Irregular watering is a common cause of disappointing allium harvests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during bulb formation -- from spring until leaves begin to yellow. Stop watering completely once leaves start to die back naturally.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Alliums need full sun for good bulb development. The bulbing trigger in onions and garlic is day length -- both need long days combined with warmth to form bulbs. In shade or under trees, they often produce only small, undeveloped bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant alliums in your sunniest, most open bed. Weed competition also significantly reduces yield -- keep allium beds completely weed-free from early spring.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: The standard UMN recommendation is to plant garlic cloves one to two weeks after first frost -- typically late September in northern Minnesota, early October in southern Minnesota. (UMN Extension) Planting too early risks shoot emergence above soil before winter; too late means roots don't develop before ground freezes. crops.description_seasoned: Plant in fall, harvest in summer. One of the most satisfying long-season crops -- almost no maintenance from October to June. Plant pointed end up, 2 inches deep.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: When 50% of lower leaves have yellowed and browned. Dig one test bulb -- wrapper should be papery. Don't wait until all leaves die or wrappers split.

crops.name: Peach

3.notes: Very challenging in Zone 3. Choose ultra-hardy varieties like Reliance or Contender. Protect from late spring frosts which kill blossoms.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. (UMN Extension 'Growing apples in the home garden'; UMN Extension 'Growing stone fruits in the home garden')

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Stone fruit harvest runs June through August for most varieties. Peaches and nectarines ripen mid-to-late summer; apricots earliest (June-July); sweet cherries June-July; sour cherries July; plums July-September depending on type (Japanese types earlier, European types later). This month-by-month synthesis of stone fruit harvest windows follows Iowa State University Extension's commercial-orchard reference material on peach, plum, and cherry harvest timing. UMN Extension is cited for complementary climate-zone guidance on northern-Midwest stone fruit cultivation.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed balanced fertilizer in early spring before blossom. Apply high-potassium feed after harvest to build next year's fruiting wood.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 10-10-10 in spring -- peaches need consistent nitrogen

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune to open-center shape in late winter. Remove crossing, dead, and inward-growing branches. Peaches fruit on 1-year-old wood so keep new growth.
Thin fruit to 6 inches apart when marble-sized. Improves fruit size and reduces branch breakage.
