pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing fruit before it fully ripens. Small maggots inside fruit. Most severe on late-maturing varieties.
pests.cause_seasoned: Drosophila suzukii fly. Female lays eggs in ripening fruit. Major pest since 2008 introduction to North America.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Kaolin clay coating. Fine mesh netting over plants during ripening. Spinosad spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Harvest fruit as soon as ripe. Remove all fallen fruit. Fine mesh netting (1mm or less) is the most effective barrier.

pests.name: Blueberry maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Maggots inside fruit. Soft, dimpled berries.
pests.cause_seasoned: Rhagoletis mendax fly. Regional pest, worst in northeastern US.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium acetate. Kaolin clay.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Hang sticky yellow traps when fruit turns green.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

diseases.name: Mummy berry
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blighted shoots in spring (salmon/tan colored). Later, berries turn pinkish and mummify on the bush.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Monilinia vaccinii-corymbosi fungus. Spores released from mummified berries on ground.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy mummified berries. Apply mulch 4 inches deep to prevent spore release.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rake and destroy mummified fruit in autumn. Apply 4-inch mulch in spring before spores release.

diseases.name: Botrytis blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gray fuzzy mold on flowers, young shoots, and berries. Shoot dieback. Worst in cool wet spring weather at bloom.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis cinerea fungus. Enters through flowers.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected material. Improve air circulation with pruning. Copper or sulfur fungicide preventively at bloom.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune to open canopy. Avoid excess nitrogen. Do not water overhead during bloom.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 3-5 days -- shallow roots dry out quickly
watering.method_seasoned: Drip at soil level -- overhead promotes botrytis

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant in spring from container. Acidify soil before planting (pH 4.5-5.5). Plant 2 different varieties for cross-pollination.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Very good in large containers -- easier to acidify container mix than garden soil. 15-gallon minimum. Use ericaceous/acid potting mix.

varieties.note_seasoned: Plant at least 2 different varieties for cross-pollination -- yields increase dramatically.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 1-2 weeks -- don't wash until ready to eat
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze raw, flat first then bag -- retains flavor perfectly
storage.notes_seasoned: Blueberries freeze better than almost any other fruit -- quality barely changes.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted plant just set. Soil level matches the original line on the stems -- not buried deeper.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), mix peat moss or pine fines into the hole, and mulch with pine needles or wood chips. Cane fruits (raspberry, blackberry): plant alongside a trellis or post-and-wire support so the canes have something to grow on. Elderberry: tolerates wetter ground than the others. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves breaking. Blueberry pushes new shoots from the base; cane fruits send up new canes from the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water consistently through the first summer -- berries have shallow roots and dry out fast. Remove all flowers in year one so the plant builds its roots and a strong base. For raspberries and blackberries, pinch off the tip of each new cane once it reaches your trellis height; this encourages side branches that will carry fruit.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Multiple stems or canes coming up from the base. Blueberry fills out as a many-stemmed bush; cane fruits send up vigorous new canes; elderberry bushes out widely.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Berries don't get scaffold-branch training the way trees do -- they're naturally multi-stemmed. Blueberry: keep the strongest 4 to 6 stems and remove weak twiggy growth. Raspberry and blackberry: train new canes onto the trellis and thin them to about 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot. Elderberry: let it bush out freely; remove only crossed or weak growth.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blueberry leaves turn red-purple and drop. Raspberry and blackberry canes go fully bare. Elderberry drops cleanly. All are dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Top up the mulch before deep freeze, especially for shallow-rooted blueberry. In cold zones, consider laying down trailing blackberry canes and covering them with mulch or burlap. Real pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bush or canes fully dormant. Late-winter window before bud break.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: cane-renewal -- remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest canes at ground level each winter. Caneberries: remove last year's spent floricanes; thin remaining primocanes to 4 to 6 per linear foot.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring bloom on blueberry, raspberry, blackberry; early-summer bloom on elderberry. Frost risk usually past.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avoid sprays during bloom. Wild bumblebees are the main blueberry pollinators.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set & Bird Netting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Berries forming. Bird pressure ramps up as fruit colors.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Cross-pollination boosts blueberry yield -- a second variety nearby helps.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe fruit pulls free with gentle pressure. Bushes and canes are hand-height -- no ladders.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for thorny canes. Refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Cleanup
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Last fruit picked. Spent floricanes on caneberries dying back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut spent floricanes at ground level if not done in late winter. Apply a potassium-rich feed (use an acidic blueberry-specific fertilizer for blueberry). Refresh mulch.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: These crops are typically grown on their own roots -- there is no graft union. Plant with the crown at the original soil line. Blueberry needs acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5); test before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed.
Caneberries (raspberry, blackberry) need a trellis or support system from year one. Build it before planting; retrofitting around established canes is awkward.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- berries are shallow-rooted and dry out fast. Blueberry especially needs steady moisture and acidic mulch (pine bark, pine needles).
Remove flowers in year one on caneberries and blueberry. The energy goes into root and cane development; you will get more fruit from years two onward by skipping year one.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Blueberry develops as a multi-stemmed shrub. Let 5 to 7 main canes establish in the first 2 to 3 years; do not prune for shape, only remove damaged wood.
Caneberries put up new canes (primocanes) from the crown each year. In year one, let everything grow -- those are next year's fruiting canes (floricanes).

dormancy.text_seasoned: These crops are deciduous and go fully dormant in winter. Pruning is done in late winter or very early spring before bud break.
Refresh mulch before winter. For caneberries, tip-prune any canes that did not harden off (still green and floppy at the tip).

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Blueberry uses cane-renewal pruning. Each winter, remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest, least-productive canes at ground level to push new cane growth from the crown. By year 5 or 6 the bush has a rotating set of young productive canes.

Caneberries: remove all canes that fruited last summer (floricanes) -- they die after fruiting and harbor disease. Leave the new green canes (primocanes) for next year. Thin remaining canes to 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot of row.

blossom.text_seasoned: Blueberry, raspberry, and blackberry bloom late enough that spring frost is rarely the problem -- usually mid-to-late spring, after most frost danger is past. Elderberry blooms even later, in early summer.
Pollinators love these flowers. Do not spray during bloom. Wild bumblebees in particular are major pollinators of blueberry.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most blueberry varieties benefit from a second variety blooming at the same time for cross-pollination -- a single bush will fruit but a pair fruits much more heavily. Caneberries and elderberry are mostly self-fertile.
Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Once birds find the patch they keep coming back.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick fruit at hand height -- no ladders here. Ripe blueberries pull off with a gentle roll of the thumb; fruit that resists is not yet ripe (color is not enough -- some varieties color days before they sweeten).

Caneberries shatter when over-ripe -- pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for blackberry and the thorny raspberries. Eat or refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: After caneberry harvest, cut the spent floricanes (now dying or dead) at ground level if you did not get them in late winter. This removes overwintering sites for cane disease and the spotted wing drosophila.
A potassium-rich feed and a mulch refresh after harvest sets up next year's bloom. For blueberry, use an acidic fertilizer formulated for ericaceous plants.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 5-10 lbs per mature highbush bush; rabbiteye and southern types can reach 12 to 25 lbs
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production typically arrives in year 4 to 7 depending on type. Berries ripen unevenly across a 2 to 4 week window, so expect to pick every few days at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Plan on no harvest in year one. Remove all flowers so the plant invests in roots and new canes. Year-two harvest is small; full production comes in year three or later.
factors_seasoned: soil pH (especially blueberry, which needs 4.5 to 5.5)
trellis or stake support for canes

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The most widely grown blueberry variety in the US. Large light-blue berries with good flavor. Mid-season ripening. Self-fertile but better with another variety. Drought and heat tolerant for a Northern Highbush.
Early-ripening (late June). Consistent heavy yields. Medium-large firm berries with mild flavor. Self-fertile. One of the most reliable commercial varieties for the Northeast.
Dwarf variety (1-2 feet), extremely cold-hardy, ideal for containers. Self-fertile. Small intensely-flavored berries. Good for cold zones where Highbush varieties struggle.
Early-ripening Rabbiteye for the Southeast. Heat and drought tolerant. Requires another Rabbiteye variety for pollination (Tifblue works well). Large productive bush (8-10 feet).

Low-chill self-fertile evergreen variety. Compact (3-4 feet), ideal for containers. Tolerates higher pH than most blueberries (5.5-6.5). The most adaptable blueberry for warm climates and container growing.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem. The more common cold issues are winter cane dieback on caneberries (canes that did not harden off in fall die back from the tips) and winter damage at the edge of blueberry's hardiness range. Some blackberry varieties are only hardy to USDA zone 6 or 7.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose varieties hardy to your zone. For caneberries, stop fertilizing by midsummer so canes harden off properly before winter. Mulch heavily in fall. In marginal zones for blackberry, lay primocanes flat under mulch for winter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Spotted wing drosophila (SWD) is now the dominant berry pest across most of the US -- it lays eggs in ripening fruit and the larvae make berries unsalvageable. Cane diseases (anthracnose, spur blight, cane blight) affect caneberries and survive in old floricanes. Blueberry maggot and mummy berry are blueberry-specific.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Remove and destroy spent floricanes immediately after harvest -- this is the main defense against cane disease and SWD overwintering. Pick ripe fruit promptly so SWD has less to lay eggs in. For blueberry mummy berry, mulch heavily in fall to bury fallen mummies.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Caneberries and elderberry are self-fertile and a single plant fruits. Blueberry is technically self-fertile but yields much more heavily with a second variety blooming at the same time -- a single bush often produces small or sparse berries. Cool wet weather during bloom keeps pollinators (especially bumblebees) grounded even when a partner is present.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant at least two compatible blueberry varieties for cross-pollination. Encourage native bumblebees with flowering plants nearby. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops want consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Blueberry hates wet feet and dies quickly in waterlogged soil; root rot from poorly-drained sites is a leading killer. Caneberries tolerate slightly more moisture but still suffer in standing water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: On heavy or low-lying soil, plant in a raised bed or mound. Blueberry especially does best in a 12-inch raised bed with bark-amended acidic soil. Ensure water drains away from the root zone.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops need full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to fruit well. Elderberry tolerates partial shade better than the others but still fruits more heavily in sun. Shaded canes and bushes grow leaves but produce few or small berries.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. For caneberries, avoid letting the row become a dense thicket -- thin canes to 4 to 6 per linear foot so light reaches all the fruiting wood.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant blueberry bushes from container stock in spring after soil thaws but before bud break. In cold zones, late April through mid-May is typical. Acidify soil before planting to pH 4. 5-5. 5 with sulfur. Plant at least 2 different varieties for cross-pollination. Blueberries are perennial shrubs producing for 20+ years with proper care. (UMN Extension, Cornell Extension)

crops.description_seasoned: The most popular edible shrub in the US. Long-lived (30+ years), beautiful ornamental, and incredibly productive once established. Soil pH is critical -- must be acidic.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Fully blue (no red or green at base). Slight gray-white bloom on skin. Pop off easily with gentle touch. Sweet, not tart. Wait 2-3 days after turning blue for maximum sweetness.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Blueberries come in four distinct types suited to different climates. Northern Highbush (Vaccinium corymbosum) are the standard commercial type for zones 4-7 -- upright 5-6 foot bushes with large sweet berries. Northern Lowbush (V. angustifolium) are short (1-2 feet) wild-type bushes native to the Northeast, hardy to zone 3, with small intensely-flavored berries. Southern Highbush are modern hybrids (Northern Highbush x Rabbiteye) for zones 7-10 where Northern types fail from inadequate chill hours. Rabbiteye (V. virgatum) are the Southeast native blueberry, heat-tolerant and productive in zones 7-9 but requiring cross-pollination. Soil pH is the make-or-break factor for all blueberries: they require strongly acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5) and fail in alkaline or neutral soils. Amend with peat moss, pine bark, or sulfur before planting, or grow in containers. Most varieties need cross-pollination from another variety of the same type for best yields.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Varies enormously -- Southern Highbush needs 150-200hrs, Northern Highbush 800-1000hrs. Match variety to zone
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Partially self-fertile but yields significantly better with a second variety. Plant two different varieties with overlapping bloom time within 6 feet.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Remove flowers in years 1-2 to direct energy into root and cane development -- this is separate from pruning. From year 3 onward, prune in late winter by removing the oldest dark canes. The patience pays off significantly in years 4-6.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Blueberries demand acidic soil (pH 4.5-5.5). Most garden soil sits at pH 6.5-7.0 -- far too alkaline. Before planting: test your soil pH, then work in elemental sulfur (1-2 lbs per 100 sq ft) or ericaceous compost. Retest after 6 weeks. Never add lime near blueberries. Use an acid-forming fertilizer (Holly-Tone, Espoma Berry-Tone) not general-purpose feeds.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root in late fall through early spring while dormant. Container-grown can be planted any time soil is workable.

crops.name: Heirloom Tomato

3.notes: Very challenging in Zone 3 -- long days-to-maturity leaves little margin. Choose faster heirlooms like Black Krim or Stupice. Use season extenders.
3.zone_notes: Short season -- start indoors 10 weeks early and choose faster 75-day varieties.

4.notes: Choose shorter-season heirlooms. Start 8 weeks early. Heavy mulching is essential.
4.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks early. Heirloom varieties push the limits of Zone 4 -- choose varieties with 75 days or fewer to maturity.

5.notes: Good heirloom zone. Stake heavily -- these get large. Consistent deep watering prevents cracking.
5.zone_notes: Start indoors 8 weeks before last frost.

6.notes: Excellent zone for heirlooms. Wide variety selection. Remove suckers for better fruit size.
6.zone_notes: Heirlooms need 80+ days -- plant by mid-May at latest for harvest before first frost.

7.notes: Long productive season. Heat above 95°F causes blossom drop -- plant early to miss peak summer.
7.zone_notes: Most heirlooms need 75-90 days -- fall planting only works with faster-maturing heirloom varieties like Stupice or Glacier (55-60 days).

8.notes: Spring crop mainly. Get harvest in before summer heat. Fall planting in August for October harvest.
8.zone_notes: Spring planting gives best results. Long-season varieties (80+ days) planted in July/August rarely mature before first frost around Oct 15; stick with Cherry, Grape, or Roma for fall plantings in Zone 8.

9.notes: Spring and fall crops. Summer is too hot. Best flavor comes from the long cool spring mornings.

10.notes: Cool season focused. Heat ruins heirloom texture and flavor faster than hybrids.
10.zone_notes: Spring is the reliable window; fall planting possible but less consistent with long-season varieties. Summer heat above 90°F stops fruit set.

11.notes: Cool season only. Afternoon shade essential. Heirlooms suffer in Zone 11 heat.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heirlooms are hungrier than hybrids. Rich compost at planting plus regular liquid feed during fruiting.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or extension literature.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring hornworm are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2-3 days -- heirlooms crack easily with irregular watering
watering.method_seasoned: Drip or soaker hose at soil level

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off carefully -- heirlooms can be more sensitive than hybrids.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Can be grown in large containers. 10-15 gallon pots. Raised beds preferred for large indeterminate varieties.

varieties.note_seasoned: Brandywine is the benchmark heirloom but is more disease-prone. Cherokee Purple and Black Krim are more reliable.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes: all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

det_indet.detail_seasoned: Most heirloom varieties are indeterminate and need strong support all season. They're slower to start fruiting but continue until frost.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Up to 1 week at room temperature
storage.fridge_seasoned: Avoid -- cold ruins flavor and texture
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole for cooking; skins slip off when thawed
storage.notes_seasoned: Never refrigerate. Heirlooms are the most flavor-sensitive of all tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil temperature between 70-80°F. A heat mat makes a real difference. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you seen any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them; they will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the humidity dome the moment sprouts appear. Get them as close to your brightest light source as possible -- leggy seedlings are caused by too little light, not too little water.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before your transplant date. A few hours outside each day, sheltered from wind. Plant deep -- bury the stem up to the lowest leaves and roots will form all along it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Switch from a balanced feed to a high-potassium fertilizer. Gently tap the flowering stems in the morning to help pollination -- or give them a gentle shake. This really does improve fruit set.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick regularly -- every tomato you harvest signals the plant to produce more. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine slows production and attracts pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips to direct energy into existing fruit. Bring any nearly-ripe tomatoes inside if frost threatens -- they will ripen on a windowsill.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start hardening off your tomatoes
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day; start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title_seasoned: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces; stay on top of it.

notifications.title_seasoned: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_seasoned: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your tomatoes doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning: protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes need deep watering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base; aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity: watch for blight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.
Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth; leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.
Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were; it builds a stronger plant.

established.text_seasoned: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.
Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.
Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium: switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.
Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments; some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.
Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 10-20 lbs over the season -- fewer but much larger fruit
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A healthy beefsteak at peak produces 1-3 large fruits per week
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First seasons are for learning. If you get enough for a salad, that is a success. You will get more each year as you learn what your specific garden needs.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early; soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering, not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently at the base, not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering, dry then suddenly wet, causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Basil
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Repels aphids and whitefly, improves flavor

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Flavor-improvement claims are classic companion-planting tradition. Not documented in peer-reviewed research or extension literature.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Deter nematodes and whitefly in soil

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrots
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Deep roots break up soil, minimal competition

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Flowering plants attracting predatory insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). Specific pairings vary in effectiveness.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start indoors 6-8 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 7-10 days.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Great container crop. 5-gallon pot minimum. Cascading varieties ideal for hanging baskets.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes: all share blight and fusarium diseases

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny white root emerging from the seed, then a pale shoot pushing upward through the soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil temperature between 70-80°F. A heat mat makes a real difference. Cover with a humidity dome until sprouts appear.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Have you seen any sprouts yet?

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves open flat, then the first true leaves emerging between them; they will look distinctly tomato-shaped.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove the humidity dome the moment sprouts appear. Get them as close to your brightest light source as possible -- leggy seedlings are caused by too little light, not too little water.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong stem, 3-4 sets of true leaves, deep green color. Ready to pot up or transplant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin hardening off 7-10 days before your transplant date. A few hours outside each day, sheltered from wind. Plant deep -- bury the stem up to the lowest leaves and roots will form all along it.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Are they outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small yellow flowers in clusters. Each flower is a potential fruit.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Switch from a balanced feed to a high-potassium fertilizer. Gently tap the flowering stems in the morning to help pollination -- or give them a gentle shake. This really does improve fruit set.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully colored fruit that gives slightly to a gentle squeeze. The skin may start to lose its sheen when perfectly ripe.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick regularly -- every tomato you harvest signals the plant to produce more. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine slows production and attracts pests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: First tomatoes picked? Log your harvest.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, yellowing lower leaves, nights cooling below 50°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips to direct energy into existing fruit. Bring any nearly-ripe tomatoes inside if frost threatens -- they will ripen on a windowsill.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your tomatoes indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost date is about {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away, the perfect window to get tomato seeds into trays. Find somewhere warm (70-80°F), keep the soil consistently moist, and cover with a dome until you see sprouts. This is where your season begins.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start hardening off your tomatoes
notifications.body_seasoned: Your last frost is {{days_until_anchor}} days away. Begin putting your plants outside for a few hours each day; start sheltered, increase exposure gradually. This week of adjustment makes a real difference to how they settle in after transplanting.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost has passed: time to transplant
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tomatoes are ready to go outside for good. Plant them deep: bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Roots will form all along the buried stem and give you a stronger, more drought-tolerant plant.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes should be flowering soon
notifications.body_seasoned: Small yellow flowers appearing means fruit is on the way. Switch to a high-potassium feed now, and give the flowering stems a gentle shake in the morning to help pollination. Each flower is a potential tomato.

notifications.title_seasoned: First tomatoes should be nearly ready
notifications.body_seasoned: Based on when you planted, you should be seeing ripe or nearly-ripe fruit about now. Pick when fully colored and slightly soft to the touch. The more you pick, the more the plant produces; stay on top of it.

notifications.title_seasoned: First frost in {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks: finish strong
notifications.body_seasoned: Your growing season is almost done. Pinch out the growing tips now so the plant puts all its remaining energy into the fruit already on the vine. Harvest anything you can and bring green tomatoes inside to ripen on a windowsill.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your tomatoes doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a couple of weeks. How is the plant looking? Any flowers, fruit, or pests worth noting? Regular check-ins help you catch problems early.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning: protect your tomatoes tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Temperatures are dropping close to freezing tonight. Cover plants with fleece or old bedsheets, or bring containers inside. Tomatoes are frost-tender and one cold night can end your season early.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress warning for your tomatoes
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Several very hot days ahead. Tomato flowers can drop when temperatures stay above 95°F. Water deeply in the early morning, add mulch around the base to retain moisture, and consider shade cloth during the hottest part of the day.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Your tomatoes need deep watering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: It has been dry. Inconsistent watering at this stage causes blossom end rot and cracked fruit. Water deeply at the base; aim for 1-2 inches this week. Mulching around the stem helps hold moisture.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity: watch for blight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions are ideal for early and late blight. Check lower leaves for dark spots with yellow halos. Remove any affected leaves immediately and do not compost them. Good airflow around the plant is your best defense.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain: harvest ripe tomatoes now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A lot of rain in a short time can split ripe fruit. Pick anything that is nearly ready before it cracks, and check for soil splash on lower leaves which can spread disease.

germination.text_seasoned: Bottom heat is the single biggest factor in germination speed. A heat mat, the top of your refrigerator, or anywhere consistently warm works well. Most tomato seeds germinate in 5-7 days at 75°F.
Cover your tray with a humidity dome or cling film until the first sprout appears. Remove it immediately when you see growth; leaving it on causes damping off.

seedling.text_seasoned: Leggy, stretched seedlings almost always mean not enough light, not overwatering. Get them as close to a bright window as possible, or use a grow light 14-16 hours a day.
Once you have two sets of true leaves, pot up into individual cells or small 3-inch pots. Tomatoes root all along their stems, so you can bury them deeper than they were; it builds a stronger plant.

established.text_seasoned: Harden off properly: a week of outdoor time before transplanting, starting with just a couple of hours in a sheltered spot. Plants that skip this step sulk for weeks after transplanting.
Plant your tomatoes deeper than they sit in the pot. Bury the stem right up to the lowest set of leaves. Every bit of buried stem becomes roots.

flowering.text_seasoned: A gentle shake of the flowering stem in the morning helps pollen transfer and improves fruit set. It sounds fussy but it genuinely makes a difference, especially in a sheltered spot without much breeze.
Stop high-nitrogen feeding the moment flowers appear. Nitrogen pushes leafy growth. What you want now is potassium: switch to a tomato-specific or high-K feed.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every ripe tomato you can find, every time you check the plant. The more you harvest, the more the plant produces. Leaving ripe fruit on the vine is the most common reason production slows mid-season.
Taste as you go. Different varieties peak at different moments; some are best just before fully ripe, others need a few more days. Your palate is the best harvest indicator you have.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: When nights drop below 50°F regularly, pinch out all the growing tips. The plant will stop trying to set new fruit and put everything into ripening what is already there.
Green tomatoes left on the plant when frost threatens can be brought inside to ripen. Lay them in a single layer somewhere cool and dark, not the refrigerator, which kills flavor.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 4-8 lbs over the season per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A good plant at peak will give you a generous bowlful every 2-3 days
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: First seasons are for learning. If you get enough for a salad, that is a success. You will get more each year as you learn what your specific garden needs.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are tropical plants and suffer the moment temperatures drop near freezing. Even a brief cold night can blacken leaves and kill young plants. If it happened at transplant, the plant was likely moved out too early; soil temperature matters as much as air temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait until both night temperatures are reliably above 50°F and soil temperature is above 60°F before transplanting. A cheap soil thermometer removes the guesswork.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes are susceptible to blight, blossom end rot, and several common pests. Blight spreads fast in wet, humid conditions and usually starts at the lower leaves. Blossom end rot is caused by calcium deficiency triggered by irregular watering, not a nutrient problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently at the base, not overhead. Remove any affected leaves immediately. Rotate tomatoes to a different bed each year and stake plants to improve airflow.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered tomatoes show yellowing lower leaves, cracked fruit, and roots that cannot get oxygen. Inconsistent watering, dry then suddenly wet, causes fruit splitting and blossom end rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply twice a week rather than a little every day. Mulching around the base dramatically improves moisture consistency.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes blossom drop; no flowers, no fruit. During fruiting, inconsistent moisture causes blossom end rot and cracked skin.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes need 1-2 inches of water per week. Mulch heavily to retain moisture, and water at the base never the leaves.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Tomatoes need a minimum of 6-8 hours of direct sun to produce well. In shade they grow leafy but set little or no fruit, and are much more prone to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Tomatoes are one of the most sun-hungry vegetables. If your current spot is marginal, prioritize this bed for tomatoes next season and move something more shade-tolerant elsewhere.
