provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark sunken lesions on ripening fruit. Fruit rots on plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum fungus. Favored by warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected fruit. Apply copper fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Harvest promptly when ripe.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 8-10 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 10 days.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Good container crop. 3-5 gallon pot.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes: all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Slice and freeze -- very good for cooking
storage.notes_seasoned: Banana peppers pickle extremely well -- classic banana pepper rings in vinegar brine last months.

varieties.note_seasoned: Sweet Banana is consistent and very productive -- hard to go wrong with it.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A small pale shoot pushing upward. Peppers are slower than tomatoes -- do not give up after a week.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Peppers need warmth more than any other vegetable. Keep soil at 80-85°F if possible. A heat mat is not optional with peppers -- it is the difference between 7 days and 21 days.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves, then the first true leaves which will be narrow and pointed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep them warm and bright. Peppers are slow at this stage -- be patient. Do not overwater; they are prone to damping off.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bushy plant with 4-6 sets of leaves, sturdy stem. Do not rush transplanting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Peppers hate cold soil more than they hate cold air. Wait until nights are reliably above 55°F and the soil temperature is 65°F+. Cold-shocked peppers stall for weeks.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white or purple flowers -- often the first one appears before you expect it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Some growers remove the first flower (the 'king flower') to encourage bushier growth and more fruit. It is optional but can increase total yield.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green peppers are ready to pick at full size. Leave them longer and they turn red, yellow or orange -- sweeter and more nutritious, but fewer total fruits.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick green to maximize total yield, or wait for color if flavor matters more. Use scissors or a knife -- pulling can snap branches.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Nights cooling, plant slowing down, remaining fruit taking longer to ripen.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Bring container peppers inside before the first frost -- they can overwinter as houseplants and come back stronger next year. In ground, harvest everything before frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Season wrapping up -- how did it go?

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your peppers indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Peppers need 8-10 weeks indoors before transplanting -- start now. They germinate slowly, especially without bottom heat. Get a heat mat under them and keep soil temperature at 80-85°F. Patience pays off with peppers.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- but check soil temperature first
notifications.body_seasoned: The air temperature is safe, but peppers care more about soil warmth than air warmth. Check your soil temperature before transplanting -- it should be 65°F or warmer. Cold soil at transplant is the most common reason peppers stall.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your peppers should be reaching full size
notifications.body_seasoned: Green bell peppers are ready to pick at full size -- usually around now. If you want colored peppers, leave them another 2-3 weeks. They will turn red, orange or yellow and get sweeter, but the plant produces fewer total fruits the longer you wait.

notifications.title_seasoned: Consider overwintering your pepper plants
notifications.body_seasoned: Peppers are perennials in warm climates. Before frost arrives, you can bring container plants inside as houseplants. Cut them back by about a third, reduce watering, and keep in a bright spot. They will come back next spring faster and stronger.

notifications.title_seasoned: Checking in on your peppers
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a while. How are they looking? Peppers can be slow and frustrating mid-season -- they often seem to stall before suddenly taking off.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect your peppers tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peppers are very frost-tender. Cover with fleece or bring containers inside tonight. Even a light frost can damage or kill the plant. Do not risk it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress -- your peppers may drop flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Very high temperatures cause pepper flowers to drop before they can set fruit. Water deeply in the early morning and consider light shade cloth during peak afternoon heat. Hot peppers handle heat better than sweet varieties.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Cold snap coming -- protect young pepper plants
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A sudden temperature drop can set pepper plants back significantly. Cover outdoor plants tonight and check soil temperature tomorrow. Peppers that get cold-shocked at transplant can stall for weeks.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- your peppers need deep watering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought stress during fruiting causes blossom drop and poor fruit development. Water deeply at the base twice a week and mulch heavily to retain moisture.

germination.text_seasoned: Peppers are the most heat-dependent seed you will germinate. A heat mat is genuinely worth it -- germination at 85°F takes 7-10 days; at 65°F it can take 3-4 weeks or fail entirely.
Soak seeds in warm water for 8 hours before sowing. It softens the seed coat and speeds up germination.

seedling.text_seasoned: Pepper seedlings are naturally slow. Do not panic if they seem stuck for a week after the seed leaves open -- they are putting energy into root development before visible growth.
Keep the heat mat going until they have 2 sets of true leaves. Peppers sulk in cool conditions at every stage.

established.text_seasoned: The most common pepper mistake is transplanting too early. Soil temperature matters more than air temperature. A cheap soil thermometer is one of the most useful tools you can have for peppers.

Pinch out the very first flower bud you see (the king flower in the center fork of the plant). It redirects energy into bushy growth and more fruit overall -- though if you cannot bear to, leave it. You will still get peppers.

flowering.text_seasoned: Hot peppers are often more reliable in the heat than sweet varieties. If your bells are struggling with flower drop in high temperatures, know that your chillies are probably loving it.
Peppers are self-pollinating but benefit from movement. A gentle breeze, or gently shaking the plant, helps pollen transfer.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick green peppers at full size to keep production going. Every pepper you leave on the plant to turn red reduces how many new ones it sets. Decide what matters more -- quantity or colored fruit.
Hot pepper heat intensifies as they ripen to red. Pick green for milder heat, red for maximum fire.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Pepper plants are true perennials -- they are only treated as annuals because of cold winters. A plant brought inside in autumn and overwintered will be much more productive the following year.
Harvest all remaining peppers before the first frost, even green ones. They can ripen slowly on a windowsill or be used green in cooking.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 6-10 bell peppers per plant, or 20-30+ hot peppers
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A healthy bell pepper plant produces fruit in flushes -- you may get several at once, then a pause
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Peppers are one of the more challenging crops in cooler climates. A good harvest in year one is something to be genuinely proud of.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers are even more cold-sensitive than tomatoes. Cold soil at transplant time is the most common cause of stunted, struggling plants -- the plant survives but sulks for weeks and never fully recovers its momentum.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check soil temperature before transplanting -- it must be 65°F or warmer. A cold snap after transplant can be just as damaging. Keep fleece handy for the first few weeks.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers can be affected by aphids, spider mites in hot dry weather, and bacterial spot in humid conditions. Spider mites thrive when plants are stressed -- usually by drought or heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Consistent watering prevents drought stress that invites spider mites. Good airflow around plants reduces humidity-related disease. Check undersides of leaves regularly.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered peppers show yellowing leaves and root rot. They prefer to dry out slightly between waterings -- unlike tomatoes they do not want consistently moist soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Ensure excellent drainage -- peppers are more drought-tolerant than most vegetables once established.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes flowers to drop before setting fruit. This is one of the most common reasons for a pepper plant with no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during the flowering period. Deep watering twice a week is better than light daily watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers need full sun -- 8 hours minimum. In less sun they grow slowly, flower poorly, and are much more susceptible to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: If your site gets less than 6 hours of direct sun, consider a different crop. Peppers planted in marginal light rarely justify the long season they require.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark sunken lesions on ripening fruit. Fruit rots on plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum fungus. Favored by warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected fruit. Apply copper fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Harvest promptly when ripe.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A small pale shoot pushing upward. Peppers are slower than tomatoes -- do not give up after a week.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Peppers need warmth more than any other vegetable. Keep soil at 80-85°F if possible. A heat mat is not optional with peppers -- it is the difference between 7 days and 21 days.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves, then the first true leaves which will be narrow and pointed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep them warm and bright. Peppers are slow at this stage -- be patient. Do not overwater; they are prone to damping off.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bushy plant with 4-6 sets of leaves, sturdy stem. Do not rush transplanting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Peppers hate cold soil more than they hate cold air. Wait until nights are reliably above 55°F and the soil temperature is 65°F+. Cold-shocked peppers stall for weeks.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white or purple flowers -- often the first one appears before you expect it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Some growers remove the first flower (the 'king flower') to encourage bushier growth and more fruit. It is optional but can increase total yield.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green peppers are ready to pick at full size. Leave them longer and they turn red, yellow or orange -- sweeter and more nutritious, but fewer total fruits.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick green to maximize total yield, or wait for color if flavor matters more. Use scissors or a knife -- pulling can snap branches.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Nights cooling, plant slowing down, remaining fruit taking longer to ripen.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Bring container peppers inside before the first frost -- they can overwinter as houseplants and come back stronger next year. In ground, harvest everything before frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Season wrapping up -- how did it go?

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your peppers indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Peppers need 8-10 weeks indoors before transplanting -- start now. They germinate slowly, especially without bottom heat. Get a heat mat under them and keep soil temperature at 80-85°F. Patience pays off with peppers.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- but check soil temperature first
notifications.body_seasoned: The air temperature is safe, but peppers care more about soil warmth than air warmth. Check your soil temperature before transplanting -- it should be 65°F or warmer. Cold soil at transplant is the most common reason peppers stall.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your peppers should be reaching full size
notifications.body_seasoned: Green bell peppers are ready to pick at full size -- usually around now. If you want colored peppers, leave them another 2-3 weeks. They will turn red, orange or yellow and get sweeter, but the plant produces fewer total fruits the longer you wait.

notifications.title_seasoned: Consider overwintering your pepper plants
notifications.body_seasoned: Peppers are perennials in warm climates. Before frost arrives, you can bring container plants inside as houseplants. Cut them back by about a third, reduce watering, and keep in a bright spot. They will come back next spring faster and stronger.

notifications.title_seasoned: Checking in on your peppers
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a while. How are they looking? Peppers can be slow and frustrating mid-season -- they often seem to stall before suddenly taking off.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect your peppers tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peppers are very frost-tender. Cover with fleece or bring containers inside tonight. Even a light frost can damage or kill the plant. Do not risk it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress -- your peppers may drop flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Very high temperatures cause pepper flowers to drop before they can set fruit. Water deeply in the early morning and consider light shade cloth during peak afternoon heat. Hot peppers handle heat better than sweet varieties.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Cold snap coming -- protect young pepper plants
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A sudden temperature drop can set pepper plants back significantly. Cover outdoor plants tonight and check soil temperature tomorrow. Peppers that get cold-shocked at transplant can stall for weeks.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- your peppers need deep watering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought stress during fruiting causes blossom drop and poor fruit development. Water deeply at the base twice a week and mulch heavily to retain moisture.

germination.text_seasoned: Peppers are the most heat-dependent seed you will germinate. A heat mat is genuinely worth it -- germination at 85°F takes 7-10 days; at 65°F it can take 3-4 weeks or fail entirely.
Soak seeds in warm water for 8 hours before sowing. It softens the seed coat and speeds up germination.

seedling.text_seasoned: Pepper seedlings are naturally slow. Do not panic if they seem stuck for a week after the seed leaves open -- they are putting energy into root development before visible growth.
Keep the heat mat going until they have 2 sets of true leaves. Peppers sulk in cool conditions at every stage.

established.text_seasoned: The most common pepper mistake is transplanting too early. Soil temperature matters more than air temperature. A cheap soil thermometer is one of the most useful tools you can have for peppers.

Pinch out the very first flower bud you see (the king flower in the center fork of the plant). It redirects energy into bushy growth and more fruit overall -- though if you cannot bear to, leave it. You will still get peppers.

flowering.text_seasoned: Hot peppers are often more reliable in the heat than sweet varieties. If your bells are struggling with flower drop in high temperatures, know that your chillies are probably loving it.
Peppers are self-pollinating but benefit from movement. A gentle breeze, or gently shaking the plant, helps pollen transfer.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick green peppers at full size to keep production going. Every pepper you leave on the plant to turn red reduces how many new ones it sets. Decide what matters more -- quantity or colored fruit.
Hot pepper heat intensifies as they ripen to red. Pick green for milder heat, red for maximum fire.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Pepper plants are true perennials -- they are only treated as annuals because of cold winters. A plant brought inside in autumn and overwintered will be much more productive the following year.
Harvest all remaining peppers before the first frost, even green ones. They can ripen slowly on a windowsill or be used green in cooking.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 30-50+ hot peppers per plant -- they are prolific once established
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Hot pepper plants at peak can produce faster than you can use them. Plan to dry, freeze or ferment the excess
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Peppers are one of the more challenging crops in cooler climates. A good harvest in year one is something to be genuinely proud of.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers are even more cold-sensitive than tomatoes. Cold soil at transplant time is the most common cause of stunted, struggling plants -- the plant survives but sulks for weeks and never fully recovers its momentum.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check soil temperature before transplanting -- it must be 65°F or warmer. A cold snap after transplant can be just as damaging. Keep fleece handy for the first few weeks.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers can be affected by aphids, spider mites in hot dry weather, and bacterial spot in humid conditions. Spider mites thrive when plants are stressed -- usually by drought or heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Consistent watering prevents drought stress that invites spider mites. Good airflow around plants reduces humidity-related disease. Check undersides of leaves regularly.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered peppers show yellowing leaves and root rot. They prefer to dry out slightly between waterings -- unlike tomatoes they do not want consistently moist soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Ensure excellent drainage -- peppers are more drought-tolerant than most vegetables once established.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes flowers to drop before setting fruit. This is one of the most common reasons for a pepper plant with no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during the flowering period. Deep watering twice a week is better than light daily watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers need full sun -- 8 hours minimum. In less sun they grow slowly, flower poorly, and are much more susceptible to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: If your site gets less than 6 hours of direct sun, consider a different crop. Peppers planted in marginal light rarely justify the long season they require.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark sunken lesions on ripening fruit. Fruit rots on plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum fungus. Favored by warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected fruit. Apply copper fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Harvest promptly when ripe.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 4-5 days -- habaneros tolerate slight drought

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 10-12 weeks before last frost -- slowest pepper to germinate. Needs soil temps above 80°F to germinate well. Patience required.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container crop -- naturally compact. 3-5 gallon pot.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes: all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole -- easiest preservation. Handle with gloves.
storage.notes_seasoned: Habaneros freeze and dry well. Wear gloves when handling.

varieties.note_seasoned: Orange Habanero is the benchmark. Peach Habanero has exceptional fruity flavor with slightly less heat.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A small pale shoot pushing upward. Peppers are slower than tomatoes -- do not give up after a week.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Peppers need warmth more than any other vegetable. Keep soil at 80-85°F if possible. A heat mat is not optional with peppers -- it is the difference between 7 days and 21 days.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Two seed leaves, then the first true leaves which will be narrow and pointed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep them warm and bright. Peppers are slow at this stage -- be patient. Do not overwater; they are prone to damping off.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bushy plant with 4-6 sets of leaves, sturdy stem. Do not rush transplanting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Peppers hate cold soil more than they hate cold air. Wait until nights are reliably above 55°F and the soil temperature is 65°F+. Cold-shocked peppers stall for weeks.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Outside yet, or still hardening off?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white or purple flowers -- often the first one appears before you expect it.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Some growers remove the first flower (the 'king flower') to encourage bushier growth and more fruit. It is optional but can increase total yield.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green peppers are ready to pick at full size. Leave them longer and they turn red, yellow or orange -- sweeter and more nutritious, but fewer total fruits.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick green to maximize total yield, or wait for color if flavor matters more. Use scissors or a knife -- pulling can snap branches.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Nights cooling, plant slowing down, remaining fruit taking longer to ripen.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Bring container peppers inside before the first frost -- they can overwinter as houseplants and come back stronger next year. In ground, harvest everything before frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Season wrapping up -- how did it go?

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your peppers indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Peppers need 8-10 weeks indoors before transplanting -- start now. They germinate slowly, especially without bottom heat. Get a heat mat under them and keep soil temperature at 80-85°F. Patience pays off with peppers.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- but check soil temperature first
notifications.body_seasoned: The air temperature is safe, but peppers care more about soil warmth than air warmth. Check your soil temperature before transplanting -- it should be 65°F or warmer. Cold soil at transplant is the most common reason peppers stall.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your peppers should be reaching full size
notifications.body_seasoned: Green bell peppers are ready to pick at full size -- usually around now. If you want colored peppers, leave them another 2-3 weeks. They will turn red, orange or yellow and get sweeter, but the plant produces fewer total fruits the longer you wait.

notifications.title_seasoned: Consider overwintering your pepper plants
notifications.body_seasoned: Peppers are perennials in warm climates. Before frost arrives, you can bring container plants inside as houseplants. Cut them back by about a third, reduce watering, and keep in a bright spot. They will come back next spring faster and stronger.

notifications.title_seasoned: Checking in on your peppers
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a while. How are they looking? Peppers can be slow and frustrating mid-season -- they often seem to stall before suddenly taking off.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect your peppers tonight
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peppers are very frost-tender. Cover with fleece or bring containers inside tonight. Even a light frost can damage or kill the plant. Do not risk it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress -- your peppers may drop flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Very high temperatures cause pepper flowers to drop before they can set fruit. Water deeply in the early morning and consider light shade cloth during peak afternoon heat. Hot peppers handle heat better than sweet varieties.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Cold snap coming -- protect young pepper plants
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A sudden temperature drop can set pepper plants back significantly. Cover outdoor plants tonight and check soil temperature tomorrow. Peppers that get cold-shocked at transplant can stall for weeks.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- your peppers need deep watering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought stress during fruiting causes blossom drop and poor fruit development. Water deeply at the base twice a week and mulch heavily to retain moisture.

germination.text_seasoned: Peppers are the most heat-dependent seed you will germinate. A heat mat is genuinely worth it -- germination at 85°F takes 7-10 days; at 65°F it can take 3-4 weeks or fail entirely.
Soak seeds in warm water for 8 hours before sowing. It softens the seed coat and speeds up germination.

seedling.text_seasoned: Pepper seedlings are naturally slow. Do not panic if they seem stuck for a week after the seed leaves open -- they are putting energy into root development before visible growth.
Keep the heat mat going until they have 2 sets of true leaves. Peppers sulk in cool conditions at every stage.

established.text_seasoned: The most common pepper mistake is transplanting too early. Soil temperature matters more than air temperature. A cheap soil thermometer is one of the most useful tools you can have for peppers.

Pinch out the very first flower bud you see (the king flower in the center fork of the plant). It redirects energy into bushy growth and more fruit overall -- though if you cannot bear to, leave it. You will still get peppers.

flowering.text_seasoned: Hot peppers are often more reliable in the heat than sweet varieties. If your bells are struggling with flower drop in high temperatures, know that your chillies are probably loving it.
Peppers are self-pollinating but benefit from movement. A gentle breeze, or gently shaking the plant, helps pollen transfer.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick green peppers at full size to keep production going. Every pepper you leave on the plant to turn red reduces how many new ones it sets. Decide what matters more -- quantity or colored fruit.
Hot pepper heat intensifies as they ripen to red. Pick green for milder heat, red for maximum fire.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Pepper plants are true perennials -- they are only treated as annuals because of cold winters. A plant brought inside in autumn and overwintered will be much more productive the following year.
Harvest all remaining peppers before the first frost, even green ones. They can ripen slowly on a windowsill or be used green in cooking.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 30-50+ hot peppers per plant -- they are prolific once established
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Hot pepper plants at peak can produce faster than you can use them. Plan to dry, freeze or ferment the excess
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Peppers are one of the more challenging crops in cooler climates. A good harvest in year one is something to be genuinely proud of.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers are even more cold-sensitive than tomatoes. Cold soil at transplant time is the most common cause of stunted, struggling plants -- the plant survives but sulks for weeks and never fully recovers its momentum.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check soil temperature before transplanting -- it must be 65°F or warmer. A cold snap after transplant can be just as damaging. Keep fleece handy for the first few weeks.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers can be affected by aphids, spider mites in hot dry weather, and bacterial spot in humid conditions. Spider mites thrive when plants are stressed -- usually by drought or heat.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Consistent watering prevents drought stress that invites spider mites. Good airflow around plants reduces humidity-related disease. Check undersides of leaves regularly.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwatered peppers show yellowing leaves and root rot. They prefer to dry out slightly between waterings -- unlike tomatoes they do not want consistently moist soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water when the top inch of soil is dry. Ensure excellent drainage -- peppers are more drought-tolerant than most vegetables once established.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering causes flowers to drop before setting fruit. This is one of the most common reasons for a pepper plant with no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during the flowering period. Deep watering twice a week is better than light daily watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peppers need full sun -- 8 hours minimum. In less sun they grow slowly, flower poorly, and are much more susceptible to disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: If your site gets less than 6 hours of direct sun, consider a different crop. Peppers planted in marginal light rarely justify the long season they require.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Nasturtiums
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Trap crop for aphids, attracts predators

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring cucumber beetle are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Flowering plants attracting predatory insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). Specific pairings vary in effectiveness.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause_seasoned: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost. Cucumbers prefer not being transplanted.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended -- for pickling, process immediately after harvest
storage.notes_seasoned: Pickle within 24 hours of harvest for crispest results -- pectin breaks down quickly.

varieties.note_seasoned: Calypso is a top performer with strong disease resistance -- very reliable for home pickling.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works in containers with a vertical trellis. 5-gallon minimum. Compact varieties work best.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cucumbers germinate fast -- you should see the seed leaves pushing up within a week.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow seeds on their edge rather than flat -- it reduces rotting and speeds germination. Keep soil warm, 70°F+.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large, round seed leaves, then the first true leaves which are rough and slightly lobed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cucumbers hate having their roots disturbed -- if starting indoors, use biodegradable pots you can plant whole. Transplant as little as possible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Vines beginning to extend and tendrils reaching for support.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Get supports in place now before the vines get tangled. Cucumbers climbing a trellis produce straighter fruit, get better airflow, and are easier to harvest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Yellow flowers appearing. Male flowers come first -- no fruit yet. Female flowers have a tiny swelling at the base that becomes the cucumber.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do not panic when the first flowers drop without producing fruit -- those are males. Female flowers follow within a week or two.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seeing flowers? Any tiny cucumbers forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Firm, dark green fruit at the size described for your variety. Skin should be smooth, not bumpy or yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days without fail. A single missed cucumber that turns yellow and seedy signals the plant to stop producing. Regular picking is the most important thing you can do.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, yellowing vines, powdery mildew appearing on leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Powdery mildew at end of season is normal -- it does not mean you did anything wrong. Pull the plant before first frost and compost the vines.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Season done? How did it go?

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your cucumbers now
notifications.body_seasoned: Cucumbers go directly into warm soil after frost. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest. If starting indoors, use biodegradable pots -- cucumbers hate having their roots disturbed at transplant.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to set up your cucumber supports
notifications.body_seasoned: Your cucumbers should be putting on growth now. Get a trellis or netting in place before the vines start sprawling -- it is much harder to do once they are tangled. Vertical growing gives you straighter fruit and better airflow.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your cucumbers should be ready to pick
notifications.body_seasoned: Check the vines carefully -- cucumbers hide under leaves and can go from perfect to overgrown very quickly. Pick every 2-3 days. A single yellow, seedy cucumber left on the plant tells it the job is done and production slows dramatically.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your cucumber vines
notifications.body_seasoned: Cucumbers need checking every few days at harvest time. One overgrown fruit can slow down the whole plant. A quick look through the leaves is worth it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- cucumbers are extremely frost-tender
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Even a light frost kills cucumber plants. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Do not risk it.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cucumbers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow around the vines, avoid watering the leaves, and pick regularly to keep the plant healthy.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress -- keep your cucumbers well watered
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Cucumbers need consistent moisture in the heat -- stress during fruiting causes bitter, misshapen fruit. Water deeply at the base every day in very hot weather and mulch well.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow cucumber seeds on their side -- the edge, not flat. It helps the root emerge more easily and reduces rotting.
Cucumbers germinate best at 70-95°F. They will not germinate well in cool soil -- wait for genuine warmth.

seedling.text_seasoned: If starting indoors, use biodegradable pots. Cucumbers genuinely hate having their roots disturbed. Plant the whole pot when transplanting.
Thin to one plant per spot -- do not try to transplant the thinned seedlings. Cucumbers do not recover well from root disturbance.

established.text_seasoned: Cucumbers climbing a trellis are easier to manage than sprawling on the ground. The fruit hangs straight, gets better airflow, and is much easier to spot at harvest.
Mulch heavily around the base. Cucumbers need consistent moisture and heat -- mulch provides both.

flowering.text_seasoned: The first flowers are male -- they produce no fruit and will drop. This is normal. Female flowers follow, identifiable by the tiny cucumber shape at their base.
In a greenhouse or polytunnel, hand-pollinate by touching a small paintbrush to each flower. Outdoors, pollinators will do the work.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days without exception during peak season. One overlarge, yellowing cucumber sends a signal to the whole plant that the season is done. Do not let that happen.
Harvest in the morning when cucumbers are at their crispest and coolest. Refrigerate immediately for best texture.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Powdery mildew appearing on leaves is normal at the end of cucumber season -- it is a sign of age, not failure. The plant has done its job.
Save seeds from an open-pollinated or heirloom variety for next year. Let one fruit go fully yellow and fat, scoop out the seeds, rinse and dry them.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 10-20 cucumbers over the season per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: At peak, a healthy plant gives you 2-3 cucumbers every few days
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Cucumbers are one of the most rewarding first crops -- fast-growing, high-yielding, and delicious straight from the vine.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from last frost. Pickling cucumbers tend to produce their crop in a concentrated burst -- useful for canning but overwhelming if you want a steady fresh supply. For steady pickles, succession planting creates a more manageable ongoing harvest. An additional benefit: if cucumber beetles hit your first batch, you have a fresh start coming in rather than a lost season.
