good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Attracts bees for pollination, deters hornworm

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring hornworm are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause_seasoned: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Cook, rake into strands, freeze -- good
storage.notes_seasoned: Spaghetti squash stores well. The hollow interior protects the flesh.

varieties.note_seasoned: Small Wonder produces smaller fruits that cook faster and fit in most microwaves -- much easier to handle than standard.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Not suited to containers -- vines grow very long. Ground or large raised bed only.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost. In zones 3-5, start indoors 3-4 weeks before in biodegradable pots.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large seed leaves pushing up fast -- squash germinates quickly in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow seeds on their edge to prevent rotting. Keep soil warm and moist.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large, hairy true leaves developing rapidly. Squash grows fast once it gets going.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give them space from the start -- squash plants get very large and do not like competition.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A strong central crown with multiple large leaves. Bush varieties stay compact; vining types will start to sprawl.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: If growing winter squash, direct the vines in the direction you want them to go now -- once established they are harder to redirect.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Growing well and in the right spot?

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large orange-yellow flowers. Male flowers come first on long straight stems. Female flowers have a swollen base -- the future squash.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hand-pollinate female flowers in the early morning if you are not seeing good fruit set. Touch a male flower to each open female flower.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowers open? Any tiny squash forming?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Summer squash: harvest small and often at 6-8 inches. Winter squash: wait until skin is hard and stem is dry and corky.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Summer squash picked small tastes better and keeps production going. Winter squash left on the vine longer develops better flavor and storage life.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production on summer squash. Winter squash stems drying and corking -- the cue to harvest before frost.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cure winter squash at room temperature for 10-14 days before storing -- it hardens the skin and sweetens the flesh. Summer squash plants can be composted after frost.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Season done? Worth noting what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your squash
notifications.body_seasoned: Squash goes in a week after last frost, once the soil has had time to warm properly. Sow 2-3 seeds per spot and thin to the strongest plant. They grow fast -- you will see real progress within a week.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your squash flowers -- pollination time
notifications.body_seasoned: Your squash should be flowering now. If you see flowers but no fruit forming, check whether you have both male and female flowers open at the same time. Female flowers have a small swollen base. Hand-pollinate in the morning if bees are scarce.

notifications.title_seasoned: Summer squash ready -- pick small and often
notifications.body_seasoned: Your courgettes or summer squash should be ready. Pick them at 6-8 inches -- they taste better small and the plant produces far more when you harvest regularly. A forgotten courgette turns into a marrow overnight.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest your winter squash before frost
notifications.body_seasoned: Frost is {{weeks_until_anchor}} weeks away -- time to check your winter squash for harvest readiness. The stem should be dry and corky, and the skin should resist a thumbnail. Harvest all squash before frost and cure them for 10-14 days at room temperature.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your squash plants
notifications.body_seasoned: Summer squash especially needs checking every few days -- they grow incredibly fast and a missed harvest sets back the whole plant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect your squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Squash is frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Winter squash still on the vine must be harvested before a hard frost -- even one frosty night can damage stored winter squash.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Powdery mildew risk for your squash
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Squash is very susceptible to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good spacing and airflow. If you see white powdery patches on leaves, remove affected leaves and spray with a dilute baking soda solution.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Your squash needs deep watering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Squash plants have large leaves and need a lot of water in dry conditions. Water deeply at the base -- not the leaves -- twice a week in drought conditions. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow squash seeds on their side, not flat. The root emerges from the pointed end and finds its way down more easily.
Squash germinates fast in warm soil -- sometimes in 4-5 days. In cold soil it rots. Wait for genuine warmth (60°F+ minimum, 70°F+ ideal).

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin ruthlessly to one plant per spot. Squash planted too close together become a tangled mass that is prone to mildew and difficult to harvest.
Do not start squash indoors too early -- 3-4 weeks maximum. They outgrow their pots quickly and transplant shock is real.

established.text_seasoned: Leave enough room -- a zucchini plant can easily cover 4-6 square feet. A butternut squash vine can run 6-10 feet. Plan for this before planting.
A thick layer of mulch around squash plants suppresses weeds, retains moisture, and keeps the fruit clean if it rests on the ground.

flowering.text_seasoned: Male flowers come before female flowers -- this is normal and not something to worry about. Female flowers (with the swollen base behind the petals) follow within a week or two.
Early morning is when squash flowers are most receptive. If you are hand-pollinating, do it between 7-10am while flowers are fully open.

harvest.text_seasoned: Winter squash is ready when the skin is hard enough that you cannot pierce it with a thumbnail and the stem has turned dry and corky. The fruit detaches easily but you should cut, not pull -- leaving 2 to 3 inches of stem dramatically extends storage life. Stemless squash rots from the wound within weeks.

Harvest before the first hard frost (28°F or below). Light frost can be tolerated if the fruit is mature, but a hard freeze damages the flesh and ruins storage potential. Watch the forecast through autumn.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Cure freshly-cut winter squash for 10 to 14 days at 70-80°F with good airflow before storing. Curing hardens the skin, heals minor stem wounds, and converts starches to sugars -- flavor improves dramatically over the cure window.

After curing, store at 50-60°F in a dry, dark spot. A well-cured butternut keeps 3 to 6 months; acorn squash 1 to 2; spaghetti squash 2 to 3. Check periodically and use any squash showing soft spots first.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 3-6 fruits per plant for butternut and acorn types
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Winter squash sets all its fruit within a window, then concentrates on ripening them
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Winter squash takes more patience than summer types -- the long growing season can feel slow. The payoff is months of stored vegetables.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits are tropical-origin tender annuals -- killed outright by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees) stunts seedlings for the rest of the season even if they survive. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to direct-sow or transplant until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before set-out, but disturb roots minimally -- cucurbits resent transplanting. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring or early-fall frosts.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucumber beetles (striped and spotted) damage seedlings directly and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease that wilts vines from the tips inward. Squash bugs target squash and pumpkin (less so cucumber and melon). Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season as white powder on leaves. Downy mildew, anthracnose, and bacterial leaf spot are humidity-driven secondary problems.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover from planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) crush easily by hand if caught early. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties (most modern cucumbers are bred for resistance) and water at the base, not overhead. Rotate cucurbits to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits need consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, sudden vine collapse, and watery flavorless fruit. Heavy rain near harvest causes ripe melons to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil or raised mounds (the traditional 'cucurbit hill' approach exists for drainage reasons). Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to even out soil moisture and reduce splash-borne disease. Stop watering watermelons 2 weeks before expected harvest to concentrate flavor.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and fruit set produces small, misshapen, or bitter fruit. Cucurbits move large volumes of water through their tissues during fruit development -- a single mature watermelon plant can use 1 to 2 gallons of water per day in peak summer. Cucumber bitterness is often a drought-stress signal.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently and deeply -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum during fruit development, more in heat. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucurbits need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally 8 or more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow leaves and even bloom, but fruit set is poor and ripening is incomplete. A late-season fruit that never sweetens is often a sun problem more than a temperature problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest spot available. Trellising vining cucurbits (vertical support for cucumbers and small-fruited squash) gets more leaf area into the sun and improves fruit set substantially. In partial-shade gardens, accept that cucurbits are not the right crop and grow leafy greens or herbs instead.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow only after last frost. Install support first to avoid root disturbance later.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note_seasoned: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent
storage.notes_seasoned: Same as bush beans -- freeze surplus immediately for best quality.

varieties.note_seasoned: Fortex is the gourmet choice -- very long, completely stringless, and exceptionally tender.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works in large containers with a trellis. 5-gallon minimum. Bush beans are easier in containers.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body_seasoned: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title_seasoned: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body_seasoned: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text_seasoned: Beans are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the brittle taproot. Wait until soil is 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better) before sowing; cold soil rots seed before it germinates.

Sow 1 to 2 inches deep, 2 to 4 inches apart in rows. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria at sowing if the bed has not grown beans recently -- this boosts the nitrogen-fixing nodulation that beans depend on.

seedling.text_seasoned: Beans germinate fast in warm soil -- typically 7 to 10 days. Seedlings are vulnerable to slugs and bean leaf beetles in their first weeks; check daily.

Thin bush beans to 4 to 6 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Pole beans need a trellis or pole structure in place at this stage -- they grow fast and resent late-installed support.

established.text_seasoned: Do not fertilize beans with nitrogen. Beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- this is when water stress most reduces yield. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds.

flowering.text_seasoned: Beans are self-pollinating and do not need pollinators. Flowers open and self-pollinate within hours; fruit set is fast.
Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during flowering -- both populations spike in this window. Check undersides of leaves daily.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick beans young and often -- bush and pole beans ready when pods snap cleanly and the seeds inside are still small. Edamame ready when pods are plump and fill 80 to 90 percent with bright green beans, before yellowing.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Beans left on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Edamame is harvested whole-pod, not shelled in the field.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: After harvest, cut bean plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen for the bed.
Rotate beans to a new bed each year. Bean diseases (anthracnose, halo blight, bean rust) survive in soil and infect next year's planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 1-2 lbs per plant over a long season
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Pole beans produce continuously for months -- far more total yield than bush beans
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Pole beans are the most productive choice if you have a support structure. They keep going all summer with regular picking.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Beans are warm-season tender annuals -- killed outright by light frost at any stage. Cold soil at sowing (below 60 degrees) rots seed; cool conditions during early growth produce stunted plants that never fully recover. Late summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to sow until soil is reliably 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better). In short-season zones, choose early-maturing bush varieties and use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring frosts. For fall harvests, time the planting so harvest finishes before first expected frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mexican bean beetle (yellow with black spots, similar to ladybug but a pest) is the dominant bean pest east of the Rockies -- larvae skeletonize leaves. Bean leaf beetle damages seedlings and pods. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Halo blight (water-soaked spots with yellow halo) and bean rust are the headline diseases. For edamame specifically, soybean aphid and Japanese beetle are also common.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For Mexican bean beetle, hand-pick adults and crush yellow egg masses on leaf undersides; in heavy infestations, parasitic wasp release works for organic gardeners. Rotate to a new bed each year. Avoid working bean plants when foliage is wet -- this spreads halo blight and bean rust. Choose disease-resistant varieties for the next planting.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Beans are also susceptible to white mold (Sclerotinia) in cool wet conditions, which produces fluffy white growth at the soil line and kills plants quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water in the morning so foliage dries before evening. Space plants for airflow. For white mold, rotate at least 3 years between bean plantings in any one bed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the leading cause of poor bean harvests. Plants drop flowers under water stress and produce small empty or partially-filled pods. Edamame is especially demanding of consistent water during the pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal because it provides consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower and produce well. In partial shade plants grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few pods. Tall pole beans can shade their own lower leaves if not pinched at the top of the support.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. For pole beans, pinch the growing tip when vines reach the top of the support to prevent excessive top growth and improve light penetration to lower flowering nodes.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3-4 weeks from last frost through early summer. Pole beans produce longer than bush beans -- a single planting can yield for 6-8 weeks of picking. But succession still helps: when the first planting hits peak production, the second is getting established. Use the longer interval (4 weeks) in zones with shorter seasons. Count back 65-80 days from first frost for your last sowing.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow in cool weather, 4-6 weeks before last frost.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note_seasoned: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 1-2 minutes, freeze -- very good
storage.notes_seasoned: Snow peas freeze better than sugar snap peas due to thinner walls.

varieties.note_seasoned: Oregon Sugar Pod II has the best disease package -- resistant to enation mosaic virus and powdery mildew.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Good container crop with a trellis. 3-gallon minimum. Dwarf varieties need less support.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body_seasoned: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title_seasoned: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body_seasoned: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text_seasoned: Peas are direct-sown 4 to 6 weeks before last frost -- they actually prefer cool soil (40 to 60 degrees) and germinate poorly above 75. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing for spring harvest works well.
Sow 1 to 1.5 inches deep, 2 inches apart. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria if the bed has not grown peas recently. Soak seeds overnight before sowing in cool soil to speed germination.

seedling.text_seasoned: Peas germinate in 7 to 14 days in cool soil. Seedlings tolerate light frost and even brief snow once established -- they are remarkably cold-hardy.
Install trellis or netting at sowing or as soon as seedlings emerge. Peas climb by tendrils and need something to grab. Even bush peas benefit from low brushwood support.

established.text_seasoned: Do not fertilize with nitrogen. Peas fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; extra N produces leafy plants with poor pod production.
Water consistently. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast -- mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and keep roots cool.

flowering.text_seasoned: Peas are self-pollinating; flowers do not need insect pollinators. Cool weather during flowering produces the most flowers and highest yields.
Watch for pea aphids on flower clusters and tender new growth. Powdery mildew often shows up as flowering peaks, especially in still humid conditions.

harvest.text_seasoned: Snow peas: pick when pods are flat and the peas inside are barely visible bumps. Sugar snap peas: pick when pods are plump and crisp but before peas inside become starchy. Both are best picked young and often.
Harvest every 1 to 2 days during peak production. Peas left on the plant signal it to stop producing new flowers; daily picking can extend the harvest by weeks.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Peas finish abruptly when daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees -- plants yellow, stop flowering, and decline. This is the natural cycle, not a problem.
Cut spent plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil for the nitrogen contribution. The freed-up bed is well-suited to a fall planting of cool-season crops or warm-season transplants.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: A good handful of pods per plant per week at peak
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Snow peas produce over several weeks -- harvest when flat and before seeds bulge
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Snow peas are delicious raw and one of the easiest crops to get right.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peas are unusual among annuals in being killed by HEAT, not cold. Young plants tolerate light frost and even brief snow; mature plants flower through cool spring weather but stop and decline once daytime temperatures consistently exceed 75 to 80 degrees. The end of pea season is heat, not cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow as early as possible -- 4 to 6 weeks before last frost in most zones. In mild-winter zones, fall sowing gives a long cool-season harvest. Choose heat-tolerant varieties (Wando, Sugar Sprint) for warmer zones. Plan succession plantings so harvest finishes before the heat hits.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pea aphid (the headline pea pest) clusters on flower buds and tender new growth, weakening plants and reducing pod set. Pea weevil larvae bore into developing peas. Pea leaf miner damages leaves but rarely affects yield substantially. Powdery mildew is the headline disease, especially in cool humid conditions or as plants approach the heat-stress end of their cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off pea aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Choose powdery-mildew-resistant varieties (most modern peas have some resistance). Space plants for airflow and avoid overhead watering. Rotate peas to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot and yellowing of inner leaves. Peas in heavy clay or low-lying spots are especially vulnerable. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew and ascochyta blight.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Use raised beds in heavy or wet sites. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill produces small empty pods or partially-filled pods. Peas have shallow roots and dry out fast; a few hot dry days during the critical flowering window can substantially reduce yield even on otherwise healthy plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and keep roots cool. Drip irrigation works well for peas because it keeps foliage dry while providing consistent water.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Peas need 6 hours of sun minimum, though they tolerate light shade better than beans. In deep shade, plants grow leggy with sparse flowers and reduced yield. Crowded planting can shade lower flowering nodes on tall pole peas.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun in cool climates; light afternoon shade is fine in warmer zones and may extend the bloom cycle by reducing heat stress. Space plants for airflow and light penetration. Trellis tall varieties properly so vines spread out rather than tangling.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 2-3 weeks from early spring, same strategy as sugar snaps. Snow peas are slightly more cold-tolerant and can go in even earlier. Pause all sowings once daytime temperatures regularly exceed 70°F -- there's no point sowing into heat. In zones 8+, autumn sowings from September work well for a winter harvest.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow in autumn (mild climates) or very early spring. Cold-tolerant -- among the first things to sow.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note_seasoned: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Shell, blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent, traditional preservation method
storage.notes_seasoned: Double-pod if beans are large (remove gray skin after blanching) for smoother texture.

varieties.note_seasoned: The Sutton is the best compact variety -- 12 inches tall, no staking, good for exposed or windy gardens.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Can be grown in containers. 5-gallon minimum per plant. Dwarf varieties like The Sutton are best.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: The fat seed leaf loop pushing up and then straightening. Beans germinate fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly -- beans and peas dislike transplanting. Soil must be at least 60°F for beans, 45°F for peas.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First true leaves developing, tendrils beginning to reach for support on climbing types.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Get supports in place for climbing varieties now. Pole beans and sugar snaps grow fast once established.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong growth with multiple sets of leaves. Climbing types reaching upward actively.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out the growing tips of broad beans when flowers appear at the top -- it deters blackfly, the most common pest.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers along the stem or at growing tips. Beans are self-pollinating -- you do not need to do anything.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep plants well watered during flowering. Drought stress at this stage causes flowers to drop before setting pods.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods swelling and filling. Pick before the pods become tough and stringy. Seeds should be visible but not bulging.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days. Regular picking is essential -- leaving pods to mature tells the plant its job is done and production stops dramatically.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing production, pods becoming tougher, plants yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave the last few pods to dry fully on the plant and save the seeds for next year. Cut plants at the base and leave the roots -- they fix nitrogen into the soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Peas are cold-hardy and can go in 6-8 weeks before your last frost. They actually prefer cool conditions -- sow directly into prepared soil as soon as the ground can be worked. Get supports in place at the same time.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your beans
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans need warm soil -- wait until a week after your last frost before sowing. Cold soil causes seeds to rot rather than germinate. Sow directly at 2-inch depth, supports already in place for pole types.

notifications.title_seasoned: Pinch out your broad bean tips
notifications.body_seasoned: As soon as your broad beans show flowers at the top of the stem, pinch out the top 4-6 inches of growth. This deters blackfly which love the soft tips, and also redirects energy to pod development. It feels drastic but it is the right thing to do.

notifications.title_seasoned: Beans ready -- pick every 2-3 days
notifications.body_seasoned: The single most important thing now is picking regularly. Beans that are left to mature on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Get out there every 2-3 days without fail.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your beans and peas
notifications.body_seasoned: Beans and peas need picking every few days at harvest time. A few days of neglect can mean tough, stringy pods. How are they looking?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect young beans
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Bean seedlings are frost-tender. Cover with fleece tonight. Peas handle light frost much better -- established pea plants usually survive without protection.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress -- water your beans during flowering
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought during flowering is the most damaging thing for beans and peas. Flowers drop before setting pods and production suffers significantly. Water deeply at the base every 2-3 days in dry weather.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on peas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Peas are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions, especially later in the season. Ensure good airflow and harvest promptly. Late in the season this is normal -- the plant has done its job.

germination.text_seasoned: Broad beans (fava beans) are cool-season legumes -- the opposite of warm-season beans. Sow in late fall in mild-winter zones (zones 8+) for spring harvest, or as early in spring as soil can be worked in colder zones. The plants tolerate light frost throughout their cycle.
Sow seeds 1.5 to 2 inches deep, 6 to 8 inches apart in rows 2 to 3 feet apart. Inoculate with rhizobium bacteria at sowing for nitrogen-fixing nodulation.

seedling.text_seasoned: Broad bean seedlings emerge in 7 to 14 days and are remarkably cold-hardy -- they tolerate light frost and even brief snow without damage in most cases.
Stake or support tall varieties as they grow -- mature plants reach 3 to 5 feet and topple in wind without support. A simple twine-and-stake corral around the planting works well.

established.text_seasoned: Do not fertilize with nitrogen. Broad beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds. Black bean aphids show up first on the growing tips at this stage.

flowering.text_seasoned: Broad bean flowers are white with distinctive black markings -- attractive to pollinators and often the first major nectar source of spring. Bumblebees especially favor them.

Pinch out the top 4 to 6 inches of growing tips once the lowest flowers begin to set pods. This is the single most effective control for black bean aphid (which clusters on the tender growing tips) and concentrates the plant's energy into pod fill.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest pods when the beans inside have swollen but the pods are still bright green and tender. Pods left too long become tough and the beans inside develop a bitter outer skin that needs blanching to remove.
Harvest every 3 to 4 days during peak production. Broad beans are usually shelled before cooking; some varieties (Aquadulce especially) can be eaten pod-and-all when very young.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: After harvest, cut plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen contribution to the bed.
Broad beans are a traditional cover crop for this reason. The bed where they grew is well-suited to nitrogen-loving warm-season crops (corn, leafy greens, brassicas) the following season.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 30-50 beans per plant across multiple pods
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Broad beans produce over 3-4 weeks then are done -- a proper seasonal crop
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Fresh broad beans double-podded and eaten immediately are extraordinary -- completely different from frozen or tinned.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Broad beans are unusual among legumes in being substantially cold-tolerant -- young plants survive light frost and even brief snow. The threats at the cold end are sustained hard freezes (below about 15 degrees) and frost during flowering or pod-fill, which damages the tender flowers and pods. Hot summer weather, not cold, ends the broad-bean cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: In mild-winter zones (8 and warmer), sow in late fall for spring harvest -- the plants overwinter and produce earlier and heavier than spring-sown plants. In colder zones, sow as early in spring as soil can be worked. Cover with row cover during sustained hard freezes if attempting to overwinter in marginal zones.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Black bean aphid (Aphis fabae, sometimes called blackfly) is the dominant broad-bean pest -- dense black colonies cluster on the growing tips during flowering and can stunt or kill plants if uncontrolled. Chocolate spot (Botrytis fabae) is the headline disease, producing characteristic chocolate-brown spots on leaves in cool wet weather. Broad bean weevil and pea aphid are secondary pests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pinch out the top 4 to 6 inches of growing tips at first flowering -- this single action removes the aphid's preferred habitat and concentrates plant energy into pods. Hose off remaining aphids with water; encourage ladybugs and lacewings. For chocolate spot, choose resistant varieties, space plants for airflow, and avoid overhead watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Broad beans tolerate moderate moisture but suffer in waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot. Wet humid conditions during flowering and pod-fill drive chocolate spot disease, which can defoliate plants and reduce yield substantially.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead. Space plants for airflow. In wet climates, choose chocolate-spot-resistant varieties and consider trellising plants to lift foliage off the ground.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill produces small pods or pods with poorly-developed beans inside. Broad beans tolerate dry conditions better than most legumes once established but still need consistent water during the critical flowering and pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and keep roots cool. The cool-weather growing window means water demands are lower than for warm-season beans, but consistent water still matters.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall weak plants with few pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Broad beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to set pods well. In partial shade plants grow tall and weak with sparse flowering and few pods. Plants that lean or topple from inadequate support similarly suffer reduced yield.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. Stake or support tall varieties as they grow -- mature plants reach 3 to 5 feet and need anchoring. A simple twine-and-stake corral around the planting prevents wind damage.

crops.description_seasoned: The cold-hardiest legume. In mild-winter zones, plant in fall for a spring harvest -- the seeds overwinter in the ground. Rich, buttery flavor unlike any other bean.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pods 6-8 inches, firm and plump. Press thumbnail into a bean -- if it leaves a mark, they're ready. For best texture, pick before beans turn mealy.

crops.name: Lettuce (Leaf)

soil.preferred_description_beginner: Lettuce likes loose, rich soil that drains well but never dries out completely. Because its roots are shallow and delicate, soggy or packed-down soil hurts lettuce more than it would a tomato, and letting the bed dry out even briefly makes the leaves turn bitter and the plant go to seed early. The simplest fix for almost any soil is to mix 2 to 3 inches of compost into the top few inches before you plant, which helps sandy soil hold water and helps heavy soil drain. Try to avoid thick clay, it forms a hard crust that small seedlings struggle to push through and stays wet around the roots.
soil.preferred_description_seasoned: Lettuce is widely adaptable on the texture front, and although it produces well in almost any soil that drains freely, a fertile loam or sandy loam that stays high in organic matter and holds moisture well is where it does best. Its root system is shallow and fine, so it is far less forgiving of compaction and waterlogging than deeper-rooted crops, and consistent moisture is essential because even brief drought stress checks vegetative growth and pushes the plant toward bolting. Working 2 to 3 inches of compost into the bed before sowing improves both drainage on heavier soils and water retention on sandy ones. Heavy clay is the main texture to avoid, it crusts as seedlings emerge and holds water around the roots.

ph.note_beginner: Soil pH measures acidity on a scale from 0 to 14, where 7 is neutral and lower numbers are more acidic. Lettuce does best between 6.0 and 6.8, slightly acidic, because that is where the nutrients it needs are easiest for the roots to take up. If your soil is more acidic than 6.0 or more alkaline than 7.0, lettuce can show yellowing leaves or browning edges even when fertilizer is present. The only way to know your number is to test, so get an inexpensive soil test from your local extension office before adding lime to raise pH or sulfur to lower it.
ph.note_seasoned: Soil pH governs nutrient availability, and lettuce is most productive in the slightly acidic 6.0 to 6.8 band where phosphorus, calcium, and magnesium stay soluble. Below about 6.0, calcium uptake falls off and aluminum and manganese grow more available, which can scorch leaf margins and stunt the fine root system. Above 7.0, iron and manganese begin to lock up and drive interveinal yellowing on new growth. Across the alkaline interior West and in alkaline-irrigation districts, growers often acidify before planting, while the naturally acidic soils of the forested East more often need lime to reach the target band.

3.notes: Direct sow early. Succession sow every 2 weeks for steady supply. Use cold frame for earliest and latest harvests.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool season crops such as spinach, leaf lettuce, peas, onions, and root crops can germinate at minimum soil temperatures of 35-40 degrees F. (MSU Extension) Sow seeds in the spring as soon as the soil is workable. Direct sow when soil consistently reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost in most zones. (UMN Extension)

uscrn_validation.zone_coverage_note_seasoned: station-years 28 below 30 confidence threshold; verdict uses available data but should not be auto-applied

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: For a fall lettuce crop, sow seeds in early to mid July so the crop matures in the cooling temperatures of late summer and fall rather than in midsummer heat, which causes bolting. Use fast-maturing looseleaf varieties so the crop is ready before the first fall frost. (NDSU Extension; UMN Extension)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leaf lettuce can begin harvest 40–60 days after direct sowing under spring conditions, depending on variety and growing conditions; leaf types are at the fast end of this range. Days to maturity for leaf lettuce range from 40 to 80 days depending on the type. (University of Maryland Extension) Harvest single leaves as soon as they reach a usable size. (UMN Extension)

harvest_start.label: secondary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall lettuce in cold zones is grown from fast-maturing looseleaf varieties, with the first leaves ready about 45 days after sowing. Cooler fall temperatures slow growth, but harvesting young leaves cut-and-come-again keeps the crop within the short window before frost. (NDSU Extension; University of Maryland Extension)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest spring cool-season crops before sustained heat causes bolting (flowering), which renders leaves bitter and unpalatable. (UMN Extension) Lettuce may bolt and taste bitter when grown in the heat of summer. (UMN Extension)

harvest_end.label: secondary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool-season greens such as lettuce and spinach tolerate light frost and can often be harvested through the first fall frost. Leaf lettuce may continue growing past the first frost with row cover protection but should be harvested before extended hard freezes. (UMN Extension; Cornell Extension; Iowa State Extension)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Harvest extends to approximately first_frost + 5 days for hardy greens; first_frost - 5 days for tender greens like lettuce.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Spring succession arm: sow looseleaf lettuce every 2 weeks from when soil reaches 40 degrees F through the bolt-driven close of the spring window. Leafy greens germinate at 35-40 degrees F minimum and mature in 40-60 days, so sequential plantings give consistent production; the arm ends as rising heat (above ~75 degrees F) triggers bolting and bitterness. (USU Extension; UMN Extension; University of Maryland Extension)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Spring arm capped at the fall-arm start so spring and fall sowings do not overlap in the coldest zones. Latest spring sow otherwise bounded by spring-harvest close minus 30-day baby-leaf maturity (Clause B).

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fall succession arm: sow fast-maturing looseleaf lettuce every 2 weeks starting about 3 months before the first fall frost, harvesting baby leaves as temperatures cool. Lettuce is semi-hardy and tolerates light frost, so the latest sowing leaves roughly 30 days to baby-leaf size near the first frost rather than a full head well before it. Zone 3 fall sow is clamped to the ~July 1 heat floor (first_frost - 76) rather than first_frost - 90, which would fall in peak summer heat and cause germination failure (thermoinhibition above 80 degrees F soil). (UMN Extension; University of Maryland Extension; USU Extension)
direct_sow.design_note_seasoned: Fall arm start = heat-floored first_frost offset (methodology v1.5 Clause A). Latest sow = first_frost - 30d (baby-leaf; light-frost-tolerant, no extra hard margin). Per-arm count derived per zone (Clause C); not the season cap.

3.safe_sowing_note_seasoned: Safest sowings: around Apr 29 in spring and Jul 1 for the fall crop. The earliest possible spring date risks slow germination in cold soil, and late-spring sowings run into bolting heat; a mid-spring sowing after the soil has warmed is the most reliable. The first fall sowing, once peak summer heat eases, establishes most dependably.
3.safe_sowing_note_beginner: If you only plant once or twice, aim for about Apr 29 in spring and Jul 1 in late summer. Very early spring is risky because cold soil makes seeds slow to sprout, and late spring gets too hot, making lettuce bitter and causing it to go to seed (bolt).

4.notes: Fast turn-around makes lettuce ideal for succession planting. Heat-tolerant varieties extend season.
