pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost. Or transplant -- collards are resilient.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent. Traditional Southern preservation.
storage.notes_seasoned: Blanched frozen collards are nearly as good as fresh for cooking.

varieties.note_seasoned: Georgia Southern is the traditional standard -- large leaves, mild flavor when cooked with pork.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Good container crop. 3-gallon minimum. Large plants -- one per pot.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body_seasoned: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text_seasoned: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text_seasoned: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text_seasoned: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text_seasoned: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Long-season crop -- one plant can feed a family for months
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Collards are productive and heat-tolerant compared to most leafy greens
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Collards are more forgiving than most leafy greens. They handle both heat and frost better than spinach or lettuce.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 4 weeks from spring through midsummer. Collards are more heat-tolerant than most brassicas and can be harvested as cut-and-come-again from the lower leaves. A summer sowing started 8-10 weeks before first frost will produce the best harvest -- collards genuinely improve in flavor after light frost. Start the autumn batch earlier than you think you need to.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost or in late summer for autumn crop.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

bolting.prevention_seasoned: Plant in steady warm-to-cool conditions. Autumn crops are more reliable than spring.
bolting.note_seasoned: Even a few cold nights can trigger bolting in young bok choy plants.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch and freeze for stir-fries -- acceptable but texture softens
storage.notes_seasoned: Best eaten fresh. Bok choy loses crunch when frozen.

varieties.note_seasoned: Win-Win Choi is the best choice for spring planting -- significantly slower to bolt than other varieties.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container crop. 2-gallon minimum. Baby varieties very well-suited.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seed leaves pushing through the soil -- leafy greens germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist but not waterlogged. Most leafy greens germinate best at 50-65°F -- they actually prefer cooler soil than tomatoes.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing, recognizable as the crop you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings to the recommended spacing -- crowded leafy greens bolt faster and produce less. The thinnings are edible.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at a harvestable size, plant looking full and healthy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now -- this encourages more growth from the center. Do not wait for the plant to be 'finished' before you start picking.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Ready to start harvesting outer leaves?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves at good size, before any yellowing or flowering stem appears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest cut-and-come-again -- remove outer leaves and let the center keep growing. For butterhead types, harvest the whole head when formed.

growth_stages.name: Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A central flower stalk shooting upward, leaves becoming smaller and more bitter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Once bolting starts the flavor changes -- harvest everything immediately. Bolted leaves are still edible but more bitter. Remove the plant and either sow again or move on to a warm-season crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens love cool weather and can go in the ground 4-6 weeks before your last frost. Sow directly into prepared soil or start indoors for transplanting. They are some of the first crops of the year -- enjoy the early start.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your greens should be ready to start picking
notifications.body_seasoned: Begin harvesting outer leaves now even if the plant seems small. Regular picking encourages more growth. Do not wait for the plant to be 'done' -- leafy greens are a harvest-as-you-go crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Heat incoming -- watch your greens for bolting
notifications.body_seasoned: Hot weather triggers leafy greens to bolt -- sending up a flower stalk and turning bitter. Harvest everything you can now before the heat arrives. Consider sowing again in late summer for a fall crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your fall leafy greens
notifications.body_seasoned: Eight weeks before first frost is the window for a second sowing of leafy greens. A fall crop often outperforms spring -- the cooling temperatures mean slower bolting and sweeter flavor. Kale especially improves after a light frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your greens looking?
notifications.body_seasoned: Leafy greens can bolt quickly in warm weather. A quick check every few days helps you catch the right harvest moment and spot any bolting before it is too late.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- harvest your greens now
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Hot weather is the enemy of leafy greens. They bolt quickly and flavor turns bitter fast. Harvest as much as you can before the heat arrives. Shade cloth can buy you another week in marginal temperatures.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Unexpected frost -- protect young greens
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Most leafy greens handle light frost well once established, but young seedlings need protection. Cover with fleece tonight if frost is forecast.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for downy mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions encourage downy mildew on leafy greens. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering late in the day. Pick regularly to keep the plant open.

germination.text_seasoned: Leafy greens are some of the easiest crops to germinate -- cool, moist soil is all they need. Sow more thickly than you think you need and thin later.
The thinnings from leafy greens are completely edible -- use them as microgreens in salads. Thinning is harvesting.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to the recommended spacing even though it feels wasteful. Crowded leafy greens bolt faster, get less airflow, and produce smaller leaves.
A light mulch around seedlings keeps moisture in and suppresses weeds -- both important for leafy greens which need consistent moisture.

established.text_seasoned: Start harvesting outer leaves as soon as they reach a useful size -- this is how leafy greens work. The center keeps producing new growth as you remove the outer leaves.
Water consistently. Irregular watering is a major trigger for bolting in many leafy greens, especially lettuce and spinach.

harvest.text_seasoned: Always harvest in the morning when leaves are full of water and at their crispest. Refrigerate immediately in a damp bag.
Leave at least half the plant intact when harvesting cut-and-come-again crops. Taking too much at once sets the plant back.

bolting.text_seasoned: Once you see a flower stalk, harvest everything immediately. The leaves are still edible but will become more bitter every day.
Bolted leafy greens are not a failure -- it is the plant completing its lifecycle. A fall sowing often outperforms spring because the weather is cooling rather than warming.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One head per plant -- harvest the whole thing
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Bok choy matures in 45-60 days -- plan for succession sowings
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Bok choy is fast and versatile. Succession sow every 3-4 weeks for a continuous supply.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most leafy greens actually handle light frost well once established -- it can even improve flavor. But young seedlings are more vulnerable. If the damage happened at the seedling stage, a late frost likely caught them.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover seedlings with fleece if frost threatens in the first few weeks. Established leafy greens generally recover from light frost on their own.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Slugs love leafy green seedlings, especially in wet conditions. Downy mildew affects plants in humid, overcrowded conditions. Flea beetles leave tiny holes in leaves -- especially on arugula and kale.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Thin seedlings properly to allow airflow. Protect from slugs in the first few weeks. Row cover helps with flea beetles on susceptible varieties.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Leafy greens in waterlogged soil develop root rot quickly. More commonly, warmth and long days trigger bolting -- the plant sends up a flower stalk and the leaves become bitter. This is the plant completing its lifecycle, not a failure of care.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bolting is largely about timing. Sow earlier in spring or switch to a fall sowing -- cooling temperatures signal the plant to keep producing leaves rather than flowering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Irregular watering is a major bolting trigger in lettuce and spinach. A dry spell followed by heat pushes them to flower and seed rapidly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Keep moisture consistent -- mulching around leafy greens makes a real difference. Water in the morning so leaves dry during the day.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heat and long days cause most leafy greens to bolt -- this is the most common reason they fail. The plant is not dying, it is doing what it is designed to do. Once bolted the leaves become bitter and inedible quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: The fall sowing is almost always more successful than spring for leafy greens. Cooling temperatures give you longer, slower-bolting plants. Shade cloth can also extend the spring crop by a couple of weeks.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks in spring and again from late summer. Bok choy bolts quickly when temperatures rise above 75°F -- spring sowings have a short window, so small frequent batches matter. The autumn succession is often more reliable in warmer zones: cooler temperatures slow bolting and improve flavor. Time your last autumn sowing to mature before hard frost.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Fast-maturing crop that doesn't need feeding. Excess nitrogen produces leafy tops and poor root development.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: radishes mature so fast they need little feeding -- compost is enough

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Many tiny holes in leaves. Plants look pepper-sprayed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Flea beetles. Radishes are a major target -- often used as trap crop.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers. Diatomaceous earth.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Radishes actually work as trap crops for other brassica-family vegetables.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces. Leaves may yellow and die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with neem oil or baking soda solution. Remove affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for airflow. Water at soil level. Choose resistant varieties.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow only -- radishes mature so fast (25 days) that starting indoors makes no sense.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container crop. Shallow roots, fast growing. Even small pots work.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

bolting.triggers: Heat, long days -- very fast to bolt
bolting.prevention_seasoned: Plant only in spring or autumn. Keep soil consistently moist. Harvest promptly.
bolting.note_seasoned: Radishes left in hot ground will bolt within days. Harvest as soon as ½ inch across.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Not recommended -- becomes mushy
storage.notes_seasoned: Radishes store best in water in the fridge. Radish greens are edible -- use promptly.

recommended: Watermelon Radish (daikon type, striking pink interior)
Easter Egg (mixed colors, fun for kids)
varieties.note_seasoned: Cherry Belle is the fastest and most reliable -- ideal for succession sowing every 2 weeks.

thinning.when: When seedlings emerge and are identifiable
thinning.method: Quick snip at soil level -- radishes grow so fast this is often the only thinning needed.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Thinnings are edible. Radishes need more space than most people give them -- crowded radishes make all tops and no root.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums are specifically named as a flea beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and USU Extension (Mohr et al.). Flea beetles have intermediate mobility, so the trap cropping protocol is a better fit here than for aphids. Note: WSU, USU, and UConn identify radishes or collards as the more heavily-documented trap crops for flea beetles on brassicas; nasturtiums are mentioned alongside but with less-specific protocol guidance.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body_seasoned: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body_seasoned: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Root check-in
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text_seasoned: Radish is one of the fastest crops in the garden -- many varieties germinate in 4 to 7 days and reach harvest in 25 to 30 days. Direct-sow shallowly (1/2 inch deep) into cool soil.
Make small successive sowings every 2 weeks rather than one large sowing. Radish bolts and turns woody in heat, so a single big planting has a narrow harvest window.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to 1 inch apart for round varieties, 2 to 3 inches for long varieties, once seedlings have their first true leaf. Crowded radishes produce all leaves and no roots.
Mulch is rarely needed -- the crop is in and out so fast that weed pressure barely matters. Hand-weed the seedling row if needed.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently -- radishes that go dry then wet split, and water-stressed radishes turn sharp and pithy fast.
Radishes are ready almost as soon as you can see the shoulder pushing above the soil. From there they go from perfect to over-mature in days, especially in warm weather.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pull the largest radishes first and let smaller ones size up for another few days. Test by feel -- a radish that resists pulling has anchored deep and is mature.
Pull young, eat young. Radishes over-mature in days; over-mature radishes turn fibrous and sharp regardless of variety. The window between perfect and pithy is shorter than for any other root crop.

storage.text_seasoned: Radishes are not really a storage crop -- the small spring varieties keep about a week in the refrigerator with tops removed. Daikon and winter-storage radish varieties keep longer (1 to 2 months) but are different varieties from the spring radish most home gardeners grow.
Pickling and fermenting (Korean kkakdugi, Japanese tsukemono) are the traditional ways to preserve a glut of radish. Refrigerator pickles take an afternoon and keep weeks.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One radish per plant -- ready in 25-30 days
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Radishes are the fastest crop in the garden -- plant a short row every 2 weeks for continuous supply
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Radishes are perfect for impatient gardeners -- harvest in under a month. They are also useful as row markers for slower crops.
factors_seasoned: harvest timing (must pick before they go woody)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Radish tolerates light frost -- a touch of cold actually improves flavor by converting root starch to sugar. Hard freeze can damage exposed shoulders pushing above the soil but rarely kills the crop. Radish goes in early spring and again in fall, dodging the heat of summer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow in early spring as soon as soil can be worked and again in late summer for fall crops. Skip midsummer sowings unless you have shade or live in a cool-summer climate -- heat is a much bigger enemy than frost for radish.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Flea beetles are the dominant radish pest, peppering leaves with tiny shot-holes. Light damage is cosmetic, but heavy populations can stunt seedlings and shorten the crop. Cabbage maggot occasionally tunnels into roots in cool wet conditions. Disease pressure is generally low because the crop is in and out fast.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest blocks both flea beetles and cabbage maggot -- this is the most effective home-garden defense. Rotate radish to a new bed each year and avoid planting after other brassicas.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Heavy water after a dry spell causes radishes to split as they swell rapidly. Persistent waterlogging causes soft rot in the root, especially in warm weather. Radish prefers consistent light moisture rather than deep soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water lightly and consistently. Mulch is generally unnecessary for such a fast crop but a light straw mulch helps stabilize moisture in dry weather. Improve drainage in heavy clay before sowing.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought-stressed radishes go straight to flower without sizing up the root, or produce small, fibrous, painfully sharp roots. Heat amplifies the problem -- water-stressed radishes in hot weather become inedible fast.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently. Sow in cool weather (early spring or fall). Avoid sowing radish in midsummer unless you can provide afternoon shade and dependable irrigation.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Radish germinates fast in 4 to 7 days when soil is moist and above about 45 degrees. Failures usually trace to dry soil during germination or seed sown too deeply. Radish seed stays viable for several years -- old seed is rarely the issue.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into pre-moistened soil and water lightly daily for the first week if rain does not provide. Sow no deeper than 1/2 inch. Successive sowings every 2 weeks reduce the cost of any single failed batch.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 1-2 weeks from early spring through autumn, pausing only in the peak summer heat. Radishes mature in as little as 25 days -- the fastest crop in the garden. They're so quick you can fit multiple successions between other crops, using them as space-fillers and row markers. Plant a pinch of seed alongside slower crops like carrots; the radishes come up first, mark the row, and are harvested before the carrots need the space.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct seed cool-season root vegetables (carrots, beets, radishes, turnips) when soil reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost. (UMN Extension) Roots do not transplant -- their long taproots develop early and transplanting damages and misdirects root growth. In Minnesota, start planting carrots beginning April 15. (UMN Extension)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant a fall crop when summer heat subsides, approximately 2-3 months before first fall frost. Fall-matured roots are sweeter due to cool-weather sugar accumulation. Autumn-matured carrots from a late sowing are noticeably sweeter. (Crop succession guidance, UMN, Iowa State Extension)

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Moderate feeder. Balanced liquid feed every 3 weeks. Boron deficiency causes hollow hearts -- use complete fertilizer.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The aphid-repellent element is mechanism-plausible: allium sulfur VOCs have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, Insects 2018, 9(4):112) described at home-gardening rigor by Mississippi State and USU Extension. However, the 'repel leaf miners and soil pests' element for garlic on beets lacks extension backing. Leaf miners (Pegomya spp. on beets/chard) are managed per extension literature (Cornell, UMN, UMass) with row covers, resistant varieties, and removal of infested foliage; allium interplanting is not on the extension-recommended list. The soil-pest sub-claim is too vague to source-check. Downgraded from extension_backed because the composite why-text pairs a mechanism-real aphid component with under-backed additional components.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Rust-red tunnels and channels inside roots. Foliage yellows and wilts. Larvae (small white maggots) visible in roots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Psila rosae. Female flies attracted by carrot scent to lay eggs near roots.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure once roots infested. Use fine mesh netting 60cm high as barrier -- flies are low-fliers.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow under fine insect mesh. Sow alongside chives or rosemary to mask scent. Avoid thinning on still evenings when smell is strongest.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Willow-carrot aphids curl leaf tips and reduce vigor. Leaves distorted. Can transmit viruses.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cavariella aegopodii. Arrives from willow trees in spring.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insecticidal soap or neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow under insect mesh. Avoid planting near willow trees.

diseases.name: Cavity spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Oval gray/brown sunken cavities on carrot roots. First appears as small lesions that enlarge.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pythium violae soil pathogen. Favored by compacted, poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No chemical control. Improve soil structure with organic matter.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Deep, well-drained, stone-free soil. Avoid waterlogging. Crop rotation.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow 4 weeks before last frost. Beet "seeds" are actually clusters -- thin to one plant per cluster after germination.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works in deep containers. Choose round varieties (Boltardy). 12 inches deep minimum.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 2-3 weeks -- remove tops, leave 1 inch of stem
storage.freezer_seasoned: Cook, slice, freeze
storage.notes_seasoned: Cooked and pickled beetroot keeps for months in jars.

varieties.note_seasoned: Chioggia has exceptional mild flavor and the candy-stripe pattern is beautiful in salads.

thinning.when: Thin when seedlings are 1-2 inches tall
thinning.method: Beet "seeds" are actually clusters of 2-4 seeds -- each cluster produces multiple seedlings. Snip all but the strongest to ground level. Don't pull -- disturbs roots.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Thinnings are edible as microgreens -- add to salads.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Spinach, chard
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate with spinach and chard.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body_seasoned: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body_seasoned: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Root check-in
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text_seasoned: These crops are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the taproot and produces forked or stunted roots. Sow seeds shallowly (1/4 to 1/2 inch deep) and keep soil surface consistently moist for the 1 to 3 week germination window.
Carrot and parsnip seed is short-lived -- use fresh seed each year. Parsnip especially can take up to 3 weeks to germinate; do not give up early.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded roots stay small and forked. Pull weaker seedlings rather than transplanting them.
Mulch lightly between rows once seedlings are established to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the row -- hoeing damages shallow seedling roots.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently. Uneven moisture causes carrot and parsnip roots to split as they swell during a wet period after dry conditions.
These crops feed lightly. Side-dress with compost mid-season if growth slows; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush leafy tops at the expense of roots.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips after the first frost for best flavor -- this is not folklore; the cold genuinely converts starch to sugar in the root. Parsnip especially needs frost exposure to develop its characteristic sweetness.

Loosen soil with a fork before pulling -- yanking by the tops snaps the root, especially on long carrots and parsnips. Cut tops off within an inch of the crown for storage; tops left on draw moisture out of the root.

storage.text_seasoned: Store carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips in layers of damp sand or sawdust in a cool location (32 to 40 degrees) at high humidity. Properly stored, these crops keep 4 to 6 months.

In zones with mild winters, you can leave the roots in the ground and harvest as needed -- mulch heavily over the row before the ground freezes. This is often easier than indoor storage and preserves quality longer.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One beet per seed -- each beetroot seed is actually a cluster of 2-3 seeds
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Pick baby beets from 6 weeks, full size from 10 weeks
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Beetroot is one of the most versatile and beautiful vegetables in the garden. Roast them, pickle them, eat them raw -- they are endlessly useful.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops actively benefit from light to moderate frost -- it improves flavor by converting root starch to sugar. Damage from frost is rare and usually only happens to exposed leaf tops on a hard freeze; the roots are insulated by soil and survive even harsh winter conditions in many zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time harvest to follow the first frost rather than precede it. In zones with mild winters, leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch and harvest as needed through winter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Carrot rust fly (carrot, parsnip) is the headline pest -- larvae tunnel through roots leaving rusty trails. Cabbage maggot (turnip, sometimes beetroot) does similar damage to brassica roots. Leaf spot diseases and powdery mildew can hit foliage but rarely affect the root harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest blocks both carrot rust fly and cabbage maggot -- this is the most effective home-garden defense. Rotate root crops to a new bed each year. Avoid planting carrot or parsnip after parsley or celery (same family, same pest).

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Uneven watering -- a dry spell followed by heavy water -- causes roots to split as they swell rapidly. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, soft black tissue, and crown collapse. Beetroot and turnip handle wet soil better than carrot and parsnip, both of which need excellent drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture rather than letting soil dry out and then soaking it. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed for carrot and parsnip especially. Mulch helps stabilize moisture.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought-stressed root crops produce small, fibrous roots with concentrated and often unpleasantly strong flavor. Parsnips become woody at the core; carrots become bitter; turnips become sharp; beetroot becomes earthy and tough.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply and consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Mulch between rows to retain moisture. In hot weather, root crops appreciate light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Carrot, parsnip, and beetroot seeds need 1 to 3 weeks of consistent surface moisture to germinate. The most common reason for failed sowings is the soil surface drying out during germination -- not poor seed or bad soil. Parsnip seed in particular loses viability fast and old seed simply does not come up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into pre-moistened soil and cover with a board or burlap until the first seedlings emerge -- this keeps the surface consistently moist without daily watering. succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from spring through midsummer. Beets store well in the ground once mature -- you don't need to harvest them all at once. But a succession of sowings means the whole season's beets aren't reaching maturity simultaneously, making harvesting more manageable. Baby beets from later sowings are excellent roasted whole -- plan a late succession specifically for this.

crops.description_seasoned: A two-for-one crop -- eat both the roots and the greens. Cold-hardy, productive, and stores well through winter. The 'seeds' are actually seed clusters -- thin to one seedling.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Roots 1.5-3 inches across. Shoulder visible at soil surface. Smaller beets are more tender.

crops.name: Potato

3.notes: Plant as soon as soil is workable and threat of hard frost passes. Early varieties essential (70-day). Harvest before first fall frost.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.source_quote_seasoned: Soil temperature should be at least 45°F. (UMD Extension)
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Early April in the Twin Cities area of Minnesota. Plant seed potatoes 2 to 4 weeks before the average last frost date. If sprouts get frosted, underground roots continue growing and the plant re-sprouts. Do not plant seed potatoes purchased at the grocery store -- use certified seed stock. (UMN, UMD, Old Farmer's Almanac)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Harvest mature potatoes after plants have died back (vines yellow and dry down) or when tubers have reached full size. (UMN Extension) Potato foliage is killed by hard frost but tubers continue developing until then. UMD: 'Tubers will continue to grow through the summer until plants are killed by frost.

10.notes: Cool season only. Fall planting in September for November--December harvest.
10.zone_notes: Zone 10 supports two potato crops per year. Spring planting (Jan-Feb) harvests Mar-May before summer heat stops tuber formation. Fall planting (Sep-Nov) harvests Dec-Feb during cool winter months. Tubers will not form in soil above 80°F -- do not plant in summer.

plant_out.label: primary

Plant in late summer for fall/winter harvest once soil cools from peak heat. (UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar; Clemson HGIC; Old Farmer's Almanac)

plant_out.label: secondary

UMD recommends planting from March 15 to May 1; plant when soil reaches 45 degrees F, then harvest before daytime temperatures consistently exceed 80 degrees F. (UMD Extension; UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar; Clemson HGIC)

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed with balanced fertilizer at planting. Apply high-potassium feed when plants flower to improve tuber development.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring Colorado beetle are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Colorado potato beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-striped beetles and orange larvae stripping leaves. Can fully defoliate plants rapidly.
pests.cause_seasoned: Leptinotarsa decemlineata. A major potato pest in much of the US.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults, larvae, and orange egg masses. Apply Bt tenebrionis spray on young larvae. Neem oil.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rotate potatoes every 3 years. Use straw mulch. Interplant with catnip or tansy.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Cutworms
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Seedlings cut off at soil level overnight. The culprit (a fat gray/brown caterpillar) hides in soil during the day.
pests.cause_seasoned: Larvae of several moth species. Active in spring when transplanting.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Place cardboard or plastic collars around stems extending 2 inches below and above soil. Hand-pick larvae from soil at night.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil before planting to expose larvae to birds. Delay transplanting if moths are active.

pests.name: Wireworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small round holes in tubers with yellow-brown wire-like larvae inside. Tubers riddled with tunnels.
pests.cause_seasoned: Agriotes click beetle larvae. Live in soil up to 5 years.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mustard seed meal applied to soil. Beneficial nematodes.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Do not plant where grass sod recently turned. Rotate crops.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark water-soaked patches on leaves that spread rapidly. White fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Tubers develop brown rot inside.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans. Same pathogen that devastated Ireland in 1845. Spreads explosively in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected foliage immediately. Copper-based fungicide preventively in wet seasons.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes. Rotate crops 3+ years. Choose blight-resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Common scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Rough, corky, scab-like patches on tuber skin. Cosmetic damage only -- flesh is fine. More common in dry alkaline soils.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Streptomyces scabies soil bacteria. Thrives at pH above 7.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No chemical treatment needed -- scab is cosmetic.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep soil pH 5.0-5.5 for potatoes. Water consistently during tuber formation. Do not add lime before planting potatoes.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly, consistent -- inconsistent watering causes hollow heart

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant certified seed potatoes (not supermarket). Cut large tubers to have 2-3 eyes each, allow cut surfaces to dry 24 hours. No hardening off needed.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes: all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Weeks -- months in cool dark place -- ideal 45-50°F
storage.fridge_seasoned: Never -- cold converts starch to sugar and turns flesh sweet
storage.freezer_seasoned: Cook first, then freeze
storage.notes_seasoned: Store in paper bags in the dark. Light causes greening (solanine). Keep away from apples and onions.

varieties.note_seasoned: Yukon Gold is the most versatile home garden potato -- excellent boiled, roasted, and mashed.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container crop -- potato bags and buckets are popular. 10-gallon minimum. Fill container in stages as plants grow.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body_seasoned: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body_seasoned: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Root check-in
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text_seasoned: Potato is grown from seed potatoes (whole small potatoes or pieces with at least 2 eyes), not from true seed. Plant 4 to 6 inches deep when soil is reliably above 45 degrees, after danger of hard frost has passed.
Cut large seed potatoes into pieces 1 to 2 days before planting and let cut surfaces dry to a callus -- this prevents rot in cool wet soil. Each piece should have at least 2 eyes.

seedling.text_seasoned: Sprouts emerge 2 to 4 weeks after planting. The first 'leaves' are actually a stem with leaves; the seed potato itself is below ground feeding the new shoot.

Hill soil up around the stems as the plant grows, burying the lower leaves. Hilling encourages tuber formation along the buried stem and protects developing tubers from sun (which turns them green and toxic).

established.text_seasoned: Continue hilling every 2 to 3 weeks until the plants begin to flower or until hills are 8 to 12 inches tall. Each hilling adds tuber-bearing stem.
Water consistently once tubers begin forming (around flowering). Uneven watering causes growth cracks and hollow heart in the tubers.

harvest.text_seasoned: For new potatoes, harvest when plants begin to flower -- gently dig at the edge of the hill and feel for marble-to-egg sized tubers. For storage potatoes, wait until the foliage has died back naturally, then wait 2 more weeks for the skin to set.
Dig on a dry day with a fork, lifting the whole hill from below. Brush soil off but do not wash potatoes intended for storage -- water on tubers shortens storage life.

storage.text_seasoned: Cure storage potatoes for 2 weeks at 50 to 60 degrees and high humidity (85 to 90 percent) in the dark. Curing toughens the skin and heals minor wounds. After curing, move to long-term storage at 40 degrees and 90 percent humidity, in the dark.
Light exposure makes potato tubers green by producing solanine, which is toxic. Always store in the dark. Inspect monthly and remove any tubers showing soft rot before it spreads.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 4-8 lbs of potatoes per plant depending on variety
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Potatoes give you a single large harvest -- earthing up well increases yield
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Digging up a plant to find a pile of potatoes underneath is one of the best moments in gardening. Genuinely exciting every time.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Potato foliage is killed by frost. Tubers underground are insulated by soil and tolerate brief hard frosts at 30 to 32 degrees, but freezing temperatures damage the tubers (the flesh turns gray or black) and shorten storage life. Frost-damaged potatoes do not sweeten the way root vegetables do -- the damage is permanent.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant after the last hard frost when soil is reliably above 45 degrees. At the end of the season, harvest within 2 weeks of foliage die-back; do not leave potatoes in cold wet soil through repeated frost cycles. Mulch heavily if a hard freeze is forecast before harvest is finished.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Colorado potato beetle is the dominant home-garden pest -- adult beetles and bright-orange larvae strip foliage fast. Late blight (Phytophthora infestans) is the headline disease, capable of wiping out a planting in a week of cool wet weather. Wireworms tunnel through tubers in soil that recently grew sod.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Inspect daily during peak beetle pressure and hand-pick adults and larvae into soapy water -- this stays ahead of populations in a home garden. Rotate potato to a new bed each year and never plant where tomato or eggplant grew the previous year. For late blight, choose resistant varieties and watch the forecast for cool wet stretches.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Waterlogged soil causes tuber rot -- soft black or brown tissue and a foul smell. Uneven watering (dry spells followed by heavy water) causes growth cracks, hollow heart (a hollow brown cavity in the tuber center), and second growth (knobby misshapen tubers).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil; on heavy clay, plant in a raised hill or a deep-mulched container. Water consistently once tubers begin forming -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Stop watering as foliage starts to die back at the end of the season.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during tuber formation produces small, knobby, or scab-prone tubers. The plant will live and even produce some harvest, but yield drops sharply if water is short during the flowering-to-die-back window when tubers actively bulk up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture during tuber formation. Mulch heavily around hills to retain moisture. In dry climates, drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering for potato.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Seed potato pieces planted in cold wet soil rot before they sprout. Pieces with cut surfaces that did not callus before planting are especially vulnerable. Diseased seed potatoes from grocery stores can also fail to sprout or sprout weakly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for soil to reach 45 degrees and dry out enough to crumble in your hand. Cut seed potatoes 1 to 2 days before planting and let cut surfaces callus. Buy certified disease-free seed potatoes rather than planting grocery-store potatoes (which are often treated with sprout inhibitors).

crops.description_seasoned: Incredibly productive -- a 10-foot row can yield 25 lbs of potatoes. Plant certified seed potatoes. Hilling soil around stems as they grow is the key technique.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: New potatoes: harvest 2-3 weeks after flowering. Maincrop: wait until tops yellow and die back, then wait 2 more weeks before digging.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Never add lime before potatoes -- it promotes scab. Ideal pH is 5.0-5.5. Potatoes love deep, loose, well-drained soil. Dig in plenty of well-rotted compost but avoid fresh manure (causes misshapen tubers and scab). Loosen soil to 12 inches deep -- potatoes need room to swell.
