good_beginner_seasoned.name: Beans
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Three Sisters -- fix nitrogen for hungry corn

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Squash
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Three Sisters -- ground cover, moisture retention

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Ground cover effects on soil temperature and moisture are real; specific pairings not well-studied.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Corn earworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Caterpillar boring into silk and tip of ear. Frass visible at tip. Damaged kernels at ear tip.
pests.cause_seasoned: Helicoverpa zea moth larvae. A major corn pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply mineral oil to silk 5-6 days after silk emergence. Bt spray on silk. Trichogramma wasp release.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Choose tight-husked varieties. Monitor with pheromone traps.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

diseases.name: Gray leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Rectangular gray-brown lesions running along leaf veins. Severe infection yellows entire plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Cercospora zeae-maydis fungus. Worst in warm humid regions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No practical organic treatment for home gardens.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant hybrids. Rotate corn crops. Till crop residue after harvest.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly, increase during silking and ear fill
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level -- overhead at silking helps pollination

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost in blocks (not rows) for pollination. Plant 4+ rows minimum. Soil must be above 60°F.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Same day -- sugars convert to starch within hours
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 4 minutes, cut from cob, freeze -- very good
storage.notes_seasoned: The famous rule: put water on to boil before you pick. Modern super-sweet varieties hold a little longer.

varieties.note_seasoned: Super-sweet varieties (SH2 types) hold their sugar much longer after picking than regular sweet corn -- good for home gardeners who can't rush to the pot.

thinning.to_spacing: 12-15 inches between plants in rows 30 inches apart
thinning.method: Thin by cutting at soil level -- corn roots intertwine and pulling disturbs neighbors.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Plant in blocks of at least 4 rows rather than long single rows -- corn is wind-pollinated and needs dense planting for good ear fill.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Not suitable for containers -- corn needs to be grown in blocks for wind pollination, which requires too many large pots to be practical.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Corn -- buildup of corn rootworm and smut diseases
rotation.good_after: Excellent after legumes (beans, peas) which fix nitrogen for heavy-feeding corn
rotation.note_seasoned: Classic rotation: corn after beans is the most efficient use of nitrogen fixation.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A strong shoot pushing up. Corn germinates fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly when soil temperature reaches 60°F. Corn does not transplant well. Sow in blocks rather than rows for wind pollination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tall narrow seedlings pushing up vigorously.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 12 inches if sown thickly. Water consistently -- corn is a heavy water user.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants 2-3 feet tall, growing strongly. Knee-high by the Fourth of July is the traditional gauge.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-nitrogen fertilizer now. Corn is a very hungry plant. Side-dress with compost if available.

growth_stages.name: Tasseling and Silking
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tassels appearing at the top of the plant, silk emerging from developing ears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: This is the pollination window. Wind carries pollen from tassels to silk. A block planting of at least 4x4 plants gives adequate pollination. Dry weather during silking causes poor kernel set.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Silks turned brown and dry. Pull back the husk to check -- kernels should be full and release milky juice when pierced.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest immediately and cook immediately. Sweet corn begins converting sugar to starch the moment it is picked. The difference between corn eaten within an hour of picking and corn bought from a shop is remarkable.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: All ears harvested, stalks turning brown and beginning to dry. Plants are 6-8 feet tall and slow to break down if left whole.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut stalks at ground level and chop into the compost or directly till in. Mark the bed in your rotation log -- corn is a heavy nitrogen feeder and should not follow itself next season.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your sweet corn
notifications.body_seasoned: Corn goes directly into warm soil a week after last frost. Sow in a block -- at least 4 plants wide in each direction. Wind pollination is how corn sets kernels, and a single row pollinates very poorly. Expect gaps and poor cobs from a single row.

notifications.title_seasoned: Corn is silking -- keep it well watered
notifications.body_seasoned: This is the most critical watering window for sweet corn. Drought stress when silks are emerging causes incomplete kernel set -- you end up with gappy, poorly-filled cobs. Water deeply every 2-3 days if it is not raining.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your corn for harvest readiness
notifications.body_seasoned: Pull back the husk on one ear and press a kernel with your thumbnail. Milky juice means perfect harvest time. Clear juice means too early. No juice and it is past peak. Cook within hours of picking for the best flavor you have ever tasted from sweet corn.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought during silking -- water immediately
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought stress when corn silk is emerging is the most damaging moment for the crop. Incomplete pollination means gaps in the cob. Water deeply today.

germination.text_seasoned: Sow corn in a block at least 4 rows wide, not in a single long row. Corn is wind-pollinated -- pollen drifts from tassel to silk -- and a block planting catches pollen efficiently while a row planting wastes most of it.

Wait for soil to reach 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 for supersweet varieties) before direct-sowing. Cold soil rots seed; supersweet types in cold soil simply do not germinate. Pre-germinate seeds on damp paper towels in cold zones if needed.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to 8 to 12 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Crowded corn produces small ears. Resist transplanting -- corn resents root disturbance and seedlings rarely catch up after transplanting.
Side-dress with nitrogen at the 4-leaf stage and again at knee-high. Corn is a heavy feeder; deficiency shows as yellowing of older leaves first.

established.text_seasoned: Hill soil up around the base of plants once they are 12 to 18 inches tall. This gives wind support and encourages prop-root development -- the brace roots that prevent toppling in summer storms.
Continue consistent watering; corn ear fill depends heavily on water during the silking and ear-development weeks. Drought during this window produces missing kernels.

tasseling.text_seasoned: Tassels emerge from the top of each stalk and shed pollen for about a week. Watch for the silk emerging from each developing ear at the same time -- proper timing of these two stages is what makes a full ear.
If the block is small or wind is limited, hand-pollinate by gently shaking tassels over the silks. This dramatically improves kernel fill in small home plantings.

harvest.text_seasoned: Use the milk test: peel back a husk, puncture a kernel with a fingernail. Clear liquid means under-ripe; milky liquid means perfect; pasty means over-ripe. Sweet corn moves from under-ripe to over-ripe in 2 to 3 days; check daily during peak.

Eat or refrigerate within hours of picking -- the sugar-to-starch conversion begins immediately and accelerates at room temperature. Supersweet varieties hold their sweetness longer (days) than older sugary varieties (hours).

end_of_season.text_seasoned: After harvest, cut stalks at ground level and chop into the compost or till in. Corn stalks are large and slow to break down; chopping accelerates decomposition.
Rotate corn to a new bed next year -- it is a heavy nitrogen feeder and should not follow itself.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 1-2 ears per plant
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: All ears mature within a 1-2 week window -- the whole harvest happens at once
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Corn eaten within an hour of picking tastes like a different vegetable from anything sold in a shop. That moment alone justifies growing it.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sweet corn is a tender annual and damaged by even a light frost at any stage. Cold soil at planting (below 60 degrees, or below 65 to 70 for supersweet types) rots seed before it germinates. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly -- ears in the milk stage at first frost are still edible but those still developing are lost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait for soil to reach 60 degrees (65 to 70 for supersweet varieties) before sowing. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil in cool zones. In short-season zones, choose early-maturing varieties (60 to 70 days) and time the sowing so harvest finishes well before expected first frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Corn earworm is the headline pest -- adult moths lay eggs on silks; larvae enter the ear tip and eat developing kernels. European corn borer tunnels into stalks. Common smut produces grotesque gray-black galls on ears (delicacy in some cuisines, ruined ear in others). Stewart's wilt is bacterial and transmitted by flea beetles in some regions.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For corn earworm, drop a few drops of vegetable oil onto the silk channel after pollination -- this physically blocks larval entry. For European corn borer, chop and compost stalks at end of season to break the overwintering cycle. Choose smut-resistant varieties. Rotate corn to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Corn tolerates more water than most vegetables but cannot handle persistent waterlogging -- roots rot and plants topple from weakened anchorage. Excessive water at silking can dilute kernel sweetness, especially in supersweet varieties.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Hill soil up around stalks at knee-high stage to encourage prop-root development and improve drainage. In flood-prone gardens, plant on raised berms.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during silking and ear-development is the leading cause of poor ears in home-grown corn. Each kernel forms only when a pollen grain successfully lands on a silk and grows down it -- water stress shortens or browns silks, producing ears with rows of missing kernels (the gap-toothed ear).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply and consistently from tasseling through ear development -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily between rows to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal for corn during the critical pollination window.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Corn needs full sun -- 8 hours minimum, ideally more. In partial shade plants grow tall and weak with small or no ears. Corn shaded by larger plants or buildings simply will not produce a meaningful crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest spot available. Plant blocks (not rows) to maximize wind pollination. Avoid planting downwind of fences or buildings that block wind movement during tasseling.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 2 weeks from last frost through early summer, or plant early-, mid-, and late-maturing varieties simultaneously. Sweet corn is only good for a 3-5 day window at peak ripeness -- succession planting means you have ears ready over weeks rather than a single overwhelming harvest. Each block needs to be large enough for pollination (at least 3-4 rows of 3-4 plants). Count back 75-90 days from first frost for your last sowing.

crops.description_seasoned: The three sisters classic. Needs to be grown in blocks (minimum 4×4) for wind pollination -- a single row gives no ears. Sweetness drops fast after picking -- eat within 30 minutes of harvest.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Silks brown and dry. Pull back husk -- kernels should be plump and milky when pierced with thumbnail. The window is 1-2 days. Eat immediately after picking.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Corn is a heavy feeder. Dig in generous amounts of well-rotted manure or compost the autumn before planting. Top-dress with balanced fertilizer before planting. Soil pH 6.0-6.8. Corn grows best in warm, well-drained soil -- wait until soil temperature is above 60°F.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Bean seed fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Seeds fail to germinate or seedlings die soon after emergence.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia platura maggots eat germinating seeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sow when soil is warm (above 60°F) for rapid germination.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Wait for warm soil. Start in pots and transplant. Pre-soak seeds to speed germination.

diseases.name: Bean rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Orange-brown powdery pustules on leaf undersides with corresponding pale spots on top.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Uromyces appendiculatus fungus. Spreads in warm humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Sulfur-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Halo blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked spots surrounded by yellow halo on leaves. Pods develop greasy patches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. phaseolicola bacteria. Seed-borne and spread by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected plants. Copper-based bactericide spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Buy certified disease-free seed. Avoid working with wet plants. Rotate crops.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost when soil is warm. Like other beans, dislikes transplanting.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Beans, peas -- some shared diseases but generally disease pressure is lower
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades, corn -- legumes fix nitrogen that these heavy feeders need
rotation.note_seasoned: Plant legumes before heavy feeders -- they'll leave nitrogen-rich soil behind.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch in pod 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent, this is what commercial frozen edamame is
storage.notes_seasoned: Edamame frozen in the pod keeps flavor best. Boil from frozen in salted water.

varieties.note_seasoned: Envy is the best choice for short-season gardens -- 75 days maturity vs 85-90 for most varieties.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Good container crop. 3-gallon minimum, 2-3 plants per pot. Compact varieties work well.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A strong shoot pushing up. Corn germinates fast in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow directly when soil temperature reaches 60°F. Corn does not transplant well. Sow in blocks rather than rows for wind pollination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tall narrow seedlings pushing up vigorously.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 12 inches if sown thickly. Water consistently -- corn is a heavy water user.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants 2-3 feet tall, growing strongly. Knee-high by the Fourth of July is the traditional gauge.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-nitrogen fertilizer now. Corn is a very hungry plant. Side-dress with compost if available.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small white or pale-purple flowers in the leaf axils. Edamame is self-pollinating, so flowers come and go quickly -- often opening and setting fruit within hours. Tiny pods begin forming directly behind successful flowers within days.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture from flowering through pod-fill -- this is the critical irrigation window for yield. Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during the flowering window; both populations spike then. Do not fertilize with nitrogen.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Silks turned brown and dry. Pull back the husk to check -- kernels should be full and release milky juice when pierced.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest immediately and cook immediately. Sweet corn begins converting sugar to starch the moment it is picked. The difference between corn eaten within an hour of picking and corn bought from a shop is remarkable.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods harvested, plant senescing -- leaves yellowing and dropping, stem stiff and dry. Edamame finishes its life cycle quickly once pods are mature.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut plants at ground level rather than pulling. Leave the roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing nodules become next season's slow-release nitrogen for whichever crop follows. Mark the bed in your rotation log.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your edamame
notifications.body_seasoned: Edamame goes directly into warm soil a week or two after last frost -- wait until soil is at least 60°F (65-70°F is better). If this is your first time growing soybeans in this bed, dust the seed with rhizobium inoculant at sowing. The bacteria settle into the root nodules and fix nitrogen for the plant; without them, edamame yield drops sharply on bean-naive soil.

notifications.title_seasoned: Edamame is flowering -- keep it consistently watered
notifications.body_seasoned: This is the start of the critical irrigation window for edamame. Water stress from flowering through pod-fill is the single biggest cause of poor yield -- pods that abort before they fill, or fill unevenly. Water deeply every 2-3 days if it is not raining, and mulch to stabilize soil moisture. Skip nitrogen fertilizer; beans fix their own and high-N suppresses nodulation.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your edamame pods for harvest readiness
notifications.body_seasoned: Squeeze a pod between thumb and finger -- when it feels plump and the beans inside fill 80 to 90 percent of the pod, it is ready. Pods should still be bright green; once they start yellowing, the beans inside have moved past their tender sweet stage. Harvest the whole pod (don't shell in the field) and either eat fresh, or blanch for 3-5 minutes and freeze whole-pod.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought during flowering or pod-fill -- water immediately
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the most damaging moment for edamame. Water stress now causes pods to abort or fill unevenly. Water deeply today and mulch heavily if you have not already.

germination.text_seasoned: Beans are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the brittle taproot. Wait until soil is 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better) before sowing; cold soil rots seed before it germinates.

Sow 1 to 2 inches deep, 2 to 4 inches apart in rows. Inoculate seed with rhizobium bacteria at sowing if the bed has not grown beans recently -- this boosts the nitrogen-fixing nodulation that beans depend on.

seedling.text_seasoned: Beans germinate fast in warm soil -- typically 7 to 10 days. Seedlings are vulnerable to slugs and bean leaf beetles in their first weeks; check daily.

Thin bush beans to 4 to 6 inches between plants once seedlings are 4 inches tall. Pole beans need a trellis or pole structure in place at this stage -- they grow fast and resent late-installed support.

Rabbits favor young soybean over most garden crops -- a single rabbit can clip an entire row of seedlings to the ground in one night. Cover seedlings with hardware cloth, chicken-wire cages, or row cover until plants are 8-10 inches tall and the stems have toughened. Damage rarely continues once plants are past the seedling stage.

established.text_seasoned: Do not fertilize beans with nitrogen. Beans fix their own nitrogen via root nodules; high-N fertilizer suppresses nodulation and produces lush leafy plants with poor pod set.
Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- this is when water stress most reduces yield. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture and suppress weeds.

flowering.text_seasoned: Beans are self-pollinating and do not need pollinators. Flowers open and self-pollinate within hours; fruit set is fast.
Watch for bean leaf beetles and aphids during flowering -- both populations spike in this window. Check undersides of leaves daily.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick beans young and often -- bush and pole beans ready when pods snap cleanly and the seeds inside are still small. Edamame ready when pods are plump and fill 80 to 90 percent with bright green beans, before yellowing.
Harvest every 2 to 3 days during peak production. Beans left on the plant signal it to stop producing new pods. Edamame is harvested whole-pod, not shelled in the field.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: After harvest, cut bean plants at ground level and leave roots in the soil -- the nitrogen-fixing root nodules become next year's slow-release nitrogen for the bed.
Rotate beans to a new bed each year. Bean diseases (anthracnose, halo blight, bean rust) survive in soil and infect next year's planting.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Pods ripen in a single 7-10 day window; whole-plant harvest yields a generous bowlful from each plant
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Edamame plants ripen all pods within a 1-2 week window -- the whole harvest happens at once
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Fresh-picked edamame is sweeter and more tender than anything you can buy frozen. The whole-plant single-harvest model is unusual but easy.
factors_seasoned: harvest timing within the 7-10 day window

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Beans are warm-season tender annuals -- killed outright by light frost at any stage. Cold soil at sowing (below 60 degrees) rots seed; cool conditions during early growth produce stunted plants that never fully recover. Late summer frost ends the season abruptly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to sow until soil is reliably 60 degrees minimum (65 to 70 is better). In short-season zones, choose early-maturing bush varieties and use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Have row cover ready for unexpected late-spring frosts. For fall harvests, time the planting so harvest finishes before first expected frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mexican bean beetle (yellow with black spots, similar to ladybug but a pest) is the dominant bean pest east of the Rockies -- larvae skeletonize leaves. Bean leaf beetle damages seedlings and pods. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Halo blight (water-soaked spots with yellow halo) and bean rust are the headline diseases. For edamame specifically, soybean aphid and Japanese beetle are also common.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For Mexican bean beetle, hand-pick adults and crush yellow egg masses on leaf undersides; in heavy infestations, parasitic wasp release works for organic gardeners. Rotate to a new bed each year. Avoid working bean plants when foliage is wet -- this spreads halo blight and bean rust. Choose disease-resistant varieties for the next planting.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Beans are also susceptible to white mold (Sclerotinia) in cool wet conditions, which produces fluffy white growth at the soil line and kills plants quickly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water in the morning so foliage dries before evening. Space plants for airflow. For white mold, rotate at least 3 years between bean plantings in any one bed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and pod-fill is the leading cause of poor bean harvests. Plants drop flowers under water stress and produce small empty or partially-filled pods. Edamame is especially demanding of consistent water during the pod-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during flowering and pod-fill -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation is ideal because it provides consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Beans need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower and produce well. In partial shade plants grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few pods. Tall pole beans can shade their own lower leaves if not pinched at the top of the support.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. For pole beans, pinch the growing tip when vines reach the top of the support to prevent excessive top growth and improve light penetration to lower flowering nodes.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Biennial -- feeds moderately. Monthly balanced feed. Avoid high nitrogen which reduces flavor intensity.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Root damage and wilting. Cilantro and dill are in carrot family and attract same pests.
pests.cause_seasoned: Psila rosae. Affects all members of the carrot family.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Grow under fine insect mesh.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Insect mesh. Grow away from carrots and parsnips.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots on leaves. Affected leaves yellow and die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot. Favored by wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Good spacing.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 10-12 weeks before last frost -- slow germination (3-4 weeks). Soak seeds overnight. Transplants fine. Harden off over 5 days.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container herb. 8 inches deep minimum (taproot). Window boxes work well.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 2 weeks in water in the fridge covered with a bag
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch briefly, squeeze dry, freeze -- or blend into oil cubes
storage.notes_seasoned: Flat-leaf parsley stores better than curly. The water-glass fridge method is highly effective.

recommended: Hamburg (root parsley -- both root and leaf edible)
varieties.note_seasoned: Flat-leaf (Italian) parsley has significantly more flavor than curly types -- use curly for garnish only.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Attracts predatory wasps that eat caterpillars

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Carrots, parsnips, celery, dill -- share carrot fly and diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Parsley is in the carrot family -- rotate away from other Apiaceae crops.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting (Year 1)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A central flower stalk shooting up from a year-one parsley plant. Leaves become smaller, sparser, and increasingly bitter as the plant redirects energy from leaf production to seed-set. This is not normal -- parsley should not bolt in its first year.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Year-one bolting is usually a stress response: seedlings exposed to prolonged cold before transplanting (vernalization), or sustained heat stress in zones 9-11. The plant is unlikely to recover meaningfully -- pull and replace with a fresh sowing of slow-bolt varieties, sown direct, mulched heavily for cooler soil. Note the cause for next year.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bolting in year 1 -- pulling for a fresh sowing?

growth_stages.name: Second-Year Bolting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Year-2 plants sending up a tall central flower stalk in spring or early summer, followed by umbel-shaped flowers and seed development. Leaves become sparse and bitter as the plant redirects energy to reproduction. This is the normal end of parsley's biennial lifecycle.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Decide whether to pull the plant for a fresh year-1 sowing, or let it flower for seed-saving and pollinator support. Once parsley bolts in year 2, the plant dies after seed-set and is finished.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Bolting in year 2 -- pulling or letting it seed?

notifications.title_seasoned: Start your parsley indoors or direct sow
notifications.body_seasoned: Parsley can be sown indoors 4 weeks before last frost or directly outside after it. It is notoriously slow to germinate -- 3 weeks is normal. Do not give up. Once it gets going it produces abundantly all season.

notifications.title_seasoned: Parsley in its second year will bolt
notifications.body_seasoned: Parsley is biennial -- it flowers in its second year and then dies. Harvest as much as you can now if this is a second-year plant, and sow fresh seed for this season's main crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text_seasoned: Parsley is famously slow to germinate -- 2 to 4 weeks is normal. Soak seeds overnight before sowing to soften the hard seed coat. Sow in early spring for summer harvest, or in fall in mild zones for winter and spring harvest.

Sow shallowly (1/4 inch) and keep the soil surface consistently moist for the entire germination window. The most common parsley failure is letting the surface dry out during the long germination period.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to 6-inch spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves. Parsley has a taproot and resents transplanting -- direct-sown plants outperform transplants over the season.
Mulch lightly between plants to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to plants -- parsley roots are shallow and easily damaged.

established.text_seasoned: Harvest outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. The plant continues producing new leaves from the center for months, even into mild winters.
Side-dress with compost mid-season for sustained leaf production. Water consistently -- parsley wilts quickly in heat and the recovery uses energy that could go into leaves.

harvest.text_seasoned: Cut individual stems at the base; do not harvest more than a third of the plant at once. Used cut-and-come-again, a single parsley plant can produce a generous harvest from spring through fall, and into winter in mild zones.
Parsley flavor concentrates in cool weather -- fall and early spring harvests are the best of the year in most zones. Hot summer growth is milder.

bolting.text_seasoned: Year-1 bolting is a stress response, not a normal stage. The most common cause is transplanting seedlings that were exposed to extended cold (a few weeks below 50°F) -- the plant interprets the cold as winter and bolts the following spring as if it were year 2.

Heat stress in zones 9-11 can also trigger early bolt. Once bolting starts, the plant rarely produces useful leaves again. Pull and resow with a slow-bolt variety like Giant of Italy or Krausa, sown direct after the soil warms past 50°F so the seedlings never see vernalization-triggering cold.

second_year_bolting.text_seasoned: Parsley is biennial -- in its second year, it bolts to flower and produces seed, then dies. The leaves that grow in the second year are sparse, bitter, and not worth harvesting.

Most home gardeners treat parsley as an annual: pull it at the end of year 1, replant fresh seed in year 2. Some growers let one or two plants bolt in year 2 specifically to save seed; the umbel-shaped flowers also attract beneficial insects to the garden.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous harvest from one plant for the whole season
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Parsley is slow to germinate but patient once established -- one plant keeps producing all season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Parsley is one of the more cold-tolerant culinary herbs. Mature plants survive light frost without damage and tolerate sustained cold weather better than basil, dill, or cilantro. In zones 7 and warmer, parsley often overwinters and resumes growth in early spring before bolting in its second year.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant parsley early in spring -- it tolerates light frost as a young transplant. In mild zones, fall planting gives an extended cool-season harvest. Cover with row cover in zone 6 and below for winter protection if attempting to overwinter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Parsley shares many pests with carrot (Apiaceae family): carrot rust fly larvae tunnel into roots; parsleyworm (the spectacular striped caterpillar that becomes the black swallowtail butterfly) eats foliage but rarely seriously damages the plant. Septoria leaf spot can hit foliage in wet weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover during the carrot rust fly emergence windows blocks the pest. Parsleyworm is generally tolerated by experienced gardeners -- the swallowtail caterpillars are striking and the damage is usually minor; relocate them to a sacrificial parsley plant if there are too many. For Septoria, water at the base and provide good airflow.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Parsley needs consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot and yellowing of inner leaves. Containerized parsley in pots without drainage fails the same way.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Use pots with drainage holes for container culture. Water deeply at the base rather than shallow overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Parsley wilts dramatically in heat and drought. Mild wilting recovers without lasting damage, but repeated severe drought stress produces small, tough, strongly-flavored leaves and accelerates bolt risk in second-year plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. In hot climates, parsley appreciates light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Parsley needs 4 to 6 hours of direct sun minimum -- it tolerates more shade than most herbs but produces sparse, leggy growth in deep shade. Indoor parsley on a windowsill often disappoints for this reason.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full to partial sun outdoors. For indoor growing, place near the brightest available window or supplement with a grow light. Light afternoon shade is fine and even helpful in hot climates.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow a second batch 4 weeks after the first. Parsley is slow to germinate (3-4 weeks) and biennial -- in its second year it bolts immediately. For practical purposes treat it as an annual and sow a fresh batch mid-season. The second sowing will be producing vigorously through autumn and into early winter in mild zones. Soak seeds overnight before sowing to improve germination speed.

3.notes: Direct sow. Cool weather is key -- bolts quickly in heat. Sow a fresh batch every 3 weeks.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Fast-growing and light feeder. One application at sowing is enough. Over-feeding speeds bolting.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Light feed time for your cilantro

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Root damage and wilting. Cilantro and dill are in carrot family and attract same pests.
pests.cause_seasoned: Psila rosae. Affects all members of the carrot family.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Grow under fine insect mesh.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Insect mesh. Grow away from carrots and parsnips.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots on leaves. Affected leaves yellow and die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot. Favored by wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Good spacing.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow -- cilantro bolts quickly and dislikes transplanting. Sow every 2-3 weeks for continuous harvest.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Good container herb. Deep pots preferred (taproot). At least 8 inches deep.

bolting.prevention_seasoned: Choose slow-bolt varieties (Leisure, Calypso). Plant in cool season. Keep well watered. Succession sow every 2 weeks. Provide shade.
bolting.note_seasoned: Once bolting starts, harvest all leaves immediately and let it go to coriander seed -- equally useful.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 3-5 days in a glass of water like flowers
storage.fridge_seasoned: 1 week in a glass of water in the fridge, covered with a bag
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blend with water, freeze in ice cube trays -- excellent for curries
storage.notes_seasoned: Cilantro is one of the most perishable herbs. The water-glass method in the fridge is the most effective.

varieties.note_seasoned: Leisure and Calypso are dramatically slower to bolt than standard varieties -- the difference is significant in warm gardens.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Structural-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Flowering plants attracting predatory insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). Specific pairings vary in effectiveness.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Carrots, parsnips, dill, parsley -- share carrot fly and diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Cilantro is in the carrot family -- avoid following other Apiaceae crops.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting / Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Central flower stem shooting up. Leaves becoming smaller and flavor intensifying or turning bitter depending on the herb.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove flower stems immediately on basil to extend harvest. For cilantro and dill, flowering is part of the lifecycle -- collect seeds for cooking or sowing.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cilantro bolting -- sow your next batch
notifications.body_seasoned: Cilantro bolts fast, especially in warm weather. When you see the first flower stem, sow your next batch immediately. Succession sowing every 3-4 weeks is the only way to have continuous cilantro through the season.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cilantro seeds -- coriander for cooking
notifications.body_seasoned: The seeds of bolted cilantro are coriander -- a completely different flavor and equally useful in the kitchen. Let some plants go to seed, collect them when the plant dries and browns, and use them whole or ground.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text_seasoned: These herbs are direct-sown or started indoors. Basil needs warm soil (70 degrees) for germination; dill and cilantro tolerate cooler soil (55 to 60 degrees) and actually germinate better in cool weather.
Sow shallowly -- 1/4 inch deep -- and keep soil surface moist. Cilantro and dill can be sown in succession every 2 to 3 weeks for continuous harvest, since both bolt fast.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded plants bolt faster and produce less leaf. Pinch basil tops at 6 inches to encourage branching.
These herbs all benefit from light afternoon shade in hot summer climates. Cilantro especially bolts within weeks of warm weather hitting.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch basil regularly to prevent flowering -- once basil flowers, leaf production slows and flavor changes. Removing flower buds extends the productive harvest by weeks.
Water consistently. Wilted plants recover but the stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill. Mulch to stabilize soil moisture.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by snipping outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. For basil, cut whole stems above a leaf pair to encourage two new shoots from each cut.
Cilantro is harvested as leaves OR seed (coriander). Same plant, same cycle: harvest leaves while plant is leafy, let it bolt, harvest dry seeds from the spent flower heads.

bolting.text_seasoned: Bolting (going to flower) signals the end of useful leaf production for these herbs. Basil bolts in heat or after flowering; dill and cilantro bolt fast in any warm weather.

Once bolting starts, decide: pinch flowers to extend leaf harvest by 1 to 2 weeks (basil), or let the plant flower and self-seed for next year (dill, cilantro). Bolted cilantro is often the original planting and reseeds prolifically.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Multiple harvests before bolting -- succession sow for continuous supply
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Cilantro is a fast, generous herb. The secret is succession sowing rather than trying to keep one plant going all season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Basil is killed outright by light frost -- it is the most frost-sensitive culinary herb. Dill and cilantro are hardier; both tolerate light frost and cilantro actually grows better in cool weather. Basil also suffers chill damage (leaf blackening) below 50 degrees even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to plant basil until soil is reliably 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. For dill and cilantro, sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring -- they prefer cool conditions. Have row cover ready for cold nights with basil; in the fall, harvest basil heavily before the first cold snap because the plants will not recover.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids cluster on tender new growth across all three. Basil downy mildew is the headline disease (yellowing and gray fuzz on leaf undersides) and has spread aggressively in recent years. Dill and cilantro may attract carrot family pests (carrot rust fly larvae, leaf miner). Powdery mildew occasionally hits all three in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose downy-mildew-resistant basil varieties -- Rutgers Devotion DMR, Prospera, and similar bred for resistance. Space plants well for airflow. Hose off aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Rotate herb-bed location each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three herbs need well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Basil is especially sensitive to wet conditions and may collapse suddenly from Pythium or Fusarium in poorly-drained sites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Use containers with drainage holes for indoor or balcony herbs. Water at the base, not overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings. Avoid heavy clay sites for basil especially.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill -- often by weeks -- and produces small, tough basil leaves with concentrated bitter flavor. Wilted herbs recover with watering but the stress shortens the productive cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently, especially in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. For cilantro and dill, succession-plant every 2 to 3 weeks rather than relying on one planting through the season -- this gives you continuous harvest even as individual plantings bolt.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs need 6 hours of direct sun minimum for full flavor and growth. In partial shade, plants grow tall, leggy, and pale, with weaker flavor. Cilantro is a partial exception -- it tolerates partial shade in hot zones, where light shade actually slows bolting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun in cool climates. In hot climates (zone 8 and warmer), cilantro and parsley tolerate and even prefer light afternoon shade. Basil and dill want full sun even in heat. For indoor growing, herbs need a sunny south-facing window or supplemental grow lights.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 2 weeks from spring through autumn. Cilantro is the most determined bolter in the herb garden -- it can go from seedling to flower in 3-4 weeks in warm weather. There is no saving a bolted cilantro plant for leaf harvest. The only reliable approach is frequent new sowings. In summer, choose slow-bolt varieties and still expect faster cycling than in spring. Let a few plants go to seed -- coriander seed is a useful spice and the plants will self-sow.

tasks.description_seasoned: Cut back to 2 inches after first frost. Divide clumps every 3 years in spring.

pests.name: Onion thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery streaks or white blotches on leaves, giving a sandblasted appearance. Leaves may yellow and dry at the tips. Tiny (under 1/16 inch) yellow to brown insects hide between leaf blades and in leaf axils.
pests.cause_seasoned: Thrips tabaci, the primary allium thrips. Multiple generations per year, worst in hot dry weather. Populations build quickly and can move between chives and nearby onions, garlic, and weeds.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blue sticky cards monitor population. Insecticidal soap or spinosad applied into the leaf axils where thrips hide. Treat in evening to protect pollinators visiting chive flowers.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Water regularly during hot weather -- drought-stressed chives are more attractive to thrips. Remove crop debris in fall where thrips overwinter.

pests.name: Onion maggot
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Plants yellow and wilt for no apparent reason. Digging up the clump reveals small white legless larvae tunneling in roots and bulb bases, often with secondary rot. Heaviest damage on spring-planted clumps.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia antiqua larvae. The adult fly lays eggs at the base of alliums in spring. UMN notes onion maggot attacks only the Alliaceae family, including chives. Cool moist conditions favor egg survival.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective rescue once larvae are in the bulb. Remove and destroy infested clumps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Floating row cover from spring emergence through early summer blocks egg-laying. Rotate chives away from last year's allium beds by at least half a mile where possible -- flies travel far. Destroy cull onions and allium debris in fall.

pests.name: Allium leafminer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Rows of small round white spots along leaf blades (from adult female feeding punctures). Later, pale tunnels inside the hollow leaves. Plants may rot from secondary infection. Distorted wavy foliage.
pests.cause_seasoned: Phytomyza gymnostoma, an invasive fly established in the Northeast since 2015. Two generations per year, active in spring (April-May) and fall (September-November). Cornell notes it now occurs throughout New York allium country.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers timed to the two flight periods. Spinosad during active flights is the primary organic tool. Remove and destroy infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Check county extension alerts for local flight timing. Harvest chives heavily before spring flight to reduce tender target tissue. Less of a concern outside the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Pale yellow or light green oval patches on leaves with fuzzy gray-violet growth on undersides in humid mornings. Leaves collapse and the clump thins out. Worst in cool wet spring weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora destructor, an oomycete that also affects onions and garlic. Overwinters in infected plant material and soil. Long dew periods favor infection.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected foliage. Cut back the clump hard to remove infected tissue and allow regrowth. Copper fungicides provide partial prevention.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level, not overhead. Divide crowded clumps every 3-4 years to improve airflow. Rotate allium plantings.

diseases.name: Rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small orange or reddish-brown pustules on leaves that release powdery spores when rubbed. Leaves yellow and die back from tips. Clump looks weakened and bloom is reduced.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Puccinia allii, a fungus specific to the Alliaceae. Spread by wind-blown spores. Most severe in damp mild weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Shear the clump back to the ground and dispose of infected foliage. New growth usually comes in clean.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overcrowding. Water at the soil line. Remove volunteer alliums and garlic mustard nearby.

diseases.name: Fusarium basal rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellowing and dieback of outer leaves. The base of the clump softens and rots, often with a white or pink fungal growth. Whole clump eventually collapses.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. cepae, a soil-borne fungus that infects onion, garlic, shallot, and chives. Persists in soil for many years and often enters through root damage caused by onion maggot or cultivation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected clumps with surrounding soil. No effective rescue.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds -- Fusarium is much worse in wet ground. Do not replant chives in the same spot for at least 4 years (UMN guideline for alliums). Control onion maggot to avoid the entry wounds Fusarium exploits.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title_seasoned: Spring cutback time for your herbs
notifications.body_seasoned: Once new growth is clearly showing, cut back last year's growth by about half. Always cut into green growth -- never into old brown wood on rosemary, sage, and thyme, as they do not regenerate from old wood. This annual trim keeps your herbs productive and compact.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest your herbs before they flower
notifications.body_seasoned: The flavor of most culinary herbs is strongest just before they flower. Harvest generous amounts now -- dry, freeze, or use fresh. Once flowers open the essential oil content changes.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text_seasoned: Chives and mint prefer fertile, consistently moist soil and tolerate partial shade -- the opposite of Mediterranean herbs. A standard compost-amended garden bed suits them well.

Mint spreads aggressively by underground runners and will take over a bed within 2 years. Plant mint in a sunken pot or contained bed unless you have unlimited space to give it. Chives stays politely in clumps.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water consistently through the first season. Both crops establish quickly and produce harvestable foliage within weeks of planting.
Mulch with compost or shredded leaves to retain moisture. Both herbs respond well to consistent moisture and benefit from organic mulch (the opposite of Mediterranean herbs).

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest chives by cutting whole leaves at the base with scissors -- avoid pulling individual leaves, which damages the bulb cluster. Cut close to the ground; the leaves regrow.
Harvest mint by snipping stems above a leaf node, which encourages branching. Frequent harvest keeps mint productive and bushy; unharvested mint becomes leggy and woody.

winter.text_seasoned: Both crops die back to the ground after hard frost. The crowns are fully hardy through USDA zone 4 (chives) and zone 3 (most mints). The dieback is normal and complete -- the plant disappears underground until spring.

Do not try to keep these herbs harvestable through winter outdoors -- they are not evergreen. For winter harvest, dig a small clump in fall and pot it for the windowsill, or simply do without and welcome the spring regrowth.

spring_cutback.text_seasoned: Cut the dead foliage to ground level in early spring before new growth emerges. Both crops regrow vigorously from the crown.

Spring is also the time to divide established clumps. Chives clumps benefit from division every 3 to 4 years; mint should be reset every 2 to 3 years to prevent decline. Lift, split, and replant the most vigorous portions; compost the rest.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous harvest all season -- snip and they regrow
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Chives are one of the easiest perennials you can grow. Divide clumps every few years to keep them vigorous.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chives and mint die back to the ground after the first hard frost -- this is normal and complete. The crowns are deeply hardy (mint to zone 3, chives to zone 4) and survive winter underground without protection. There is no frost damage to worry about; the dieback is the plant's normal life cycle, not a failure.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Expect complete dieback and welcome regrowth in spring. Mulch lightly over the dormant crowns in zones 3 and 4 to insulate against repeated freeze-thaw cycles, but no special protection is needed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chives can develop allium rust (orange pustules on leaves) in humid summers. Mint occasionally suffers mint rust (similar orange pustules) and verticillium wilt. Aphids cluster on chive flower stalks. Pest pressure is otherwise low -- both herbs deter many insects with their volatile oils.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut affected foliage to the ground at first sign of rust -- both crops regrow clean. Remove and destroy verticillium-affected mint plants; do not replant mint in the same spot for 4 years. For aphids, hose off with water or wait for ladybugs to find them.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs prefer moist soil but cannot tolerate sustained waterlogging. Symptoms are yellowing leaves and crown rot in poorly-drained soil, especially over winter when growth is dormant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage if soil holds water through winter. Container-grown chives and mint need pots with drainage holes and never need to sit in a saucer of water. Adjust watering by season -- much less in winter, when growth is dormant.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Both herbs prefer consistent moisture and stress quickly under drought. Mint especially wilts dramatically when dry -- it usually recovers when watered, but repeated drought stress reduces the harvest and toughens the leaves. Chives in dry soil produces narrow, fibrous leaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently. Mulch to retain soil moisture. In hot weather, light afternoon shade benefits both herbs. Mint thrives in moisture conditions that would rot Mediterranean herbs.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Both herbs prefer full sun but tolerate partial shade -- chives accepts as little as 4 hours of sun, and mint actively prefers afternoon shade in hot climates. In deep shade both grow leggy and lose flavor strength.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun to partial shade. Chives placed in light shade in hot summers stays more tender. Mint in dry sunny spots needs more water; mint in shade needs less.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause_seasoned: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Easiest from cuttings or division -- mint seeds are unreliable. Grow in containers to prevent spreading.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Containers are the preferred way to grow mint -- it spreads aggressively in the ground. Any size pot.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 3-5 days in a glass of water like flowers
storage.fridge_seasoned: 1 week wrapped in damp paper towel
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch briefly, freeze on a tray, bag -- or make mint oil cubes
storage.notes_seasoned: Mint dries well -- hang bunches upside down for 2 weeks for long-term storage.

varieties.note_seasoned: Grow each variety in its own container -- mint varieties cross-pollinate and lose their character when mixed.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant your mint in a container
notifications.body_seasoned: Mint spreads aggressively by underground runners and will take over a bed within a season. Plant in a pot sunk into the ground, or in a dedicated container. This is not optional advice -- it is the most important thing to know about mint.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cut mint back for winter
notifications.body_seasoned: Cut mint back hard to a few inches above the soil as it dies back in autumn. It will come back strongly from the roots in spring. Mulch the container or bed to protect the roots in colder zones.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text_seasoned: Chives and mint prefer fertile, consistently moist soil and tolerate partial shade -- the opposite of Mediterranean herbs. A standard compost-amended garden bed suits them well.

Mint spreads aggressively by underground runners and will take over a bed within 2 years. Plant mint in a sunken pot or contained bed unless you have unlimited space to give it. Chives stays politely in clumps.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water consistently through the first season. Both crops establish quickly and produce harvestable foliage within weeks of planting.
Mulch with compost or shredded leaves to retain moisture. Both herbs respond well to consistent moisture and benefit from organic mulch (the opposite of Mediterranean herbs).

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest chives by cutting whole leaves at the base with scissors -- avoid pulling individual leaves, which damages the bulb cluster. Cut close to the ground; the leaves regrow.
Harvest mint by snipping stems above a leaf node, which encourages branching. Frequent harvest keeps mint productive and bushy; unharvested mint becomes leggy and woody.

winter.text_seasoned: Both crops die back to the ground after hard frost. The crowns are fully hardy through USDA zone 4 (chives) and zone 3 (most mints). The dieback is normal and complete -- the plant disappears underground until spring.

Do not try to keep these herbs harvestable through winter outdoors -- they are not evergreen. For winter harvest, dig a small clump in fall and pot it for the windowsill, or simply do without and welcome the spring regrowth.

spring_cutback.text_seasoned: Cut the dead foliage to ground level in early spring before new growth emerges. Both crops regrow vigorously from the crown.

Spring is also the time to divide established clumps. Chives clumps benefit from division every 3 to 4 years; mint should be reset every 2 to 3 years to prevent decline. Lift, split, and replant the most vigorous portions; compost the rest.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Prolific -- one plant produces more mint than most people can use
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Mint is one of the most rewarding and forgiving herbs to grow. The containment is the only rule.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chives and mint die back to the ground after the first hard frost -- this is normal and complete. The crowns are deeply hardy (mint to zone 3, chives to zone 4) and survive winter underground without protection. There is no frost damage to worry about; the dieback is the plant's normal life cycle, not a failure.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Expect complete dieback and welcome regrowth in spring. Mulch lightly over the dormant crowns in zones 3 and 4 to insulate against repeated freeze-thaw cycles, but no special protection is needed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Chives can develop allium rust (orange pustules on leaves) in humid summers. Mint occasionally suffers mint rust (similar orange pustules) and verticillium wilt. Aphids cluster on chive flower stalks. Pest pressure is otherwise low -- both herbs deter many insects with their volatile oils.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cut affected foliage to the ground at first sign of rust -- both crops regrow clean. Remove and destroy verticillium-affected mint plants; do not replant mint in the same spot for 4 years. For aphids, hose off with water or wait for ladybugs to find them.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs prefer moist soil but cannot tolerate sustained waterlogging. Symptoms are yellowing leaves and crown rot in poorly-drained soil, especially over winter when growth is dormant.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage if soil holds water through winter. Container-grown chives and mint need pots with drainage holes and never need to sit in a saucer of water. Adjust watering by season -- much less in winter, when growth is dormant.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Both herbs prefer consistent moisture and stress quickly under drought. Mint especially wilts dramatically when dry -- it usually recovers when watered, but repeated drought stress reduces the harvest and toughens the leaves. Chives in dry soil produces narrow, fibrous leaves.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently. Mulch to retain soil moisture. In hot weather, light afternoon shade benefits both herbs. Mint thrives in moisture conditions that would rot Mediterranean herbs.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Both herbs prefer full sun but tolerate partial shade -- chives accepts as little as 4 hours of sun, and mint actively prefers afternoon shade in hot climates. In deep shade both grow leggy and lose flavor strength.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun to partial shade. Chives placed in light shade in hot summers stays more tender. Mint in dry sunny spots needs more water; mint in shade needs less.

crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Very cold hardy. Most common mints (peppermint, spearmint, applemint) are reliably perennial in Z3-Z10. Spreads aggressively via runners -- plant in containers or bordered beds to contain.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Light feeder -- excess feeding reduces aromatic oils. One light feed in spring when growth begins is all that's needed.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: low N -- over-feeding reduces flavor intensity

tasks.description_seasoned: Cut back by one-third in spring as new growth emerges. Never cut into woody stems. Replace plants every 4-5 years as productivity declines.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause_seasoned: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Root rot, yellowing -- very common mistake

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost or start indoors 6-8 weeks before. Harden off transplants. Or buy plants -- thyme from seed is slow.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container herb. Good drainage is essential. Terracotta pots ideal.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 1 week at room temperature in a glass of water
storage.freezer_seasoned: Strip leaves and freeze dry -- maintains excellent flavor
storage.notes_seasoned: Thyme dries exceptionally well -- arguably better dried than fresh for most cooking.

varieties.note_seasoned: English Thyme is the most cold-hardy and reliable. French Thyme is more flavorful but slightly less hardy.
