rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title_seasoned: Spring cutback time for your herbs
notifications.body_seasoned: Once new growth is clearly showing, cut back last year's growth by about half. Always cut into green growth -- never into old brown wood on rosemary, sage, and thyme, as they do not regenerate from old wood. This annual trim keeps your herbs productive and compact.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest your herbs before they flower
notifications.body_seasoned: The flavor of most culinary herbs is strongest just before they flower. Harvest generous amounts now -- dry, freeze, or use fresh. Once flowers open the essential oil content changes.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil and full sun. Skip the compost amendment and the rich potting mix -- these herbs evolved on dry rocky hillsides and produce stronger flavor on lean soil. A handful of grit or coarse sand in the planting hole helps drainage.
Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Space generously -- mature rosemary and sage can spread 3 to 4 feet across; thyme and oregano spread by creeping stems.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water regularly through the first season to establish roots, then step back. Established Mediterranean herbs need very little supplemental water and actively dislike consistently moist soil.
Mulch with gravel or coarse sand around the base rather than organic mulch -- organic mulch holds moisture against the crown and invites rot in these herbs.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by snipping the top 2 to 3 inches of stem rather than pulling individual leaves. Regular harvest encourages bushy compact growth; unharvested plants become woody and sparse.
Harvest is most intense in early-to-mid summer when leaves carry peak essential oil. A morning harvest after dew has dried but before the heat of the day captures the strongest flavor.

winter.text_seasoned: Hardy Mediterranean herbs (thyme, oregano, sage, hardy rosemary varieties) overwinter outdoors through USDA zone 6 or 7 and can be harvested through mild winters -- the leaves stay green and usable. Less-hardy rosemary varieties need protection or container culture in zones 6 and below.
Avoid wet feet in winter -- waterlogged dormant roots are the most common cause of Mediterranean herb death. A thick gravel mulch and excellent drainage matter more in winter than in summer.

spring_cutback.text_seasoned: In early spring before new growth starts, cut back about a third of the previous year's growth. Never cut into old brown wood -- new growth comes only from green-stemmed wood, and a hard cut into the woody base often kills the plant.

Older plants (4 to 5 years and up) become woody and sparse despite annual cutback. When the woody portion exceeds the productive portion, replace the plant rather than trying to rejuvenate it -- propagate replacements from cuttings the previous fall.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Generous continuous harvest from established plants
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Thyme is one of the hardiest and most forgiving of all herbs. Once established it looks after itself.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs vary widely in cold tolerance. Thyme and oregano are hardy through USDA zone 4 or 5. Hardy sage varieties survive zone 5; tender varieties only zone 7. Common rosemary is reliably hardy only to zone 7 or 8; hardy varieties (Arp, Madeline Hill) extend to zone 6 with protection. Cold damage shows as blackened tips and dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range and choose hardy varieties for cold zones. In marginal zones, plant on the south side of a wall or in a sheltered spot, and mulch crown with gravel before winter. For rosemary in zones 5 and below, treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors near a sunny window.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are remarkably pest-resistant -- their essential oils deter most insects and they evolved without typical garden pest pressure. The main problems are root rot (from too much water), powdery mildew (in humid conditions or shade), and spider mites (in dry hot conditions, especially indoors).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage and reduce watering -- nearly all disease problems on Mediterranean herbs trace back to wet feet. Increase airflow with light pruning. For spider mites on indoor plants, increase humidity and rinse foliage occasionally.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage is the single most common killer of Mediterranean herbs. Symptoms are yellowing leaves at the base, sudden wilting despite moist soil, and a rotten smell at the crown. The damage is often irreversible by the time symptoms show.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil, on a slope or raised bed if necessary. Water only when the top 2 inches of soil are dry; in cool weather and through winter, water rarely or not at all. Use gravel mulch instead of organic mulch.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Light feeder. A single balanced feed at planting is sufficient. Over-feeding reduces aromatic oils.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Light feed time for your dill

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Carrot fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Root damage and wilting. Cilantro and dill are in carrot family and attract same pests.
pests.cause_seasoned: Psila rosae. Affects all members of the carrot family.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Grow under fine insect mesh.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Insect mesh. Grow away from carrots and parsnips.

diseases.name: Leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots on leaves. Affected leaves yellow and die.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Bacterial or fungal leaf spot. Favored by wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Good spacing.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow -- taproots dislike disturbance. Succession sow every 3 weeks.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works in deep pots (taproot). 8-12 inches deep minimum. Can grow tall -- stake if needed.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze fronds dry on a tray, then bag -- very good. Or freeze in oil cubes.
storage.notes_seasoned: Dried dill loses flavor quickly. Freezing is better for preserving the green, fresh taste.

varieties.note_seasoned: Fernleaf is the best container dill -- compact and slower to bolt than standard varieties.

rotation.note_seasoned: Dill is in the carrot family. Avoid near or after carrots.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seedlings emerging. Annual herbs germinate readily in warm conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist. Most annual herbs germinate better in warmth -- 65-75°F is ideal.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- already recognizable as the herb you planted.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 6-9 inches. The thinnings are edible -- add them to salads.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: A bushy, fragrant plant ready for regular harvesting.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Begin harvesting by pinching out the growing tips -- this encourages bushy side growth rather than a tall, lanky plant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plenty of leafy growth, plant not yet showing flowering stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest little and often by pinching growing tips. Never remove more than a third of the plant at once. Regular harvesting is what keeps herbs producing.

growth_stages.name: Bolting / Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Central flower stem shooting up. Leaves becoming smaller and flavor intensifying or turning bitter depending on the herb.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove flower stems immediately on basil to extend harvest. For cilantro and dill, flowering is part of the lifecycle -- collect seeds for cooking or sowing.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cilantro bolting -- sow your next batch
notifications.body_seasoned: Cilantro bolts fast, especially in warm weather. When you see the first flower stem, sow your next batch immediately. Succession sowing every 3-4 weeks is the only way to have continuous cilantro through the season.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cilantro seeds -- coriander for cooking
notifications.body_seasoned: The seeds of bolted cilantro are coriander -- a completely different flavor and equally useful in the kitchen. Let some plants go to seed, collect them when the plant dries and browns, and use them whole or ground.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

germination.text_seasoned: These herbs are direct-sown or started indoors. Basil needs warm soil (70 degrees) for germination; dill and cilantro tolerate cooler soil (55 to 60 degrees) and actually germinate better in cool weather.
Sow shallowly -- 1/4 inch deep -- and keep soil surface moist. Cilantro and dill can be sown in succession every 2 to 3 weeks for continuous harvest, since both bolt fast.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded plants bolt faster and produce less leaf. Pinch basil tops at 6 inches to encourage branching.
These herbs all benefit from light afternoon shade in hot summer climates. Cilantro especially bolts within weeks of warm weather hitting.

established.text_seasoned: Pinch basil regularly to prevent flowering -- once basil flowers, leaf production slows and flavor changes. Removing flower buds extends the productive harvest by weeks.
Water consistently. Wilted plants recover but the stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill. Mulch to stabilize soil moisture.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by snipping outer leaves first, leaving the central growing tip intact. For basil, cut whole stems above a leaf pair to encourage two new shoots from each cut.
Cilantro is harvested as leaves OR seed (coriander). Same plant, same cycle: harvest leaves while plant is leafy, let it bolt, harvest dry seeds from the spent flower heads.

bolting.text_seasoned: Bolting (going to flower) signals the end of useful leaf production for these herbs. Basil bolts in heat or after flowering; dill and cilantro bolt fast in any warm weather.

Once bolting starts, decide: pinch flowers to extend leaf harvest by 1 to 2 weeks (basil), or let the plant flower and self-seed for next year (dill, cilantro). Bolted cilantro is often the original planting and reseeds prolifically.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Generous leaf harvest before bolting, then seeds for cooking
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Dill self-seeds prolifically -- once you grow it, you may have it forever.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Basil is killed outright by light frost -- it is the most frost-sensitive culinary herb. Dill and cilantro are hardier; both tolerate light frost and cilantro actually grows better in cool weather. Basil also suffers chill damage (leaf blackening) below 50 degrees even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to plant basil until soil is reliably 60 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. For dill and cilantro, sow as soon as soil can be worked in spring -- they prefer cool conditions. Have row cover ready for cold nights with basil; in the fall, harvest basil heavily before the first cold snap because the plants will not recover.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids cluster on tender new growth across all three. Basil downy mildew is the headline disease (yellowing and gray fuzz on leaf undersides) and has spread aggressively in recent years. Dill and cilantro may attract carrot family pests (carrot rust fly larvae, leaf miner). Powdery mildew occasionally hits all three in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose downy-mildew-resistant basil varieties -- Rutgers Devotion DMR, Prospera, and similar bred for resistance. Space plants well for airflow. Hose off aphids with water; for serious infestations, insecticidal soap. Rotate herb-bed location each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three herbs need well-drained soil. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and crown collapse. Basil is especially sensitive to wet conditions and may collapse suddenly from Pythium or Fusarium in poorly-drained sites.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Use containers with drainage holes for indoor or balcony herbs. Water at the base, not overhead, and let the soil surface dry slightly between waterings. Avoid heavy clay sites for basil especially.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress accelerates bolting in cilantro and dill -- often by weeks -- and produces small, tough basil leaves with concentrated bitter flavor. Wilted herbs recover with watering but the stress shortens the productive cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently, especially in heat. Mulch around plants to retain soil moisture. For cilantro and dill, succession-plant every 2 to 3 weeks rather than relying on one planting through the season -- this gives you continuous harvest even as individual plantings bolt.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs need 6 hours of direct sun minimum for full flavor and growth. In partial shade, plants grow tall, leggy, and pale, with weaker flavor. Cilantro is a partial exception -- it tolerates partial shade in hot zones, where light shade actually slows bolting.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun in cool climates. In hot climates (zone 8 and warmer), cilantro and parsley tolerate and even prefer light afternoon shade. Basil and dill want full sun even in heat. For indoor growing, herbs need a sunny south-facing window or supplemental grow lights.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from spring through midsummer. Dill bolts in heat but more slowly than cilantro -- you get 4-6 weeks of good leaf production before flowering. Succession keeps a supply of fresh feathery fronds through the season. Note that dill at different stages serves different purposes: young plants for fronds, mature plants for flower heads (great with cucumbers), seeds for pickling. Plan your succession with the end use in mind.

crops.description_seasoned: Fast, feathery, and self-seeding. Plant once and you'll have it forever -- it reseeds prolifically. Harvest young leaves for flavor; let some plants set seed for pickling.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick feathery leaves any time. For seeds, wait until seed heads turn brown.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Very light feeder. Rich feeding reduces aromatic oil content and makes plants more susceptible to cold. One annual feed in spring.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: low N -- over-feeding reduces flavor and oil content

tasks.description_seasoned: Light prune after flowering in spring. Never cut into woody stems -- rosemary does not regenerate from old wood.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause_seasoned: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Root rot -- most common rosemary killer

start_method.notes_seasoned: Buy as a plant -- rosemary from seed is very slow and unreliable. Harden off over 7 days before planting out.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Good container plant. 3-5 gallon minimum. Excellent drainage essential. Can overwinter indoors in cold zones.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 1-2 weeks in a glass of water
storage.freezer_seasoned: Strip needles, freeze dry -- very good
storage.notes_seasoned: Rosemary dries perfectly. Hang branches or lay flat on a screen.

recommended: Barbecue Rosemary (very long stems for skewers)
varieties.note_seasoned: Arp and Salem are the key cold-hardy varieties -- essential for zones 5-6 where standard rosemary dies over winter.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title_seasoned: Prune your rosemary in spring
notifications.body_seasoned: Trim rosemary back by a third once new growth begins in spring. Cut back to healthy green growth -- never into old brown wood, which does not regenerate. Regular light pruning keeps rosemary compact and productive for years.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil and full sun. Skip the compost amendment and the rich potting mix -- these herbs evolved on dry rocky hillsides and produce stronger flavor on lean soil. A handful of grit or coarse sand in the planting hole helps drainage.
Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Space generously -- mature rosemary and sage can spread 3 to 4 feet across; thyme and oregano spread by creeping stems.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water regularly through the first season to establish roots, then step back. Established Mediterranean herbs need very little supplemental water and actively dislike consistently moist soil.
Mulch with gravel or coarse sand around the base rather than organic mulch -- organic mulch holds moisture against the crown and invites rot in these herbs.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by snipping the top 2 to 3 inches of stem rather than pulling individual leaves. Regular harvest encourages bushy compact growth; unharvested plants become woody and sparse.
Harvest is most intense in early-to-mid summer when leaves carry peak essential oil. A morning harvest after dew has dried but before the heat of the day captures the strongest flavor.

winter.text_seasoned: Hardy Mediterranean herbs (thyme, oregano, sage, hardy rosemary varieties) overwinter outdoors through USDA zone 6 or 7 and can be harvested through mild winters -- the leaves stay green and usable. Less-hardy rosemary varieties need protection or container culture in zones 6 and below.
Avoid wet feet in winter -- waterlogged dormant roots are the most common cause of Mediterranean herb death. A thick gravel mulch and excellent drainage matter more in winter than in summer.

spring_cutback.text_seasoned: In early spring before new growth starts, cut back about a third of the previous year's growth. Never cut into old brown wood -- new growth comes only from green-stemmed wood, and a hard cut into the woody base often kills the plant.

Older plants (4 to 5 years and up) become woody and sparse despite annual cutback. When the woody portion exceeds the productive portion, replace the plant rather than trying to rejuvenate it -- propagate replacements from cuttings the previous fall.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Year-round harvest from established plants in mild zones
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Rosemary grows into a magnificent shrub over the years. Give it a good spot and it will be there for a decade.
factors_seasoned: frost protection in zone 6 and below

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs vary widely in cold tolerance. Thyme and oregano are hardy through USDA zone 4 or 5. Hardy sage varieties survive zone 5; tender varieties only zone 7. Common rosemary is reliably hardy only to zone 7 or 8; hardy varieties (Arp, Madeline Hill) extend to zone 6 with protection. Cold damage shows as blackened tips and dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range and choose hardy varieties for cold zones. In marginal zones, plant on the south side of a wall or in a sheltered spot, and mulch crown with gravel before winter. For rosemary in zones 5 and below, treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors near a sunny window.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are remarkably pest-resistant -- their essential oils deter most insects and they evolved without typical garden pest pressure. The main problems are root rot (from too much water), powdery mildew (in humid conditions or shade), and spider mites (in dry hot conditions, especially indoors).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage and reduce watering -- nearly all disease problems on Mediterranean herbs trace back to wet feet. Increase airflow with light pruning. For spider mites on indoor plants, increase humidity and rinse foliage occasionally.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage is the single most common killer of Mediterranean herbs. Symptoms are yellowing leaves at the base, sudden wilting despite moist soil, and a rotten smell at the crown. The damage is often irreversible by the time symptoms show.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil, on a slope or raised bed if necessary. Water only when the top 2 inches of soil are dry; in cool weather and through winter, water rarely or not at all. Use gravel mulch instead of organic mulch.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

crops.description_seasoned: Mediterranean perennial that becomes a large evergreen shrub. Extremely drought-tolerant once established. Slow from seed -- buy a plant instead. Hardy to about 10°F.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Clip young soft stems any time. Avoid cutting into old woody growth.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Typically hardy Z7-Z10. Hardy varieties like 'Arp' and 'Hill Hardy' can survive Z6 with protection. In Z3-Z5 treat as an annual or grow in a container and overwinter indoors.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Excellent drainage is essential -- rosemary will die in waterlogged soil. Add grit to heavy soil. Low fertility is fine -- avoid rich compost. pH 6.0-7.0.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Like all Mediterranean herbs, over-feeding reduces flavor. One light feed in spring is ideal.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: low N -- too much feed weakens flavor

tasks.description_seasoned: Cut back to 2 inches in early spring. Harvest heavily before flowering for best flavor. Divide every 3-4 years.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause_seasoned: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost or buy plants. Harden off transplants.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container herb. Any size pot with good drainage.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Strip leaves and freeze dry -- very good
storage.notes_seasoned: Oregano is actually more flavorful dried. Hang bunches upside down.

recommended: Greek Oregano (most pungent -- the one you want for cooking)
varieties.note_seasoned: Greek Oregano is the only variety with strong enough flavor for cooking -- decorative varieties are nearly tasteless.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title_seasoned: Spring cutback time for your herbs
notifications.body_seasoned: Once new growth is clearly showing, cut back last year's growth by about half. Always cut into green growth -- never into old brown wood on rosemary, sage, and thyme, as they do not regenerate from old wood. This annual trim keeps your herbs productive and compact.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest your herbs before they flower
notifications.body_seasoned: The flavor of most culinary herbs is strongest just before they flower. Harvest generous amounts now -- dry, freeze, or use fresh. Once flowers open the essential oil content changes.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil and full sun. Skip the compost amendment and the rich potting mix -- these herbs evolved on dry rocky hillsides and produce stronger flavor on lean soil. A handful of grit or coarse sand in the planting hole helps drainage.
Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Space generously -- mature rosemary and sage can spread 3 to 4 feet across; thyme and oregano spread by creeping stems.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water regularly through the first season to establish roots, then step back. Established Mediterranean herbs need very little supplemental water and actively dislike consistently moist soil.
Mulch with gravel or coarse sand around the base rather than organic mulch -- organic mulch holds moisture against the crown and invites rot in these herbs.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by snipping the top 2 to 3 inches of stem rather than pulling individual leaves. Regular harvest encourages bushy compact growth; unharvested plants become woody and sparse.
Harvest is most intense in early-to-mid summer when leaves carry peak essential oil. A morning harvest after dew has dried but before the heat of the day captures the strongest flavor.

winter.text_seasoned: Hardy Mediterranean herbs (thyme, oregano, sage, hardy rosemary varieties) overwinter outdoors through USDA zone 6 or 7 and can be harvested through mild winters -- the leaves stay green and usable. Less-hardy rosemary varieties need protection or container culture in zones 6 and below.
Avoid wet feet in winter -- waterlogged dormant roots are the most common cause of Mediterranean herb death. A thick gravel mulch and excellent drainage matter more in winter than in summer.

spring_cutback.text_seasoned: In early spring before new growth starts, cut back about a third of the previous year's growth. Never cut into old brown wood -- new growth comes only from green-stemmed wood, and a hard cut into the woody base often kills the plant.

Older plants (4 to 5 years and up) become woody and sparse despite annual cutback. When the woody portion exceeds the productive portion, replace the plant rather than trying to rejuvenate it -- propagate replacements from cuttings the previous fall.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Generous harvest, best before flowering
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Greek oregano varieties have the strongest flavor. Harvest before the flowers open for maximum essential oil content.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs vary widely in cold tolerance. Thyme and oregano are hardy through USDA zone 4 or 5. Hardy sage varieties survive zone 5; tender varieties only zone 7. Common rosemary is reliably hardy only to zone 7 or 8; hardy varieties (Arp, Madeline Hill) extend to zone 6 with protection. Cold damage shows as blackened tips and dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range and choose hardy varieties for cold zones. In marginal zones, plant on the south side of a wall or in a sheltered spot, and mulch crown with gravel before winter. For rosemary in zones 5 and below, treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors near a sunny window.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are remarkably pest-resistant -- their essential oils deter most insects and they evolved without typical garden pest pressure. The main problems are root rot (from too much water), powdery mildew (in humid conditions or shade), and spider mites (in dry hot conditions, especially indoors).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage and reduce watering -- nearly all disease problems on Mediterranean herbs trace back to wet feet. Increase airflow with light pruning. For spider mites on indoor plants, increase humidity and rinse foliage occasionally.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage is the single most common killer of Mediterranean herbs. Symptoms are yellowing leaves at the base, sudden wilting despite moist soil, and a rotten smell at the crown. The damage is often irreversible by the time symptoms show.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil, on a slope or raised bed if necessary. Water only when the top 2 inches of soil are dry; in cool weather and through winter, water rarely or not at all. Use gravel mulch instead of organic mulch.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune lightly in spring after new growth appears. Remove about one-third of growth. Replace every 4-5 years when plants become woody and unproductive.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Rosemary beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Metallic striped beetles eating leaves and flowers. Most active autumn and spring.
pests.cause_seasoned: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme, marjoram.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake over a sheet. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Check plants regularly. Avoid hiding spots at base.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White coating on leaves. Leaves yellow and drop. Common on sage and mint.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Various Erysiphe fungi.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve airflow. Neem oil spray.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Water at soil level. Ensure good spacing.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 6-8 weeks before last frost or buy plants. Harden off over 7 days.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Good container herb. 3-gallon minimum. Can overwinter indoors in cold zones.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze leaves individually on a tray then bag -- or fry in butter and freeze
storage.notes_seasoned: Dried sage is excellent -- more intense than fresh. Hang bunches to dry.

varieties.note_seasoned: Berggarten has the largest leaves and rarely flowers -- keeps producing for cooking rather than going to seed.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant settling in after planting or propagation.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most perennial herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil -- do not over-fertilize. Good drainage is more important than rich soil.

growth_stages.name: Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New growth appearing, roots establishing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water regularly in the first season to establish roots. Once established, most perennial herbs are drought-tolerant.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Abundant leafy growth -- harvest anytime the plant has plenty.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest by cutting stems back by a third. Never cut into old woody growth on rosemary, sage, and thyme -- they do not regenerate from old wood.

growth_stages.name: Winter
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plant slowing down or going dormant. Hardy perennials stay evergreen; tender ones die back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give a light haircut before winter to tidy up but avoid heavy pruning -- leave it for spring. Mulch around the base in colder zones.

growth_stages.name: Spring Cutback
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New green growth beginning to push from the base or lower stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut back last year's growth by about half once new growth appears. This annual cutback keeps perennial herbs from going woody and keeps them productive.

notifications.title_seasoned: Spring cutback time for your herbs
notifications.body_seasoned: Once new growth is clearly showing, cut back last year's growth by about half. Always cut into green growth -- never into old brown wood on rosemary, sage, and thyme, as they do not regenerate from old wood. This annual trim keeps your herbs productive and compact.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest your herbs before they flower
notifications.body_seasoned: The flavor of most culinary herbs is strongest just before they flower. Harvest generous amounts now -- dry, freeze, or use fresh. Once flowers open the essential oil content changes.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender herbs
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Basil, cilantro, and lemongrass are extremely frost-tender. Bring containers inside or cover with fleece tonight. Hardy herbs like thyme, rosemary, and mint are much more frost-tolerant.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat alert -- herbs may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Heat triggers bolting in cilantro, dill, and parsley. Harvest as much as possible before temperatures peak. Basil, on the other hand, loves heat -- just remove any flowers that appear.

planting.text_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs prefer poor, well-drained soil and full sun. Skip the compost amendment and the rich potting mix -- these herbs evolved on dry rocky hillsides and produce stronger flavor on lean soil. A handful of grit or coarse sand in the planting hole helps drainage.
Plant in spring after the last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Space generously -- mature rosemary and sage can spread 3 to 4 feet across; thyme and oregano spread by creeping stems.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water regularly through the first season to establish roots, then step back. Established Mediterranean herbs need very little supplemental water and actively dislike consistently moist soil.
Mulch with gravel or coarse sand around the base rather than organic mulch -- organic mulch holds moisture against the crown and invites rot in these herbs.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest by snipping the top 2 to 3 inches of stem rather than pulling individual leaves. Regular harvest encourages bushy compact growth; unharvested plants become woody and sparse.
Harvest is most intense in early-to-mid summer when leaves carry peak essential oil. A morning harvest after dew has dried but before the heat of the day captures the strongest flavor.

winter.text_seasoned: Hardy Mediterranean herbs (thyme, oregano, sage, hardy rosemary varieties) overwinter outdoors through USDA zone 6 or 7 and can be harvested through mild winters -- the leaves stay green and usable. Less-hardy rosemary varieties need protection or container culture in zones 6 and below.
Avoid wet feet in winter -- waterlogged dormant roots are the most common cause of Mediterranean herb death. A thick gravel mulch and excellent drainage matter more in winter than in summer.

spring_cutback.text_seasoned: In early spring before new growth starts, cut back about a third of the previous year's growth. Never cut into old brown wood -- new growth comes only from green-stemmed wood, and a hard cut into the woody base often kills the plant.

Older plants (4 to 5 years and up) become woody and sparse despite annual cutback. When the woody portion exceeds the productive portion, replace the plant rather than trying to rejuvenate it -- propagate replacements from cuttings the previous fall.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Generous harvest from established plants
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sage grows into a beautiful shrub. It lasts for years with annual pruning and improves with age.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs vary widely in cold tolerance. Thyme and oregano are hardy through USDA zone 4 or 5. Hardy sage varieties survive zone 5; tender varieties only zone 7. Common rosemary is reliably hardy only to zone 7 or 8; hardy varieties (Arp, Madeline Hill) extend to zone 6 with protection. Cold damage shows as blackened tips and dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range and choose hardy varieties for cold zones. In marginal zones, plant on the south side of a wall or in a sheltered spot, and mulch crown with gravel before winter. For rosemary in zones 5 and below, treat as a container plant and overwinter indoors near a sunny window.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are remarkably pest-resistant -- their essential oils deter most insects and they evolved without typical garden pest pressure. The main problems are root rot (from too much water), powdery mildew (in humid conditions or shade), and spider mites (in dry hot conditions, especially indoors).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage and reduce watering -- nearly all disease problems on Mediterranean herbs trace back to wet feet. Increase airflow with light pruning. For spider mites on indoor plants, increase humidity and rinse foliage occasionally.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Root rot from overwatering or poor drainage is the single most common killer of Mediterranean herbs. Symptoms are yellowing leaves at the base, sudden wilting despite moist soil, and a rotten smell at the crown. The damage is often irreversible by the time symptoms show.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil, on a slope or raised bed if necessary. Water only when the top 2 inches of soil are dry; in cool weather and through winter, water rarely or not at all. Use gravel mulch instead of organic mulch.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mediterranean herbs are drought-tolerant but not drought-immune. Severe drought during the first establishing season kills young plants. Established plants drop older leaves as a normal response to prolonged drought; this is recoverable but reduces the harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water young plants regularly through their first season. Established plants need water only during prolonged dry spells -- a deep watering once every 2 to 3 weeks is plenty. A well-established Mediterranean herb thrives on neglect once roots are deep.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These herbs need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to develop strong essential oils and compact growth. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy and floppy, lose their characteristic flavor intensity, and become more disease-prone.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. If your only sunny spots are filled, container-grown Mediterranean herbs do well on a sunny patio or balcony. Move pots seasonally to track the sun if needed.

fertilizer.timing: switch to high-potassium at first flower
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heavy feeder like peppers and tomatoes. Start with balanced feed, switch to high-potassium when flowers appear. Consistent feeding produces larger, more tender fruit.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Tomato hornworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large green caterpillars (up to 4 inches) stripping foliage. Leaves disappear rapidly. Black droppings on leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Manduca quinquemaculata moth larvae. Mid to late summer pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick; they are well camouflaged but easy to remove. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray. If white cocoons visible on back, leave them; parasitic wasps are doing the work.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Till soil in autumn to kill overwintering pupae. Plant dill and basil nearby to attract predatory wasps.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Most active in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Use row covers on seedlings. Apply diatomaceous earth. Neem oil spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay transplanting until plants are large. Use transplants rather than seeds.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Early blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown spots with concentric rings on lower leaves first. Affected leaves yellow and drop. Spreads upward through plant.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria fungus. Favored by warm wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves immediately. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively. Mulch soil to prevent splash-up.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate tomatoes every 3-4 years. Water at soil level. Space plants for airflow. Stake to keep foliage off ground.

diseases.name: Blossom end rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark, sunken, leathery patch at the bottom (blossom end) of fruit. Affects first fruits most. Not contagious.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Calcium deficiency in developing fruit, caused by irregular watering or root damage, not a pest or disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Mulch to maintain even soil moisture. Water consistently. Foliar calcium spray provides some relief. Remove affected fruit.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Consistent watering is the key prevention. Avoid root disturbance. Do not over-fertilize with nitrogen.

diseases.name: Septoria leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular spots with dark borders and pale gray centers, starting on lower leaves. Spots may have yellow halos.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Septoria lycopersici fungus. One of the most common tomato diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper fungicide. Ensure good air circulation.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate crops. Water at soil level. Mulch around plants.

diseases.name: Late blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked, rapidly expanding brown patches on leaves and stems. White fuzzy growth on undersides in humid conditions. Can destroy plants in days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora infestans oomycete. The same pathogen that caused the Irish potato famine. Spreads rapidly in cool wet weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected material immediately; do not compost. Apply copper fungicide preventively in wet conditions.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure excellent airflow. Never leave tomato debris in the garden over winter.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 8-10 weeks before last frost. Eggplant loves heat -- don't rush transplanting.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, potatoes: all share blight and fusarium diseases
rotation.note_seasoned: Always rotate nightshades to a fresh bed -- blight and fusarium can persist in soil for years.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Roast/cook first, then freeze -- raw frozen eggplant is poor quality
storage.notes_seasoned: Eggplant deteriorates rapidly. Cook it or freeze as a cooked dish (baba ganoush, caponata).

varieties.note_seasoned: Ichiban is excellent for beginners -- sets fruit in cool conditions better than many varieties, very prolific.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Marigolds
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Deter Colorado beetle, nematodes, and aphids

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring aphids, Colorado beetle are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small seedlings emerging. Eggplant germinates more slowly than tomatoes.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep at 80-85°F. Heat mat essential. Eggplant is even more heat-demanding than peppers at germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves with a distinctive purple sheen on the underside.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep consistently warm. Eggplant is slow -- do not worry if progress seems minimal in the first few weeks.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Compact, sturdy plant ready for outdoor conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do not transplant until nights are reliably above 60°F. Eggplant is more cold-sensitive than peppers.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Purple star-shaped flowers with yellow centers.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer. Tap flowering stems gently to aid pollination.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Glossy, firm skin -- harvest before the shine fades. Eggplant past its prime becomes bitter and seedy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut rather than pull -- eggplants have thorny calyx. Use secateurs. Pick when the skin is shiny and the fruit gives slightly to pressure.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing fruit set, smaller fruit, nights cooling below 55°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest any remaining fruit before first frost -- eggplant does not ripen off the plant. Pull and compost spent plants; the stems can be tough so chop or shred before composting.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your eggplant season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start your eggplant indoors -- 10 weeks before last frost
notifications.body_seasoned: Eggplant is even slower than peppers and needs 10-12 weeks indoors. Start now with a heat mat at 80-85°F. They are rewarding once established but demand patience early on.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Cold snap -- protect your eggplant
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Eggplant is more cold-sensitive than any other common vegetable. Even temperatures in the 50s at night slow them significantly. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text_seasoned: Eggplant needs warm soil to germinate -- 75 to 85 degrees is the sweet spot. Start indoors 8 to 10 weeks before last frost; eggplant is even more heat-loving than peppers and gets a slow start.
Use a heat mat under the seed tray for reliable germination -- room temperature is too cold for fast germination. Seedlings emerge in 7 to 14 days at the right temperature.

seedling.text_seasoned: Pot up seedlings to 4-inch pots once they have 2 true leaves. Eggplant resents cold and slow growth; keep seedlings warm (70+ degrees day, 60+ night) until transplant.
Harden off slowly over 7 to 10 days before transplanting outdoors. Eggplant transplanted into cold soil sulks for weeks and may never fully recover.

established.text_seasoned: Transplant outdoors only after night temperatures stay reliably above 55 degrees and soil reaches 65. Black plastic mulch and row cover help substantially in cool zones.
Eggplant prefers more consistent soil moisture than peppers -- closer to tomato needs. Water deeply 1 to 2 times per week and mulch heavily. Side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer mid-season.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick eggplant when the skin is glossy and the fruit feels firm but yields slightly to thumb pressure. Dull skin means the fruit is overripe -- the seeds inside have hardened and the flesh has turned bitter.
Use pruners or a sharp knife to cut the stem cleanly -- eggplant stems are tough and twisting damages the plant. Harvest every 3 to 5 days during peak production to encourage continued fruit set.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Eggplant production drops as nights cool below 55 degrees. Harvest all developing fruit before first expected frost -- frost kills the plant and damages fruit.
Pull and compost spent plants. Rotate eggplant to a new bed each year; avoid planting in any spot where tomato, pepper, or potato grew last year (Solanaceae rotation).

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 4-8 fruits per plant over the season
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: A productive plant front-loads in late summer -- expect a steady run of fruit for 4 to 6 weeks before cooler nights slow it down.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Eggplant is challenging in cooler climates but deeply satisfying when it works.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Eggplant is one of the most heat-loving and frost-sensitive vegetables. Cold soil at transplant (below 65 degrees) stunts plants for the rest of the season. Light frost kills the plant outright. Cool nights below 55 degrees during fruit set reduce yield substantially even without frost.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to transplant until soil reaches 65 degrees and night temperatures stay above 55. Use black plastic mulch to warm soil and row cover for the first weeks. In short-season zones, choose early-maturing varieties (Patio Baby, Hansel) and start indoors 8 to 10 weeks before transplant date.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Flea beetles are the headline eggplant pest -- they make countless tiny shotholes in leaves, especially on young plants. Heavy flea-beetle damage on seedlings can kill plants outright. Colorado potato beetle, tomato hornworm, and aphids also attack eggplant. Verticillium wilt and bacterial wilt are the headline diseases in long-rotation gardens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover at transplant blocks flea beetles -- remove at flowering for pollination. Hand-pick larger pests (Colorado potato beetle, hornworm). Rotate eggplant to a new bed and avoid spots where Solanaceae grew last year. Choose disease-resistant varieties for areas with verticillium history.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Eggplant prefers more consistent moisture than peppers but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot, yellowing leaves, and fruit drop. Wet humid conditions also drive flea beetle and Colorado potato beetle activity.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture. Avoid heavy clay sites for eggplant.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during flowering and fruit development causes blossom drop and produces small, bitter, often misshapen fruit. Eggplant is more sensitive to inconsistent watering than peppers -- the fruit develops fast and water-stressed plants cannot fill them properly.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply 1 to 2 times per week and increase frequency in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation works well for eggplant by providing consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Eggplant needs full sun -- 8 hours minimum -- and serious heat to set fruit well. In partial shade or cool conditions, plants may grow leaves but flower sparsely and set few fruit. Eggplant in cool coastal climates often disappoints for this reason.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest, hottest spot available. Plant against a south-facing wall or fence for reflected heat in cool climates. In genuinely cool-summer regions, grow in containers that can be moved or accept that eggplant is not the right crop.
