tasks.description_seasoned: After harvest, mow foliage to 1 inch above crowns, thin plants to 6 inches apart, and apply fertilizer. This renovation extends bed life.
Replace strawberry beds every 3-4 years as production declines. Root new runners from healthy plants.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Attracts pollinators, may improve strawberry flavor

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: The pollinator-attraction portion of this claim is extension-documented (Xerces), but the flavor-improvement assertion is the distinguishing content and matches the traditional flavor-improvement claim pattern. Reclassify as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring slugs are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Ground cover effects on soil temperature and moisture are real; specific pairings not well-studied.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

pests.name: Vine weevil
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Notched semi-circular bites from leaf edges (adults -- less serious). Plants wilt and die suddenly -- white C-shaped larvae found eating roots.
pests.cause_seasoned: Otiorhynchus sulcatus. Larvae feed on roots autumn-spring. Worst in containers.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Apply beneficial nematodes (Steinernema or Heterorhabditis) in late summer when soil is warm. Hand-pick adults at night.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Nematode treatment in late summer is the key prevention in containers.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing fruit. Tiny maggots inside. Develops in ripening fruit before harvest.
pests.cause_seasoned: Drosophila suzukii fly. Lays eggs in ripening soft fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Harvest ripe fruit immediately. Fine mesh netting during ripening.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Do not leave overripe fruit on plant. Harvest frequently.

diseases.name: Botrytis (gray mold)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gray fluffy mold on fruit, especially in cool wet weather. Fruit rots rapidly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis cinerea fungus. Enters through damaged skin or petals.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected fruit immediately. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Straw mulch lifts fruit off soil. Ensure plant spacing for airflow.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White coating on upper leaf surfaces. Leaf margins roll upward. Purple discoloration on upper side.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Podosphaera aphanis fungus. Worst in warm conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Neem oil or sulfur-based spray. Remove affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Ensure good airflow. Avoid excess nitrogen.

watering.method_seasoned: Drip or soaker -- overhead watering promotes gray mold
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Root rot, gray mold on fruit

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root crowns in early spring. Crown should sit at soil level -- too deep causes rot, too shallow causes drying. In year 1, remove all flowers to build plant strength.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Perfect container crop. Hanging baskets, strawberry planters, window boxes all work. Everbearing varieties best for containers.

varieties.note_seasoned: Albion is the standout variety for flavor -- widely considered the best-tasting modern strawberry.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 3-5 days -- don't wash until ready to eat
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole on a tray, then bag -- excellent for smoothies and baking
storage.notes_seasoned: Very perishable -- pick and use quickly. Hulled berries stored in a single layer last longest.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Tomatoes, peppers, potatoes -- share verticillium wilt
rotation.note_seasoned: Strawberry beds should be refreshed every 3-4 years and moved to new ground.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Plants established with crowns at soil level -- not buried, not exposed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant with the crown exactly at soil level. Too deep and it rots; too shallow and it dries out. Net immediately against birds.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Healthy green growth, no crown rot.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove flowers in year one of planting to direct energy to root establishment. You will get far more fruit in subsequent years.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: White flowers with yellow centers opening.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Lay straw under the developing fruit to keep them clean and away from slugs. This is what gives strawberry beds their name.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fully red, fragrant fruit. Do not pick until fully colored -- green shoulders indicate underripe.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick in the morning when cool. Eat the same day -- homegrown strawberries do not keep. Net against birds before they get there first.

growth_stages.name: Managing Runners
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Long trailing stems with baby plants forming at the tips.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pin runners down to root new plants, or cut them off to keep energy on fruit production. After 3-4 years, replace old plants with rooted runners.

notifications.title_seasoned: Strawberries flowering -- net them now
notifications.body_seasoned: Birds can strip a strawberry crop overnight once fruit starts forming. Net before the fruit appears, not after. One night without nets during ripening can cost you the whole harvest.

notifications.title_seasoned: Lay straw under your strawberry plants
notifications.body_seasoned: Lay straw or strawberry mats around the plants now. This keeps developing fruit clean, retains moisture, and keeps slugs away from the ripening berries. This is what gives strawberry beds their name.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently and feed every 2 weeks with a balanced fertilizer.
Watch for pests -- check undersides of leaves regularly.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick when fully red and fragrant. Eat the same day -- homegrown strawberries do not keep.
Harvest at the right moment -- timing makes a significant difference to flavor.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 0.5-1 lb of strawberries per plant per year
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: June-bearing varieties give one heavy 2 to 3 week flush in early summer; everbearing and day-neutral varieties spread a smaller harvest from early summer through fall.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Established strawberry plants produce more each year until they peak at year 3-4 then decline. Replace with rooted runners.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These three perennials handle winter cold differently. Asparagus is fully cold-hardy through zone 3, dies back to the ground each winter, and emerges from the crown each spring. Strawberry is cold-hardy through zone 3 with mulch, sometimes loses leaves but the crown survives. Artichoke is the cold-tender one -- hardy only to zone 7 reliably, often grown as an annual in colder zones. Late spring frost can damage emerging asparagus spears and strawberry blossoms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For asparagus, cover emerging spears with row cover during late spring frosts; damaged spears are tough and bitter. For strawberry, mulch heavily over the crowns before winter and uncover in early spring. For artichoke in zones 6 and below, grow as an annual or dig and overwinter the crown indoors. Hardy artichoke varieties (Imperial Star) survive zone 6 with heavy mulching.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Each of these crops has its own primary pest: asparagus beetle (both common and spotted) chews ferns and lays eggs on spears; spotted wing drosophila (SWD), slugs, and gray mold (Botrytis) are the headline strawberry problems; artichoke is generally low-pest but artichoke aphid clusters in the bracts and slugs damage tender new growth. Asparagus rust and Fusarium crown rot affect asparagus over time; strawberry is also vulnerable to verticillium wilt.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For asparagus beetle, hand-pick adults and crush egg masses; in heavy infestations, neem or pyrethrin sprays in the cool of the day work. For SWD on strawberry, harvest ripe fruit promptly and clean up drops; row cover during fruit ripening helps. For artichoke aphid, hose off with water or use insecticidal soap. Choose disease-resistant strawberry varieties and renovate beds every 3 to 4 years.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three crops fail in waterlogged soil. Asparagus crowns rot in standing water -- a single wet season can kill an established bed. Strawberry crowns rot at the soil-stem interface in persistently wet conditions, and the fruit develops gray mold in damp weather. Artichoke is similarly intolerant of wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds. For asparagus, the bed is a multi-year commitment -- excellent drainage at planting prevents 20 years of disappointment. For strawberry, raised beds and straw mulch (the source of the name) keep fruit and crowns dry. For artichoke, mound up the planting site if drainage is marginal.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress in the establishment year is the leading cause of failed asparagus and artichoke plantings. Strawberry tolerates short drought once established but fruit size and number drop substantially with water stress during fruiting. Asparagus that goes dry in summer produces fewer and smaller spears the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply through the establishment season for all three. Asparagus needs consistent moisture in summer (when it is feeding the crown for next year's spears) more than in spring (when it is producing spears from already-stored energy). Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture for all three.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three want full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to produce well. Shaded asparagus produces fewer and thinner spears; shaded strawberry produces small pale fruit with weak flavor; shaded artichoke grows leaves but produces few or no buds. These are not shade-tolerant crops.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. Asparagus is a long-term commitment (15 to 20 years productive life), so the site choice matters more than for annual crops. For strawberry, full sun is also better for disease management because foliage dries faster after rain or dew.

crops.description_seasoned: One of the most beloved fruits to grow at home. Three types: June-bearing (one big crop), everbearing (two crops), and day-neutral (continuous fruiting). Year one is establishment -- year two is harvest.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Fully red, easily detaches from stem, slight give when squeezed. Aroma is the best indicator. Pick every 1-2 days during peak season.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: June-bearing and everbearing strawberries are reliably perennial Z3-Z10. Mulch heavily in coldest zones to protect crowns. Day-neutral varieties sometimes grown as annuals in warm zones.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: June-bearing (short-day) varieties need 200-800 chill hours depending on variety; day-neutral and everbearing varieties have low to no chill requirement. This is why day-neutrals ship to warm zones and June-bearing stays in cold zones.
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile but yields improve with pollinator visits. Honey bees and native bees both work.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Remove flowers in year one for June-bearing types to strengthen runners and crowns. Everbearing types can be lightly harvested.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Remove all perennial weeds before planting -- they're nearly impossible to remove once strawberries are established. Dig in well-rotted compost. pH 5.5-6.5 (slightly acidic). Raised beds are ideal for drainage. Never plant where tomatoes, potatoes, or peppers grew in the last 3 years (verticillium wilt risk).

crops.name: Pumpkin

3.notes: Very tight window. Start 3 weeks early. Small-sized varieties essential -- no time for giants.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: In cold zones (Z3-Z5), pumpkin growing is challenging due to 90-120 day DTM crowding the frost-free window. Direct-sow as soon as soil reaches 65 degrees F after last frost. Choose fast-maturing varieties (90 days). Start indoors 3 weeks before last frost in biodegradable pots for best results in short-season zones. (UMN Extension; NDSU Extension; UMaine Extension)

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Attracts bees for pollination, deters hornworm

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant that blooms concurrently with tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, drawing the same bees that pollinate those crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat. The claim's additional assertions about deterring hornworm are not supported in extension literature; they recur widely in popular gardening sources but without rigorous backing and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Inter-plant competition for N, P, K is a real agronomic concept. Specific 'bad pair' claims often extrapolate beyond what research has shown.

pests.name: Cucumber beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green beetles with black spots or stripes feeding on leaves, flowers, and fruit. Plants wilt suddenly (bacterial wilt transmission). Holey leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Spotted and striped cucumber beetles. Also transmit bacterial wilt disease.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers until flowering. Yellow sticky traps. Neem oil spray. Spinosad-based insecticide.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting until plants are large. Use row covers early season. Interplant with radishes and nasturtiums.

pests.name: Squash bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gray-brown flat insects on stems and undersides of leaves. Wilting leaves with yellow then brown patches. Bronze egg clusters on leaf undersides.
pests.cause_seasoned: Anasa tristis. Overwinters as adults in garden debris.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and egg masses. Trap under boards at night. Neem oil spray on nymphs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Remove all garden debris in autumn. Rotate cucurbit crops. Use row covers early season.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

diseases.name: Bacterial wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of individual leaves, then whole stems, then entire plant. No recovery even with watering. Plants die within days.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia tracheiphila bacteria spread by cucumber beetles feeding.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure -- remove and destroy infected plants immediately. Control cucumber beetles to prevent spread.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use row covers to exclude cucumber beetles early in season. Plant resistant varieties.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow-green patches on upper leaf surface with corresponding gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaf undersides. Leaves die rapidly.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudoperonospora cubensis fungus. Spreads rapidly in wet humid conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Apply copper-based fungicide preventively.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Choose resistant varieties. Water at soil level. Ensure good air circulation.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost. In zones 3-5, start indoors 3 weeks before in biodegradable pots.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Cucumbers, squash, pumpkins, melons -- share cucumber beetle, bacterial wilt, downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Rotate to prevent cucumber beetle and disease buildup.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Cook, puree, freeze -- excellent
storage.notes_seasoned: Cure pumpkins for 10 days at 80°F before long storage -- hardens skin and heals blemishes.

varieties.note_seasoned: Jarrahdale is the best eating pumpkin -- dense, dry, sweet orange flesh. Better flavor than most "pie pumpkins."

thinning.when: When seedlings have first true leaf
thinning.to_spacing: 1 plant per hill (2-3 feet spacing between plants)
thinning.method: Thin to strongest plant per hill. Cut rather than pull.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Plant 3 seeds per hill, thin to 1. Hills warm up faster than flat ground -- good for cold starts.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Not suited to containers except for miniature varieties (Jack Be Little, Baby Boo) which can be grown in 15-gallon pots.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large seed leaves emerging fast.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow on their edge to prevent rotting. Warm soil 65°F+.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large hairy leaves developing quickly.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Give them space from the start -- pumpkins sprawl enormously.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Vines running in multiple directions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Direct the main vine. Remove any secondary vines if space is limited -- one strong vine gives better pumpkins than many weak ones.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large orange flowers. Hand-pollinate for better fruit set.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hand-pollinate in the morning -- touch a male flower to each open female flower. Pumpkins need reliable pollination for large fruit.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Flowers open? Any tiny pumpkins forming?

growth_stages.name: Fruit Development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pumpkins swelling and coloring. Limit to 1-3 fruits per plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Place a tile or board under each developing pumpkin to prevent ground rot. Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to encourage ripening.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Skin hardened to resist a thumbnail, stem corky and dry, color fully developed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest before first frost and cure for 10-14 days at room temperature. A cured pumpkin stores for months and tastes better than an uncured one.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Vines yellowing and dying back, rinds hardening so a fingernail does not pierce the skin, stems beginning to cork.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut pumpkins from the vine leaving 3-4 inches of stem. Cure in a warm dry spot for 10-14 days before storage. Pull and compost the dead vines; chop large stems first.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your pumpkin harvest? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your pumpkins
notifications.body_seasoned: Pumpkins go directly into warm soil after last frost. They grow fast and sprawl enormously -- give them as much space as you can spare. Sow on their edge to prevent rotting.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest pumpkins before frost
notifications.body_seasoned: Harvest all pumpkins before first frost and cure for 10-14 days at room temperature. A cured pumpkin stores for months. Do not leave them in the ground through frost -- it damages the skin and shortens storage dramatically.

germination.text_seasoned: Pumpkin is direct-sown after soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees -- typically 1 to 2 weeks after last frost. In short-season zones, start transplants indoors 2 to 3 weeks before transplant date but disturb roots minimally; pumpkin resents transplanting.
Sow 4 to 5 seeds in a hill (a low mound), 1 inch deep. Hills should be 4 to 8 feet apart depending on variety -- pumpkin vines run aggressively and need room.

seedling.text_seasoned: Once seedlings have 2 to 3 true leaves, thin to the 2 strongest plants per hill. Pull the others rather than transplanting -- damaged roots set seedlings back significantly.
Cucumber beetles attack seedlings hard -- floating row cover at planting through first flower blocks them. Watch for squash bug egg masses (orange-red, on undersides of leaves) and crush by hand.

established.text_seasoned: Pumpkin vines run 10 to 20 feet by midsummer. Train vines into the bed rather than letting them root at every node, which produces many small fruit instead of fewer large ones.
Side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer at flowering and again at fruit set. Pumpkin is a heavy feeder; deficiency shows as yellowing of older leaves and reduced fruit size.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pumpkin is ready when the skin is fully colored, the rind is hard enough that a thumbnail does not pierce it, and the stem has begun to dry and crack. Hollow sound when tapped is another good indicator.
Cut pumpkins from the vine with 4 to 6 inches of stem attached -- a stemless pumpkin rots from the wound much faster. Use pruners or a sharp knife; do not pull or twist off.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Cure pumpkins in a warm dry spot (75 to 85 degrees) for 1 to 2 weeks after harvest. Curing hardens the skin and heals minor wounds, dramatically extending storage life.
After curing, store at 50 to 55 degrees in a dry location. Properly cured pumpkins keep 3 to 6 months. Rotate pumpkin to a new bed each year.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 1-5 pumpkins depending on variety and space
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Pumpkins ripen together over a 2 to 4 week window in early fall -- one main flush rather than a long staggered harvest.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: A row of cured pumpkins lining a porch is one of the most satisfying things you can grow.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pumpkin is a tropical-origin tender annual killed by light frost. Cold soil at planting (below 65 degrees) stunts seedlings. Late-summer frost ends the season abruptly -- mature pumpkins on the vine survive light frost but the foliage dies and the fruit must be harvested immediately.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to direct-sow until soil reaches 65 to 70 degrees and night temperatures stay above 50. In short-season zones, choose short-maturity varieties (Sugar Pie, New England Pie at 90 to 100 days; mini pumpkins at 80 days) and use black plastic mulch to warm soil. Track expected harvest date carefully so the crop matures before first frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cucumber beetles damage seedlings and transmit bacterial wilt -- a fatal disease. Squash bugs target pumpkin specifically (worse than on cucumber or melon). Squash vine borer larvae bore into stems, often killing plants suddenly at midseason. Powdery mildew shows up reliably late in the season.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover at planting through first flower blocks cucumber beetles and squash vine borer adults. Squash bug egg masses (orange-red on leaf undersides) crush easily by hand. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties and water at the base. Rotate pumpkin to a new bed each year.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pumpkin needs consistent water but cannot tolerate waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot and sudden vine collapse. Heavy rain near harvest causes mature fruit to crack and split. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew, downy mildew, and bacterial leaf spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in raised hills or well-drained soil. Water deeply at the base 1 to 2 times per week rather than shallow daily. Mulch heavily to stabilize soil moisture. Stop watering 2 weeks before expected harvest to firm up fruit and improve storage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development produces small or misshapen pumpkins. Pumpkin vines move large volumes of water through tissues during fruit fill -- a single mature pumpkin plant uses 1 to 2 gallons per day in peak summer. Severe drought can also cause fruit to drop before reaching usable size.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently and deeply through fruit development -- 1 to 2 inches per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. Drip irrigation works well by providing consistent water without wetting foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pumpkin needs full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum, ideally more -- to set and ripen fruit. In partial shade vines grow long and leafy but flower sparsely and set few fruit. The huge leaves of a healthy pumpkin plant can also shade their own flowering nodes if vines are not trained.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest spot available. Train vines outward into the bed to expose flowers to pollinators and sun. Avoid planting downwind of large structures or trees that will cast shade as the season progresses.

crops.description_seasoned: Needs space -- a lot of space. But few crops beat the satisfaction of growing a Halloween pumpkin. Small varieties like Baby Boo need much less room. Plant in a hill with heaps of compost.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Skin hard and deep colored. Hollow sound when tapped. Stem dries completely. Leave as long as possible before frost.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Pumpkins are very heavy feeders. Dig a planting hole 18 inches deep and 18 wide and fill with half compost, half garden soil -- the "pumpkin hill" method. This creates a rich, well-drained mound. pH 6.0-6.8.

3.notes: European plums (Damson, Stanley) are most cold-hardy. Japanese plums risky in Zone 3.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. (UMN Extension 'Growing apples in the home garden'; UMN Extension 'Growing stone fruits in the home garden')

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Stone fruit harvest runs June through August for most varieties. This month-by-month synthesis of stone fruit harvest windows follows Iowa State University Extension's commercial-orchard reference material on peach, plum, and cherry harvest timing. fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Established plums are light feeders. Young trees benefit from a balanced spring feed. Over-feeding produces sappy growth susceptible to silver leaf disease.

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune to open-center in late winter. Less aggressive than peach -- remove about 20% of growth.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, 'Companion Plants for Aphid Pest Management,' Insects 2018, 9(4):112). The companion application is described by several extensions at home-gardening rigor: Mississippi State University Extension ('Companion planting improves gardens,' Snyder via Reeves) explicitly states 'Chives tend to repel aphids'; Utah State University Extension ('Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting,' Mohr et al.) lists onions, garlic, and chives as repelling common garden pests; UC Cooperative Extension Master Gardener publications (Butte County 'Best Friends in the Garden' and Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects') likewise list allium VOCs among aphid-repellent companions. These extension sources describe the pairing at tradition-plus-plausible-mechanism rigor rather than validated protocol -- the Kansas State Extension / Johnson County 'Companion Planting' page caveats that allium sulfur repellency is 'centralized to the garlic itself -- and only with certain pests.' The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's Pest Notes on aphids (pn7404), which focus on reflective mulches, water sprays, soaps, and natural enemies rather than allium interplanting.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 3-5 days at room temperature to ripen
storage.freezer_seasoned: Halve, remove stone, freeze flat then bag -- good for baking and jam
storage.notes_seasoned: Plums ripen quickly -- check daily once they soften. Freeze any surplus immediately.

varieties.note_seasoned: Methley is self-fertile and very early -- ideal where space allows only one tree.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text_seasoned: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text_seasoned: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 60-100 lbs from a mature standard tree (European plums) or 30-60 lbs (Japanese types)
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors_seasoned: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Japanese-American hybrid developed for cold climates. Large red-skinned fruit with yellow flesh. Requires a pollinator (Toka works well). One of the hardiest named cultivars.
Classic prune-type European plum. Self-pollinating. Dark purple skin, sweet yellow flesh. Excellent for fresh eating, drying, and preserves. Late-blooming reduces frost risk.
Wide-adaptability Japanese plum. Self-pollinating. Red-purple skin, juicy red flesh. Low chill requirement makes it one of few plums that fruits in zone 9.
Heirloom European plum prized for exceptional sweet flavor. Small green-yellow fruit. Self-fertile but better with a pollinator. Considered one of the finest dessert plums.
Most widely planted Japanese plum in the US. Self-pollinating. Reddish-purple skin, amber flesh. Best flavor when tree-ripened. Performs well across a wide climate range.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Stone fruit harvest runs June through August for most varieties. Peaches and nectarines ripen mid-to-late summer; apricots earliest (June-July); sweet cherries June-July; sour cherries July; plums July-September depending on type (Japanese types earlier, European types later). This month-by-month synthesis of stone fruit harvest windows follows Iowa State University Extension's commercial-orchard reference material on peach, plum, and cherry harvest timing. crops.description_seasoned: One of the most adaptable stone fruits. Japanese plums are earlier and sweeter; European plums (including prunes) are later and more cold-hardy. Wide zone range makes plums a great beginner fruit tree.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Slight give when squeezed. Background color change from green to yellow-red. Easy detachment. Sweet aroma.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Plum is a broad category covering three distinct species with different hardiness profiles. European plums (Prunus domestica, e.g., Stanley, Italian, Green Gage) are the most cold-hardy of the fresh-market plums, reliably fruiting in zones 5a-8b with later spring bloom that escapes most frost events. Japanese plums (Prunus salicina, e.g., Santa Rosa, Methley, Shiro) are more cold-sensitive and bloom earlier, making them better-suited to zones 6a-9b where late frosts are less likely. American and American-hybrid plums (e.g., Superior, Toka, Underwood) are the hardiest of all, with some rated to zone 3; these are the right choice for zones 4a-4b where both European and Japanese types struggle. For all types, black knot disease is a significant concern in humid eastern zones -- choose resistant varieties. Most plums require cross-pollination from another compatible variety blooming at the same time; Japanese pollen does not fertilize European flowers.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Japanese plums need less chill than European. Low-chill varieties exist for zone 8+
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Varies by variety. Japanese plums (Santa Rosa, Satsuma) are partially self-fertile but produce better with a partner. European plums (Stanley, Italian) are self-fertile.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Light harvest in year 3 is fine. Remove fruit in years 1-2 to encourage root establishment.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly young, drought tolerant when mature

storage.freezer_seasoned: Halve, stone, freeze flat -- excellent for jam and baking
storage.notes_seasoned: Apricots have the shortest shelf life of stone fruits. Freeze immediately at peak ripeness.

varieties.note_seasoned: Goldcot is the most reliable for northern gardens -- significantly more cold-hardy than Moorpark.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text_seasoned: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text_seasoned: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 80-150 lbs from a mature standard tree, less on dwarf rootstocks
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors_seasoned: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Manchurian-type apricot (Prunus armeniaca mandshurica). One of the cold-hardiest apricots available. Fruit is smaller and less refined than standard cultivars but reliable in the coldest zones. Good for drying, canning, preserves.
Canadian-bred cultivar, considered the go-to apricot for zone 4 growers. Produces good-quality fruit by cold-climate standards. Self-fertile but better with a pollinator. Ripens early August.
Late-blooming cultivar from Canada's Harrow research station. The late bloom significantly reduces spring frost crop losses. Firm, medium-sized orange fruit with good flavor. Self-pollinating.
Classic heirloom apricot, prized for exceptional flavor. Large fruit with distinctive speckled skin. Self-pollinating. Best fresh-eating apricot but susceptible to split stones and uneven ripening.
Low-chill California-bred apricot. For warm climates where standard apricots fail to break dormancy. Large yellow fruit with red blush. Early ripening (May-June). Self-fertile.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.
