crops.description_seasoned: Blooms early -- the earliest of all stone fruits -- making it highly vulnerable to late spring frosts. Site on a north-facing slope or near a building to delay bloom. Worth it when the timing works.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Orange all over, slight give near stem, detaches easily, sweet aroma. Ripen quickly once picked.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Apricots present a significant disconnect between tree survival and fruit production. The tree itself is genuinely cold-hardy -- standard varieties survive to zone 5a, and Manchurian-type apricots (Mandan, Sungold, Moongold) survive to zone 3. However, apricots are notorious early bloomers, often flowering a full month before the official last-frost date. Late spring frosts frequently kill the blossoms even though the tree is unharmed, making reliable crops rare north of zone 6a. In marginal zones, growers report harvesting a full crop only once every 3-5 years. Strategies to improve fruit production include late-blooming varieties (Harglow, Goldrich, Harlayne, Canadian White Blenheim), north-facing siting to delay bloom, and frost-protection coverings during bloom. Apricots need well-drained soil -- they are particularly susceptible to root rot in heavy or wet soils. Most varieties are self-fertile. In warm climates (zones 8-9), low-chill varieties (Katy, Gold Kist, Royal Rosa) are required since standard apricots need 600-900 chill hours to break dormancy properly.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Flowers early -- late frost risk is higher concern than chill hours in most zones
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Most varieties are self-fertile. Some (Perfection, Riland, Rival) require cross-pollination.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Remove blossoms years 1-2. Apricots bloom early and are frost-sensitive -- site selection matters most in year one.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.source_quote_seasoned: The most common mistake novice pear growers make is to let the fruit ripen on the tree. Fruit that ripens on the tree ends up gritty and unpleasant. Instead, fruit should be picked at a mature stage and then allowed to ripen indoors. (UMN Extension)
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: European pear harvest window is August through October in cold and temperate zones, with exact timing by variety. Pick fruit when mature (full size) but still firm, not when fully ripe. Use a gentle lift-and-twist motion to detach the fruit from the spur. Ripen indoors at room temperature for 5 to 10 days, or cold-store winter varieties (Anjou, Bosc, Comice) for 2 to 3 months before ripening. First significant harvest occurs 3 to 5 years after planting per crop-level years_to_first_harvest field. (UMN Extension; UMD Extension; UMaine Extension)

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Light feeder once established. Annual spring application of balanced fertilizer is sufficient for mature trees.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 10-10-10 in spring -- pears need less N than peaches

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune in late winter to central leader shape. Pears are prone to fire blight -- disinfect tools between cuts.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Ground cover effects on soil temperature and moisture are real; specific pairings not well-studied.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The aphid-repellent element is mechanism-plausible: allium sulfur VOCs have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, Insects 2018, 9(4):112) and are described at home-gardening rigor by Mississippi State and USU Extension. However, the 'repel scab fungus' element is mechanism-fabricated. Apple scab (Venturia inaequalis) is a fungal disease whose extension-recommended management (UMN Extension 'Apple scab of apples and crabapples'; Cornell apple IPM guidelines) consists of resistant-variety selection, fallen-leaf sanitation, canopy pruning for rapid leaf-drying, and fungicide timing. No extension source endorses chives or other alliums as a scab management tactic, and there is no documented mechanism by which allium VOCs would suppress a foliar fungal pathogen that requires leaf surface moisture to infect. The scab-repellent claim is folk-remedy framing rather than extension-backed. Downgraded from extension_backed because the composite why-text mixes a mechanism-real aphid component with a mechanism-fabricated scab component.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small entry holes in fruit with brown frass (sawdust-like droppings). Maggot inside apple tunnelling to core. Often mistaken for worm in apple.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella moth. Larvae tunnel into developing fruit from June-August.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pheromone traps to monitor and disrupt mating. Apply kaolin clay to fruit. Remove fallen fruit daily.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Hang pheromone traps from late May. Use sticky tree bands to trap crawling larvae.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoots wilt and turn black/brown. Shepherd's crook shape. Spreads rapidly in warm wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora bacteria. Pears are more susceptible than apples.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune infected wood 12 inches below infection. Sterilize tools. Copper spray before bloom.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Avoid excess nitrogen. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark olive-green/black spots on leaves and fruit. Cracked, deformed fruit.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pirina fungus. Similar to apple scab.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Copper or sulfur fungicide from bud break. Rake and destroy leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Remove leaf debris in autumn.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Pick firm and green, ripen on counter 3-5 days
storage.fridge_seasoned: Once ripe: 3-5 days. Unripe pears: 1-3 months in fridge -- they ripen on removal
storage.freezer_seasoned: Peel, slice, poach lightly and freeze -- good for cooking
storage.notes_seasoned: Never ripen pears on the tree -- pick firm. Fridge storage actually ripens them slowly over months.

varieties.note_seasoned: Conference is the most reliable for backyard growers -- heavy cropper, partial self-fertile, and excellent disease resistance.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted tree planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the soil. Trunk vertical and supported by a stake.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots, same depth. Plant so the graft union is clearly above ground -- if it gets buried, the dwarfing rootstock stops working and the tree gets too big. Stake firmly. Water in deeply.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree planted with graft union above soil?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First buds breaking on the young tree. Slow start -- pome fruits put almost all year-one energy into roots, not visible top growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off all year-one flowers and any fruit that sets. Keep grass and weeds cleared in a 3-foot circle around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Trunk extending. Side branches developing. The early structure of the tree is taking shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pome fruit trees are trained to a central-leader form: one strong vertical trunk with side branches angled outward at roughly 60 to 80 degrees and spaced along it. Pick the first set of side branches about 2 to 3 feet off the ground. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) -- narrow branch angles break under fruit weight.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Main trunk and first side branches chosen?

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight. Tree is fully dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the real pruning happens later. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Mulch deeply around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk. Hold off on major pruning until late winter.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant -- no green tissue, buds tight. Late winter, before bud-break.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain a central-leader form: one dominant vertical leader, with scaffold branches spaced along it. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood first; then crossing branches and water sprouts. Aim for an open, airy canopy.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink-bud opening into white or pale-pink bloom; pollinators active on warm days.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast for frost. Avoid all sprays during bloom -- pollinators are working. If frost is forecast, cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece overnight.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and June Drop
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Petals fall, small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop of excess fruitlets follows in early summer (the 'June drop').
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: After June drop, thin remaining fruit to one per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart. Hand-thinning sets next year's bud quality.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit color shift complete, seeds darkening when sliced (apple), background color shift from green to yellow (pear). Fruit lifts and twists free easily when ready.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick over multiple visits as fruit ripens unevenly. Cup the fruit, lift, and twist; do not pull. Place in baskets gently -- bruises shorten storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves yellowing or dropped; fallen fruit on ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Rake and remove all fallen fruit and leaves. Codling moth larvae and apple/pear scab spores overwinter in this debris. Apply a potassium feed once leaves have dropped to support next year's bud.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Position the graft union -- the swollen knob low on the trunk -- a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake firmly for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the planting hole before the tree goes in to avoid damaging roots later.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season, even in summer rain. Roots have not yet reached out of the planting hole and the original root ball dries quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture and suppress competing weeds. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Choose 3 or 4 scaffold branches evenly spaced up the trunk and around the compass. Remove competing leaders so a single central trunk dominates.
Train scaffolds to wide angles with spreaders or weights. Wide-angled branches are stronger and bear more fruit than narrow upright ones.

dormancy.text_seasoned: First dormancy is when you set the tree's permanent shape. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make every cut clean and just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged cuts and stubs invite disease.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Work the three Ds first: dead, diseased, damaged. Then thin crossing branches and remove inward-pointing growth. The goal is an open canopy that light and spray can reach.
Maintain a central leader: one dominant vertical with scaffolds stepping out and down. On older trees, remove no more than a quarter of total wood in any one winter.

blossom.text_seasoned: Frost during bloom is the single largest risk to the year's crop. Watch the overnight forecast and cover small trees with fleece if frost threatens.
Do not spray anything -- including organic options -- while the tree is in bloom. Pollinators are at work and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin to one fruit per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart, after the June drop has finished. Unthinned trees produce many small fruit and tend toward biennial bearing.
The June drop is the tree shedding what it cannot ripen. It looks alarming but is healthy -- additional hand-thinning is still usually needed afterward.

harvest.text_seasoned: Apples and pears ripen unevenly across the tree. Walk the tree every few days and pick what lifts and twists free with a gentle motion.
Pears finish ripening off the tree -- pick when the background color shifts from deep green toward yellow but the fruit is still firm. Apples ripen on the tree.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves from under the tree. This debris is where codling moth larvae overwinter and where apple/pear scab spores survive to reinfect next spring.
Apply a potassium-rich feed after harvest while leaves are still working. This is the feed that goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 50-150 lbs on a mature dwarf, 150-300 lbs on a mature standard tree
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Dwarf rootstocks bear at year 2 to 4 and reach full production by year 5 to 7. Semi-dwarf and standard trees take longer (year 4 to 8 for first crop, year 8 to 12 for full production) but carry larger crops for far longer.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. Pome fruits are the slowest of the common backyard fruits to come into bearing. Remove any first-year flowers so energy goes to the trunk and scaffold.
factors_seasoned: annual fruit thinning to one fruit per cluster
cross-pollination -- almost all varieties need a different variety nearby
fire blight, codling moth, and apple scab management
rootstock choice (dwarf bears earlier, standard bears longer)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The world's most widely grown pear. Classic bell-shaped yellow fruit. Requires pollinator. Highly susceptible to fire blight -- avoid in humid eastern zones. Best in Pacific Northwest and California.
Long-necked russet-brown pear with sweet-spicy flavor. Excellent for baking and poaching. Moderately fire-blight susceptible. Requires pollinator. Cold-hardier than Bartlett.
Green or red skin varieties. Smooth-textured, mild sweet flavor. Long storage life (up to 6 months). Moderate fire blight resistance. Requires pollinator.
The gift-box gourmet pear. Considered the best-tasting European pear -- rich buttery flavor. Greenish-yellow with red blush. Moderate fire blight resistance. Requires pollinator.

European x Asian hybrid. Strong fire blight resistance, tolerates heat and humidity. Partially self-fertile. Large golden pears best for cooking, canning, preserves. The safest pear for the humid South.
Fire-blight resistant with Bartlett-like quality. Yellow skin with red blush. Good universal pollinator for other European pears. Released by USDA in 1960. Excellent beginner pear.
Small 'sugar pear' -- intensely sweet, snack-size. Late-blooming reduces frost risk. Fire blight resistant. Note: cannot cross-pollinate with Bartlett (shared S-alleles). Pair with Bosc or Anjou.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A frost during bloom kills the open flowers and any fruitlets just set. Apple and pear bloom in early to mid spring, often when frost is still possible. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Watch the overnight forecast through the bloom window and cover small trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. For a frost-prone site, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- bloom timing varies by variety by 1 to 3 weeks.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Codling moth larvae tunnel into apples and pears, leaving small holes with frass at the entry. Apple scab and pear scab cause olive-brown lesions on leaves and fruit. Fire blight on pear blackens shoots from the tip down. These three are the dominant pome problems across the country.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves at the end of each season -- this is where codling moth and scab overwinter. For codling moth, pheromone traps and well-timed sprays during the egg-hatch windows are the standard home-orchard tools. Prune for an open canopy that dries quickly after rain to suppress scab.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most apples and pears need pollen from a different but compatible variety to set fruit. A single tree alone, or two trees of the same variety, will bloom heavily and set little or no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant a second variety with overlapping bloom time within about 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is in range. Crabapple is an effective universal pollinator for apple. For pear, European and Asian pears can cross-pollinate if bloom overlaps.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pome fruit trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoot growth, and dieback that worsens through the season. The roots suffocate and cannot take up water or nutrients, so the tree behaves as if it is drought-stressed even with wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Drainage is set at planting and is hard to improve afterward. If the site holds water, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move to a different site. Avoid amending only the planting hole -- this creates a sump.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pome fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color and sweeten properly. In shade, trees flower and set fruit but the fruit is small, pale, and low in sugar. A dense, unpruned canopy creates the same problem within a sunny site by shading its own interior.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site new trees in full sun. On established trees, prune to open the canopy: remove inward-growing branches and water sprouts so light reaches every fruiting spur. A well-pruned tree in full sun outyields a crowded one of the same age.

crops.description_seasoned: Long-lived, productive tree that outlasts its planter. Harvest slightly underripe and ripen indoors -- tree-ripened pears go mealy. Bartlett, Bosc, and Anjou are the classics. Needs cross-pollination.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pears ripen from the inside out. Pick while still firm and green/yellow. Ripen at room temperature. Check by pressing near the stem -- ready when it yields slightly.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: European pears (Pyrus communis) are hardy across a wide range but fire blight is the defining limitation in humid eastern zones. Susceptible varieties (Bartlett, Bosc) can be killed outright by fire blight in warm humid climates where the bacterial disease thrives. Resistant varieties (Kieffer, Moonglow, Warren, Harrow Delight) are the practical choice for the South and humid Midwest. European pears also require 2-8 weeks of cold storage after harvest before they develop proper flavor and texture -- they ripen from the inside out and are picked green, unlike Asian pears which ripen on the tree. Almost all European pears require cross-pollination with a compatible variety; pollen-incompatible pairs exist (Bartlett and Seckel cannot pollinate each other). Asian pears can cross-pollinate European pears when bloom times overlap. Trees begin bearing in year 4-6 and can produce for 50+ years.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: High chill requirement -- best in zones 4-7
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Partially self-fertile but yields much better with a second variety. Bartlett and Anjou are common pairs.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Remove blossoms years 1-2. Pears are slow -- patience in early years means decades of production.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Slightly heavier feeder than European pears. Feed spring and post-harvest.

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune to central leader or modified central leader in late winter.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Ground cover effects on soil temperature and moisture are real; specific pairings not well-studied.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, 'Companion Plants for Aphid Pest Management,' Insects 2018, 9(4):112). The companion application is described by several extensions at home-gardening rigor: Mississippi State University Extension ('Companion planting improves gardens,' Snyder via Reeves) explicitly states 'Chives tend to repel aphids'; Utah State University Extension ('Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting,' Mohr et al.) lists onions, garlic, and chives as repelling common garden pests; UC Cooperative Extension Master Gardener publications (Butte County 'Best Friends in the Garden' and Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects') likewise list allium VOCs among aphid-repellent companions. These extension sources describe the pairing at tradition-plus-plausible-mechanism rigor rather than validated protocol -- the Kansas State Extension / Johnson County 'Companion Planting' page caveats that allium sulfur repellency is 'centralized to the garlic itself -- and only with certain pests.' The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's Pest Notes on aphids (pn7404), which focus on reflective mulches, water sprays, soaps, and natural enemies rather than allium interplanting.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Codling moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small entry holes in fruit with brown frass (sawdust-like droppings). Maggot inside apple tunnelling to core. Often mistaken for worm in apple.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cydia pomonella moth. Larvae tunnel into developing fruit from June-August.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Pheromone traps to monitor and disrupt mating. Apply kaolin clay to fruit. Remove fallen fruit daily.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Hang pheromone traps from late May. Use sticky tree bands to trap crawling larvae.

diseases.name: Fire blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Blossoms and shoots wilt and turn black/brown. Shepherd's crook shape. Spreads rapidly in warm wet weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Erwinia amylovora bacteria. Pears are more susceptible than apples.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune infected wood 12 inches below infection. Sterilize tools. Copper spray before bloom.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Avoid excess nitrogen. Improve airflow.

diseases.name: Pear scab
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark olive-green/black spots on leaves and fruit. Cracked, deformed fruit.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Venturia pirina fungus. Similar to apple scab.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Copper or sulfur fungicide from bud break. Rake and destroy leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties. Remove leaf debris in autumn.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Ripe off tree -- eat within 1-2 weeks
storage.fridge_seasoned: Up to 3 months -- Asian pears keep much longer than European
storage.freezer_seasoned: Slice and freeze for cooking
storage.notes_seasoned: Asian pears are crisp and ready to eat right off the tree, unlike European pears.

varieties.note_seasoned: Hosui is consistently rated the best-tasting Asian pear -- needs a second variety for pollination.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted tree planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the soil. Trunk vertical and supported by a stake.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots, same depth. Plant so the graft union is clearly above ground -- if it gets buried, the dwarfing rootstock stops working and the tree gets too big. Stake firmly. Water in deeply.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree planted with graft union above soil?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First buds breaking on the young tree. Slow start -- pome fruits put almost all year-one energy into roots, not visible top growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off all year-one flowers and any fruit that sets. Keep grass and weeds cleared in a 3-foot circle around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Trunk extending. Side branches developing. The early structure of the tree is taking shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pome fruit trees are trained to a central-leader form: one strong vertical trunk with side branches angled outward at roughly 60 to 80 degrees and spaced along it. Pick the first set of side branches about 2 to 3 feet off the ground. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) -- narrow branch angles break under fruit weight.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Main trunk and first side branches chosen?

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight. Tree is fully dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the real pruning happens later. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Mulch deeply around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk. Hold off on major pruning until late winter.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant -- no green tissue, buds tight. Late winter, before bud-break.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain a central-leader form: one dominant vertical leader, with scaffold branches spaced along it. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood first; then crossing branches and water sprouts. Aim for an open, airy canopy.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink-bud opening into white or pale-pink bloom; pollinators active on warm days.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast for frost. Avoid all sprays during bloom -- pollinators are working. If frost is forecast, cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece overnight.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and June Drop
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Petals fall, small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop of excess fruitlets follows in early summer (the 'June drop').
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: After June drop, thin remaining fruit to one per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart. Hand-thinning sets next year's bud quality.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit color shift complete, seeds darkening when sliced (apple), background color shift from green to yellow (pear). Fruit lifts and twists free easily when ready.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick over multiple visits as fruit ripens unevenly. Cup the fruit, lift, and twist; do not pull. Place in baskets gently -- bruises shorten storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves yellowing or dropped; fallen fruit on ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Rake and remove all fallen fruit and leaves. Codling moth larvae and apple/pear scab spores overwinter in this debris. Apply a potassium feed once leaves have dropped to support next year's bud.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Position the graft union -- the swollen knob low on the trunk -- a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake firmly for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the planting hole before the tree goes in to avoid damaging roots later.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season, even in summer rain. Roots have not yet reached out of the planting hole and the original root ball dries quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture and suppress competing weeds. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Choose 3 or 4 scaffold branches evenly spaced up the trunk and around the compass. Remove competing leaders so a single central trunk dominates.
Train scaffolds to wide angles with spreaders or weights. Wide-angled branches are stronger and bear more fruit than narrow upright ones.

dormancy.text_seasoned: First dormancy is when you set the tree's permanent shape. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make every cut clean and just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged cuts and stubs invite disease.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Work the three Ds first: dead, diseased, damaged. Then thin crossing branches and remove inward-pointing growth. The goal is an open canopy that light and spray can reach.
Maintain a central leader: one dominant vertical with scaffolds stepping out and down. On older trees, remove no more than a quarter of total wood in any one winter.

blossom.text_seasoned: Frost during bloom is the single largest risk to the year's crop. Watch the overnight forecast and cover small trees with fleece if frost threatens.
Do not spray anything -- including organic options -- while the tree is in bloom. Pollinators are at work and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin to one fruit per cluster, spaced about 6 inches apart, after the June drop has finished. Unthinned trees produce many small fruit and tend toward biennial bearing.
The June drop is the tree shedding what it cannot ripen. It looks alarming but is healthy -- additional hand-thinning is still usually needed afterward.

harvest.text_seasoned: Apples and pears ripen unevenly across the tree. Walk the tree every few days and pick what lifts and twists free with a gentle motion.
Pears finish ripening off the tree -- pick when the background color shifts from deep green toward yellow but the fruit is still firm. Apples ripen on the tree.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves from under the tree. This debris is where codling moth larvae overwinter and where apple/pear scab spores survive to reinfect next spring.
Apply a potassium-rich feed after harvest while leaves are still working. This is the feed that goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 100-300 lbs on a mature standard tree, with each fruit larger and heavier than European pears
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Dwarf rootstocks bear at year 2 to 4 and reach full production by year 5 to 7. Semi-dwarf and standard trees take longer (year 4 to 8 for first crop, year 8 to 12 for full production) but carry larger crops for far longer.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. Pome fruits are the slowest of the common backyard fruits to come into bearing. Remove any first-year flowers so energy goes to the trunk and scaffold.
factors_seasoned: annual fruit thinning to one fruit per cluster
cross-pollination -- almost all varieties need a different variety nearby
fire blight, codling moth, and apple scab management
rootstock choice (dwarf bears earlier, standard bears longer)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Most popular Asian pear in the US. Large russeted golden fruit with brandy-like aroma and low acid. Bears young. Susceptible to fire blight despite Asian pear reputation. Partially self-fertile; better with Shinseiki or 20th Century as pollinator.
Yellow-skinned, crisp, mild-flavored fruit. Self-fertile (one of the few). Moderate fire blight resistance. Vigorous, reliable producer. Good beginner Asian pear. Ripens late August.
World's most widely-grown Asian pear. Yellow-green skin, juicy sweet-tart flesh. Self-fertile. Stores 4-5 months refrigerated. Fire-blight susceptible. Excellent cold hardiness for an Asian pear.

Old variety with distinctive butterscotch flavor. Russeted brown skin, flat shape. Moderate fire blight resistance. Stores up to 5 months. Earliest-blooming Asian pear -- pairs well with Anjou for pollination.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A frost during bloom kills the open flowers and any fruitlets just set. Apple and pear bloom in early to mid spring, often when frost is still possible. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Watch the overnight forecast through the bloom window and cover small trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. For a frost-prone site, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- bloom timing varies by variety by 1 to 3 weeks.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Codling moth larvae tunnel into apples and pears, leaving small holes with frass at the entry. Apple scab and pear scab cause olive-brown lesions on leaves and fruit. Fire blight on pear blackens shoots from the tip down. These three are the dominant pome problems across the country.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Clear all fallen fruit and leaves at the end of each season -- this is where codling moth and scab overwinter. For codling moth, pheromone traps and well-timed sprays during the egg-hatch windows are the standard home-orchard tools. Prune for an open canopy that dries quickly after rain to suppress scab.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most apples and pears need pollen from a different but compatible variety to set fruit. A single tree alone, or two trees of the same variety, will bloom heavily and set little or no fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant a second variety with overlapping bloom time within about 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is in range. Crabapple is an effective universal pollinator for apple. For pear, European and Asian pears can cross-pollinate if bloom overlaps.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pome fruit trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoot growth, and dieback that worsens through the season. The roots suffocate and cannot take up water or nutrients, so the tree behaves as if it is drought-stressed even with wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Drainage is set at planting and is hard to improve afterward. If the site holds water, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move to a different site. Avoid amending only the planting hole -- this creates a sump.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pome fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color and sweeten properly. In shade, trees flower and set fruit but the fruit is small, pale, and low in sugar. A dense, unpruned canopy creates the same problem within a sunny site by shading its own interior.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site new trees in full sun. On established trees, prune to open the canopy: remove inward-growing branches and water sprouts so light reaches every fruiting spur. A well-pruned tree in full sun outyields a crowded one of the same age.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. (UMN Extension 'Growing apples in the home garden'; UMN Extension 'Growing stone fruits in the home garden')

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Asian pears ripen on the tree unlike European pears. Harvest when fruit is fully colored (green to yellow, hazel, or golden depending on variety) and the skin is fragrant; Asian pears can be eaten immediately after picking. (USU Extension Asian Pear; UMN Extension Pear) Asian pear harvest window is August through October in cold and temperate zones. Unlike European pears, Asian varieties ripen fully on the tree and do not require a post-harvest ripening period. Test ripeness by smell (fresh and fruity) and by tasting a sample fruit. First significant harvest occurs 3 to 5 years after planting per crop-level years_to_first_harvest field. (USU Extension; UMN Extension)

crops.description_seasoned: Apple-like texture, crisp and sweet. Harvested tree-ripe (unlike European pears). Earlier bearing than European pears -- often fruit in 2-3 years. Shinseiki and 20th Century are popular varieties.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Asian pears ripen on the tree unlike European. Pick when full sized and colored. Should feel crisp and heavy.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Asian pears (Pyrus pyrifolia) are crisp like apples rather than buttery like European pears, and ripen on the tree rather than off. They have generally lower chill requirements (300-600 hours) than European pears, making them more adaptable to zones 8-9. They also have better fire blight resistance as a group, though no Asian pear is truly immune. Most are partially self-fertile but produce significantly larger crops with a compatible pollinator -- Asian pears can cross-pollinate each other or compatible European pears (Bartlett and 20th Century have overlapping bloom, Chojuro blooms with Anjou). Asian pears bruise easily and don't ship well, which makes them a home-garden-favorable fruit that rarely appears in grocery stores. Trees begin bearing in year 3-4, earlier than European pears. Prune aggressively -- Asian pears set more fruit than the tree can properly size without thinning.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Lower chill than European pears -- better suited to zones 6-9
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Partially self-fertile. Two varieties recommended for best yields. Can cross-pollinate with European pear if bloom times overlap.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Remove blossoms in year one. Asian pears fruit sooner than European but still benefit from early restraint.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Flat brown or white waxy lumps on stems and leaves. Sooty black mold follows from honeydew. Leaves yellow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Various scale species. Common on indoor/container citrus.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scrape off by hand. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap. Horticultural oil spray in winter.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect regularly. Keep plants healthy and well-fed. Good air circulation.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Mottled yellow-green leaves in blotchy pattern. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Tree slowly declines. No cure.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Candidatus Liberibacter bacteria spread by Asian citrus psyllid insect. A devastating citrus disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove affected trees.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control Asian citrus psyllid with neem oil or spinosad. Inspect purchased trees before planting.

diseases.name: Root rot (Phytophthora)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow leaves, declining vigor, branch dieback. Bark at soil line may show brown discoloration.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged or poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Apply phosphonate fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Well-drained soil essential. Never let roots sit in water. Graft onto resistant rootstock.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Juice in ice cube trays. Zest separately.

varieties.note_seasoned: Persian Lime is the standard supermarket lime -- seedless and productive. Key Lime has more intense flavor but smaller fruit.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Buy as a container plant. Harden off if moving from indoors to outdoors in spring. In zones below 9, grow in a large pot and bring indoors before first frost.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Container-grown tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil level. Trunk often staked briefly to support against wind.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole the same depth as the rootball but twice as wide. Plant high -- the top of the rootball should sit slightly above ground level. Don't add fertilizer at planting. Water deeply, then mulch around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves emerging in the first weeks after planting. Citrus pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist (not soggy) through year one. Begin a light citrus-specific feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers so the tree builds its leafy canopy before fruiting.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree filling out with leaves and side branches. Canopy taking shape; some shoots may appear from below the graft union.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus needs almost no training -- it builds its own canopy. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union and any tall vertical shoots from inside the canopy. Keep pruning light; citrus fruits at the outer edges of the canopy, so a dense outer leaf surface matters more than a defined branch structure.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Citrus does not lose its leaves -- it's evergreen. Growth slows in cool weather, foliage may darken slightly, and the tree holds its shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. In marginal zones, watch overnight forecasts and protect with frost cloth or warm holiday lights when temperatures approach 28°F. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball go bone-dry.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After main harvest, before spring flush. Citrus does not truly go dormant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light shape pruning: remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, water sprouts, crossing branches. Avoid heavy heading -- citrus fruits at the canopy edge.

growth_stages.name: Main Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Honey-scented spring bloom. Smaller flushes possible in summer or fall on healthy trees.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avoid sprays during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruit forming after petal fall. Heavy early-summer drop is the tree shedding excess set, normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus is self-fertile; no thinning needed in most cases. Maintain consistent moisture to limit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Variable -- some types ripen for months. Citrus does not ripen off the tree; pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which tears bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Main harvest done. Tree preparing for next bloom flush.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, with iron, zinc, manganese micronutrients). Inspect for scale and consider a horticultural oil application.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Citrus is grafted on rootstock chosen for cold tolerance, disease resistance, and tree size. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions defeat the purpose of the rootstock and invite Phytophthora.
Plant in spring once soil is reliably above 60 degrees. Skip nitrogen fertilizer in the planting hole; a thin layer of compost is enough.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Citrus has shallow roots and dries out faster than other tree fruit -- but also rots faster in standing water. Aim for evenly moist, never soggy.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Citrus collar and crown rot from Phytophthora is the single most common young-tree killer.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Citrus is grown as a balanced canopy or hedge form, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- those are where most of the fruit will come from.
Remove suckers from below the graft union immediately. Rootstock suckers grow fast and have wicked thorns; left in place they take over the tree.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Citrus does not have true dormancy -- it is evergreen and grows year-round wherever frost does not knock it back. There is no winter pruning window in the way deciduous fruit has.
In the colder end of citrus range, freeze protection (frost cloth, string lights, banking soil around the trunk) is the winter task rather than pruning.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Citrus pruning is light and shape-focused, done after the main harvest in late winter or early spring before new growth. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts, and crossing branches.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Citrus fruits on previous and current-year growth at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Citrus often blooms multiple times per year. The main bloom in spring is the largest, but a healthy tree may also flush in summer or fall. Honey-scented flowers are normal.
Do not spray insecticide during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most citrus is self-fertile and a single tree fruits well. Some mandarin varieties are seedy when cross-pollinated and seedless when isolated -- check your variety preference.
Heavy fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent drop later in the season usually indicates water stress.

harvest.text_seasoned: Citrus does not ripen off the tree. Pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors -- many citrus types color before they are sweet, and others stay green when ripe.
Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which can tear bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, micronutrients including iron, zinc, manganese) after the main harvest. Citrus is heavier-feeding than other fruit trees.
Inspect for scale and ant trails year-round; the post-harvest window is a good time for a horticultural-oil application before the next bloom.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 20-50 lbs from a mature dooryard tree, smaller fruit but heavy bearer
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Grafted citrus typically reaches full production in 3 to 5 years and stays productive for decades. Many varieties hold ripe fruit on the tree for months, so harvest is often a slow steady pick rather than a single window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Light or no fruit in year one is normal. Grafted citrus can flower early; remove early blossoms in year one so the tree builds canopy and roots first.
factors_seasoned: consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set
nitrogen feeding split across the year
iron and zinc availability (citrus leaves yellow when these are deficient)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Thornless commercial standard Persian lime. Large seedless green fruit. Self-fertile. More cold-hardy than Key lime. The practical choice for California and Florida home growers.

Classic small yellow-green lime with intense aromatic flavor. Thorny shrubby tree. Self-fertile. The true Key lime from Key Lime Pie fame. Less cold-hardy than Bearss -- Florida Keys and South Florida only.

Grown primarily for aromatic leaves used in Thai and Southeast Asian cooking. Distinctive double-lobed leaves. Small bumpy fruit is minimally juicy. Self-fertile. Essential herb tree for Asian cooking.

Lime x kumquat hybrid -- much more cold-hardy than true limes, surviving to about 20°F. Small oval yellow fruit with lime-like flavor. Self-fertile. The only way to grow a lime-flavored fruit in zones 8-9.
Sweet non-acidic lime, eaten like an orange rather than juiced. Yellow-green skin. Popular in Middle Eastern and South Asian cuisines. Self-fertile. Interesting specialty citrus.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus is evergreen and does not become fully dormant, so freeze damage is a whole-tree phenomenon (leaves, twigs, fruit) rather than the blossom-frost issue deciduous fruit faces. Lemons and limes are most cold-sensitive (damaged below about 30 degrees); oranges and grapefruit tolerate brief drops to about 26 degrees; mandarins are typically the hardiest. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split or mushy fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights and string old-style incandescent lights through the canopy if possible. Bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties (satsuma mandarin, kumquat, calamondin) or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Scale insects (cottony cushion scale, citrus mealybug, California red scale) and Asian citrus psyllid are the dominant citrus pests. Asian citrus psyllid spreads Huanglongbing (HLB, citrus greening), the disease threatening commercial citrus in Florida, Texas, and California. Phytophthora root and crown rot kills more young trees than any insect.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Inspect for scale year-round and treat with horticultural oil. In HLB-affected areas, follow your state's quarantine guidance; healthy trees on resistant rootstock and aggressive psyllid control are the home-garden defense. For Phytophthora prevention, keep mulch off the trunk and avoid overwatering.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most citrus is self-fertile -- a single tree should fruit well. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often a water-stress, temperature-extreme, or alternate-bearing issue than a pollination one. Some mandarin varieties produce seedless fruit only when isolated from other citrus.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set. If the tree blooms heavily one year and barely the next, it is alternate-bearing -- thinning fruit in the heavy year levels the cycle out. Avoid moving citrus during bloom; flowers and small fruit drop from stress.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus is more prone to Phytophthora than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in waterlogged soil and at the trunk-soil interface. Symptoms are yellowing leaves with green veins, dieback, gum oozing from the lower trunk, and bark that lifts off the wood at the base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on a raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Keep mulch a hand-width back from the trunk. Water deeply but infrequently, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. There is no good cure once Phytophthora is established.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to develop sugar and color. In shade the tree grows leaves and may bloom but fruit stays small, sour, and green. South or southwest exposure is ideal in most US citrus zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun -- if a wall or building is reflecting heat, even better. Light pruning to keep the inside of the canopy open helps inner fruit ripen. In containers, rotate the pot a quarter turn every few weeks for even growth.

crops.description_seasoned: More cold-sensitive than lemon. Persian lime is most common (seedless, thornless); Key lime is smaller but more flavorful. Container growing works well in cooler zones -- bring indoors in winter.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick green when full sized and slightly yielding. Limes can be left to turn yellow for more juice.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Limes (Citrus aurantiifolia and C. latifolia) are the least cold-hardy common citrus -- leaves are damaged at 30°F, trees killed at 24-28°F. True Key limes (C. aurantiifolia) are more cold-sensitive than Persian/Bearss limes (C. latifolia). In zones 8-9, grow in containers and move indoors for winter. Limes are year-round producers in true tropical conditions but have a strong winter/spring harvest peak in subtropical zones. Most limes are self-fertile. Key limes are thorny, small-fruited, and have the classic intense lime flavor; Persian limes are thornless, larger, less acidic, and are the commercial standard. The Kaffir lime is grown for its leaves (used in Thai cooking) rather than its fruit. Lime trees are smaller than lemon trees (10-15 feet) and work well in containers. Begin bearing in year 3-4 from grafted trees.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: No chill requirement -- among the least cold-hardy citrus
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile.

tasks.description_seasoned: Light prune after harvest. Remove suckers, dead wood, and branches growing into canopy center.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.
