pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Flat brown or white waxy lumps on stems and leaves. Sooty black mold follows from honeydew. Leaves yellow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Various scale species. Common on indoor/container citrus.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scrape off by hand. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap. Horticultural oil spray in winter.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect regularly. Keep plants healthy and well-fed. Good air circulation.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Mottled yellow-green leaves in blotchy pattern. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Tree slowly declines. No cure.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Candidatus Liberibacter bacteria spread by Asian citrus psyllid insect. A devastating citrus disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove affected trees.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control Asian citrus psyllid with neem oil or spinosad. Inspect purchased trees before planting.

diseases.name: Root rot (Phytophthora)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow leaves, declining vigor, branch dieback. Bark at soil line may show brown discoloration.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged or poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Apply phosphonate fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Well-drained soil essential. Never let roots sit in water. Graft onto resistant rootstock.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Juice in ice cube trays. Segments freeze well.
storage.notes_seasoned: Navel oranges have the thickest peel and best keeping quality of citrus.

varieties.note_seasoned: Cara Cara is gaining rapidly in popularity -- pink flesh with low acidity and a distinctive berry note.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Buy as a container plant. Harden off if moving from indoors to outdoors in spring. In zones below 9, grow in a large pot and bring indoors before first frost.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container plants in cold climates -- bring indoors before frost. Use citrus-specific potting mix. 15-gallon minimum for productive fruiting.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Container-grown tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil level. Trunk often staked briefly to support against wind.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole the same depth as the rootball but twice as wide. Plant high -- the top of the rootball should sit slightly above ground level. Don't add fertilizer at planting. Water deeply, then mulch around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves emerging in the first weeks after planting. Citrus pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist (not soggy) through year one. Begin a light citrus-specific feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers so the tree builds its leafy canopy before fruiting.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree filling out with leaves and side branches. Canopy taking shape; some shoots may appear from below the graft union.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus needs almost no training -- it builds its own canopy. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union and any tall vertical shoots from inside the canopy. Keep pruning light; citrus fruits at the outer edges of the canopy, so a dense outer leaf surface matters more than a defined branch structure.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Citrus does not lose its leaves -- it's evergreen. Growth slows in cool weather, foliage may darken slightly, and the tree holds its shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. In marginal zones, watch overnight forecasts and protect with frost cloth or warm holiday lights when temperatures approach 28°F. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball go bone-dry.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After main harvest, before spring flush. Citrus does not truly go dormant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light shape pruning: remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, water sprouts, crossing branches. Avoid heavy heading -- citrus fruits at the canopy edge.

growth_stages.name: Main Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Honey-scented spring bloom. Smaller flushes possible in summer or fall on healthy trees.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avoid sprays during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruit forming after petal fall. Heavy early-summer drop is the tree shedding excess set, normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus is self-fertile; no thinning needed in most cases. Maintain consistent moisture to limit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Variable -- some types ripen for months. Citrus does not ripen off the tree; pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which tears bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Main harvest done. Tree preparing for next bloom flush.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, with iron, zinc, manganese micronutrients). Inspect for scale and consider a horticultural oil application.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Citrus is grafted on rootstock chosen for cold tolerance, disease resistance, and tree size. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions defeat the purpose of the rootstock and invite Phytophthora.
Plant in spring once soil is reliably above 60 degrees. Skip nitrogen fertilizer in the planting hole; a thin layer of compost is enough.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Citrus has shallow roots and dries out faster than other tree fruit -- but also rots faster in standing water. Aim for evenly moist, never soggy.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Citrus collar and crown rot from Phytophthora is the single most common young-tree killer.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Citrus is grown as a balanced canopy or hedge form, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- those are where most of the fruit will come from.
Remove suckers from below the graft union immediately. Rootstock suckers grow fast and have wicked thorns; left in place they take over the tree.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Citrus does not have true dormancy -- it is evergreen and grows year-round wherever frost does not knock it back. There is no winter pruning window in the way deciduous fruit has.
In the colder end of citrus range, freeze protection (frost cloth, string lights, banking soil around the trunk) is the winter task rather than pruning.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Citrus pruning is light and shape-focused, done after the main harvest in late winter or early spring before new growth. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts, and crossing branches.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Citrus fruits on previous and current-year growth at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Citrus often blooms multiple times per year. The main bloom in spring is the largest, but a healthy tree may also flush in summer or fall. Honey-scented flowers are normal.
Do not spray insecticide during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most citrus is self-fertile and a single tree fruits well. Some mandarin varieties are seedy when cross-pollinated and seedless when isolated -- check your variety preference.
Heavy fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent drop later in the season usually indicates water stress.

harvest.text_seasoned: Citrus does not ripen off the tree. Pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors -- many citrus types color before they are sweet, and others stay green when ripe.
Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which can tear bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, micronutrients including iron, zinc, manganese) after the main harvest. Citrus is heavier-feeding than other fruit trees.
Inspect for scale and ant trails year-round; the post-harvest window is a good time for a horticultural-oil application before the next bloom.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 100-200 lbs from a mature dooryard tree at full production
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Grafted citrus typically reaches full production in 3 to 5 years and stays productive for decades. Many varieties hold ripe fruit on the tree for months, so harvest is often a slow steady pick rather than a single window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Light or no fruit in year one is normal. Grafted citrus can flower early; remove early blossoms in year one so the tree builds canopy and roots first.
factors_seasoned: consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set
nitrogen feeding split across the year
iron and zinc availability (citrus leaves yellow when these are deficient)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The original navel orange (1870s California). Large seedless fruit with classic flavor. Peak ripeness December-February. Self-fertile by nature. The commercial standard for winter-harvest oranges in California.
Pink-fleshed navel with berry-like flavor notes. Medium-large fruit. Same ripening period as Washington (December-February). Self-fertile. Popular premium variety at farmers markets.
Earlier-ripening navel (October-December). Heavy bearing. Self-fertile. Good for growers wanting fresh oranges before the Washington navel season.
Late-ripening navel (March-June). Extends the navel orange season. Fruit holds on the tree for months. Self-fertile. Plant alongside Washington for continuous harvest fall through summer.
Technically not a navel -- a true sweet orange. Summer harvest (May-October). Excellent juice orange. Self-fertile. Pair with a Washington navel for year-round oranges from just two trees.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus is evergreen and does not become fully dormant, so freeze damage is a whole-tree phenomenon (leaves, twigs, fruit) rather than the blossom-frost issue deciduous fruit faces. Lemons and limes are most cold-sensitive (damaged below about 30 degrees); oranges and grapefruit tolerate brief drops to about 26 degrees; mandarins are typically the hardiest. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split or mushy fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights and string old-style incandescent lights through the canopy if possible. Bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties (satsuma mandarin, kumquat, calamondin) or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Scale insects (cottony cushion scale, citrus mealybug, California red scale) and Asian citrus psyllid are the dominant citrus pests. Asian citrus psyllid spreads Huanglongbing (HLB, citrus greening), the disease threatening commercial citrus in Florida, Texas, and California. Phytophthora root and crown rot kills more young trees than any insect.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Inspect for scale year-round and treat with horticultural oil. In HLB-affected areas, follow your state's quarantine guidance; healthy trees on resistant rootstock and aggressive psyllid control are the home-garden defense. For Phytophthora prevention, keep mulch off the trunk and avoid overwatering.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most citrus is self-fertile -- a single tree should fruit well. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often a water-stress, temperature-extreme, or alternate-bearing issue than a pollination one. Some mandarin varieties produce seedless fruit only when isolated from other citrus.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set. If the tree blooms heavily one year and barely the next, it is alternate-bearing -- thinning fruit in the heavy year levels the cycle out. Avoid moving citrus during bloom; flowers and small fruit drop from stress.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus is more prone to Phytophthora than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in waterlogged soil and at the trunk-soil interface. Symptoms are yellowing leaves with green veins, dieback, gum oozing from the lower trunk, and bark that lifts off the wood at the base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on a raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Keep mulch a hand-width back from the trunk. Water deeply but infrequently, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. There is no good cure once Phytophthora is established.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to develop sugar and color. In shade the tree grows leaves and may bloom but fruit stays small, sour, and green. South or southwest exposure is ideal in most US citrus zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun -- if a wall or building is reflecting heat, even better. Light pruning to keep the inside of the canopy open helps inner fruit ripen. In containers, rotate the pot a quarter turn every few weeks for even growth.

crops.description_seasoned: Classic seedless eating orange. Needs warm days, cool nights, and a long growing season to develop sweetness. Washington Navel is most widely grown. Harvest Dec-Apr for peak flavor.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deep orange skin, heavy for size. Taste is the best test -- a navel that looks orange can still be tart inside.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Navel oranges (Citrus sinensis) are moderately cold-hardy among citrus -- mature trees tolerate 20-22°F, making them viable in zones 8b-9a with protection. Navels are the winter-eating orange (peel-and-eat, no juice); Valencia oranges are the juice orange (tougher peel, more juice, summer harvest). Navels produce seedless fruit because the flowers cannot produce viable pollen -- they are seedless by nature. This also means they're self-fertile by definition (no pollination needed). They set fruit from late fall through early winter, with the classic winter-holiday ripening pattern. Cold stress actually improves flavor by increasing sugar content -- warm climates like Florida produce less-flavorful navel oranges than cooler climates like California. Trees are sensitive to wet feet and alkaline soils. Most commercial navels are grafted on trifoliate orange rootstock which increases cold-hardiness by 5-10°F. Begin bearing year 3-5.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Minimal chill -- suited to zones 9-11
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Navel oranges are seedless because they are parthenocarpic.

tasks.description_seasoned: Light prune in early spring. Remove dead wood, suckers, and branches below the graft union.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Flat brown or white waxy lumps on stems and leaves. Sooty black mold follows from honeydew. Leaves yellow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Various scale species. Common on indoor/container citrus.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Scrape off by hand. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap. Horticultural oil spray in winter.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect regularly. Keep plants healthy and well-fed. Good air circulation.

pests.name: Spider mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Fine stippling or yellow dots on leaves. Fine webbing on leaf undersides. Leaves may bronze, dry out, and drop. Worst in hot dry weather.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetranychus urticae and related species. Thrives in heat and drought.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water repeatedly. Apply neem oil or insecticidal soap to leaf undersides. Increase humidity around plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep plants well-watered in hot weather. Avoid dusty conditions. Introduce predatory mites.

diseases.name: Citrus greening (HLB)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Mottled yellow-green leaves in blotchy pattern. Small, lopsided, bitter fruit. Tree slowly declines. No cure.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Candidatus Liberibacter bacteria spread by Asian citrus psyllid insect. A devastating citrus disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove affected trees.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control Asian citrus psyllid with neem oil or spinosad. Inspect purchased trees before planting.

diseases.name: Root rot (Phytophthora)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow leaves, declining vigor, branch dieback. Bark at soil line may show brown discoloration.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged or poorly drained soil.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve drainage. Avoid overwatering. Apply phosphonate fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Well-drained soil essential. Never let roots sit in water. Graft onto resistant rootstock.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze peeled segments -- good for smoothies
storage.notes_seasoned: Mandarins dry out faster than oranges. Best eaten fresh within 1 week.

varieties.note_seasoned: Owari Satsuma is the most cold-hardy mandarin -- reliable in zones 7-8 where most citrus fails.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Buy as a container plant. Harden off if moving from indoors to outdoors in spring. In zones below 9, grow in a large pot and bring indoors before first frost.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container plants in cold climates -- bring indoors before frost. Use citrus-specific potting mix. 15-gallon minimum for productive fruiting.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Container-grown tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil level. Trunk often staked briefly to support against wind.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole the same depth as the rootball but twice as wide. Plant high -- the top of the rootball should sit slightly above ground level. Don't add fertilizer at planting. Water deeply, then mulch around the base, keeping mulch a few inches off the trunk.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves emerging in the first weeks after planting. Citrus pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist (not soggy) through year one. Begin a light citrus-specific feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers so the tree builds its leafy canopy before fruiting.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree filling out with leaves and side branches. Canopy taking shape; some shoots may appear from below the graft union.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus needs almost no training -- it builds its own canopy. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union and any tall vertical shoots from inside the canopy. Keep pruning light; citrus fruits at the outer edges of the canopy, so a dense outer leaf surface matters more than a defined branch structure.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Citrus does not lose its leaves -- it's evergreen. Growth slows in cool weather, foliage may darken slightly, and the tree holds its shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. In marginal zones, watch overnight forecasts and protect with frost cloth or warm holiday lights when temperatures approach 28°F. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball go bone-dry.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After main harvest, before spring flush. Citrus does not truly go dormant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light shape pruning: remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, water sprouts, crossing branches. Avoid heavy heading -- citrus fruits at the canopy edge.

growth_stages.name: Main Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Honey-scented spring bloom. Smaller flushes possible in summer or fall on healthy trees.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avoid sprays during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruit forming after petal fall. Heavy early-summer drop is the tree shedding excess set, normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Citrus is self-fertile; no thinning needed in most cases. Maintain consistent moisture to limit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Variable -- some types ripen for months. Citrus does not ripen off the tree; pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which tears bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Main harvest done. Tree preparing for next bloom flush.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, with iron, zinc, manganese micronutrients). Inspect for scale and consider a horticultural oil application.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Citrus is grafted on rootstock chosen for cold tolerance, disease resistance, and tree size. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions defeat the purpose of the rootstock and invite Phytophthora.
Plant in spring once soil is reliably above 60 degrees. Skip nitrogen fertilizer in the planting hole; a thin layer of compost is enough.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Citrus has shallow roots and dries out faster than other tree fruit -- but also rots faster in standing water. Aim for evenly moist, never soggy.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Citrus collar and crown rot from Phytophthora is the single most common young-tree killer.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Citrus is grown as a balanced canopy or hedge form, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- those are where most of the fruit will come from.
Remove suckers from below the graft union immediately. Rootstock suckers grow fast and have wicked thorns; left in place they take over the tree.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Citrus does not have true dormancy -- it is evergreen and grows year-round wherever frost does not knock it back. There is no winter pruning window in the way deciduous fruit has.
In the colder end of citrus range, freeze protection (frost cloth, string lights, banking soil around the trunk) is the winter task rather than pruning.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Citrus pruning is light and shape-focused, done after the main harvest in late winter or early spring before new growth. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts, and crossing branches.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Citrus fruits on previous and current-year growth at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Citrus often blooms multiple times per year. The main bloom in spring is the largest, but a healthy tree may also flush in summer or fall. Honey-scented flowers are normal.
Do not spray insecticide during bloom. The smell brings pollinators from a distance.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most citrus is self-fertile and a single tree fruits well. Some mandarin varieties are seedy when cross-pollinated and seedless when isolated -- check your variety preference.
Heavy fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent drop later in the season usually indicates water stress.

harvest.text_seasoned: Citrus does not ripen off the tree. Pick when the fruit tastes right, not when it colors -- many citrus types color before they are sweet, and others stay green when ripe.
Use clippers or a gentle twist; do not pull, which can tear bark. Most citrus can hang on the tree for weeks or months once ripe -- treat the tree as the storage.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Apply citrus-specific fertilizer (higher in nitrogen, micronutrients including iron, zinc, manganese) after the main harvest. Citrus is heavier-feeding than other fruit trees.
Inspect for scale and ant trails year-round; the post-harvest window is a good time for a horticultural-oil application before the next bloom.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 50-100 lbs from a mature dooryard tree, often with a concentrated winter harvest window
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Grafted citrus typically reaches full production in 3 to 5 years and stays productive for decades. Many varieties hold ripe fruit on the tree for months, so harvest is often a slow steady pick rather than a single window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Light or no fruit in year one is normal. Grafted citrus can flower early; remove early blossoms in year one so the tree builds canopy and roots first.
factors_seasoned: consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set
nitrogen feeding split across the year
iron and zinc availability (citrus leaves yellow when these are deficient)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Most cold-hardy sweet citrus -- survives to 15°F when mature. Loose-peeled easy-peeling fruit ripens October-December. Essentially seedless. Self-fertile. The go-to citrus for the Gulf Coast and zone 8 growers.
Small very sweet fruit with loose peel. The 'Cuties' marketing name. Requires cross-pollination for heavy bearing. Sensitive to heat and humidity -- best in Mediterranean climates.
Classic Christmas tangerine. Deep red-orange skin and flesh, tight peel but snap-peel type. Heavy bearing. Self-fertile. The traditional Florida tangerine.
Miniature seedless mandarin, bite-size fruit with intense sweet flavor. Ripens December-January. Self-fertile. Premium variety at high-end markets.
Clementine x Minneola tangelo cross. Medium red-orange fruit with exceptional sweet-tart flavor and rich aroma. Requires cross-pollination. Ripens November-January. Popular home-garden variety.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus is evergreen and does not become fully dormant, so freeze damage is a whole-tree phenomenon (leaves, twigs, fruit) rather than the blossom-frost issue deciduous fruit faces. Lemons and limes are most cold-sensitive (damaged below about 30 degrees); oranges and grapefruit tolerate brief drops to about 26 degrees; mandarins are typically the hardiest. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split or mushy fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights and string old-style incandescent lights through the canopy if possible. Bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties (satsuma mandarin, kumquat, calamondin) or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Scale insects (cottony cushion scale, citrus mealybug, California red scale) and Asian citrus psyllid are the dominant citrus pests. Asian citrus psyllid spreads Huanglongbing (HLB, citrus greening), the disease threatening commercial citrus in Florida, Texas, and California. Phytophthora root and crown rot kills more young trees than any insect.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Inspect for scale year-round and treat with horticultural oil. In HLB-affected areas, follow your state's quarantine guidance; healthy trees on resistant rootstock and aggressive psyllid control are the home-garden defense. For Phytophthora prevention, keep mulch off the trunk and avoid overwatering.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most citrus is self-fertile -- a single tree should fruit well. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often a water-stress, temperature-extreme, or alternate-bearing issue than a pollination one. Some mandarin varieties produce seedless fruit only when isolated from other citrus.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture through bloom and fruit set. If the tree blooms heavily one year and barely the next, it is alternate-bearing -- thinning fruit in the heavy year levels the cycle out. Avoid moving citrus during bloom; flowers and small fruit drop from stress.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus is more prone to Phytophthora than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in waterlogged soil and at the trunk-soil interface. Symptoms are yellowing leaves with green veins, dieback, gum oozing from the lower trunk, and bark that lifts off the wood at the base.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on a raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Keep mulch a hand-width back from the trunk. Water deeply but infrequently, and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. There is no good cure once Phytophthora is established.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Citrus needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to develop sugar and color. In shade the tree grows leaves and may bloom but fruit stays small, sour, and green. South or southwest exposure is ideal in most US citrus zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun -- if a wall or building is reflecting heat, even better. Light pruning to keep the inside of the canopy open helps inner fruit ripen. In containers, rotate the pot a quarter turn every few weeks for even growth.

crops.description_seasoned: More cold-tolerant than oranges, easier to peel, and beloved by kids. Satsuma mandarin is the hardiest type -- survives down to 20°F for short periods. Great container plant.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deep orange, easy to peel, skin slightly loose. Segments separate easily.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Mandarins and clementines (Citrus reticulata) are the most cold-hardy of the sweet citrus -- Satsuma mandarins tolerate 15-18°F when mature, making them viable in zone 8a. This hardiness makes mandarins the right citrus for Gulf Coast growers (Louisiana, Alabama, Mississippi, Florida Panhandle) where winters are too cold for oranges or lemons. Fruit characteristics vary widely across varieties: Satsumas are early-ripening and virtually seedless with loose peels; clementines are small and very sweet; Tangerines have more intense flavor and tighter peels. Most mandarins require cross-pollination from another citrus variety for heavy fruit set; pollination by bees from neighboring citrus is usually sufficient. Fruit matures fall through winter depending on variety. Trees are small (8-15 feet) and well-suited to container growing. Begin bearing year 3-4 from grafted trees. Satsumas are particularly forgiving and make good beginner citrus for cold-winter zones.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Minimal chill -- one of the more cold-tolerant citrus varieties
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Some varieties (Clementine) produce seedless fruit when isolated from other citrus.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed monthly during the growing season. High-potassium feed from midsummer improves fruit ripening. Over-feeding produces lots of leaf and little fruit.

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune in late winter while dormant. Remove dead wood and crossing branches. Can cut hard to control size.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Borage
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Attracts pollinators, improves general garden health

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Xerces Society documents borage as a pollinator-attractant plant. While Xerces specifically names tomato, squash, and cucumber crops, the pollinator-attraction mechanism generalizes reasonably to other insect-pollinated crops. Source: xerces.org/blog/plants-you-can-eat-are-pollinator-treat.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: White cottony masses along stems, at leaf axils, and inside ripening fruit eyes. Sticky honeydew on leaves and ground below, followed by sooty mold. Ants often tend the colonies.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several mealybug species, including Pseudococcus longispinus and Planococcus species. UF/IFAS lists mealybug as one of the most common fig insects. Heaviest in warm humid weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray colonies with insecticidal soap or horticultural oil, focusing on leaf axils and fruit clusters. Control ants (which farm mealybugs) with sticky bands on the trunk. Prune out heavily infested branches.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect new plants before planting. Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen. Remove fruit mummies where mealybugs overwinter.

pests.name: Fig mites
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow or russet discoloration on leaves, curled or distorted new growth, and reduced vigor. Most important as vectors of fig mosaic virus, which causes permanent yellow mottling and leaf distortion.
pests.cause_seasoned: Aceria ficus (fig blister mite) and related eriophyid mites. Too small to see without magnification. Transmit fig mosaic virus from infected trees to healthy ones.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil or sulfur sprays applied in late winter or early spring (before bud break) are the standard control. Remove and destroy severely virus-infected trees -- there is no cure for mosaic.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Only propagate cuttings from symptom-free trees. Disinfect pruning tools between trees. Control is especially important if mites were a problem the previous year.

pests.name: Fig beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large (1 inch) iridescent green beetles feed on ripe figs, chewing into fruits from the eye. Birds often follow beetle damage and finish off the fruit.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cotinis mutabilis (green fig beetle) in the West and Cotinis nitida (green June beetle) in the Southeast. Attracted to ripe and overripe fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick beetles in early morning when they are sluggish. Drop into soapy water. Bag developing fruit in fine-mesh organza bags to exclude beetles.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Pick fruit daily as it ripens. Remove fallen and overripe figs so beetles move elsewhere. Closed-eye varieties are less vulnerable.

pests.name: Ants
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Ants trailing up the trunk and through the canopy. Ants tending mealybugs and scale, protecting them from natural enemies. May enter fruit through the eye.
pests.cause_seasoned: Argentine ants and other species are attracted by honeydew produced by mealybugs and scale. UF/IFAS lists ants among the most common fig pests.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sticky trunk bands (Tanglefoot on tree wrap, not directly on bark) block ants from climbing. Bait stations with boric acid along ant trails.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep tree base clear of mulch and weeds that shelter ants. Control the sap-sucking insects (mealybugs, scale) that ants tend.

diseases.name: Fig rust
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small yellow to yellow-green spots on upper leaf surface that turn reddish-brown as they enlarge. Undersides of leaves develop small blister-like pustules. Heavy infection causes leaves to yellow and drop prematurely, weakening the tree and reducing cold tolerance.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Cerotelium fici, a fungus. UF/IFAS identifies fig rust as the most common fig disease in the southeastern US. Favored by warm humid weather.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Once leaves show symptoms, no cure -- focus on sanitation. Rake and dispose of fallen leaves in fall (they harbor overwintering spores).
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune for good air circulation. Water at soil level -- avoid overhead irrigation. Apply 5-5-50 Bordeaux spray (copper sulfate + lime + water) preventively during the growing season in high-pressure areas. 2-3 inches of mulch under the tree. Fig rust resistance varies by variety.

diseases.name: Fig mosaic virus
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow mottling or mosaic pattern on leaves, often with diffuse margins that blend into green. Older lesions may develop a brown-red band. Leaf distortion and reduced vigor. No cure.
diseases.cause_seasoned: One or more viruses transmitted by fig mites (Aceria ficus) and through infected cuttings. Widespread in backyard figs.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Severely affected trees should be removed and replaced.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Only take cuttings from trees with no mosaic symptoms. Control fig mites with horticultural oil or sulfur. Many tolerant varieties carry low-level virus without major yield loss.

diseases.name: Thread blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Fine white fungal threads run along twigs and leaf undersides, matting leaves together. Leaves turn brown and die but remain attached, hanging in the canopy.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pellicularia koleroga (syn. Rhizoctonia), a fungus favored by humid summer conditions and dense canopies. Listed by UF/IFAS as a regional fig disease.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out affected branches well back into healthy wood. Dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Thin canopy annually to improve airflow. Avoid overhead watering. Space trees for light penetration.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 2 weeks -- figs are drought tolerant

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Figs are classic container plants in cold climates -- bring into unheated garage for winter. 15-gallon minimum. Root restriction actually improves fruiting.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 1-2 days -- very perishable at peak ripeness
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole or halved -- good for baking, less good for eating fresh
storage.notes_seasoned: Figs are the most perishable tree fruit. Pick and use same day when possible.

varieties.note_seasoned: Chicago Hardy is the key variety for Z5-6 -- survives cold by dying to the ground and resprouting.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Container-grown or bare-root fig just planted. Often a multi-stem shrub-like form rather than a single trunk.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant in the warmest, most sheltered spot you have -- against a south-facing wall is ideal in cold zones. Dig wide, plant at the original soil line, water in deeply. In zone 6 and colder, plant in a large container so you can move it into shelter for winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Fig planted in sheltered spot or container?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves emerging from the dormant stems. Fig often pushes new growth quickly once warm weather arrives.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water consistently through the first summer; figs handle drought once established but need steady moisture in year one. Remove any small fruit that sets in year one. In containers, keep the rootball moist but never standing in water.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Multiple stems extending from the base or main trunk. Fig can grow as a single-trunk tree or a multi-stem bush.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Decide on the form now: single-trunk for warm zones (more vertical growth, easier to harvest), multi-stem for cold zones (insurance -- if one stem dies back, others survive). Remove competing growth to settle the form. Pinch the tips of long shoots to encourage side branching.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves drop. In warm zones (8-10) figs may hold leaves into early winter; in colder zones they go fully dormant by the first hard freeze.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cold-zone protection is critical for fig. Wrap the trunk and main stems with burlap or insulation, mound mulch deeply over the root zone, or move container figs into an unheated garage or shed. The colder the zone, the more aggressive the wrapping should be. Light pruning is OK now but main pruning waits until late winter.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Heavy pruning OK. Hard prune in cold zones (sacrifices breba crop); light prune in warm zones to keep both crops.

growth_stages.name: (No Visible Bloom)
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fig has no visible flowers -- the syconium is the flower structure.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most home varieties are parthenocarpic; no pollinator needed.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Development
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Breba crop on year-old wood, main crop on current-year wood.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture to prevent fruit drop.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Neck softens, fruit hangs down, nectar at eye.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick daily during peak; ripe figs go over fast.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest & Winter Prep
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit done; tree heading to dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Clear drops. Mulch refresh. Wrap trunk in cold zones.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Fig is grown on its own roots in home gardens -- there is no graft union to worry about. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Plant in spring after frost danger passes. Fig is more tolerant of poor and alkaline soil than most fruit trees but appreciates a generous compost amendment at planting.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Established figs are remarkably drought-tolerant but young trees need consistent moisture for the first two years.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the base. Fig roots are shallow and benefit from a deep organic mulch year-round.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Fig can be grown as a single-trunk tree, a multi-stemmed shrub, or even an espalier against a wall. Multi-stem form is common in cold zones because it allows the tree to regenerate from the crown after winter dieback.
Pinch the growing tips at 24 to 30 inches to encourage branching. Otherwise fig grows fast and gangly.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Fig is fully deciduous and goes dormant in winter. In the warmer end of fig range, dormancy is brief; in cold zones the tree may die back to the ground each winter and regrow from the crown.
In USDA zones 6 and below, wrap the trunk and main scaffolds with insulating material before winter, or grow as a multi-stem so regeneration from the crown is easy.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Fig tolerates heavy pruning. Most varieties bear two crops per year: an early 'breba' crop on previous-year wood and a main crop on current-year wood. Heavy winter pruning reduces the breba crop but does not affect the main crop.
In cold zones where the breba crop rarely ripens before frost anyway, prune hard to maintain a manageable size. In warm zones, prune lightly to preserve the breba crop.

blossom.text_seasoned: Fig has no visible flowers -- the 'fruit' is actually a syconium, an enclosed structure with the flowers inside. There is no bloom stage to protect from frost.

Most home-garden fig varieties (Common figs) are parthenocarpic, meaning they set fruit without pollination. Some varieties (Smyrna, San Pedro types) need a specific wasp pollinator that is not present in most US gardens -- avoid these unless you live in California's fig belt.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Fruit develops over several months. A breba crop ripens in early summer on year-old wood; the main crop ripens in late summer to early fall on current-year wood.
Heavy early fruit drop indicates water stress. Fig is drought-tolerant but drops fruit before it drops leaves when water-stressed.

harvest.text_seasoned: Fig is ripe when the fruit hangs down on its stem (the neck softens), the skin gives to gentle pressure, and a tiny drop of nectar may appear at the eye. Underripe figs are starchy and disappointing; ripe figs are floral and intensely sweet.
Harvest daily during peak ripening. Ripe figs do not hold on the tree -- they go from underripe to over-ripe in 24 to 48 hours and attract birds, wasps, and yellow jackets fast.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clean up dropped fruit immediately. Fermenting figs attract wasps, yellow jackets, and dried-fruit beetles in serious numbers.
Apply mulch refresh and a balanced feed in fall before dormancy. In cold zones, this is also when to wrap the trunk for winter protection.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 20-50 lbs from a mature in-ground tree in a warm zone; 5-15 lbs from a mature container fig
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production typically by year 3 to 5. A mature in-ground fig in a warm zone produces heavily; a container fig produces more modestly but gives reliable fruit even in cold zones.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Light or no harvest in year one. Figs are precocious for a fruit tree and may set a few in year two. Year one is still a root and trunk year.
factors_seasoned: winter protection in zones 6 and colder (wrap, mulch heavy, or grow in container)
consistent moisture during fruit sizing -- drought causes drop
balance between breba (year-old wood) and main crop (current-year wood) when pruning
container growing for cold zones extends viable range significantly

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The gold standard for cold-climate fig growing. Roots survive to -20°F even when top growth dies back. Medium purple-mahogany fruit with sweet berry flavor. Self-fertile. The safest fig for zones 5-6.
Small sweet brown-purple fruit -- one of the sweetest figs. Closed eye keeps out moisture in rainy climates, reducing spoilage. Self-fertile. Heat-tolerant and southern-adapted.
Most widely planted fig in the southern US. Large medium-brown fruit, sometimes produces two crops per year. Self-fertile. Heat-tolerant. Less cold-hardy than Chicago Hardy.
Naturally dwarf (6-10 feet), ideal for containers and small spaces. Small purple-black fruit with intense strawberry-like flavor. Self-fertile. A 17th-century French heirloom still prized for flavor.

Louisiana State University release. Heavy producer of medium dark-purple fruit. Bred for hot humid southern conditions. Self-fertile. Fast-growing and productive. Top choice for the Gulf Coast and Southeast.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fig blooms inside the syconium (no exposed flowers), so spring frost during bloom is not an issue. The cold problem for fig is winter dieback at the edge of its hardiness range -- USDA zone 7 reliably, zones 6 and 5 with protection. Cold-damaged trees often regenerate from the crown but lose the breba crop and may produce only the late main crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: In cold zones, grow as a multi-stem shrub so regeneration from the crown is easy. Wrap the trunk and main scaffolds with insulation in fall, or bend young trees over and bury them under mulch for winter (the traditional 'fig coffin' approach).

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fig has remarkably few serious pests in most of the US. Fig rust (orange spots on leaves leading to defoliation) shows up in humid climates. Fig mites cause leaf curling but rarely affect crop. Birds, wasps, and yellow jackets are often more destructive than insects -- they go after ripe fruit hard.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For fig rust, rake and destroy fallen leaves in fall to break the cycle. For wasps and yellow jackets, harvest daily and clean up drops immediately. Bird netting helps in serious bird-pressure areas; a single ripe fig can attract a flock.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pollination is not the issue for fig in most home gardens. Common fig varieties are parthenocarpic and set fruit without pollination. Smyrna and San Pedro varieties need a specific fig wasp (only present in California's fig belt and a few similar areas); planting one of these outside its range gives you a tree that flowers internally but never sets fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety is a Common fig (parthenocarpic) before planting. Brown Turkey, Celeste, Chicago Hardy, Black Mission, and Kadota are all Common figs. Persistent fruit drop is more often water stress than pollination failure.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fig tolerates a wider moisture range than most fruit trees but cannot survive standing water. Roots in waterlogged soil suffocate; symptoms include yellowing leaves and dieback. Excessive irrigation in summer can also reduce fruit quality (less sugar, more cracking).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Once established, water deeply but infrequently -- weekly is plenty in most climates. Avoid the daily-shallow-watering pattern that suits some other fruit.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Fig needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to ripen fruit properly. In partial shade the tree grows leaves but produces fewer and lower-quality figs that may not reach full sweetness before fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun -- a south or southwest wall provides reflected heat that helps in cooler zones. Light pruning to open the canopy helps inner fruit ripen.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: In zones below their hardiness minimum, fig and pomegranate can be grown in containers and overwintered in an unheated garage or basement. Persimmon is not practical as a container plant due to size. Avocado requires Z9+ and is container-impractical for most home growers in cold zones. (UMN Extension; Iowa State Extension; UC Master Gardeners)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fig, pomegranate, and persimmon are warm-climate perennials. Plant bare-root or container stock in spring after last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Fig is hardy to Zone 6 with winter protection (die-back hardy to Z5). Pomegranate Z7+. Persimmon (American) Z5+, Asian Z7+. Harvest late summer through fall once trees reach bearing age (2-4 years for fig and persimmon, 2-3 years for pomegranate). (UGA Extension Fig Production; Clemson HGIC Fig; UF/IFAS Pomegranate; UC Master Gardeners Persimmon)

crops.description_seasoned: One of the easiest fruit trees. Self-fertile, drought-tolerant, and beautiful as a garden specimen. Two crops per year in warm zones -- a breba crop in early summer and main crop in late summer/fall.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Fruit droops downward on stem. Skin slightly wrinkled. Tip may show a small drop of nectar. Skin gives easily to gentle pressure.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Figs (Ficus carica) have a unique hardiness pattern: roots are significantly more cold-tolerant than the above-ground canes. In zones 5-6, the top growth frequently dies back to the ground in winter, but the roots survive and resprout vigorously in spring, fruiting on new wood the same year. This makes figs genuinely viable in zones 5-6 as die-back-and-regrow shrubs (expect 6-8 feet of growth per season), though crop timing gets tight in zones 5a-5b. In zones 7+, figs grow as full-sized trees (15-25 feet) with normal fig tree habit. Common figs (the type grown for backyard fruit) are parthenocarpic -- they produce fruit without pollination and don't need another tree. Many varieties produce two crops: an early breba crop on previous-year wood in June-July, and a main crop on current-year wood in August-October. In cold zones where canes die back, only the main crop is possible. Winter protection (wrapping, mulching, or the Minnesota Tip method of burying canes) is essential in zones 5-6 and recommended in zone 7. Trees begin bearing in year 2-3.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Essentially no chill requirement -- ideal for zones 7-11
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Common figs (Brown Turkey, Celeste, Black Mission) produce without pollination.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: May produce a small crop in year 2-3. Remove any fruit forming in year one to direct energy to roots.
