pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth. Curled and yellowed young leaves. Sticky honeydew on lower leaves and fruit, followed by sooty mold that disfigures the skin.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cotton/melon aphid (Aphis gossypii) is most common. UF/IFAS CREC notes aphids are common to most pomegranate-growing regions, especially on young plants and at the propagation stage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast with water. Insecticidal soap or neem oil. Ladybugs and lacewings provide strong control. Tolerate light populations -- natural enemies need prey to stay around.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid over-fertilizing. Control ants that tend aphid colonies. Protect young plants most carefully.

pests.name: Leaffooted bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Hard darkened spots or sunken areas on fruit rind where bugs have fed. Fruit may develop internal browning and off-flavors. Long narrow brown bugs (3/4 inch) with flared hind legs visible on fruit clusters, often in groups.
pests.cause_seasoned: Leptoglossus zonatus and related species. Major warm-region fruit pest. Feeds by piercing the rind and sucking juice from arils.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and nymphs in morning when sluggish. Knock clusters into soapy water. Pyrethrin products if infestations are heavy.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout fruit weekly. Remove weedy borders where bugs overwinter. Netting fruit clusters when fruits begin to size up protects against both bugs and birds.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: White cottony masses in leaf axils, on fruit, and inside the calyx. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold. Fruit may crack at the calyx where mealybugs feed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several mealybug species affect pomegranate. Often farmed by ants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap sprayed into calyx and leaf axils. Control ants with sticky trunk bands.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect nursery stock. Prune for airflow so spray coverage reaches hidden areas.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery or bronzy scarring on fruit skin where thrips have rasped the surface. Distorted new leaves. Heaviest damage during bloom and early fruit development.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several thrips species including Scirtothrips and Frankliniella. Active during warm dry weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blue sticky traps to monitor. Spinosad applied in the evening during bloom (to protect bees). Reflective mulch deters thrips from landing.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain even irrigation to reduce stress. Remove weedy hosts around the orchard.

diseases.name: Anthracnose fruit rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Circular brown or black sunken lesions on fruit skin that may show concentric rings. Lesions spread rapidly in warm wet weather. Fruit drops prematurely or rots on the tree. Leaves may show dark spots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides fungus. UF/IFAS research identifies this as the most damaging pomegranate disease in the humid Southeast, causing severe fruit rot and premature fruit drop.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected fruits. Copper-based fungicide during extended wet weather.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant resistant varieties where available -- UF/IFAS trials show significant variation. Prune for airflow. Rake and remove fallen fruit and leaves. Avoid overhead irrigation. Mulch under canopy.

diseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot & fruit blemish
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown to black circular leaf spots, sometimes coalescing. Early leaf drop. On fruit, small dark blemishes that may enlarge into sunken lesions. Fruit quality and appearance reduced.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Cercospora punicae fungus. UF/IFAS CREC lists this as a primary pomegranate concern in humid climates. Spreads by rain splash.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves and fruits. Copper fungicide may reduce spread during wet periods.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for air circulation. Water at soil level. Rake and destroy fallen leaves in winter.

diseases.name: Branch canker & dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting and dieback of individual branches. Elliptical cankers on branches that may ooze sap. Interior wood shows brown streaking. Whole branches may die back from the tip.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Neofusicoccum parvum, Lasiodiplodia theobromae, and related fungi in the Botryosphaeriaceae. UF/IFAS surveys isolate these regularly from diseased branches. Stressed and pruning-wounded trees are most vulnerable.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune affected branches well below the cankered tissue (at least 6 inches into healthy wood). Disinfect pruning tools between cuts. Burn or dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune during dry weather with clean cuts at a slight angle so water drains. Avoid pruning in wet weather when spores are active. Keep trees unstressed -- healthy vigorous trees resist canker.

diseases.name: Fruit heart rot (Alternaria)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Fruit looks normal from outside but interior arils are rotted dark brown or black when cut open. Often no external symptoms -- the first sign is biting into a ruined fruit.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Alternaria alternata infects flowers and developing fruit during wet bloom weather, then grows inside the fruit undetected. Worse in years with heavy spring rain.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective organic rescue once infection is internal. Discard affected fruits.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant less-susceptible varieties where possible. Avoid overhead irrigation during bloom. Thin fruit clusters to improve airflow.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze arils (seeds) in a bag -- excellent, lasts 6 months
storage.notes_seasoned: Whole pomegranates have remarkable shelf life. The thick skin is nature's packaging.

varieties.note_seasoned: Sienevyi is the most cold-hardy pomegranate -- recommended for zones 6-7 where Wonderful is unreliable.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree or multi-trunk shrub just planted. Pomegranate often arrives as a multi-stem clump; mulberry and persimmon as single-trunk trees.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant high in well-drained soil. Stake mulberry and persimmon firmly; pomegranate usually doesn't need staking once the multi-trunk form is set. Water in deeply, mulch around the base, and avoid burying the lowest stems.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking. Pomegranate often pushes new shoots from the base in a clump; mulberry and persimmon push from existing stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Remove any first-year flowers or developing fruit. For pomegranate, decide now whether to keep the multi-trunk form (let 3 to 5 main trunks grow) or train it to a single trunk; remove the extra base shoots accordingly.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension. Mulberry grows quickly and may need its first directional pruning. Persimmon is slower. Pomegranate fills its multi-trunk clump.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulberry: pick one main vertical trunk and remove low side branches you don't want long-term -- mulberry grows large fast. Persimmon: light shaping only; both American and Asian persimmons fruit on last year's wood, so heavy pruning costs you crops. Pomegranate: keep the chosen 3 to 5 main trunks clear of small side shoots below knee height.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate all drop their leaves in late fall. Frost-hardy when fully dormant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulch around the base before hard freeze. Pomegranate benefits from extra mulch over the root zone in zone 7 and colder. Wrap young trunks in young-tree wrap if rabbits or sunscald are concerns. Major pruning waits until late winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Mulch and trunk protection in place?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant, leaves down. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon -- both fruit on previous-year wood. Pomegranate suckers freely; remove suckers and limit to 3 to 5 main trunks.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring or early-summer bloom -- well after main spring frost risk has passed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: These crops bloom late, so frost protection is rarely needed. Avoid spraying during bloom.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small green fruit forming after petal fall. Most home varieties are self-fertile.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thinning is rarely needed for this group. On heavy pomegranate set, thin lightly to prevent limb breakage.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mulberry summer-ripens over weeks; persimmon and pomegranate ripen in fall.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulberry: lay a sheet under the tree and shake, or pick ripe fruit daily. Persimmon: astringent types after first frost; non-astringent when fully colored. Pomegranate: when fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Last fruit picked. Drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Clear fallen fruit. Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed. Refresh mulch before winter.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: These trees are typically grown on their own roots in home gardens, so there is no graft union to worry about. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Water in well at planting and mulch a 3-foot circle around the base, kept a few inches back from the trunk. Staking is usually not needed unless the site is very windy.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- even after rain. Establishment takes one to two years; do not skip irrigation just because the tree looks fine.
These crops are slow to bear -- mulberry typically 2 to 3 years, persimmon 3 to 5, pomegranate 2 to 3. Patience is the main first-season skill.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Train to a modified central-leader or open-vase form depending on the species. Pomegranate is often grown as a multi-stemmed shrub; mulberry and persimmon take well to a single-trunk form.
Remove low water sprouts and any suckers. Pomegranate especially suckers freely and needs annual sucker removal.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter pruning is the rule for this group. Wait until leaves are fully down and the tree is dormant.
A mulch refresh and a deep watering before the ground freezes help winter survival, especially in the colder end of each species' hardiness range.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon. Both bear on previous-year wood and heavy heading reduces the next crop. Remove dead, diseased, damaged, and crossing branches; leave the rest.
Pomegranate is the exception -- it tolerates and benefits from heavier annual pruning to limit suckers and keep the canopy open. Limit to 3 to 5 main trunks if growing as a multi-stem.

blossom.text_seasoned: These crops bloom later than pome and stone fruit, so spring frost is rarely the problem. Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate flower from late spring into early summer in most zones.
Avoid spraying during bloom. Pollinators are doing the year's most important work in this window even on self-fertile crops.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile (American persimmon needs a male; Asian persimmon does not; pomegranate and mulberry are self-fertile). Confirm your variety before assuming.
Thinning is rarely needed -- the tree's natural set is usually appropriate. A heavy pomegranate set on a young tree may benefit from light thinning to avoid limb breakage.

harvest.text_seasoned: Mulberry ripens over 3 to 4 weeks; harvest by laying a sheet under the tree and shaking, or by picking ripe fruit daily. Persimmon and pomegranate ripen later -- persimmon is best after the first frost (astringent types) and pomegranate when the fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.
Handle ripe fruit gently. Mulberry and ripe persimmon stain badly and bruise even more easily than stone fruit.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear fallen fruit from under the tree. Sticky drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed after harvest to build reserves. Refresh mulch before winter.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 30-60 lbs from a mature multi-trunk shrub, typically 50-100 fruits
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production in year 4 to 6. Mature plants produce reliably for decades with very little intervention compared to deciduous fruit trees.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No useful crop in year one. These are tough, low-input plants once established, but year one is still a root-building year. Remove fruit if any sets.
factors_seasoned: light structural pruning -- these crops fruit on previous-year wood (mulberry, persimmon) or freely from suckers (pomegranate)
fruit drop when stressed in pomegranate

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The commercial standard -- the pomegranate you see in grocery stores. Large deep-red fruit with tart-sweet juice. Self-fertile. Hardy to 15°F. Best in California and Arizona climates.
Russian-bred cold-hardy variety. Survives to 0°F. Large red fruit with sweet-tart flavor. Self-fertile. The top choice for zone 7 growers and anywhere winter cold limits standard pomegranates.
Another Russian-bred cold-hardy variety. Medium orange-red fruit with exceptional sweet flavor. Self-fertile. Lower chill requirement makes it productive in moderate-winter zones.
Modern variety bred for superior flavor -- often ranked the best-tasting pomegranate. Soft seeds (edible without spitting). Medium-large red fruit. Self-fertile. Popular with culinary growers.
Virtually seedless variety with sweet non-acidic juice. Unique clear non-staining juice. Self-fertile. Less cold-hardy than Salavatski. Best for California coastal growers.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem -- the more common cold issue is winter cold damage at the edge of each species' hardiness range. Pomegranate is hardy to about USDA zone 7; persimmon and mulberry are hardier (zones 4 to 5 for hardy varieties). Cold-damaged wood shows as dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety is hardy to your zone -- there is wide variation within each species. In marginal zones, plant in a sheltered south-facing site, mulch heavily before winter, and accept some annual dieback on pomegranate.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pest pressure on this group is generally lower than on pome or stone fruit. Mulberry attracts birds heavily once fruit ripens. Persimmon is sometimes hit by persimmon psyllid (curling new growth) or persimmon wilt. Pomegranate can suffer leaffooted bug damage and heart rot in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bird netting on mulberry once fruit colors. For persimmon psyllid, a dormant horticultural oil spray reduces overwintering populations. For pomegranate heart rot, choose resistant varieties and improve airflow with light pruning.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile. American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is the main exception -- it needs a male tree nearby. Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki), which is what most named varieties sold in the US are, sets fruit without a pollinator (sometimes seedless).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm whether your variety is American or Asian persimmon and whether it needs a male. For pomegranate and mulberry, persistent fruit-drop usually points to drought stress or extreme heat at bloom rather than pollination.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops want well-drained soil. Pomegranate is the most drought-tolerant; mulberry tolerates a wider moisture range; persimmon prefers consistent moisture but hates standing water. Symptoms of waterlogging are yellowing leaves, dieback, and root rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage before planting on heavy or low-lying soil -- plant on a 12-inch mound if needed. Pomegranate especially does best on the dry side once established.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to ripen and develop sugar. Pomegranate especially struggles in shade and may flower without setting fruit. Persimmon ripens unevenly without enough sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. Light pruning to keep the canopy open helps fruit ripen on the inside of the tree -- particularly important for pomegranate and persimmon.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: In zones below their hardiness minimum, fig and pomegranate can be grown in containers and overwintered in an unheated garage or basement. Persimmon is not practical as a container plant due to size. Avocado requires Z9+ and is container-impractical for most home growers in cold zones. (UMN Extension; Iowa State Extension; UC Master Gardeners)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fig, pomegranate, and persimmon are warm-climate perennials. Plant bare-root or container stock in spring after last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Fig is hardy to Zone 6 with winter protection (die-back hardy to Z5). Pomegranate Z7+. Persimmon (American) Z5+, Asian Z7+. Harvest late summer through fall once trees reach bearing age (2-4 years for fig and persimmon, 2-3 years for pomegranate). (UGA Extension Fig Production; Clemson HGIC Fig; UF/IFAS Pomegranate; UC Master Gardeners Persimmon)

crops.description_seasoned: Stunning in autumn with orange-red fruit and fiery foliage. Drought-tolerant, heat-loving, and long-lived. Needs a long hot summer (200+ frost-free days) for fruit to ripen fully.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deep red skin, fruit feels heavy for its size, skin begins to crack slightly. Tap -- sounds metallic rather than dull.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Pomegranates (Punica granatum) are remarkably drought-tolerant and adaptable to the arid Southwest and Mediterranean-climate California. They need a hot dry summer to properly develop fruit sugars -- in humid climates, fruit may split and rot before ripening. Cold hardiness varies significantly by variety: the standard 'Wonderful' is hardy to about 15°F (zone 8a+), while 'Salavatski' and other Russian-bred varieties survive to 0°F (zone 7a). Most pomegranates are self-fertile. They flower heavily but drop most blossoms; don't panic at a pile of fallen flowers. Fruit matures 5-7 months after flowering. Trees are multi-stemmed shrubs or small trees (10-15 feet) and tolerate significant pruning. Begin bearing in year 2-3. In humid climates, fruit cracking and fungal disease limit success even where winter temperatures are adequate.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Very low chill -- thrives in zones 7-10 with hot summers
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Single tree bears well. Bees improve fruit set.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: No fruit expected years 1-2. Plant in full sun -- location drives everything with pomegranates.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed in spring as growth begins. After fruiting, apply sulphate of potash to build next year's canes.

tasks.description_seasoned: Summer-bearing: cut all fruited canes to ground after harvest. Leave new green canes for next year. Everbearing: cut all canes to ground in late winter for one big fall crop.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring aphids are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: The aphid-repellent element is mechanism-plausible: allium sulfur VOCs have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, Insects 2018, 9(4):112) at home-gardening extension rigor (Mississippi State, USU). However, the 'repel beetles' sub-claim for garlic on raspberry is not extension-documented. Raspberry beetle/cane borer/Japanese beetle management in extension publications (Cornell Berry Diagnostic Tool, PNW Extension) relies on cultural controls, pruning, and targeted insecticides; allium interplanting is not listed. Downgraded from extension_backed because the composite claim mixes a mechanism-real aphid component with an unbacked beetle component.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing fruit before full ripeness. Tiny maggots inside ripening berries.
pests.cause_seasoned: Drosophila suzukii fly. Major pest of soft fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Fine mesh netting (1mm) over plants during ripening. Spinosad spray. Harvest frequently.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Fine netting is most effective. Remove overripe fruit promptly.

diseases.name: Cane diseases (botrytis/anthracnose)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Purple/brown spots on canes. Die-back of canes. Gray mold on fruit in wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis and Elsinoe fungal diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected canes. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune out old canes after fruiting. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead irrigation.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze flat then bag -- excellent quality preserved
storage.notes_seasoned: The most perishable fruit. Freeze immediately if not eating same day.

varieties.note_seasoned: Heritage is the most widely planted home raspberry -- reliable, prolific, two crops per year.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant from container in spring. Bare-root plants available in winter -- plant immediately on receipt.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted plant just set. Soil level matches the original line on the stems -- not buried deeper.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), mix peat moss or pine fines into the hole, and mulch with pine needles or wood chips. Cane fruits (raspberry, blackberry): plant alongside a trellis or post-and-wire support so the canes have something to grow on. Elderberry: tolerates wetter ground than the others. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves breaking. Blueberry pushes new shoots from the base; cane fruits send up new canes from the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water consistently through the first summer -- berries have shallow roots and dry out fast. Remove all flowers in year one so the plant builds its roots and a strong base. For raspberries and blackberries, pinch off the tip of each new cane once it reaches your trellis height; this encourages side branches that will carry fruit.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Multiple stems or canes coming up from the base. Blueberry fills out as a many-stemmed bush; cane fruits send up vigorous new canes; elderberry bushes out widely.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Berries don't get scaffold-branch training the way trees do -- they're naturally multi-stemmed. Blueberry: keep the strongest 4 to 6 stems and remove weak twiggy growth. Raspberry and blackberry: train new canes onto the trellis and thin them to about 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot. Elderberry: let it bush out freely; remove only crossed or weak growth.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blueberry leaves turn red-purple and drop. Raspberry and blackberry canes go fully bare. Elderberry drops cleanly. All are dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Top up the mulch before deep freeze, especially for shallow-rooted blueberry. In cold zones, consider laying down trailing blackberry canes and covering them with mulch or burlap. Real pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bush or canes fully dormant. Late-winter window before bud break.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: cane-renewal -- remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest canes at ground level each winter. Caneberries: remove last year's spent floricanes; thin remaining primocanes to 4 to 6 per linear foot.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring bloom on blueberry, raspberry, blackberry; early-summer bloom on elderberry. Frost risk usually past.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avoid sprays during bloom. Wild bumblebees are the main blueberry pollinators.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set & Bird Netting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Berries forming. Bird pressure ramps up as fruit colors.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Cross-pollination boosts blueberry yield -- a second variety nearby helps.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe fruit pulls free with gentle pressure. Bushes and canes are hand-height -- no ladders.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for thorny canes. Refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Cleanup
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Last fruit picked. Spent floricanes on caneberries dying back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut spent floricanes at ground level if not done in late winter. Apply a potassium-rich feed (use an acidic blueberry-specific fertilizer for blueberry). Refresh mulch.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: These crops are typically grown on their own roots -- there is no graft union. Plant with the crown at the original soil line. Blueberry needs acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5); test before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed.
Caneberries (raspberry, blackberry) need a trellis or support system from year one. Build it before planting; retrofitting around established canes is awkward.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- berries are shallow-rooted and dry out fast. Blueberry especially needs steady moisture and acidic mulch (pine bark, pine needles).
Remove flowers in year one on caneberries and blueberry. The energy goes into root and cane development; you will get more fruit from years two onward by skipping year one.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Blueberry develops as a multi-stemmed shrub. Let 5 to 7 main canes establish in the first 2 to 3 years; do not prune for shape, only remove damaged wood.
Caneberries put up new canes (primocanes) from the crown each year. In year one, let everything grow -- those are next year's fruiting canes (floricanes).

dormancy.text_seasoned: These crops are deciduous and go fully dormant in winter. Pruning is done in late winter or very early spring before bud break.
Refresh mulch before winter. For caneberries, tip-prune any canes that did not harden off (still green and floppy at the tip).

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Blueberry uses cane-renewal pruning. Each winter, remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest, least-productive canes at ground level to push new cane growth from the crown. By year 5 or 6 the bush has a rotating set of young productive canes.

Caneberries: remove all canes that fruited last summer (floricanes) -- they die after fruiting and harbor disease. Leave the new green canes (primocanes) for next year. Thin remaining canes to 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot of row.

blossom.text_seasoned: Blueberry, raspberry, and blackberry bloom late enough that spring frost is rarely the problem -- usually mid-to-late spring, after most frost danger is past. Elderberry blooms even later, in early summer.
Pollinators love these flowers. Do not spray during bloom. Wild bumblebees in particular are major pollinators of blueberry.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most blueberry varieties benefit from a second variety blooming at the same time for cross-pollination -- a single bush will fruit but a pair fruits much more heavily. Caneberries and elderberry are mostly self-fertile.
Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Once birds find the patch they keep coming back.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick fruit at hand height -- no ladders here. Ripe blueberries pull off with a gentle roll of the thumb; fruit that resists is not yet ripe (color is not enough -- some varieties color days before they sweeten).

Caneberries shatter when over-ripe -- pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for blackberry and the thorny raspberries. Eat or refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: After caneberry harvest, cut the spent floricanes (now dying or dead) at ground level if you did not get them in late winter. This removes overwintering sites for cane disease and the spotted wing drosophila.
A potassium-rich feed and a mulch refresh after harvest sets up next year's bloom. For blueberry, use an acidic fertilizer formulated for ericaceous plants.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 1-2 lbs per cane, or roughly 4-8 lbs per mature plant grown on a trellis
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production typically arrives in year 4 to 7 depending on type. Berries ripen unevenly across a 2 to 4 week window, so expect to pick every few days at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Plan on no harvest in year one. Remove all flowers so the plant invests in roots and new canes. Year-two harvest is small; full production comes in year three or later.
factors_seasoned: soil pH (especially blueberry, which needs 4.5 to 5.5)
trellis or stake support for canes

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The most widely grown everbearing raspberry. Medium-large firm red berries with good flavor. Heavy fall crop late August to frost. Self-fertile. Vigorous and adaptable. Good beginner variety.
Extremely cold-hardy -- developed for Manitoba. Heavy producer of medium-sized sweet berries. Summer harvest in early July. Self-fertile. Top choice for zones 3-4.
Pale yellow berries with distinctive sweet banana-apricot flavor. Fall-bearing. Self-fertile. Ornamental as well as productive. Birds ignore yellow berries, reducing crop losses.

Highest-quality black raspberry available. Glossy black berries with rich flavor, ripen in July. Self-fertile. More disease-resistant than most black raspberries. Susceptible to anthracnose in humid years.
Heat-tolerant everbearing red -- better than Heritage in zones 7-9. Large sweet berries. Heavy fall crop. Self-fertile. Root rot resistant. Good choice for the Mid-Atlantic and upper South.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem. The more common cold issues are winter cane dieback on caneberries (canes that did not harden off in fall die back from the tips) and winter damage at the edge of blueberry's hardiness range. Some blackberry varieties are only hardy to USDA zone 6 or 7.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose varieties hardy to your zone. For caneberries, stop fertilizing by midsummer so canes harden off properly before winter. Mulch heavily in fall. In marginal zones for blackberry, lay primocanes flat under mulch for winter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Spotted wing drosophila (SWD) is now the dominant berry pest across most of the US -- it lays eggs in ripening fruit and the larvae make berries unsalvageable. Cane diseases (anthracnose, spur blight, cane blight) affect caneberries and survive in old floricanes. Blueberry maggot and mummy berry are blueberry-specific.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Remove and destroy spent floricanes immediately after harvest -- this is the main defense against cane disease and SWD overwintering. Pick ripe fruit promptly so SWD has less to lay eggs in. For blueberry mummy berry, mulch heavily in fall to bury fallen mummies.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Caneberries and elderberry are self-fertile and a single plant fruits. Blueberry is technically self-fertile but yields much more heavily with a second variety blooming at the same time -- a single bush often produces small or sparse berries. Cool wet weather during bloom keeps pollinators (especially bumblebees) grounded even when a partner is present.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant at least two compatible blueberry varieties for cross-pollination. Encourage native bumblebees with flowering plants nearby. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops want consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Blueberry hates wet feet and dies quickly in waterlogged soil; root rot from poorly-drained sites is a leading killer. Caneberries tolerate slightly more moisture but still suffer in standing water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: On heavy or low-lying soil, plant in a raised bed or mound. Blueberry especially does best in a 12-inch raised bed with bark-amended acidic soil. Ensure water drains away from the root zone.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops need full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to fruit well. Elderberry tolerates partial shade better than the others but still fruits more heavily in sun. Shaded canes and bushes grow leaves but produce few or small berries.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. For caneberries, avoid letting the row become a dense thicket -- thin canes to 4 to 6 per linear foot so light reaches all the fruiting wood.

crops.description_seasoned: One of the most productive garden shrubs. Summer-bearing (one big crop) or everbearing (two crops). Manage with a simple T-trellis and annual cane pruning. Very cold-hardy.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deep red (or yellow/black by variety). Pulls away from white core easily with no resistance. Soft and fragrant. Harvest daily.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Raspberries come in two bearing types that affect pruning and harvest timing. Summer-bearing (floricane) raspberries produce on 2-year-old canes, yielding one large crop in early summer. Everbearing (primocane) raspberries produce on first-year canes, yielding a fall crop and (if canes are left standing) a smaller summer crop the following year. For simplicity, cut primocane varieties to the ground each winter and enjoy one heavy fall harvest. Red and yellow raspberries are the most cold-hardy (zones 3-9). Black and purple raspberries are slightly less hardy (zones 4-8) and more disease-prone. Raspberries prefer cool summers -- fruit quality declines sharply above 85°F at ripening. In warm zones (8-9), grow in dappled afternoon shade. Plants spread by underground rhizomes and can become invasive; contain with a root barrier or mow around the patch. Establishment is fast: expect light crops in year 2, full crops in year 3.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Good chill requirement -- zones 4-8 ideal. Ever-bearing varieties more adaptable
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Bees improve yield.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: First-year canes (primocanes) don't fruit in summer types. Let them grow -- they'll fruit next year as floricanes.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root canes in late fall through early spring. Spring planting preferred in cold zones.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring aphids are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing fruit before full ripeness. Tiny maggots inside ripening berries.
pests.cause_seasoned: Drosophila suzukii fly. Major pest of soft fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Fine mesh netting (1mm) over plants during ripening. Spinosad spray. Harvest frequently.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Fine netting is most effective. Remove overripe fruit promptly.

diseases.name: Cane diseases (botrytis/anthracnose)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Purple/brown spots on canes. Die-back of canes. Gray mold on fruit in wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis and Elsinoe fungal diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected canes. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune out old canes after fruiting. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead irrigation.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze flat then bag -- very good quality.
storage.notes_seasoned: More robust than raspberries but still very perishable. Freeze surplus immediately.

varieties.note_seasoned: Triple Crown has the best flavor of thornless types -- the thorny Ouachita has even better flavor but needs gloves.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant from container in spring. Bare-root plants available in winter -- plant immediately on receipt.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted plant just set. Soil level matches the original line on the stems -- not buried deeper.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), mix peat moss or pine fines into the hole, and mulch with pine needles or wood chips. Cane fruits (raspberry, blackberry): plant alongside a trellis or post-and-wire support so the canes have something to grow on. Elderberry: tolerates wetter ground than the others. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves breaking. Blueberry pushes new shoots from the base; cane fruits send up new canes from the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water consistently through the first summer -- berries have shallow roots and dry out fast. Remove all flowers in year one so the plant builds its roots and a strong base. For raspberries and blackberries, pinch off the tip of each new cane once it reaches your trellis height; this encourages side branches that will carry fruit.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Multiple stems or canes coming up from the base. Blueberry fills out as a many-stemmed bush; cane fruits send up vigorous new canes; elderberry bushes out widely.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Berries don't get scaffold-branch training the way trees do -- they're naturally multi-stemmed. Blueberry: keep the strongest 4 to 6 stems and remove weak twiggy growth. Raspberry and blackberry: train new canes onto the trellis and thin them to about 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot. Elderberry: let it bush out freely; remove only crossed or weak growth.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blueberry leaves turn red-purple and drop. Raspberry and blackberry canes go fully bare. Elderberry drops cleanly. All are dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Top up the mulch before deep freeze, especially for shallow-rooted blueberry. In cold zones, consider laying down trailing blackberry canes and covering them with mulch or burlap. Real pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bush or canes fully dormant. Late-winter window before bud break.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: cane-renewal -- remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest canes at ground level each winter. Caneberries: remove last year's spent floricanes; thin remaining primocanes to 4 to 6 per linear foot.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring bloom on blueberry, raspberry, blackberry; early-summer bloom on elderberry. Frost risk usually past.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avoid sprays during bloom. Wild bumblebees are the main blueberry pollinators.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set & Bird Netting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Berries forming. Bird pressure ramps up as fruit colors.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Cross-pollination boosts blueberry yield -- a second variety nearby helps.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe fruit pulls free with gentle pressure. Bushes and canes are hand-height -- no ladders.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for thorny canes. Refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Cleanup
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Last fruit picked. Spent floricanes on caneberries dying back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut spent floricanes at ground level if not done in late winter. Apply a potassium-rich feed (use an acidic blueberry-specific fertilizer for blueberry). Refresh mulch.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: These crops are typically grown on their own roots -- there is no graft union. Plant with the crown at the original soil line. Blueberry needs acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5); test before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed.
Caneberries (raspberry, blackberry) need a trellis or support system from year one. Build it before planting; retrofitting around established canes is awkward.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- berries are shallow-rooted and dry out fast. Blueberry especially needs steady moisture and acidic mulch (pine bark, pine needles).
Remove flowers in year one on caneberries and blueberry. The energy goes into root and cane development; you will get more fruit from years two onward by skipping year one.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Blueberry develops as a multi-stemmed shrub. Let 5 to 7 main canes establish in the first 2 to 3 years; do not prune for shape, only remove damaged wood.
Caneberries put up new canes (primocanes) from the crown each year. In year one, let everything grow -- those are next year's fruiting canes (floricanes).

dormancy.text_seasoned: These crops are deciduous and go fully dormant in winter. Pruning is done in late winter or very early spring before bud break.
Refresh mulch before winter. For caneberries, tip-prune any canes that did not harden off (still green and floppy at the tip).

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Blueberry uses cane-renewal pruning. Each winter, remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest, least-productive canes at ground level to push new cane growth from the crown. By year 5 or 6 the bush has a rotating set of young productive canes.

Caneberries: remove all canes that fruited last summer (floricanes) -- they die after fruiting and harbor disease. Leave the new green canes (primocanes) for next year. Thin remaining canes to 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot of row.

blossom.text_seasoned: Blueberry, raspberry, and blackberry bloom late enough that spring frost is rarely the problem -- usually mid-to-late spring, after most frost danger is past. Elderberry blooms even later, in early summer.
Pollinators love these flowers. Do not spray during bloom. Wild bumblebees in particular are major pollinators of blueberry.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most blueberry varieties benefit from a second variety blooming at the same time for cross-pollination -- a single bush will fruit but a pair fruits much more heavily. Caneberries and elderberry are mostly self-fertile.
Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Once birds find the patch they keep coming back.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick fruit at hand height -- no ladders here. Ripe blueberries pull off with a gentle roll of the thumb; fruit that resists is not yet ripe (color is not enough -- some varieties color days before they sweeten).

Caneberries shatter when over-ripe -- pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for blackberry and the thorny raspberries. Eat or refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: After caneberry harvest, cut the spent floricanes (now dying or dead) at ground level if you did not get them in late winter. This removes overwintering sites for cane disease and the spotted wing drosophila.
A potassium-rich feed and a mulch refresh after harvest sets up next year's bloom. For blueberry, use an acidic fertilizer formulated for ericaceous plants.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 10-20 lbs per mature plant on a trellis -- the heaviest yielder of the cane fruits
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production typically arrives in year 4 to 7 depending on type. Berries ripen unevenly across a 2 to 4 week window, so expect to pick every few days at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Plan on no harvest in year one. Remove all flowers so the plant invests in roots and new canes. Year-two harvest is small; full production comes in year three or later.
factors_seasoned: soil pH (especially blueberry, which needs 4.5 to 5.5)
trellis or stake support for canes

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Cold-hardiest thornless blackberry. Vigorous trailing canes need a trellis. Large sweet berries, late ripening (August). Self-fertile. Disease resistant. The go-to thornless variety for zones 5-6.
Arkansas/USDA release. Huge sweet berries (among the largest blackberries). Heavy yields. Thornless canes need trellising. Mid-season ripening. Self-fertile. Good flavor and productivity.
Self-supporting thornless canes -- no trellising required. Medium-sized very sweet berries. Disease resistant. Self-fertile. Good choice for small gardens where space for trellising is limited.
First thornless primocane-fruiting blackberry. Produces on first-year canes -- cut to ground each winter for one heavy fall crop, or leave for two crops. Self-fertile. University of Arkansas release.

University of Illinois release specifically for cold zones. Thorny but reliably productive in zones 4-5 where most blackberries suffer cane die-back. Medium berries, good flavor. Self-supporting canes.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem. The more common cold issues are winter cane dieback on caneberries (canes that did not harden off in fall die back from the tips) and winter damage at the edge of blueberry's hardiness range. Some blackberry varieties are only hardy to USDA zone 6 or 7.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose varieties hardy to your zone. For caneberries, stop fertilizing by midsummer so canes harden off properly before winter. Mulch heavily in fall. In marginal zones for blackberry, lay primocanes flat under mulch for winter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Spotted wing drosophila (SWD) is now the dominant berry pest across most of the US -- it lays eggs in ripening fruit and the larvae make berries unsalvageable. Cane diseases (anthracnose, spur blight, cane blight) affect caneberries and survive in old floricanes. Blueberry maggot and mummy berry are blueberry-specific.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Remove and destroy spent floricanes immediately after harvest -- this is the main defense against cane disease and SWD overwintering. Pick ripe fruit promptly so SWD has less to lay eggs in. For blueberry mummy berry, mulch heavily in fall to bury fallen mummies.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Caneberries and elderberry are self-fertile and a single plant fruits. Blueberry is technically self-fertile but yields much more heavily with a second variety blooming at the same time -- a single bush often produces small or sparse berries. Cool wet weather during bloom keeps pollinators (especially bumblebees) grounded even when a partner is present.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant at least two compatible blueberry varieties for cross-pollination. Encourage native bumblebees with flowering plants nearby. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops want consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Blueberry hates wet feet and dies quickly in waterlogged soil; root rot from poorly-drained sites is a leading killer. Caneberries tolerate slightly more moisture but still suffer in standing water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: On heavy or low-lying soil, plant in a raised bed or mound. Blueberry especially does best in a 12-inch raised bed with bark-amended acidic soil. Ensure water drains away from the root zone.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops need full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to fruit well. Elderberry tolerates partial shade better than the others but still fruits more heavily in sun. Shaded canes and bushes grow leaves but produce few or small berries.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. For caneberries, avoid letting the row become a dense thicket -- thin canes to 4 to 6 per linear foot so light reaches all the fruiting wood.

crops.description_seasoned: Thornless varieties (Triple Crown, Navaho) make this a genuinely easy fruit. Enormous harvests from established canes. Everbearing types give two crops. More heat-tolerant than raspberries.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deep black, dull finish (not glossy). Soft, easily detached. Glossy black means one more day. Harvest every 2-3 days.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Blackberries come in three growth habits: erect (self-supporting thorny canes), semi-erect (need a trellis, mostly thornless), and trailing (need extensive trellising, best flavor). Thornless varieties are strongly preferred for home gardens -- the difference in harvesting experience is dramatic. Most blackberries are summer-bearing on second-year canes, but primocane-fruiting varieties (Prime-Ark series from University of Arkansas) produce on first-year canes like everbearing raspberries. Hardiness varies significantly by variety: erect types are generally hardy to zone 5, trailing types only to zone 6-7, and thornless semi-erect types to zone 5-6. In zones 4 and colder, cane die-back is common -- choose specifically cold-hardy varieties (Illini Hardy, Chester Thornless). Blackberries tolerate warmer climates than raspberries and are the small-fruit crop of choice in zones 8-9. Expect light harvests in year 2, full production in years 3-5.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Variable by variety -- thornless varieties tend toward lower chill
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Bees improve yield.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: First-year canes won't fruit until year two. Tip them at 3-4 feet to encourage lateral growth.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root in late fall through early spring. Space 3-4 feet apart in rows.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Very light feeder. Annual spring feed is sufficient. Elderberries are woodland plants that thrive in average soil without much intervention.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 10-10-10 in spring -- elderberries are largely self-sufficient

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune in late winter. Remove oldest canes and any dead wood. Keep plant to 5-6 main canes.
