pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Spotted wing drosophila
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Soft, collapsing fruit before full ripeness. Tiny maggots inside ripening berries.
pests.cause_seasoned: Drosophila suzukii fly. Major pest of soft fruit.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Fine mesh netting (1mm) over plants during ripening. Spinosad spray. Harvest frequently.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Fine netting is most effective. Remove overripe fruit promptly.

diseases.name: Cane diseases (botrytis/anthracnose)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Purple/brown spots on canes. Die-back of canes. Gray mold on fruit in wet conditions.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis and Elsinoe fungal diseases.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy affected canes. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune out old canes after fruiting. Improve airflow. Avoid overhead irrigation.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly when young, drought tolerant when mature

storage.fridge_seasoned: 3-5 days (only cooked elderberries -- raw are mildly toxic in quantity)
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze raw on stems, strip frozen -- freeze for months. Cook before eating.
storage.notes_seasoned: Always cook elderberries before eating -- raw elderberries contain sambunigrin which causes nausea. Cooked is safe and delicious.

varieties.note_seasoned: Plant two different varieties -- elderberries cross-pollinate and yield dramatically improves with two plants.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant from container in spring. Bare-root plants available in winter -- plant immediately on receipt.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted plant just set. Soil level matches the original line on the stems -- not buried deeper.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: plant in acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5), mix peat moss or pine fines into the hole, and mulch with pine needles or wood chips. Cane fruits (raspberry, blackberry): plant alongside a trellis or post-and-wire support so the canes have something to grow on. Elderberry: tolerates wetter ground than the others. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaves breaking. Blueberry pushes new shoots from the base; cane fruits send up new canes from the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water consistently through the first summer -- berries have shallow roots and dry out fast. Remove all flowers in year one so the plant builds its roots and a strong base. For raspberries and blackberries, pinch off the tip of each new cane once it reaches your trellis height; this encourages side branches that will carry fruit.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Multiple stems or canes coming up from the base. Blueberry fills out as a many-stemmed bush; cane fruits send up vigorous new canes; elderberry bushes out widely.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Berries don't get scaffold-branch training the way trees do -- they're naturally multi-stemmed. Blueberry: keep the strongest 4 to 6 stems and remove weak twiggy growth. Raspberry and blackberry: train new canes onto the trellis and thin them to about 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot. Elderberry: let it bush out freely; remove only crossed or weak growth.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Blueberry leaves turn red-purple and drop. Raspberry and blackberry canes go fully bare. Elderberry drops cleanly. All are dormant and frost-hardy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Top up the mulch before deep freeze, especially for shallow-rooted blueberry. In cold zones, consider laying down trailing blackberry canes and covering them with mulch or burlap. Real pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bush or canes fully dormant. Late-winter window before bud break.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Blueberry: cane-renewal -- remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest canes at ground level each winter. Caneberries: remove last year's spent floricanes; thin remaining primocanes to 4 to 6 per linear foot.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring bloom on blueberry, raspberry, blackberry; early-summer bloom on elderberry. Frost risk usually past.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avoid sprays during bloom. Wild bumblebees are the main blueberry pollinators.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set & Bird Netting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Berries forming. Bird pressure ramps up as fruit colors.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Cross-pollination boosts blueberry yield -- a second variety nearby helps.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Ripe fruit pulls free with gentle pressure. Bushes and canes are hand-height -- no ladders.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for thorny canes. Refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Cleanup
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Last fruit picked. Spent floricanes on caneberries dying back.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut spent floricanes at ground level if not done in late winter. Apply a potassium-rich feed (use an acidic blueberry-specific fertilizer for blueberry). Refresh mulch.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: These crops are typically grown on their own roots -- there is no graft union. Plant with the crown at the original soil line. Blueberry needs acidic soil (pH 4.5 to 5.5); test before planting and amend with elemental sulfur if needed.
Caneberries (raspberry, blackberry) need a trellis or support system from year one. Build it before planting; retrofitting around established canes is awkward.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- berries are shallow-rooted and dry out fast. Blueberry especially needs steady moisture and acidic mulch (pine bark, pine needles).
Remove flowers in year one on caneberries and blueberry. The energy goes into root and cane development; you will get more fruit from years two onward by skipping year one.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Blueberry develops as a multi-stemmed shrub. Let 5 to 7 main canes establish in the first 2 to 3 years; do not prune for shape, only remove damaged wood.
Caneberries put up new canes (primocanes) from the crown each year. In year one, let everything grow -- those are next year's fruiting canes (floricanes).

dormancy.text_seasoned: These crops are deciduous and go fully dormant in winter. Pruning is done in late winter or very early spring before bud break.
Refresh mulch before winter. For caneberries, tip-prune any canes that did not harden off (still green and floppy at the tip).

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Blueberry uses cane-renewal pruning. Each winter, remove 1 or 2 of the oldest, thickest, least-productive canes at ground level to push new cane growth from the crown. By year 5 or 6 the bush has a rotating set of young productive canes.

Caneberries: remove all canes that fruited last summer (floricanes) -- they die after fruiting and harbor disease. Leave the new green canes (primocanes) for next year. Thin remaining canes to 4 to 6 strong canes per linear foot of row.

blossom.text_seasoned: Blueberry, raspberry, and blackberry bloom late enough that spring frost is rarely the problem -- usually mid-to-late spring, after most frost danger is past. Elderberry blooms even later, in early summer.
Pollinators love these flowers. Do not spray during bloom. Wild bumblebees in particular are major pollinators of blueberry.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most blueberry varieties benefit from a second variety blooming at the same time for cross-pollination -- a single bush will fruit but a pair fruits much more heavily. Caneberries and elderberry are mostly self-fertile.
Drape bird netting after fruit colors and before any berry softens fully. Once birds find the patch they keep coming back.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick fruit at hand height -- no ladders here. Ripe blueberries pull off with a gentle roll of the thumb; fruit that resists is not yet ripe (color is not enough -- some varieties color days before they sweeten).

Caneberries shatter when over-ripe -- pick every 1 to 2 days during peak. Wear long sleeves for blackberry and the thorny raspberries. Eat or refrigerate immediately; berries do not store at room temperature.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: After caneberry harvest, cut the spent floricanes (now dying or dead) at ground level if you did not get them in late winter. This removes overwintering sites for cane disease and the spotted wing drosophila.
A potassium-rich feed and a mulch refresh after harvest sets up next year's bloom. For blueberry, use an acidic fertilizer formulated for ericaceous plants.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 12-15 lbs per mature shrub, harvested as cymes (not individual berries)
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production typically arrives in year 4 to 7 depending on type. Berries ripen unevenly across a 2 to 4 week window, so expect to pick every few days at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Plan on no harvest in year one. Remove all flowers so the plant invests in roots and new canes. Year-two harvest is small; full production comes in year three or later.
factors_seasoned: soil pH (especially blueberry, which needs 4.5 to 5.5)
trellis or stake support for canes

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Large vigorous shrub (8-10 feet). Heavy producer of large black fruit clusters. Ripens late August. Needs cross-pollination (York makes a good partner). The commercial standard for US elderberries.
Self-fertile but still produces better with a pollinator. Largest fruit of any elderberry variety. Late ripening. Pairs naturally with Adams for mutual pollination. Good disease resistance.
Canadian-bred. Very cold-hardy. Large sweet berries. Self-fertile but crops better with pollinator. Compact growth habit (6-8 feet). Early-ripening. Good choice for cold zones 3-4.
Vigorous large shrub -- produces huge yields. Earlier-ripening than Adams. Excellent pollinator for Adams and other varieties. Blue-black berries with good flavor. Often grown for wine-making.

European elderberry with ornamental deep-purple lacy foliage and pink flowers. Dual-purpose ornamental and edible. Less productive than American varieties but striking in the landscape. Requires cross-pollination.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem. The more common cold issues are winter cane dieback on caneberries (canes that did not harden off in fall die back from the tips) and winter damage at the edge of blueberry's hardiness range. Some blackberry varieties are only hardy to USDA zone 6 or 7.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose varieties hardy to your zone. For caneberries, stop fertilizing by midsummer so canes harden off properly before winter. Mulch heavily in fall. In marginal zones for blackberry, lay primocanes flat under mulch for winter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Spotted wing drosophila (SWD) is now the dominant berry pest across most of the US -- it lays eggs in ripening fruit and the larvae make berries unsalvageable. Cane diseases (anthracnose, spur blight, cane blight) affect caneberries and survive in old floricanes. Blueberry maggot and mummy berry are blueberry-specific.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Remove and destroy spent floricanes immediately after harvest -- this is the main defense against cane disease and SWD overwintering. Pick ripe fruit promptly so SWD has less to lay eggs in. For blueberry mummy berry, mulch heavily in fall to bury fallen mummies.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Caneberries and elderberry are self-fertile and a single plant fruits. Blueberry is technically self-fertile but yields much more heavily with a second variety blooming at the same time -- a single bush often produces small or sparse berries. Cool wet weather during bloom keeps pollinators (especially bumblebees) grounded even when a partner is present.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant at least two compatible blueberry varieties for cross-pollination. Encourage native bumblebees with flowering plants nearby. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops want consistent moisture but well-drained soil. Blueberry hates wet feet and dies quickly in waterlogged soil; root rot from poorly-drained sites is a leading killer. Caneberries tolerate slightly more moisture but still suffer in standing water.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: On heavy or low-lying soil, plant in a raised bed or mound. Blueberry especially does best in a 12-inch raised bed with bark-amended acidic soil. Ensure water drains away from the root zone.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops need full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to fruit well. Elderberry tolerates partial shade better than the others but still fruits more heavily in sun. Shaded canes and bushes grow leaves but produce few or small berries.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. For caneberries, avoid letting the row become a dense thicket -- thin canes to 4 to 6 per linear foot so light reaches all the fruiting wood.

crops.description_seasoned: Fast-growing native shrub that earns its place. Berries for syrup, wine, and preserves. Wildlife magnet. Very cold-hardy and adaptable. Plant two varieties for cross-pollination.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deep purple-black in heavy drooping clusters. Not all berries in a cluster ripen at once -- harvest when 80%+ are dark.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Elderberry (Sambucus canadensis, American elderberry) is a native North American shrub genuinely adaptable across most of the continental US. It tolerates wet soils that kill other fruit crops, shade better than most fruiting plants, and neglect better than almost anything. Fruit is never eaten raw -- it must be cooked to break down mildly toxic compounds. Primary uses are syrups, wines, jellies, and immune-support supplements. American elderberry is the correct species for the US; European elderberry (S. nigra) is less adapted and more susceptible to pests here. Elderberries are partially self-fertile but produce significantly larger crops with a second compatible variety planted within 50 feet. Plants are fast-growing (reach 8-12 feet in 2-3 years) and produce useful crops in year 2. They spread by root suckers and need occasional thinning, but are not aggressively invasive like some brambles.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Good chill requirement -- thrives in zones 3-8
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Partially self-fertile. Two different varieties dramatically increase yield. Bob Gordon and Nova are popular combinations.
crops.planting_method_notes_seasoned: Plant in early spring or fall. Can root from hardwood cuttings in late winter.

plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: In zones below their hardiness minimum, fig and pomegranate can be grown in containers and overwintered in an unheated garage or basement. harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Fig, pomegranate, and persimmon are warm-climate perennials. Plant bare-root or container stock in spring after last frost, or in fall in mild-winter zones. Fig is hardy to Zone 6 with winter protection (die-back hardy to Z5). Pomegranate Z7+. Persimmon (American) Z5+, Asian Z7+. Harvest late summer through fall once trees reach bearing age (2-4 years for fig and persimmon, 2-3 years for pomegranate). (UGA Extension Fig Production; Clemson HGIC Fig; UF/IFAS Pomegranate; UC Master Gardeners Persimmon)

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Light to moderate feeder. Balanced feed in spring and midsummer. Avoid excess nitrogen which delays fruit ripening.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 10-10-10 in spring -- persimmons need little feeding

tasks.description_seasoned: Minimal pruning needed. Remove dead wood and crossing branches in late winter. Scaffold branches set in years 1-3.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.reason: Legume rhizobial nitrogen fixation is textbook plant science. The mechanism is real; the specific pairing benefit is mechanistically plausible but often not pair-tested.

provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Raised bumps (1/8 inch or less) on twigs, branches, and sometimes fruit -- tan, gray, or white depending on species. Yellowing leaves, stunted growth, and twig dieback. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower foliage from soft scale species.
pests.cause_seasoned: Armored scales (White peach scale Pseudaulacaspis pentagona, Greedy scale Hemiberlesia rapax) and soft scales are primary persimmon pests per UF/IFAS. Protected under their waxy coating they are hard to kill with contact sprays.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant horticultural oil spray applied in late winter (before bud break) smothers overwintering scale and is the most effective organic treatment. Summer oil at reduced rate can be used during the growing season but only in cool weather. Prune out heavily infested branches.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect trees regularly -- early populations are easy to miss. Protect beneficial insects (parasitic wasps) that provide biological control. Avoid over-fertilizing.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: White cottony masses at leaf nodes, under calyxes, and on undersides of leaves. Sticky honeydew on lower leaves followed by sooty mold. Fruit drop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Longtailed mealybug (Pseudococcus longispinus) and related species. UF/IFAS lists persimmon among the mealybug's important hosts.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap targeting hidden areas (under leaves, in calyxes). Strong water spray for smaller infestations. Control ants that farm mealybugs.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect nursery stock. Prune for airflow so natural predators can reach colonies.

pests.name: Persimmon psyllid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Curled, puckered, and distorted young leaves. White mildew-like secretion on new leaves and small galls at leaf buds. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold. Hot weather usually reduces populations.
pests.cause_seasoned: Trioza diospyri (psyllid species specific to persimmon). Feeds by sucking sap from new growth. Overuse of broad-spectrum pesticides disrupts natural control.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant horticultural oil in late winter targets overwintering eggs. Insecticidal soap on nymphs during the spring flush. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill beneficial parasitic wasps.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Prune out heavily distorted shoots in spring. Support generalist predators by maintaining flowering groundcover.

diseases.name: Anthracnose leaf & fruit spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small dark brown to black circular spots on leaves, sometimes with a pale center. Leaves may yellow and drop early. On fruit, sunken black lesions that enlarge and can cause fruit drop or render fruit inedible.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides and related species. Spreads by rain splash in warm wet weather. Overwinters on fallen leaves and mummified fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rake and destroy fallen leaves and dropped fruit. Copper-based fungicide during extended wet weather, especially before and during bloom.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune for air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Keep the area under the tree clear of debris in fall and winter.

diseases.name: Persimmon wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting and browning of leaves in summer. Wilted leaves remain attached to dead branches. Dark vascular streaking visible when bark is peeled. Whole tree dies, often within one season. Affects American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana), not Asian persimmon.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Acremonium diospyri, a fungus specific to American persimmon. Spread by bark beetles that carry spores between trees. Historically caused widespread persimmon die-off in the southeastern US.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and burn affected trees promptly to reduce spread to healthy persimmons nearby.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki) or Asian-American hybrids where persimmon wilt is a known problem. Avoid wounding tree bark. Control bark beetle activity on nearby hardwoods.

diseases.name: Cercospora leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Numerous small circular brown spots on leaves, often with a yellow halo. Affected leaves yellow and drop prematurely. Heavy pressure can weaken the tree over multiple seasons.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Cercospora kaki and related fungi. Favored by warm humid weather with long leaf wetness periods.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rake and dispose of fallen leaves. Copper fungicide at bud break and again during wet weather if pressure is high.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune for airflow. Water at soil level. Clean up leaf litter in fall.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly young, drought tolerant when mature

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Fuyu: 1-2 weeks. Hachiya: until very soft (essential)
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze whole Hachiya -- freezing softens them perfectly for eating
storage.notes_seasoned: Astringent Hachiya persimmons must be completely soft before eating. Freezing is an excellent way to ripen them.

varieties.note_seasoned: Fuyu is the easy choice -- non-astringent, eat like an apple. Nikita's Gift is the best cold-hardy non-astringent option.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree or multi-trunk shrub just planted. Pomegranate often arrives as a multi-stem clump; mulberry and persimmon as single-trunk trees.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant high in well-drained soil. Stake mulberry and persimmon firmly; pomegranate usually doesn't need staking once the multi-trunk form is set. Water in deeply, mulch around the base, and avoid burying the lowest stems.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking. Pomegranate often pushes new shoots from the base in a clump; mulberry and persimmon push from existing stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Remove any first-year flowers or developing fruit. For pomegranate, decide now whether to keep the multi-trunk form (let 3 to 5 main trunks grow) or train it to a single trunk; remove the extra base shoots accordingly.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension. Mulberry grows quickly and may need its first directional pruning. Persimmon is slower. Pomegranate fills its multi-trunk clump.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulberry: pick one main vertical trunk and remove low side branches you don't want long-term -- mulberry grows large fast. Persimmon: light shaping only; both American and Asian persimmons fruit on last year's wood, so heavy pruning costs you crops. Pomegranate: keep the chosen 3 to 5 main trunks clear of small side shoots below knee height.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate all drop their leaves in late fall. Frost-hardy when fully dormant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulch around the base before hard freeze. Pomegranate benefits from extra mulch over the root zone in zone 7 and colder. Wrap young trunks in young-tree wrap if rabbits or sunscald are concerns. Major pruning waits until late winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Mulch and trunk protection in place?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant, leaves down. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon -- both fruit on previous-year wood. Pomegranate suckers freely; remove suckers and limit to 3 to 5 main trunks.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring or early-summer bloom -- well after main spring frost risk has passed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: These crops bloom late, so frost protection is rarely needed. Avoid spraying during bloom.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small green fruit forming after petal fall. Most home varieties are self-fertile.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thinning is rarely needed for this group. On heavy pomegranate set, thin lightly to prevent limb breakage.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mulberry summer-ripens over weeks; persimmon and pomegranate ripen in fall.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulberry: lay a sheet under the tree and shake, or pick ripe fruit daily. Persimmon: astringent types after first frost; non-astringent when fully colored. Pomegranate: when fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Last fruit picked. Drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Clear fallen fruit. Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed. Refresh mulch before winter.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: These trees are typically grown on their own roots in home gardens, so there is no graft union to worry about. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Water in well at planting and mulch a 3-foot circle around the base, kept a few inches back from the trunk. Staking is usually not needed unless the site is very windy.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- even after rain. Establishment takes one to two years; do not skip irrigation just because the tree looks fine.
These crops are slow to bear -- mulberry typically 2 to 3 years, persimmon 3 to 5, pomegranate 2 to 3. Patience is the main first-season skill.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Train to a modified central-leader or open-vase form depending on the species. Pomegranate is often grown as a multi-stemmed shrub; mulberry and persimmon take well to a single-trunk form.
Remove low water sprouts and any suckers. Pomegranate especially suckers freely and needs annual sucker removal.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter pruning is the rule for this group. Wait until leaves are fully down and the tree is dormant.
A mulch refresh and a deep watering before the ground freezes help winter survival, especially in the colder end of each species' hardiness range.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon. Both bear on previous-year wood and heavy heading reduces the next crop. Remove dead, diseased, damaged, and crossing branches; leave the rest.
Pomegranate is the exception -- it tolerates and benefits from heavier annual pruning to limit suckers and keep the canopy open. Limit to 3 to 5 main trunks if growing as a multi-stem.

blossom.text_seasoned: These crops bloom later than pome and stone fruit, so spring frost is rarely the problem. Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate flower from late spring into early summer in most zones.
Avoid spraying during bloom. Pollinators are doing the year's most important work in this window even on self-fertile crops.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile (American persimmon needs a male; Asian persimmon does not; pomegranate and mulberry are self-fertile). Confirm your variety before assuming.
Thinning is rarely needed -- the tree's natural set is usually appropriate. A heavy pomegranate set on a young tree may benefit from light thinning to avoid limb breakage.

harvest.text_seasoned: Mulberry ripens over 3 to 4 weeks; harvest by laying a sheet under the tree and shaking, or by picking ripe fruit daily. Persimmon and pomegranate ripen later -- persimmon is best after the first frost (astringent types) and pomegranate when the fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.
Handle ripe fruit gently. Mulberry and ripe persimmon stain badly and bruise even more easily than stone fruit.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear fallen fruit from under the tree. Sticky drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed after harvest to build reserves. Refresh mulch before winter.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 50-100 lbs from a mature American or Asian persimmon tree, often alternate-bearing
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production in year 4 to 6. Mature plants produce reliably for decades with very little intervention compared to deciduous fruit trees.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No useful crop in year one. These are tough, low-input plants once established, but year one is still a root-building year. Remove fruit if any sets.
factors_seasoned: light structural pruning -- these crops fruit on previous-year wood (mulberry, persimmon) or freely from suckers (pomegranate)
fruit drop when stressed in pomegranate

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The most popular Asian persimmon. Flat-round orange fruit can be eaten crisp like an apple. Self-fertile. Low chill requirement. The introductory persimmon for most new growers.
Large acorn-shaped orange fruit. Must be eaten fully soft and jelly-like; unripe fruit is painfully astringent. Self-fertile. Excellent for drying (hoshigaki). Classic for persimmon pudding.
Most cold-hardy Asian persimmon. Small-medium yellow-orange fruit, exceptionally sweet when ripe. Self-fertile. The Asian persimmon for zone 6 growers who can't grow Fuyu reliably.

Self-fertile American persimmon -- no male tree required. University of New Hampshire release. Small sweet orange fruit. Extremely cold-hardy. Essential for zones 4-5 where Asian persimmons cannot survive.
Selected seedling American persimmon with large sweet fruit (by native persimmon standards). Self-fertile. Excellent flavor. Popular choice among American persimmon enthusiasts for fruit quality.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem -- the more common cold issue is winter cold damage at the edge of each species' hardiness range. Pomegranate is hardy to about USDA zone 7; persimmon and mulberry are hardier (zones 4 to 5 for hardy varieties). Cold-damaged wood shows as dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety is hardy to your zone -- there is wide variation within each species. In marginal zones, plant in a sheltered south-facing site, mulch heavily before winter, and accept some annual dieback on pomegranate.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pest pressure on this group is generally lower than on pome or stone fruit. Mulberry attracts birds heavily once fruit ripens. Persimmon is sometimes hit by persimmon psyllid (curling new growth) or persimmon wilt. Pomegranate can suffer leaffooted bug damage and heart rot in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bird netting on mulberry once fruit colors. For persimmon psyllid, a dormant horticultural oil spray reduces overwintering populations. For pomegranate heart rot, choose resistant varieties and improve airflow with light pruning.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile. American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is the main exception -- it needs a male tree nearby. Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki), which is what most named varieties sold in the US are, sets fruit without a pollinator (sometimes seedless).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm whether your variety is American or Asian persimmon and whether it needs a male. For pomegranate and mulberry, persistent fruit-drop usually points to drought stress or extreme heat at bloom rather than pollination.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops want well-drained soil. Pomegranate is the most drought-tolerant; mulberry tolerates a wider moisture range; persimmon prefers consistent moisture but hates standing water. Symptoms of waterlogging are yellowing leaves, dieback, and root rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage before planting on heavy or low-lying soil -- plant on a 12-inch mound if needed. Pomegranate especially does best on the dry side once established.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to ripen and develop sugar. Pomegranate especially struggles in shade and may flower without setting fruit. Persimmon ripens unevenly without enough sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. Light pruning to keep the canopy open helps fruit ripen on the inside of the tree -- particularly important for pomegranate and persimmon.

crops.description_seasoned: Spectacular in autumn -- brilliant orange fruit hanging on bare branches is one of the garden's great sights. American persimmon is very cold-hardy (Zone 4); Asian/Fuyu is milder and sweeter.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Fuyu: pick when orange and firm. Hachiya: must be very soft and jelly-like before eating or very astringent. Frost or freezing softens them.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Persimmons come in two distinct species with very different hardiness profiles. American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is native to the eastern US and is remarkably cold-hardy, growing in zones 4-10. Fruits are small (1-2 inches) and intensely astringent until fully ripe (typically after the first fall frost), then become honey-sweet. Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki, also called Japanese persimmon or kaki) is hardy in zones 6-10 with larger 2-4 inch fruits. Asian persimmons come in two pollination classes: astringent (Hachiya, Saijo) which must be eaten fully soft, and non-astringent (Fuyu, Jiro) which can be eaten crisp like an apple. Most American persimmons require a male and female tree for fruit set (dioecious), though some self-fertile varieties exist. Asian persimmons are usually self-fertile. Both types are slow to begin bearing (year 4-7) but long-lived (50+ years) and essentially disease-free. Trees develop a deep taproot -- transplant when young or from containers only.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Low chill -- American varieties hardier than Japanese
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: American and Asian persimmons are self-fertile. Fruit is seedless when grown alone.

tasks.description_seasoned: Light prune after harvest or in early spring. Avocados bleed sap heavily -- keep pruning minimal. Remove dead wood and shape for size control.

pests.name: Persea mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Circular yellow spots on leaf undersides that become brown necrotic patches. Fine webbing on leaf undersides visible with a hand lens. Severe infestations cause widespread leaf browning and premature leaf drop, exposing fruit and trunk to sunburn.
pests.cause_seasoned: Oligonychus perseae. UC ANR identifies this as a key California avocado pest. Populations build April-June, peak July-August on the undersides of mature leaves.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil or narrow-range summer oil applied to leaf undersides. Direct water sprays to knock down populations. Predatory mites (Neoseiulus californicus) provide biological control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Monitor leaf undersides from spring onward. Avoid dusty conditions near groves. Protect beneficial mite populations by avoiding broad-spectrum miticides.

pests.name: Avocado thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silvery or tan scarring on fruit skin with a leathery 'alligator skin' appearance as fruit expands. Damage occurs while fruit is 5-15 mm long (early spring). Internal fruit quality is unaffected but market appearance is ruined. Tiny (2 mm) brown-orange insects on new leaves and young fruit.
pests.cause_seasoned: Scirtothrips perseae. UC ANR cites avocado thrips as responsible for large California industry losses. Each female lays up to 300 eggs; multiple generations per season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spinosad (evening applications to protect bees) during early fruit set. Horticultural oil reduces populations. Protect native predatory thrips (Franklinothrips spp.).
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout weekly during bloom and early fruit development. Reduce tender flush growth that thrips prefer -- careful pruning and moderate nitrogen help.

pests.name: Armored scale
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular or oval raised bumps on leaves, twigs, and sometimes fruit. Yellowing and premature leaf drop in heavy infestations. Unlike soft scales, armored scales do not produce honeydew.
pests.cause_seasoned: Latania scale, greedy scale, and oleander scale are most commonly found on avocado per UC ANR. Protected under their waxy covers, they are hard to control with contact sprays.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Narrow-range horticultural oil at delayed-dormant timing and again as needed during the growing season. Parasitic wasps provide biological control if not disrupted by broad-spectrum sprays.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect nursery stock. Avoid ant-tended areas (ants protect scale from parasitoid wasps). Control dust, which interferes with parasitic wasps.

pests.name: Avocado lace bug
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow stippling visible on upper leaf surfaces. Undersides of leaves show dark spots of lace bug excrement and tiny clear-winged insects. In severe infestations, whole leaves brown and drop.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pseudacysta perseae. Most damaging during hot dry weather. An established pest in Florida and increasing in California.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil sprayed on leaf undersides where lace bugs live. Multiple applications during population buildup. Remove heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Monitor leaf undersides starting in early summer. Maintain consistent irrigation -- drought-stressed trees suffer worse damage.

diseases.name: Phytophthora root rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small pale leaves that wilt in afternoon heat. Sparse canopy with many small leaves. Twig dieback from the tips inward. Fruit small and misshapen. Digging reveals dark, rotted, sparse feeder roots instead of the healthy white mat a healthy tree should have.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora cinnamomi, a soil-borne oomycete. UC ANR and international sources identify this as the single most destructive avocado disease worldwide. Thrives in waterlogged soils.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective cure. Reduce tree stress with careful irrigation (avoid waterlogging) and mulching. Phosphonate products (systemic, available to commercial growers) can slow decline but do not eliminate the pathogen.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on resistant rootstocks (Duke 7, Dusa, Toro Canyon) -- this is the single most important prevention step. Plant on well-drained sites or mounded beds. Do not over-irrigate. Inspect nursery stock carefully; do not introduce infested soil or plants.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small sunken dark lesions on fruit, often first appearing at the stem end and expanding as fruit ripens. May show concentric ring pattern. Black spots on stems and leaves. Severely affected fruit rots on the tree or in storage.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides. Infects during humid weather but may remain latent until fruit ripens, which is why losses often appear post-harvest. Overwinters on infected twigs, leaves, and mummified fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove infected fruit from tree and ground. Copper fungicide preventively during wet weather. Handle fruit carefully -- bruises invite anthracnose.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune for airflow. Rake fallen leaves and remove mummified fruit. Avoid overhead irrigation. Plant anthracnose-resistant varieties if available.

diseases.name: Branch canker & dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dead or dying branches with discolored bark. Dark staining visible in the wood beneath. Small white or pink spore masses may appear on infected wood. Whole branches die back from the tip over weeks to months.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Neofusicoccum and related Botryosphaeriaceae fungi (formerly called Dothiorella canker). Enter through pruning wounds and stressed tissue. Drought-stressed trees are most vulnerable.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out affected branches well below visible damage. Disinfect tools between cuts. Dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Keep trees adequately irrigated but not waterlogged. Prune during dry weather. Avoid sunburn by whitewashing exposed trunks on young trees.

diseases.name: Laurel wilt (regional)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of upper canopy followed by rapid whole-tree death, sometimes within weeks. Dark blue-black streaks visible in the sapwood. Small entry holes from the beetle vector on the trunk. Primarily a Florida concern.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Raffaelea lauricola fungus vectored by the redbay ambrosia beetle (Xyleborus glabratus). UF/IFAS documents laurel wilt as a major and devastating Florida avocado disease since roughly 2012. Not yet established in California.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Affected trees must be removed and destroyed to slow spread to neighboring trees. Systemic fungicide injections may give temporary protection for high-value trees but are not a home-gardener treatment.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant disease-free nursery stock. Remove dying laurel-family trees (redbay, swampbay, camphor) nearby, which serve as beetle reservoirs. Contact local extension if you suspect laurel wilt -- it is a reportable disease in some states.

watering.amount_seasoned: Deep soak -- avocados are sensitive to both over and underwatering
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level, good drainage essential
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellowing, root rot -- very common problem

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Ripen at room temperature -- hard avocados take 3-5 days
storage.fridge_seasoned: Once ripe: 2-3 days. Unripe: up to 2 weeks
storage.freezer_seasoned: Mash with lemon juice and freeze -- good for guacamole
storage.notes_seasoned: Speed ripening by placing next to a banana in a paper bag.

varieties.note_seasoned: Bacon is the most cold-tolerant Guatemalan-type avocado -- reliable in Z8 where Hass struggles. Wurtz stays under 8 feet -- ideal for containers.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Avocados grow in containers in cold climates but need very large pots (25+ gallons) and excellent drainage. Use avocado/citrus potting mix. They rarely fruit in containers outside tropical zones.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Container-grown grafted tree just planted. The graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits well above soil. Often staked briefly while establishing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avocado has fragile roots and is prone to root rot -- plant on a small mound to ensure good drainage, with the top of the rootball slightly above ground level. Avoid lawn locations; avocado roots compete poorly with turfgrass. Water deeply, mulch generously, keeping mulch off the trunk.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree planted on mound with good drainage?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf flush emerging. Avocado pushes growth in flushes rather than steadily.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water 2 to 3 times a week the first summer, less near the coast. Check soil moisture before each watering -- avocado hates wet feet. Begin light nitrogen feeding once new growth appears. Remove any first-year flowers (most won't set fruit anyway).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: New flush and watering schedule set?

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree filling out with leaves; lower branches sometimes drooping. Canopy taking shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avocado needs almost no training. Fruit forms at the outer edges of the canopy, so a wide, dense canopy matters more than a defined branch structure. Pinch the tips of long lanky shoots to encourage side branching. Remove any shoots growing from below the graft union. Avoid heavy pruning -- avocado wood is brittle and exposed bark sunburns easily.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Avocado is evergreen and does not drop its leaves. Growth slows in cool weather; the tree holds its shape and color.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Avocado's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not a leaf-fall. Frost is the year-one killer -- young trees are damaged below 30°F and killed below 25. Cover with frost cloth or string warm holiday lights through the canopy when overnight lows threaten. Reduce watering frequency but don't let the rootball dry out.

growth_stages.name: Light Annual Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After main harvest or in late winter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light shape pruning. Remove dead wood, suckers, ground-dragging branches.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Heavy bloom in spring. A-type or B-type pattern.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant both A and B types nearby for best set. Do not spray.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruit forming. Heavy early-summer drop is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruit in heavy years to level alternate bearing.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mature fruit by size and variety-specific color. Tree is the storage.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick mature fruit, ripen at room temperature.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Feeding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Main harvest done.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Apply fertilizer with extra zinc and iron. Refresh mulch.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Avocado is grafted on rootstock chosen for soil tolerance and disease resistance, especially Phytophthora resistance. The graft union must sit 2 to 4 inches above soil level -- buried unions invite root rot.
Plant in spring once nights are reliably above 50 degrees. Avocado roots are extremely sensitive to disturbance -- handle the root ball gently and avoid loosening the bottom of the hole.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply but infrequently. Avocado has shallow brittle roots that drown easily in waterlogged soil and die quickly in drought -- the sweet spot is moist-but-never-soggy. Aim for the top 2 inches of soil to dry slightly between waterings.
Mulch heavily with coarse organic mulch (wood chips, bark) but keep mulch 6 inches back from the trunk. Avocado evolved in tropical leaf-litter environments and the deep mulch genuinely matters.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Avocado is grown as a balanced canopy or pyramidal tree, not as central-leader or open-center. Do not strip lower branches -- avocado fruits at the canopy edge and the lower limbs are productive.
Pinch the growing tip at 24 to 30 inches to encourage branching. Otherwise avocado tends to grow as a tall whip with few side branches.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Avocado is evergreen and does not have true dormancy. Growth slows in winter but the tree is never bare.

In the cooler end of avocado range, freeze protection (frost cloth, banking soil around the trunk, string lights) is the winter task. Mature trees of cold-hardy varieties (Mexican-race) survive brief drops to about 24 degrees; tropical varieties die at 30.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Avocado pruning is light and shape-focused, done in late winter or after the main harvest. Remove dead wood, suckers from below the graft union, and any branches dragging on the ground.
Avoid heavy heading cuts. Avocado fruits on the previous year's wood at the canopy edge -- removing that growth removes next year's fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Avocado has an unusual bloom system: each flower opens twice, once as functionally female and once as functionally male, but a tree's flowers are synchronized to be female and male at different times. 'A-type' varieties are female in the morning; 'B-type' varieties are female in the afternoon.
A single tree of either type sets fruit because flowers overlap in many conditions, but planting both types nearby boosts fruit set significantly. Do not spray during bloom.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Avocado often shows alternate bearing -- a heavy crop year followed by a light year. This is partly genetic and partly fixable by thinning fruit on heavy years.
Persistent fruit drop in early summer is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Drop later in the season usually indicates water stress or boron deficiency.

harvest.text_seasoned: Avocado does not ripen on the tree. Pick mature fruit (size and skin color appropriate to the variety) and ripen at room temperature -- 5 to 14 days depending on the variety. The tree is the storage; mature fruit can hang on the tree for weeks or months.
Use a picking pole with a basket on the end for high fruit, or a clipper for low fruit. Twist gently rather than pulling; pulling tears bark.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Avocado is heavy-feeding -- apply a balanced fertilizer with extra zinc and iron after the main harvest. Yellowing leaves between green veins indicates iron deficiency, especially in alkaline soil.
Refresh mulch annually. Avocado roots need the leaf-litter environment year-round.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 60-200 lbs from a mature dooryard tree in a typical year, with strong alternate-bearing common -- a heavy year followed by a much lighter one
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Grafted trees bear in year 3 to 4 and reach full production around year 5 to 8. Mature trees often alternate -- a heavy crop one year followed by a lighter crop the next.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. Avocado trees produce huge numbers of flowers but only about 1 in 10,000 sets fruit even at maturity, so first-year flowers can be ignored or removed without loss.
factors_seasoned: frost protection -- avocados are damaged or killed below about 28°F
well-drained soil (avocado is highly susceptible to root rot)

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Most cold-hardy commonly available avocado. Small black-skinned fruit with excellent rich flavor -- many consider it superior to Hass. Type A. Self-fertile. The avocado for zone 8 growers.

The commercial standard -- the avocado you buy in stores. Medium-large pebbly-skinned fruit that blackens when ripe. Type A. Partially self-fertile but bears heavier with a Type B pollinator (Fuerte works well).
Green-skinned pear-shaped avocado. Milder and creamier than Hass, stays green at ripeness. Type B. Classic pollinator for Hass in home orchards. More cold-hardy than Hass.
Medium green-skinned fruit, earlier ripening than most avocados. Type B. Good pollinator for Hass. More cold-hardy than Hass, making it a better zone 9a choice. Mild flavor.

Purple-black-skinned fruit with rich flavor. Cold-hardy for a Mexican-West Indian type. Type A. Good choice for Gulf Coast growers (Texas, Louisiana, Florida Panhandle) where heat and humidity defeat California varieties.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Avocado is evergreen and does not become fully dormant; freeze damage is whole-tree (leaves, twigs, fruit, and even bark splitting) rather than blossom-frost. Mexican-race varieties (Bacon, Mexicola, Stewart) tolerate brief drops to about 24 degrees; West Indian varieties die at 30 to 32. Damage shows as leaf drop, blackened twigs, and split bark.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover with frost cloth on freeze nights; bank soil up around the graft union before winter so the rootstock survives even if the top is killed. In marginal zones, choose the most cold-hardy varieties or grow in a movable container.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Phytophthora root rot is by far the most serious avocado problem -- it kills more avocados than any other cause. Persea mite and avocado lace bug damage leaves but rarely kill trees. Laurel wilt (a fungal disease spread by an invasive beetle) is now killing avocados in parts of Florida.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose Phytophthora-resistant rootstock (Dusa, Toro Canyon) when planting. Keep mulch off the trunk and ensure excellent drainage. For persea mite, encourage predatory mites with reduced spraying. In Florida, follow state guidance on laurel wilt.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Avocado has the unusual A-type / B-type flower system: a single tree's flowers are synchronized male or female at different times of day, so any one tree's pollen is rarely available when its own flowers are receptive. A single tree often sets some fruit (because conditions can shift the timing) but pairs of A and B types crank up the set substantially.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant an A-type and a B-type nearby (within 30 feet). Hass is A-type; Bacon, Fuerte, and Zutano are B-type. Encourage native bees and avoid spraying during the long bloom window.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Avocado is more prone to Phytophthora root rot than any other backyard fruit tree. The pathogen thrives in wet soil and kills feeder roots; the tree slowly declines with yellowing leaves, dieback, and eventually death. Once established it cannot be cured.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on a 12-inch raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Choose Phytophthora-resistant rootstock. Water deeply but infrequently and let the top inch of soil dry between waterings. Keep mulch off the trunk.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Avocado needs full sun, 6 to 8 hours minimum, to bloom and ripen fruit properly. In partial shade the tree grows leaves but bears poorly. Wind exposure also hurts -- avocado leaves and fruit damage easily in strong wind.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun in a wind-sheltered spot. South or southwest exposure is ideal. Avoid planting close to eucalyptus or other trees with allelopathic root chemistry.

crops.description_seasoned: Large, beautiful tree that fruits heavily once established. Very frost-sensitive -- even 29°F can damage young trees. Two types (A and B) flower at different times -- plant one of each for best yields.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick when full sized. Leave on tree until needed -- they ripen after harvest. Test by picking one and ripening at room temperature -- takes 5-7 days.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Avocados (Persea americana) come in three racial types with dramatically different cold tolerances. Mexican varieties (Persea americana var. drymifolia) are the most cold-hardy, tolerating 16-18°F -- these are the practical choice for zone 8-9 growers. Guatemalan varieties tolerate to 24°F and are zone 10. West Indian varieties are true tropicals, damaged below 32°F, and are really only for zone 11. Commercial Hass is a Guatemalan-Mexican hybrid hardy to about 24°F (zone 9b). Most avocados require cross-pollination between Type A and Type B varieties (flowers open as female one day and male the next on complementary schedules); this is why commercial orchards always have pollinator trees interspersed. Home growers often plant a Type A + Type B pair. Avocados are shallow-rooted, drought-sensitive once bearing, and intolerant of wet feet. Trees begin bearing in year 3-5 from grafted trees, 7-10 years from seed. Seed-grown trees produce fruit but usually not true to type.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: No chill requirement -- frost protection critical. Zones 9-11
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Avocados are technically self-fertile but have Type A and Type B flower timing. Plant one of each type for significantly better yields (e.g. Hass + Fuerte, or Hass + Bacon).
