pests.name: Mulberry whitefly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small white winged insects flush up in clouds when leaves are disturbed. Oval dark nymphs fringed with white wax cling to leaf undersides. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold on lower foliage. Light to moderate infestations rarely threaten an established tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Tetraleurodes mori, named for mulberry although it feeds on other hosts. The Connecticut Agricultural Experiment Station identifies this as a mulberry-specific pest, though control is rarely needed.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Strong water spray to knock down adults. Insecticidal soap or horticultural oil on leaf undersides. Yellow sticky traps for monitoring. Beneficial wasps usually keep populations in check.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill parasitic wasps. Most home trees never need treatment.

pests.name: Scale insects
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Raised bumps (light tan to gray) on twigs, branches, and sometimes leaf stems. Yellowing leaves, twig dieback, and reduced vigor in heavy infestations. Sometimes sticky honeydew from soft-scale species.
pests.cause_seasoned: Armored scales in the family Diaspididae are common on mulberry. Protected under waxy covers that resist contact sprays. Crawlers (the mobile juvenile stage) are the vulnerable stage.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dormant horticultural oil in late winter smothers overwintering scale. Summer oil at reduced rate during crawler activity (typically early summer). Prune out heavily infested branches.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect trunk and branches annually. Control ants that farm scale. Prune for airflow.

pests.name: Mealybugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: White cottony masses at leaf axils and on twigs. Slowed plant growth, twig dieback, premature leaf drop. Sooty mold on lower leaves. Worst on young trees and in warm climates.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several Pseudococcus species. Often tended by ants, which protect them from parasitic wasps.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap, focusing on hidden areas. Control ants with sticky trunk bands.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Inspect new trees before planting. Maintain healthy tree vigor -- stressed mulberries attract more pests.

pests.name: Japanese beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Skeletonized leaves (only the major veins remain), starting at the top of the tree and moving downward. Masses of metallic green-and-copper beetles feeding together, especially in sunny weather. July is the usual peak.
pests.cause_seasoned: Popillia japonica adults. Mulberry is listed among the 275+ plants they attack. Damage is usually cosmetic on a mature tree but can defoliate young trees.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick in early morning when beetles are sluggish -- knock into soapy water. Avoid pheromone traps in the home garden (they attract more beetles than they catch). Neem oil deters feeding on young trees.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Encourage ground-nesting predators by leaving some bare ground. Healthy lawns with parasitic nematodes have fewer grubs.

diseases.name: Bacterial blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Water-soaked spots on young leaves that turn brown or black with yellow halos. Leaf distortion. Black stripes or lesions on young shoots. Twig tip dieback. Heaviest in cool wet spring weather. On fruit: dark irregular spots.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas syringae pv. mori. TAMU and PNW Handbook both identify this as the primary bacterial disease of mulberry. Favored by cool, wet weather. Young leaves are most susceptible.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy affected shoots during dry weather. Copper-based bactericide at late-dormant timing and again at bud break in high-pressure years.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Prune only in dry weather. Minimize wounds to limbs and new shoots. Mulch to reduce soil splash.

diseases.name: Leaf spot (false mildew)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Whitish indefinite patches on undersides of leaves appearing in mid-summer. Yellowish spores emerge from leaf stomata, spreading out as a white cobweb-like coating. Leaves yellow and fall prematurely. In the South this can be severe.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Mycosphaerella mori fungus. TAMU notes this is a significant disease on mulberries growing in southern states. Overwinters on fallen leaves.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn to reduce overwintering inoculum. Copper fungicide at first sign of infection in high-pressure areas.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune for airflow. Water at soil level. Gather and remove or compost fallen leaves in fall.

diseases.name: Cankers & branch dieback
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken discolored areas on twigs and branches. Black masses of spores sometimes visible in infected bark. Branches beyond the canker die back. Cankers on main trunks can kill the tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Multiple fungi including Cytospora, Dothiorella, Gibberella, and Fusarium species per TAMU. Often follows freeze damage, pruning wounds, or drought stress.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out cankered branches well below the visible damage. Disinfect pruning tools between cuts. Trees with trunk cankers generally cannot be saved.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune in dry weather with clean, sharp cuts. Avoid wounding the trunk (mower and string-trimmer damage). Keep the tree watered during drought but not waterlogged.

diseases.name: Root-knot nematodes
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Stunted, slow-growing young trees. Yellowing leaves. Afternoon wilting despite adequate water. Pulling a young tree reveals galled, knobby roots. Less impact on established mature trees.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Meloidogyne spp., microscopic roundworms. TAMU notes seedling mulberries in the East and Southwest are vulnerable. Sandy soils favor the pest.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective in-ground chemical treatment for home growers. Amend with compost to support beneficial soil microbes.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Test soil for nematodes before planting. In known-infested soils, plant elsewhere or use resistant rootstocks where available. French marigolds as a cover crop before planting can reduce population.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze immediately -- lasts 6 months, excellent quality
storage.notes_seasoned: Mulberries are one of the most perishable fruits. The reason you never see them in stores. Freeze everything you can't eat same day.

varieties.note_seasoned: Illinois Everbearing is the most reliable backyard mulberry -- productive over 6-8 weeks rather than 2 weeks for other varieties.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree or multi-trunk shrub just planted. Pomegranate often arrives as a multi-stem clump; mulberry and persimmon as single-trunk trees.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant high in well-drained soil. Stake mulberry and persimmon firmly; pomegranate usually doesn't need staking once the multi-trunk form is set. Water in deeply, mulch around the base, and avoid burying the lowest stems.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking. Pomegranate often pushes new shoots from the base in a clump; mulberry and persimmon push from existing stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Remove any first-year flowers or developing fruit. For pomegranate, decide now whether to keep the multi-trunk form (let 3 to 5 main trunks grow) or train it to a single trunk; remove the extra base shoots accordingly.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension. Mulberry grows quickly and may need its first directional pruning. Persimmon is slower. Pomegranate fills its multi-trunk clump.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulberry: pick one main vertical trunk and remove low side branches you don't want long-term -- mulberry grows large fast. Persimmon: light shaping only; both American and Asian persimmons fruit on last year's wood, so heavy pruning costs you crops. Pomegranate: keep the chosen 3 to 5 main trunks clear of small side shoots below knee height.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate all drop their leaves in late fall. Frost-hardy when fully dormant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulch around the base before hard freeze. Pomegranate benefits from extra mulch over the root zone in zone 7 and colder. Wrap young trunks in young-tree wrap if rabbits or sunscald are concerns. Major pruning waits until late winter.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Mulch and trunk protection in place?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant, leaves down. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon -- both fruit on previous-year wood. Pomegranate suckers freely; remove suckers and limit to 3 to 5 main trunks.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring or early-summer bloom -- well after main spring frost risk has passed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: These crops bloom late, so frost protection is rarely needed. Avoid spraying during bloom.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small green fruit forming after petal fall. Most home varieties are self-fertile.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thinning is rarely needed for this group. On heavy pomegranate set, thin lightly to prevent limb breakage.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mulberry summer-ripens over weeks; persimmon and pomegranate ripen in fall.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mulberry: lay a sheet under the tree and shake, or pick ripe fruit daily. Persimmon: astringent types after first frost; non-astringent when fully colored. Pomegranate: when fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Last fruit picked. Drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Clear fallen fruit. Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed. Refresh mulch before winter.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: These trees are typically grown on their own roots in home gardens, so there is no graft union to worry about. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Water in well at planting and mulch a 3-foot circle around the base, kept a few inches back from the trunk. Staking is usually not needed unless the site is very windy.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season -- even after rain. Establishment takes one to two years; do not skip irrigation just because the tree looks fine.
These crops are slow to bear -- mulberry typically 2 to 3 years, persimmon 3 to 5, pomegranate 2 to 3. Patience is the main first-season skill.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Train to a modified central-leader or open-vase form depending on the species. Pomegranate is often grown as a multi-stemmed shrub; mulberry and persimmon take well to a single-trunk form.
Remove low water sprouts and any suckers. Pomegranate especially suckers freely and needs annual sucker removal.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Winter pruning is the rule for this group. Wait until leaves are fully down and the tree is dormant.
A mulch refresh and a deep watering before the ground freezes help winter survival, especially in the colder end of each species' hardiness range.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Light structural pruning only on mulberry and persimmon. Both bear on previous-year wood and heavy heading reduces the next crop. Remove dead, diseased, damaged, and crossing branches; leave the rest.
Pomegranate is the exception -- it tolerates and benefits from heavier annual pruning to limit suckers and keep the canopy open. Limit to 3 to 5 main trunks if growing as a multi-stem.

blossom.text_seasoned: These crops bloom later than pome and stone fruit, so spring frost is rarely the problem. Mulberry, persimmon, and pomegranate flower from late spring into early summer in most zones.
Avoid spraying during bloom. Pollinators are doing the year's most important work in this window even on self-fertile crops.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile (American persimmon needs a male; Asian persimmon does not; pomegranate and mulberry are self-fertile). Confirm your variety before assuming.
Thinning is rarely needed -- the tree's natural set is usually appropriate. A heavy pomegranate set on a young tree may benefit from light thinning to avoid limb breakage.

harvest.text_seasoned: Mulberry ripens over 3 to 4 weeks; harvest by laying a sheet under the tree and shaking, or by picking ripe fruit daily. Persimmon and pomegranate ripen later -- persimmon is best after the first frost (astringent types) and pomegranate when the fruit cracks slightly or sounds metallic when tapped.
Handle ripe fruit gently. Mulberry and ripe persimmon stain badly and bruise even more easily than stone fruit.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Clear fallen fruit from under the tree. Sticky drops attract wasps and yellow jackets in late summer.
Apply a balanced or potassium-rich feed after harvest to build reserves. Refresh mulch before winter.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Heavy bearer once mature -- expect 50+ lbs from a mature tree, ripening over a 2 to 6 week window with daily pickings
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production in year 4 to 6. Mature plants produce reliably for decades with very little intervention compared to deciduous fruit trees.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No useful crop in year one. These are tough, low-input plants once established, but year one is still a root-building year. Remove fruit if any sets.
factors_seasoned: light structural pruning -- these crops fruit on previous-year wood (mulberry, persimmon) or freely from suckers (pomegranate)
fruit drop when stressed in pomegranate

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Most popular mulberry for US home gardens. Large sweet dark berries over a long bearing season (6+ weeks). Self-fertile. Cold-hardy. Produces heavily even in light shade. Nearly seedless.
Produces enormous berries (3-4 inches long) with excellent sweet flavor. Self-fertile. Requires warm climate. Not hardy in cold zones. The most impressive mulberry for warm-climate growers.
Compact tree (6-10 feet) suitable for containers or small gardens. Self-fertile. Small sweet black berries over long season. More cold-hardy than most black mulberries. Good patio tree.
Cold-hardy cultivar from Minnesota. Very productive with large sweet black-purple fruit. Self-fertile. Good choice for zone 4-5 growers where Illinois Everbearing may struggle in severe winters.
True black mulberry with the species' legendary flavor -- widely regarded as the best-tasting mulberry. Compact tree (10-15 feet). Self-fertile. Only for warm-winter zones; not cold-hardy.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops bloom late enough that spring frost during bloom is rarely the problem -- the more common cold issue is winter cold damage at the edge of each species' hardiness range. Pomegranate is hardy to about USDA zone 7; persimmon and mulberry are hardier (zones 4 to 5 for hardy varieties). Cold-damaged wood shows as dieback the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety is hardy to your zone -- there is wide variation within each species. In marginal zones, plant in a sheltered south-facing site, mulch heavily before winter, and accept some annual dieback on pomegranate.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pest pressure on this group is generally lower than on pome or stone fruit. Mulberry attracts birds heavily once fruit ripens. Persimmon is sometimes hit by persimmon psyllid (curling new growth) or persimmon wilt. Pomegranate can suffer leaffooted bug damage and heart rot in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Bird netting on mulberry once fruit colors. For persimmon psyllid, a dormant horticultural oil spray reduces overwintering populations. For pomegranate heart rot, choose resistant varieties and improve airflow with light pruning.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most home varieties of these crops are self-fertile. American persimmon (Diospyros virginiana) is the main exception -- it needs a male tree nearby. Asian persimmon (Diospyros kaki), which is what most named varieties sold in the US are, sets fruit without a pollinator (sometimes seedless).
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm whether your variety is American or Asian persimmon and whether it needs a male. For pomegranate and mulberry, persistent fruit-drop usually points to drought stress or extreme heat at bloom rather than pollination.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops want well-drained soil. Pomegranate is the most drought-tolerant; mulberry tolerates a wider moisture range; persimmon prefers consistent moisture but hates standing water. Symptoms of waterlogging are yellowing leaves, dieback, and root rot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage before planting on heavy or low-lying soil -- plant on a 12-inch mound if needed. Pomegranate especially does best on the dry side once established.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to ripen and develop sugar. Pomegranate especially struggles in shade and may flower without setting fruit. Persimmon ripens unevenly without enough sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. Light pruning to keep the canopy open helps fruit ripen on the inside of the tree -- particularly important for pomegranate and persimmon.

crops.description_seasoned: The fastest-fruiting tree you can plant -- may fruit year one. Massive production, almost zero maintenance. Fruit stains everything, so don't plant over paths or parking. Incredibly productive.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Berries turn from red to deep purple-black. Pick by spreading a sheet and shaking branches. Stain everything -- wear old clothes.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Mulberry (Morus species) is an easy, adaptable fruit tree that fits well in a backyard but has two quirks worth knowing. First, ripe mulberries drop readily and stain hard surfaces -- don't plant over a patio, sidewalk, or driveway. Second, fruit doesn't ripen uniformly on the tree, so harvest happens daily over 4-6 weeks rather than in one big pick. Three main species are grown: White mulberry (Morus alba) is the Asian import, very hardy, less flavorful fruit, considered invasive in some regions. Red mulberry (Morus rubra) is the North American native, better-flavored, zones 5-9. Black mulberry (Morus nigra) has the best flavor of all but is only hardy to zone 7-8. Most varieties sold in US nurseries are red-white hybrids chosen for cold hardiness and flavor. Mulberries are self-fertile; one tree produces abundantly. Trees bear in year 2-3 and are long-lived (100+ years). In zones 4-5, choose named varieties bred for cold hardiness rather than seedling trees.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Low to moderate chill -- adaptable across zones 5-10
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Some varieties have male and female flowers on same tree.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed balanced fertilizer in spring and midsummer during establishment. Mature trees are light feeders.

tasks.description_seasoned: Minimal pruning. Remove suckers and dead wood in late winter. Pawpaw forms a natural pyramid shape.

provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Carrion flower
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Pawpaw flowers are pollinated by flies -- rotting organic matter nearby helps

provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

pests.name: Pawpaw peduncle borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Individual flowers wither, dry, and drop shortly after opening. Cutting open an affected flower reveals a small (5 mm) whitish larva tunneling through the flower tissue and into the peduncle (the flower stem) at the base. In bad years, most of a crop's flowers can be destroyed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Talponia plummeriana, a small native moth. Kentucky State University identifies this as the single most damaging pawpaw pest. Typically provides a beneficial thinning effect in normal years; destructive only in outbreak years.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: No reliable organic spray -- larvae are protected inside the flower tissue. Hand-remove and destroy affected flowers when damage appears.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout flowers daily during bloom. Clean up flower debris under trees to reduce overwintering population. Avoid broad-spectrum sprays that kill parasitic wasps.

pests.name: Zebra swallowtail larvae
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Chewed young leaves on new growth. Green-and-black striped caterpillars (up to 1 1/2 inches) on young foliage. Damage is almost always minor on established trees and does not affect fruit yield.
pests.cause_seasoned: Eurytides marcellus. Pawpaw is the exclusive host plant for this butterfly's larvae. Kentucky State notes the adult butterfly is of such beauty that this should be considered a blessing rather than a curse.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Generally not recommended -- the damage is minor and the adult butterfly is ecologically valuable. On young seedlings only, hand-relocate caterpillars to mature trees.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Generally not needed. Established pawpaws tolerate this feeding easily.

pests.name: Asimina webworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Leaves at branch tips pulled together with silk webbing to form a shelter. Caterpillars feed inside the webbing. Damage is unsightly but occurs late in the season after growth has finished, so impact is minimal.
pests.cause_seasoned: Omphalocera munroei, reported as an occasional pawpaw pest by Ohio State extension. Appears in late summer or early fall.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out and destroy affected branch tips with their webbing. Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) is effective on caterpillars if treatment is warranted.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Rarely needed. Clean up leaf litter under trees in fall.

diseases.name: Phyllosticta leaf spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Small circular brown or black spots on leaves, sometimes with a lighter center ('bordered' spots). In high-pressure years, fruit may also develop spots that can crack. Usually a cosmetic issue on a healthy tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phyllosticta species, fungi. Ohio State lists this among the common pawpaw diseases. Spreads by rain splash in wet weather. Overwinters on fallen leaves.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Rake and destroy fallen leaves in autumn. Copper fungicide only in severe cases; most pawpaw leaf spot does not warrant treatment.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune for air circulation. Water at soil level. Remove leaf litter annually.

diseases.name: Sooty blotch & flyspeck
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dark smudgy patches (sooty blotch) and tiny black dots grouped in flyspeck patterns on fruit skin. Surface blemish only -- does not penetrate the fruit or affect flavor.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Complex of surface fungi, including Zygophiala and Schizothyrium species, favored by warm humid weather and dense canopies. Reported by Ohio State on pawpaw fruit.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Gently wipe fruit with a damp cloth at harvest -- much of the blemish washes off. Copper fungicide may suppress in high-pressure orchards but is rarely needed in home plantings.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Prune for better air circulation and light penetration. Thin heavy fruit clusters to improve airflow.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Scoop out flesh, mash with lemon juice, freeze in portions -- excellent
storage.notes_seasoned: Pawpaws are the most perishable large temperate fruit -- freeze surplus immediately.

varieties.note_seasoned: Shenandoah is the most widely recommended introduction variety -- milder flavor appeals to beginners, reliable producer.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Container-grown tree just planted. Pawpaw seedlings have a long tap root; potted trees may show some root circling.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant carefully -- pawpaw doesn't like root disturbance. Loosen any roots that are circling the rootball. Plant at the original soil line, water in well, mulch deeply. Plant at least two genetically different pawpaws within 30 feet of each other so the flowers can cross-pollinate.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Two or more pawpaws planted within range?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves emerging. Pawpaw is famously slow to start -- most year-one energy goes into the tap root, with little visible top growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pawpaw needs partial shade in years 1 to 2 -- full sun can scorch young leaves. Use a shade cloth or plant on the east side of a taller plant. Water consistently. Don't expect dramatic top growth; the tree is building an exceptional root system underground.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree finally putting on visible top growth. Tropical-looking long leaves; growth shape is naturally pyramidal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pawpaw needs almost no training. The natural pyramidal shape is the right shape. Pick one main vertical trunk if two are competing, and clear any shoots from the base. The shade requirement ends around year 3 -- by then the tree handles full sun fine.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves turn yellow and drop -- pawpaw is fully deciduous. Buds tight on the stems through winter.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pawpaw is generally cold-hardy through zone 5 once established, so first-year dormancy needs only standard care: mulch the root zone, wrap young trunks if rodents are a concern. The shade cloth comes off if it was up. Pawpaw shrugs off cold winters.

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant. Late-winter window.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light pruning only: dead, diseased, damaged. Pawpaw needs little structural pruning.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Maroon bell flowers before leaves emerge. Faintly fetid smell -- normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hand-pollinate between trees with a small brush to boost fruit set.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small green fruit forming. Self-incompatible -- need 2+ trees.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Confirm cross-pollination from different variety nearby.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late summer to early fall. Fruit gives to pressure and often falls.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Catch falling fruit on a sheet or pick daily. Refrigerate or pulp-freeze immediately.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit done; tree heading toward dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Minimal cleanup. Light spring feeding.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Pawpaw is grown from grafted named varieties or from seedlings. Both are own-rooted in practice -- there is no dwarfing rootstock concern. Plant with the crown at the original soil line.
Young pawpaws need shade for the first 2 to 3 years. Plant under existing tree shade or set up shade cloth on stakes; full sun on a young pawpaw burns the foliage.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first two seasons. Pawpaw roots are notoriously slow to establish and the tree may look like it is sulking for the first year -- this is normal, not a problem.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the base. Pawpaw thrives in a forest-floor environment of deep leaf litter; replicate that with an inch of compost annually under the mulch.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Pawpaw grows naturally as a small understory tree with a pyramidal form. No structural pruning is needed in the first few years; let the tree establish its natural shape.
Once established, gradually reduce shade -- pawpaw needs increasing sun as it matures to set fruit. By year 3 or 4 it should be in mostly full sun.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Pawpaw is fully deciduous and goes dormant in winter. It is one of the latest trees to leaf out in spring -- do not panic if neighboring trees have leaves and yours does not yet.
Refresh mulch before the ground freezes. Pawpaw is hardy through USDA zone 5; no special winter protection needed in zone.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Pawpaw needs little pruning. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood and any low suckers. Avoid heavy structural pruning -- the tree's natural shape is what you want.
Pawpaw fruits on previous-year wood. Heavy heading reduces the next crop. Less is more.

blossom.text_seasoned: Pawpaw flowers are dark maroon, bell-shaped, and faintly fetid -- they are pollinated by flies and beetles, not bees. The smell is the point and is normal.
Bloom happens before the leaves emerge in mid-spring. Frost during bloom can damage flowers but is rarely catastrophic; pawpaw blooms over a 2 to 3 week window.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Pawpaw is self-incompatible -- a single tree, even a grafted named variety, will produce little or no fruit. You need at least two genetically different trees (different varieties, or seedlings from different parents) within about 30 feet for pollination.

Hand-pollination with a small brush significantly boosts fruit set in home gardens. Move pollen between flowers on different trees during the bloom window. Many serious pawpaw growers do this every year.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pawpaw ripens in late summer to early fall. Ripe fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure (like a ripe peach) and often falls from the tree on its own. Catch ripening fruit by laying a sheet under the canopy or check daily.

Pawpaw does not store. Refrigerate immediately for up to a week, or pulp and freeze for use in baking or smoothies. The flavor is best at peak ripeness; under-ripe fruit is starchy and over-ripe fruit ferments quickly.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Pawpaw is one of the lowest-maintenance fruit trees once established -- no major post-harvest cleanup is needed. Clear any fallen leaves from the immediate trunk area.
A balanced organic fertilizer in early spring is usually sufficient. Pawpaw is a light feeder compared to most fruit trees.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 25-50 lbs from a mature grafted tree, harvested over a 2 to 4 week window in late summer or fall
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: First fruit typically in year 5 to 7 from grafted trees, longer from seedlings. Mature pawpaws produce a moderate but very reliable crop with almost no spray or thinning input.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. Pawpaws are slow to establish, often putting almost all their first-year energy into a tap root. Don't expect visible top growth until the root system is set.
factors_seasoned: shade in years 1 to 2 (pawpaw seedlings are shade-obligate when young)
cross-pollination -- pawpaws need at least two genetically different trees
fly pollination, not bee -- some growers hang carrion bait near trees
very few pest or disease problems once established

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Partially self-fertile (still better with a pollinator). Medium-large fruit with rich custardy flavor and relatively few seeds. Kansas-origin variety. The pawpaw for beginners who want reliable fruit from a single tree.
Peterson Pawpaws release. Mild sweet flavor and relatively firm flesh -- considered the best pawpaw for people who are new to the fruit's tropical flavor. Requires pollinator. Released 2003.
Peterson Pawpaws release. Large fruit (up to a pound each) with rich deep flavor. The fruit-quality benchmark among modern pawpaws. Requires pollinator. Ripens late.
Florida-origin variety, the best low-chill pawpaw for the southern end of the range. Medium fruit with distinctive mango-tropical flavor. Requires pollinator. Earlier ripening than most varieties.
Indiana-origin heirloom. Large fruit with excellent flavor. Cold-hardy. Requires pollinator. Classic variety available from most specialty fruit nurseries. A good reliable choice for zones 5-7.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pawpaw is hardy through USDA zone 5 -- one of the most cold-hardy fruit trees in this group. Spring frost during bloom can damage some flowers but rarely eliminates the crop because pawpaw blooms over a 2 to 3 week window. Winter cold is rarely the limiting factor.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Pawpaw needs little frost protection in its zone range. If you are at the southern edge of its range, ensure the tree gets enough winter chill (over 400 hours below 45 degrees) for proper bloom.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pawpaw is famously pest-resistant -- deer leave it alone, and the leaves contain natural insecticides. The main pest is pawpaw peduncle borer, which causes premature fruit drop. Phyllosticta leaf spot may show up in wet years but rarely affects the crop.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Clear and destroy any prematurely-dropped fruit to break the peduncle borer cycle. No spraying is generally needed. Pawpaw's pest profile is one of the reasons to plant it -- it needs less intervention than nearly any other backyard fruit.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pawpaw is self-incompatible. A single tree -- including a grafted named variety -- will not set significant fruit. Even two seedlings with the same parent may share enough genes to be incompatible. This is the single most common reason pawpaws bloom heavily but fruit poorly in home gardens.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant at least two genetically different pawpaws within 30 feet -- two different named varieties, or seedlings from different sources. Hand-pollinate with a small brush between trees during bloom; this can multiply fruit set several times over.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pawpaw tolerates moist soil better than most fruit trees -- it is naturally a streambank species. Standing water still damages roots, but pawpaw fails more often from drought during establishment than from waterlogging.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture, especially during the first 2 to 3 years. Mulch deeply with leaf litter or compost to mimic the forest-floor environment pawpaw evolved in.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pawpaw is unusual in needing shade as a young tree but full sun as a mature tree. A mature pawpaw in deep shade grows leaves but bears little or no fruit. A young pawpaw in full sun burns and may die.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Provide shade for the first 2 to 3 years (existing tree shade or shade cloth on stakes), then gradually reduce shade as the tree matures. By year 4 or 5 the tree should be in mostly full sun.

crops.description_seasoned: North America's largest native fruit -- tropical-tasting custard flavor unlike anything else. Extremely cold-hardy. Doesn't ship (too soft) so homegrown is the only way. Plant two for cross-pollination.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Skin softens and yellows. Strong tropical aroma. Slight give to thumb pressure. Short shelf life -- eat within days.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Pawpaw (Asimina triloba) is North America's largest native fruit and one of the most interesting tree fruits a home grower can plant. It tolerates shade better than almost any fruiting tree, thrives in humid eastern zones where stone fruits struggle with disease, and has essentially no serious pests or diseases in the US. The fruit has a tropical custard flavor (compared to banana, mango, and pineapple) but the trees are fully hardy to zone 5 and marginal in zone 4. Pawpaws require cross-pollination between two different varieties -- a single pawpaw tree will not fruit. Pollination is by flies and beetles rather than bees, as the maroon flowers smell mildly of rotting meat; some growers hand-pollinate for better fruit set. Pawpaws need protection from direct sunlight in their first 2-3 years; they are naturally understory trees. Mature trees tolerate full sun. Fruit doesn't store -- it must be eaten within a few days of ripening, which is why you rarely see pawpaws in grocery stores. Trees begin bearing in year 5-8 from seed, year 3-5 from grafted trees.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Native to eastern US -- zones 5-8. Needs a pollinator partner
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Requires cross-pollination from a different pawpaw variety or seedling. Flowers are pollinated by flies and beetles, not bees. Hand-pollination improves fruit set significantly.

pests.name: Olive fruit fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small brown puncture (sting) on olive fruit that darkens as the larva tunnels inside. Cut fruit shows tan tunnels and sometimes a small cream-colored maggot. Fruit drops early or rots on the tree. Affected fruit ruins oil quality and cannot be cured.
pests.cause_seasoned: Bactrocera oleae. UC ANR identifies this as the most damaging pest of California olives and the most important olive pest worldwide. Regional -- primarily a California concern in the US. Multiple generations per season.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hang yellow sticky traps baited with ammonium carbonate for monitoring. Spinosad-based GF-120 NF Naturalyte bait (OMRI-listed) applied weekly to a few branches during fruit development attracts and kills egg-laying females. Kaolin clay spray (Surround WP) deters egg-laying.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Pick up and destroy all dropped olives -- they harbor pupae. Consider not leaving fruit on trees past January. Strip unpicked olives at season end on ornamental (non-fruiting) trees to deny the fly a breeding site. Regionally, protected or closed fruit clusters help.

pests.name: Black scale
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dark brown to black domed bumps on twigs, branches, and leaves -- about 1/8 inch across with a characteristic H-shaped ridge on the back. Copious sticky honeydew coating leaves and fruit, followed by heavy sooty mold that reduces photosynthesis. Leaf drop and twig dieback.
pests.cause_seasoned: Saissetia oleae, a soft scale listed by UC ANR as a key olive pest. Worse in humid coastal conditions and in dense canopies. Farmed by ants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Narrow-range horticultural oil timed to crawler emergence (typically late spring into summer). Prune out heavily infested branches. Control ants with sticky trunk bands.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Prune to open the canopy -- scale populations crash in well-ventilated trees. Protect parasitic wasps (Metaphycus spp.) that provide biological control.

pests.name: Olive psyllid (regional)
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Waxy white filaments on new growth tips. Distorted, curled young leaves. Flower buds malformed or dropping. Sticky honeydew and sooty mold. Most severe on flush growth in spring.
pests.cause_seasoned: Euphyllura olivina, an invasive psyllid established in California since roughly 2007. UC ANR lists it as a regional olive pest. Multiple generations per year.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Horticultural oil or insecticidal soap during the spring flush. Parasitic wasps provide partial control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Prune out infested tips in spring. Support natural enemies by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.

pests.name: Olive mite
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pale stippling or silvery discoloration on leaves. Heavy infestations cause leaf bronzing and early leaf drop. Visible only with a hand lens.
pests.cause_seasoned: Oxycenus maxwelli and related eriophyid mites. UC ANR lists this as an olive pest, mostly a concern on stressed trees and in hot dry weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Sulfur dust or horticultural oil (not together -- they interact). Most established trees tolerate mite damage.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain even irrigation. Avoid drought stress, which favors mite buildup.

diseases.name: Olive knot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Rough, woody, gall-like swellings on twigs, branches, and occasionally trunk and leaves. Knots start as small swellings and grow to 1-2 inches or more. Branches beyond heavy knots lose vigor, fail to leaf out, and die back. Fruit from infected trees may carry off-flavors.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Pseudomonas savastanoi pv. savastanoi, a bacterium. UC ANR identifies this as a primary olive disease, with incidence strongly tied to rainfall and freeze injury (openings that let the bacteria in). Spreads by water and contaminated pruning tools.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out knotted tissue during dry weather, cutting 6-12 inches into healthy wood. Disinfect tools between cuts with 10% bleach or 70% alcohol. Destroy (burn or bag) all prunings. No effective bactericide registered for home use.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Only prune in dry weather. Avoid injuring bark with mowers, pruners, or picking equipment. Plant disease-free nursery stock (pathogen exclusion is the primary defense). Protect trees from freeze damage in marginal zones. Copper sprays before winter rains can reduce new infections in commercial orchards.

diseases.name: Peacock spot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Circular dark olive-green to black spots (1/10 to 1/2 inch) on upper leaf surfaces, sometimes with a yellow halo -- the 'peacock eye' or 'bird's eye' pattern. Lower-canopy leaves most affected. Heavy infection causes defoliation, weakening the tree and reducing bloom the following year.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Spilocaea oleaginea (also called Cycloconium oleaginum), a fungus. UC ANR and oliveoilsource.com both document this as a common olive disease worldwide. Infection occurs in cool wet fall and winter weather (35-80°F); inactive in hot dry summer.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Copper-based fungicide applied in late October before winter rains, and again in spring if wet weather persists. Rake and destroy fallen leaves that harbor overwintering spores.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Plant on well-drained sites with good air circulation. Avoid overhead irrigation. Prune to open the canopy. Cultivar resistance varies but no variety is immune.

diseases.name: Verticillium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting and yellowing of leaves on one side of the tree or on individual branches. Dark vascular streaking visible when a cut is made in affected wood. Leaves may remain attached after dying (unlike frost damage, which drops leaves). Young trees often die; mature trees may decline over years.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Verticillium dahliae, a soil-borne fungus with a very wide host range (tomatoes, peppers, eggplant, cotton, many others). Persists in soil for over a decade. Particularly bad on sites previously planted to susceptible annual crops.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Prune out affected branches. Severely infected young trees should be removed.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Do not plant olives where solanaceous crops (tomatoes, peppers, eggplants) have grown recently. Plant on verticillium-tested soil in replant situations. Some rootstocks show tolerance. Avoid over-irrigation.

diseases.name: Botryosphaeria blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Dead flower clusters that fail to emerge in spring, or blighted clusters with blackened rachises appearing in late spring. Fruit rot with silvery covering. Elliptical cankers on branches that girdle and kill twigs.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Neofusicoccum parvum, Diplodia, and related Botryosphaeriaceae fungi. Often enters through olive knot galls, pruning wounds, or freeze-damaged tissue. Compounds the damage caused by olive knot.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out dead branches and blighted clusters. Disinfect pruning tools between cuts. Dispose of prunings; do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Control olive knot (which provides entry points). Prune during dry weather with clean cuts. Keep trees adequately watered but not waterlogged.

watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Root rot -- most common olive killer

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Freshly picked olives must be cured immediately -- they are inedible raw
storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze cured olives in brine -- quality drops somewhat but acceptable
storage.notes_seasoned: Cure in brine (12-18 months), lye (1-2 weeks), or dry salt (6 weeks). Home-cured olives are very satisfying.

varieties.note_seasoned: Arbequina is the best choice for most backyard growers -- self-fertile (no partner needed), compact, and produces oil and table olives.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Olive is a classic container tree for cold-zone growers. Use a 15+ gallon container with excellent drainage. In zones below 8, bring indoors to an unheated but frost-free space for winter (olives need a cool dormancy -- don't keep in a heated room). Choose dwarf varieties like Arbequina for best container performance. Expect reduced vigor and fruit set versus in-ground trees in warm zones.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Container-grown olive just planted. Often a small multi-stem form or a single-trunk young tree.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil -- olives die fast in wet feet. Site in full sun and a sheltered spot if your zone is marginal for cold. Water in deeply, mulch generously, but keep mulch off the trunk. Stake briefly if the tree was tall and slim from the nursery.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Olive planted in well-drained sunny spot?

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves greening up and new shoots extending. Olive is slow but steady in year one.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply but infrequently -- about every 10 to 14 days, depending on heat and soil. Olive prefers a deep soak followed by drying out over constant moisture. Remove any first-year flowers or olives. Watch for olive fruit fly if you're in a warm coastal zone.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Branch structure becoming visible. Olive naturally wants to be multi-stemmed unless trained otherwise.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Olive trains to an open-vase form similar to stone fruit -- 3 to 5 main branches angled outward, no central trunk. Decide on the form now: single-trunk for an orchard look, multi-stem for ornamental use or as insurance against cold damage. Remove any shoots from below the soil line and any crossing growth.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Form decided and main branches chosen?

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Olive is evergreen -- leaves stay on through winter. Growth slows visibly; the silver-green foliage may darken slightly.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Olive's version of dormancy is a winter slowdown, not true leaf-fall. Cold-hardiness varies sharply by variety -- some olives tolerate brief drops to about 15°F, others lose wood at 25. Check your variety's cold tolerance and don't rely on the tree past its limit. Use frost cloth or warm holiday lights if a hard freeze threatens. Reduce watering frequency.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Variety cold limit known and protection ready?

growth_stages.name: Late Winter Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late winter, before bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light pruning. Open canopy. Remove dead wood, suckers, water sprouts.

growth_stages.name: Bloom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Late-spring creamy-yellow flower clusters. Wind-pollinated.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant a second variety nearby for boosted set.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small green fruit. Heavy early-summer drop is normal.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin in heavy years to level alternate-bearing cycle.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green for table olives, fully-darkened for oil or black-cured.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick by hand or net-shake. Plan 6+ weeks of curing.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Main harvest done.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Light feeding only. Refresh coarse mulch.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Olive is grown on its own roots or grafted -- both are common. The graft union, if present, should sit at or just above soil level. Olive tolerates planting depth better than most fruit trees.
Plant in spring after frost danger passes. Olive thrives in poor, rocky, alkaline soil -- do not over-amend with compost or manure. Excellent drainage matters more than fertility.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first season. Once established (2 to 3 years), olive is among the most drought-tolerant fruit trees and thrives on infrequent deep watering.
Mulch a 3-foot circle but use a coarse, dry mulch (gravel works well). Olive resents the moist organic mulch that other fruit trees prefer.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Olive can be trained as a single-trunk tree or a multi-stemmed shrub. Both are traditional. For single-trunk form, select a strong leader and remove competing trunks at the base.
Olive grows slowly. Do not over-fertilize trying to push growth -- excess nitrogen produces vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and shortens the tree's life.

dormancy.text_seasoned: Olive is evergreen and never fully dormant. Growth pauses through winter cold but the tree is never bare.

Olive needs winter chill (above freezing but below about 50 degrees) to set fruit -- about 200 to 300 hours below 50 in winter. In subtropical zones with no winter chill, olive grows but rarely fruits.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Olive pruning is done in late winter or early spring before bloom. Olive fruits on previous-year wood; heavy heading reduces the next crop substantially.
Open the canopy enough that light reaches all the fruiting wood. Olive can become a thicket if left unpruned. Remove dead wood, suckers, and water sprouts.

blossom.text_seasoned: Olive blooms in late spring with creamy-yellow flower clusters. The bloom is wind-pollinated -- bees rarely visit -- so isolation from pollinator gardens does not matter.
Most olive varieties are self-fertile but most also benefit from a second variety nearby. Mission and Manzanillo are good cross-pollinators.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Olive is famously alternate-bearing -- a heavy crop year followed by a light year. Thinning fruit in heavy years partly evens the cycle out.
Heavy early-summer fruit drop is normal -- the tree sheds excess set. Persistent later drop usually means drought stress.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest timing depends on use. For green olives, pick when fruit is fully sized but still green-yellow. For oil or black-cured olives, wait until fruit darkens fully.
All raw olives are bitter from oleuropein and inedible without curing. Plan for a 6-week minimum cure (lye, brine, or salt) before eating.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Light feeding only after harvest -- a balanced organic fertilizer at half the usual rate. Olive is a light feeder and over-fertilizing causes problems.
Refresh mulch with coarse material. Inspect for olive fruit fly damage in the harvested fruit and remove any infested drops from under the tree.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 20-60 lbs from a mature dooryard tree in an on year, much less in an off year (alternate-bearing is the norm)
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production in year 5 to 8 and continuing for decades. Mature olives often alternate, with a heavy crop one year and a lighter one the next.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No useful crop in year one. Olives are slow to bear but very long-lived. Year one is canopy and root development.
factors_seasoned: cold-hardiness varies sharply by variety -- some tolerate brief drops to about 15°F, others lose wood at 25°F
drought-tolerant once established but moisture during fruit sizing improves yield
olive fruit fly in warm coastal zones

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Spanish variety. Partially self-fertile -- one of few olive varieties that fruits alone. Small brown-purple fruit, excellent for oil production. Cold-hardy. The home-garden standard olive. Earlier bearing than most varieties.
Classic California olive, brought by Franciscan missionaries in the 1700s. Medium black fruit, dual-purpose for table olives and oil. Requires pollinator. The cultural heritage olive of California.

Spanish variety, the classic green table olive. Large oval fruit. Requires pollinator (Sevillano, Mission). Most widely-planted table olive variety globally. Lower oil content; grown specifically for eating.
Greek variety producing the famous purple-black Kalamata olives. Large almond-shaped fruit. Requires pollinator. Classic Mediterranean table olive with distinctive rich flavor. Good cold tolerance.
Italian oil olive, the standard for premium Tuscan olive oil. Small black fruit with very high oil content. Requires pollinator. Top choice for serious home oil production.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Olive is evergreen and tolerates light frost but is killed back by hard freezes -- mature trees suffer leaf and twig damage at about 22 degrees and severe damage below about 15. Olive needs some winter chill (200 to 300 hours below 50 degrees) to set fruit, so subtropical zones grow olive trees that rarely fruit.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: In marginal zones, plant in the warmest microclimate available (south wall, sheltered courtyard) and choose cold-hardy varieties (Arbequina, Mission). In no-chill zones, accept that olive is an ornamental tree.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Olive fruit fly is the headline pest in California and increasingly in other Western states -- it lays eggs in developing fruit, ruining the crop for table or oil use. Olive knot bacteria causes warty growths on twigs and branches. Verticillium wilt is an occasional serious problem.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For olive fruit fly, hang yellow sticky traps and bait traps from late spring through harvest. Pick up all dropped fruit. For olive knot, prune out infected branches in dry weather and disinfect tools. Verticillium has no cure -- avoid planting in soil where tomatoes or other susceptible crops have suffered the disease.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Olive is wind-pollinated and most varieties are self-fertile, so missing pollination is rarely the issue. Heavy bloom with no fruit set is more often insufficient winter chill, drought stress, or alternate bearing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your zone provides enough winter chill (below 50 degrees for several hundred hours). Plant a second variety nearby (Mission, Manzanillo) for cross-pollination boost. In hot windy sites, irrigate during bloom.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Olive evolved in poor, rocky, dry-summer Mediterranean soils. It cannot tolerate waterlogged soil; standing water kills roots quickly and the tree never recovers. Over-irrigation also produces vegetative growth at the expense of fruit and shortens the tree's productive life.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant on a 12-inch raised mound on heavy or poorly-drained soil. Water deeply but infrequently once established; many mature olives do well with no irrigation at all in their native climate range.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Olive needs full sun, all day if possible. In partial shade the tree grows leaves but barely fruits. Olive is also the most heat-tolerant common backyard fruit tree -- the hottest spot in the yard is usually the right spot.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest, hottest spot available. Light pruning to open the canopy helps inner fruit ripen. Reflective surfaces (white walls, gravel mulch) can help in marginal zones.
