varieties.note_seasoned: Lapins and Stella are self-fertile -- if you can only plant one tree, these are your only choices.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text_seasoned: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text_seasoned: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 30-50 lbs from a mature semi-standard tree
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors_seasoned: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Cold-hardiest named sweet cherry, bred in Geneva NY and field-tested in Montana and Norway. Large dark-red fruit. Requires pollinator. Pick this for zone 4 or challenging continental climates.

Self-pollinating Canadian-bred Stella x Van cross. Large dark-red crack-resistant fruit. Late-ripening. One of the best all-around sweet cherries for home growers -- tolerates late frost and is hardier than Bing.

First self-fertile sweet cherry widely available. Dark red heart-shaped fruit. Acts as universal pollinator for many other sweet cherries including Bing. Cornell notes some cold-sensitivity in harsh winters.

Classic commercial sweet cherry and quality benchmark. Large firm dark-red fruit with superior flavor. Requires pollinator (Stella works well). Highly susceptible to rain-cracking and brown rot -- not recommended for humid eastern zones.
Low-chill cherry bred for warm climates where standard cherries fail to break dormancy. Medium-large red heart-shaped fruit. Requires Minnie Royal as pollinator. Makes cherries possible in zones 8-9.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. (UMN Extension 'Growing apples in the home garden'; UMN Extension 'Growing stone fruits in the home garden')

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Stone fruit harvest runs June through August for most varieties. Peaches and nectarines ripen mid-to-late summer; apricots earliest (June-July); sweet cherries June-July; sour cherries July; plums July-September depending on type (Japanese types earlier, European types later). This month-by-month synthesis of stone fruit harvest windows follows Iowa State University Extension's commercial-orchard reference material on peach, plum, and cherry harvest timing. UMN Extension is cited for complementary climate-zone guidance on northern-Midwest stone fruit cultivation.

crops.description_seasoned: The most spectacular fruit tree in bloom. Needs cross-pollination from another variety. Birds will compete for every fruit -- netting is essential before fruit colors. Needs 700-1,200 chill hours.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deep red-black color, firm but giving to squeeze. Glossy skin. Taste a few -- best indicator is flavor.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Sweet cherries are among the fussiest stone fruits about climate. Traditional varieties thrive in zones 5-7 with dry summers and cold-but-not-frigid winters -- conditions found in the Pacific Northwest and inland California. In humid eastern zones, summer rain during ripening causes fruit cracking that ruins crops. In warmer zones (8+), most varieties fail to get enough chill hours (700-800) to break dormancy properly. Newer cold-hardy varieties (Kristin, Whitegold, BlackGold, Lapins) push the cold limit to zone 4 with reliable survival, though reliable fruit production remains marginal. Sweet cherries are self-sterile and typically require a pollination partner; self-fertile varieties (Stella, Lapins, Black Gold) are a relatively recent breeding achievement and are the practical choice for home growers with limited space. Sensitivity to summer heat above 95°F and winter bud damage below -20°F are both common. Trees typically begin bearing in year 4 and produce 30-50 quarts at maturity.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: High chill requirement -- best in zones 5-7. Struggle in zones 8+
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Requires a compatible sweet cherry variety for cross-pollination. Bing, Rainier, and Stella are popular combinations. Stella is self-fertile and pollinates others.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: No harvest years 1-3. Focus on building scaffold. Stake tree in first year.

crops.name: Artichoke

3.notes: Annual treatment only. Start indoors 8-10 weeks early. May not produce in short seasons.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: Start artichoke seeds indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost. Artichokes require brief cold exposure (vernalization) to trigger budding; expose seedlings to nighttime temps below 50 degrees F for 10 days before transplanting. Harden off over 7 days. (UC Master Gardeners, existing dataset start_method.notes). Transplant out after last frost.

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Artichokes mature 85-100 days from transplant in cold zones. Harvest buds while still firm, before petals open. In perennial zones (Z7+), expect spring and fall harvests; in annual zones, a single harvest occurs from late summer through first frost. (UC Master Gardeners Artichoke; Clemson HGIC)

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heavy feeder. Monthly nitrogen-rich feed during the growing season. Mulch well -- artichokes are perennials that benefit from rich soil year after year.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your artichoke -- it's a hungry plant

tasks.description_seasoned: Cut stalks to 8-10 inches after harvest season ends and after first frost. Mulch crowns with 4 inches of straw to protect through winter.
Divide clumps every 3-4 years in early spring. Replant offsets (suckers) 4 feet apart.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Artichoke plume moth
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Larvae tunnel into stems and buds. Wilting shoots. Entry holes in base.
pests.cause_seasoned: Platyptilia carduidactyla moth. Western US pest.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy infested buds. Bt spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Cut plants to ground level after harvest to remove overwintering sites.

diseases.name: Botrytis (gray mold)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gray fuzzy mold on leaves and buds in wet cool weather.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Botrytis cinerea.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected tissue. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Good air circulation. Avoid overhead watering.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 3-5 days -- heavy feeder and drinker

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 8-10 weeks before last frost. Briefly expose to cold (vernalization) by putting near a window on cold nights -- this triggers better budding. Harden off over 7 days.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 1 week in a bag with a few drops of water
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch hearts, freeze -- good for cooking
storage.notes_seasoned: Trim the stem end and spritz with water before refrigerating to keep fresh.

varieties.note_seasoned: Imperial Star produces in year one if started early -- essential for zones 3-6 where artichokes are grown as annuals.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Not practical in containers -- artichokes grow to 4-6 feet tall and wide. Ground planting only.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Perennial herbs don't need annual rotation, but they can be divided and moved if needed. Choose a permanent-ish spot with the right sun and drainage; plan to divide every 3-4 years to keep plants vigorous.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Established plant or germinating seed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Artichokes grown from seed are variable -- buy named variety plants for reliable results. Plant in a permanent spot with excellent drainage.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large, deeply lobed silver-green leaves developing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water generously. Artichokes are large plants and heavy feeders -- they benefit from regular feeding with a balanced fertilizer.

growth_stages.name: Flower Buds Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tight, scaly buds forming at the top of stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest the central bud first and largest. Side buds follow -- they will be smaller but just as delicious.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds tight and firm before the scales begin to open. Once scales open the heart becomes fibrous.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut with 2-3 inches of stem. Cook immediately or store in water in the refrigerator for up to a week.

yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Established plants produce a main flush of buds in late spring with a smaller fall flush in mild-winter climates -- expect 5 to 8 buds from a mature plant per main flush.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Artichokes in year one are establishing. Year two and three plants are far more productive.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These three perennials handle winter cold differently. Asparagus is fully cold-hardy through zone 3, dies back to the ground each winter, and emerges from the crown each spring. Strawberry is cold-hardy through zone 3 with mulch, sometimes loses leaves but the crown survives. Artichoke is the cold-tender one -- hardy only to zone 7 reliably, often grown as an annual in colder zones. Late spring frost can damage emerging asparagus spears and strawberry blossoms.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For asparagus, cover emerging spears with row cover during late spring frosts; damaged spears are tough and bitter. For strawberry, mulch heavily over the crowns before winter and uncover in early spring. For artichoke in zones 6 and below, grow as an annual or dig and overwinter the crown indoors. Hardy artichoke varieties (Imperial Star) survive zone 6 with heavy mulching.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Each of these crops has its own primary pest: asparagus beetle (both common and spotted) chews ferns and lays eggs on spears; spotted wing drosophila (SWD), slugs, and gray mold (Botrytis) are the headline strawberry problems; artichoke is generally low-pest but artichoke aphid clusters in the bracts and slugs damage tender new growth. Asparagus rust and Fusarium crown rot affect asparagus over time; strawberry is also vulnerable to verticillium wilt.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: For asparagus beetle, hand-pick adults and crush egg masses; in heavy infestations, neem or pyrethrin sprays in the cool of the day work. For SWD on strawberry, harvest ripe fruit promptly and clean up drops; row cover during fruit ripening helps. For artichoke aphid, hose off with water or use insecticidal soap. Choose disease-resistant strawberry varieties and renovate beds every 3 to 4 years.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three crops fail in waterlogged soil. Asparagus crowns rot in standing water -- a single wet season can kill an established bed. Strawberry crowns rot at the soil-stem interface in persistently wet conditions, and the fruit develops gray mold in damp weather. Artichoke is similarly intolerant of wet feet.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil or raised beds. For asparagus, the bed is a multi-year commitment -- excellent drainage at planting prevents 20 years of disappointment. For strawberry, raised beds and straw mulch (the source of the name) keep fruit and crowns dry. For artichoke, mound up the planting site if drainage is marginal.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress in the establishment year is the leading cause of failed asparagus and artichoke plantings. Strawberry tolerates short drought once established but fruit size and number drop substantially with water stress during fruiting. Asparagus that goes dry in summer produces fewer and smaller spears the following spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply through the establishment season for all three. Asparagus needs consistent moisture in summer (when it is feeding the crown for next year's spears) more than in spring (when it is producing spears from already-stored energy). Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture for all three.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: All three want full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to produce well. Shaded asparagus produces fewer and thinner spears; shaded strawberry produces small pale fruit with weak flavor; shaded artichoke grows leaves but produces few or no buds. These are not shade-tolerant crops.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun. Asparagus is a long-term commitment (15 to 20 years productive life), so the site choice matters more than for annual crops. For strawberry, full sun is also better for disease management because foliage dries faster after rain or dew.

crops.description_seasoned: A dramatic, architectural perennial that produces edible flower buds. In warm zones it's a long-lived perennial -- cut back after harvest and it regrows. In colder zones, treat as an annual.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut bud when plump and tight, before scales begin to open. Size varies by position on plant -- central bud is largest.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Perennial in Z7-Z11. In Z3-Z6 typically grown as an annual from transplants started early indoors, or mulched heavily to attempt overwintering (inconsistent results).
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: May produce a small harvest in year one from annual varieties. Perennial types fruit more heavily from year two.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Artichokes are heavy feeders. Dig in generous amounts of well-rotted manure or compost. They prefer a rich, moisture-retentive but well-drained soil. pH 6.5-7.5. In cold climates, raised beds help warm soil earlier.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Light feeder. Work a balanced fertilizer into the bed before sowing. No additional feeding needed.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Cube, blanch, freeze -- good for soups and mash
storage.notes_seasoned: Can be left in the ground through light frosts -- flavor improves with cold.

varieties.note_seasoned: Hakurei is exceptional eaten raw -- sweet and crisp with no bitterness. Completely different from standard turnips.

thinning.method: Snip at soil level. Thinnings edible.
thinning.tip_seasoned: Thinning is especially important for turnip -- they bulk up quickly and need the space.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Works in deep containers. 3-gallon minimum, 8 inches deep. Compact varieties like Tokyo Cross work well.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow 4-6 weeks before last frost for spring, or in late summer. Fast-maturing -- no need to start indoors.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Thread-like shoots pushing up from the soil. Carrots and parsnips are notoriously slow -- do not give up.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil surface consistently moist -- the most common reason carrots fail is the surface drying out during the 2-3 week germination period. Lay a plank of wood over the row and check daily.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Feathery or distinctive first true leaves -- carrots look like tiny ferns, beetroot has deep red stems.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin seedlings carefully and promptly. Crowded root vegetables fork and stay small. Thin in stages -- once at 2 inches, again at 4 inches.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong leaf growth above ground. Roots are developing below -- resist the urge to dig and check.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep consistently watered -- irregular watering causes cracking and forking in root crops. Weed carefully to avoid disturbing roots.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shoulders of root visible at soil surface, or reach the days to maturity for your variety. Test pull one before harvesting the row.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water well before harvesting to loosen the soil. Pull at an angle rather than straight up to prevent snapping. Many root crops improve with frost.

growth_stages.name: In Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Roots harvested and stored properly. Potatoes in a dark cool place. Carrots in damp sand.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Check stored roots monthly for any that are rotting -- one bad root can spread to others. Remove immediately.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to sow your root vegetables
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables go directly into the ground -- they do not transplant. Prepare your bed deeply, remove any stones that could cause forking, and sow thinly. Most root crops can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to thin your root crops
notifications.body_seasoned: Thinning is the most important thing you can do for root vegetables right now. Crowded roots fork and stay small. Thin to the recommended spacing -- eat the thinnings if they are big enough.

notifications.title_seasoned: Your root vegetables should be approaching harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Do a test pull of one root before harvesting the row. Water the ground well first to loosen the soil. Most root crops can stay in the ground for several weeks after reaching full size -- they store well in situ.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest before the ground freezes
notifications.body_seasoned: Most root vegetables need to be out of the ground before it freezes solid. Carrots, parsnips, and beetroot can handle light frost -- it actually sweetens them. But harvest everything before a hard freeze locks them in.

notifications.title_seasoned: Root check-in
notifications.body_seasoned: Root vegetables mostly look after themselves once established, but it is worth checking for weeds and keeping the soil consistently moist. How are they looking above ground?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Dry spell -- water your root crops consistently
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Irregular watering during root development causes carrots and parsnips to fork, beetroot to become woody, and potatoes to crack. Water deeply and consistently -- not a little every day but a good soak twice a week.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heavy rain -- check for waterlogging
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Root vegetables sitting in waterlogged soil can rot. Check drainage in your bed and consider harvesting any roots that are near maturity before they split from the rapid moisture uptake.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost coming -- parsnips and carrots will thank you
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: A light frost actually improves the flavor of carrots and parsnips by converting starch to sugar. Leave them in the ground through light frosts if you can. Potatoes and beetroot should be harvested before a hard frost.

germination.text_seasoned: These crops are direct-sown -- transplanting damages the taproot and produces forked or stunted roots. Sow seeds shallowly (1/4 to 1/2 inch deep) and keep soil surface consistently moist for the 1 to 3 week germination window.
Carrot and parsnip seed is short-lived -- use fresh seed each year. Parsnip especially can take up to 3 weeks to germinate; do not give up early.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves -- crowded roots stay small and forked. Pull weaker seedlings rather than transplanting them.
Mulch lightly between rows once seedlings are established to suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the row -- hoeing damages shallow seedling roots.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently. Uneven moisture causes carrot and parsnip roots to split as they swell during a wet period after dry conditions.
These crops feed lightly. Side-dress with compost mid-season if growth slows; avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers, which produce lush leafy tops at the expense of roots.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips after the first frost for best flavor -- this is not folklore; the cold genuinely converts starch to sugar in the root. Parsnip especially needs frost exposure to develop its characteristic sweetness.

Loosen soil with a fork before pulling -- yanking by the tops snaps the root, especially on long carrots and parsnips. Cut tops off within an inch of the crown for storage; tops left on draw moisture out of the root.

storage.text_seasoned: Store carrots, parsnips, beetroot, and turnips in layers of damp sand or sawdust in a cool location (32 to 40 degrees) at high humidity. Properly stored, these crops keep 4 to 6 months.

In zones with mild winters, you can leave the roots in the ground and harvest as needed -- mulch heavily over the row before the ground freezes. This is often easier than indoor storage and preserves quality longer.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One turnip per plant -- fast crop at 40-60 days
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Best harvested young at golf ball size for best flavor
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Young turnips are sweet and delicious -- a world away from the woody, bitter specimens you might remember. Pick them small.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These crops actively benefit from light to moderate frost -- it improves flavor by converting root starch to sugar. Damage from frost is rare and usually only happens to exposed leaf tops on a hard freeze; the roots are insulated by soil and survive even harsh winter conditions in many zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Time harvest to follow the first frost rather than precede it. In zones with mild winters, leave roots in the ground under heavy mulch and harvest as needed through winter.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Carrot rust fly (carrot, parsnip) is the headline pest -- larvae tunnel through roots leaving rusty trails. Cabbage maggot (turnip, sometimes beetroot) does similar damage to brassica roots. Leaf spot diseases and powdery mildew can hit foliage but rarely affect the root harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Floating row cover from sowing through harvest blocks both carrot rust fly and cabbage maggot -- this is the most effective home-garden defense. Rotate root crops to a new bed each year. Avoid planting carrot or parsnip after parsley or celery (same family, same pest).

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Uneven watering -- a dry spell followed by heavy water -- causes roots to split as they swell rapidly. Persistent waterlogging causes root rot, soft black tissue, and crown collapse. Beetroot and turnip handle wet soil better than carrot and parsnip, both of which need excellent drainage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain consistent moisture rather than letting soil dry out and then soaking it. On heavy clay, plant in a raised bed for carrot and parsnip especially. Mulch helps stabilize moisture.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought-stressed root crops produce small, fibrous roots with concentrated and often unpleasantly strong flavor. Parsnips become woody at the core; carrots become bitter; turnips become sharp; beetroot becomes earthy and tough.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply and consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Mulch between rows to retain moisture. In hot weather, root crops appreciate light afternoon shade.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Carrot, parsnip, and beetroot seeds need 1 to 3 weeks of consistent surface moisture to germinate. The most common reason for failed sowings is the soil surface drying out during germination -- not poor seed or bad soil. Parsnip seed in particular loses viability fast and old seed simply does not come up.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow into pre-moistened soil and cover with a board or burlap until the first seedlings emerge -- this keeps the surface consistently moist without daily watering. Use fresh parsnip seed each year. Pre-sprout difficult seed on damp paper towels indoors before sowing if needed.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from early spring and again from late summer. Turnips mature in 40-60 days and taste best pulled young and small. Like radishes, they're a quick-turnaround crop that benefits from small frequent sowings. The autumn succession is often the better season -- cool nights sweeten the flavor. Stop spring sowings when temperatures consistently exceed 75°F.

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Direct seed cool-season root vegetables (carrots, beets, radishes, turnips) when soil reaches 40 degrees F, typically 2-4 weeks before last frost. (UMN Extension) Roots do not transplant -- their long taproots develop early and transplanting damages and misdirects root growth. In Minnesota, start planting carrots beginning April 15. (UMN Extension)

direct_sow.label: secondary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant a fall crop when summer heat subsides, approximately 2-3 months before first fall frost. Fall-matured roots are sweeter due to cool-weather sugar accumulation. Autumn-matured carrots from a late sowing are noticeably sweeter. (Crop succession guidance, UMN, Iowa State Extension)

harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool-season root crops develop off flavors, bitterness, or toughness when forced to mature in summer heat. harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Conservative harvest_end for spring crop: bolt_threshold_start - 5 days.

harvest_end.label: secondary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cool-season root crops tolerate light frost. Beets, carrots, radishes, and turnips can be left in the ground past first frost and stored in place in cold zones with mulch protection. (UMN Extension; Iowa State Extension; Cornell Extension)
harvest_end.design_note_seasoned: Fall harvest window extends to approximately first_frost + 14d for most; parsnips extend much further.

crops.description_seasoned: One of the fastest root crops -- baby turnips in 35 days. Both root and greens are edible. Cool-season crop that tolerates light frost.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick roots at 2-3 inches -- any bigger and they get woody and peppery. Leaves can be harvested any time.

crops.name: Leek

3.notes: Start indoors 10-12 weeks early. Short-season varieties only.

start_indoors.label: primary
start_indoors.synthesis_note_seasoned: In cold zones (Z3-Z6), start leek seeds indoors 10 weeks before last frost and transplant in spring for summer and fall harvest. (Clemson HGIC; UMN Extension) Leeks mature best during temperatures averaging below 75 degrees F. They require about 120 days from seed to maturity. Plant in late summer or early fall for harvesting during early winter in warm zones. Leeks may be grown from seeds or transplants. (Clemson HGIC)

Plant in late summer or early fall for harvesting during early winter in warm zones. Leeks may be grown from seeds or transplants. (Clemson HGIC)

harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Leeks tolerate cold well and can be harvested through light frost, and continue into winter in mild-winter zones with mulch protection.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Heavy nitrogen feeder for long, thick stems. Feed monthly throughout the season.

pests.name: Onion fly
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt and die. White maggots at the base of bulb eating roots and inner leaves.
pests.cause_seasoned: Delia antiqua fly. Lays eggs near onion seedlings in spring.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Insect mesh over bed. Remove and destroy affected plants.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Grow under fine mesh. Rotate alliums every 3 years. Interplant with carrots -- mutual pest confusion.

pests.name: Thrips
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Silver streaking and speckling on leaves. Stunted growth. Tiny yellow-brown insects visible.
pests.cause_seasoned: Thrips tabaci. Worse in hot dry summers.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Neem oil spray. Insecticidal soap.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reflective mulch. Adequate watering in dry weather.

diseases.name: White rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants yellow and die. White fluffy growth at base with small black seed-like sclerotia. Roots and base rotted.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Sclerotium cepivorum soil fungus. Persists in soil for 20+ years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove all plant material. Do not replant alliums in infected soil.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Strict crop rotation. Buy allium seed sets from reputable sources.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gray-purple fuzzy growth on leaves. Leaves yellow and collapse. Worst in wet cool springs.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora destructor fungus.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Copper-based fungicide.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants for airflow. Rotate crops.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 10-12 weeks before transplant. Harden off over 7 days. Transplant into deep holes -- drop in and water, don't fill with soil. This blanches the stems.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Onions, garlic, leeks, shallots -- share white rot and onion fly
rotation.note_seasoned: White rot can persist indefinitely in soil -- strict rotation is essential once present.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Slice, blanch 1 minute, freeze -- good for soups and cooking
storage.notes_seasoned: Leeks can be left in the ground through mild frosts as living storage.

varieties.note_seasoned: Musselburgh is the standout variety for cold hardiness -- can be harvested through winter in zones 5-7.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Cloves, sets, or seeds in the ground. No visible growth yet.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Plant garlic and onion sets pointed end up, just below the surface. For leeks, sow seeds in modules and transplant as pencil-thin seedlings.

growth_stages.name: Early Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Green shoots pushing up from sets or cloves. Slow growth initially -- alliums establish roots first.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep weed-free -- alliums are poor competitors with weeds, especially in early growth.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong upright leaves, healthy green color. Onions and garlic developing the bulb underground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stop feeding garlic and onions with nitrogen once the bulb starts forming -- it encourages leafy growth at the expense of the bulb.

growth_stages.name: Bulb Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: For garlic: scapes curling upward on hardneck varieties. For onions: leaves beginning to yellow from the tips and fall over.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest garlic scapes when curled -- they are delicious and removing them redirects energy to the bulb. For onions, bending down any remaining upright leaves once half have fallen speeds final ripening.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Seeing scapes on garlic, or leaves beginning to fall?

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Garlic: leaves 2/3 brown. Onions: all leaves yellow and fallen. Leeks: any size -- harvest young for mild flavor.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Lift carefully with a fork to avoid bruising. Cure in a warm, airy spot for 2-4 weeks before storing -- this is essential for long storage life.

growth_stages.name: Curing and Storage
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Skin papery and tight, neck dry and closed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Hang or lay in a single layer in good airflow, out of direct rain, for 2-4 weeks. Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store well.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your garlic
notifications.body_seasoned: Garlic is planted in autumn and overwinters in the ground -- it needs a cold period to develop properly. Plant cloves now, pointed end up, 2 inches deep and 6 inches apart. You will not see much happen until spring, and that is exactly right.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your onion sets
notifications.body_seasoned: Onion sets can go in 3-4 weeks before last frost. Plant pointed end up with just the tip showing at the surface. They establish quickly and are more reliable than growing from seed.

notifications.title_seasoned: Harvest your garlic scapes
notifications.body_seasoned: Hardneck garlic sends up curled green shoots called scapes in early summer. Cut them off now -- they are delicious in stir fries and pestos, and removing them directs energy back into the bulb for a larger harvest.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your garlic for harvest readiness
notifications.body_seasoned: When two thirds of the leaves have turned brown, your garlic is ready. Do not wait for all leaves to die -- the outer wrapper deteriorates. Lift carefully with a fork, do not pull by the stem, and handle gently to avoid bruising.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cure your alliums properly -- it is worth it
notifications.body_seasoned: Garlic and onions not properly cured will not store through winter. Hang or lay them in a single layer in a warm, airy space out of rain for 3-4 weeks. The necks should be completely dry before storage. This step makes the difference between 3-month storage and 6-month storage.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for rust on your alliums
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid conditions. It weakens the plant but rarely kills it. Remove badly affected leaves and ensure good airflow. Rotate alliums to a different bed next year.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Keep curing alliums dry
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Rain on curing garlic and onions undoes the drying process and encourages rot. Make sure they are under cover -- a shed, garage, or covered porch is ideal.

planting.text_seasoned: Plant garlic in your best, most fertile bed. It is in the ground for 9 months -- give it good conditions from the start.
Save the largest cloves from each bulb for planting and eat the small ones. Larger cloves produce larger bulbs.

early_growth.text_seasoned: Keep allium beds completely weed-free. Onions and garlic have poor, shallow root systems and are easily out-competed. Even small weeds reduce yields significantly.
No need to water garlic in autumn and winter -- rainfall is usually sufficient. Begin watering in spring if it is dry.

established.text_seasoned: Stop feeding with nitrogen once bulbs start to form. High nitrogen at this stage produces soft, poorly-stored bulbs with thick necks.
Leeks can be earthed up as they grow to blanch the lower stem -- this gives you a longer white shaft and milder flavor.

bulb_forming.text_seasoned: When onion leaves begin to yellow and fall over, stop watering. The plant is telling you it is finishing -- let it dry down naturally.
Do not bend onion tops manually until at least half the leaves have yellowed on their own. Bending them too early exposes the neck to disease.

harvest.text_seasoned: Lift rather than pull. A garden fork under the bulb loosens the roots and prevents the stem tearing -- which exposes the bulb to rot during curing.
Harvest on a dry day and leave on top of the soil for a few hours before bringing in. The sun begins the drying process.

curing.text_seasoned: Curing is the most important step most gardeners skip. 3-4 weeks in warm, airy conditions transforms a perishable vegetable into one that stores for 6-9 months.
Braid garlic and onions for storage if you have enough -- it looks beautiful and is functional. Store in a cool, dry, dark place.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One leek per plant -- sizeable at full growth
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Leeks stand in the ground all winter and are harvested as needed
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Leeks are a genuinely useful winter vegetable. They store in the ground and you can harvest all winter as you need them.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Established alliums are among the hardiest vegetables and handle frost well. Garlic overwintering in the ground is designed for frost. Young onion seedlings are more vulnerable to late hard freezes.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Protect young onion sets if a hard freeze threatens in the first few weeks after planting. Established plants need no protection from ordinary frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Allium rust appears as orange powder on leaves in humid summers -- it weakens but rarely kills the plant. White rot is more serious: a soil-borne fungus that causes bulbs to rot at the base. Once white rot is in soil it persists for decades.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Rotate alliums to a new bed every year. White rot cannot be eliminated from infected soil -- grow alliums elsewhere if you see it. Rust is largely cosmetic -- harvest early and the bulbs are usually fine.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Garlic and onion bulbs rot in waterlogged soil, especially during curing. Rain on curing alliums reverses the drying process and causes neck rot -- one of the most common storage failures.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Ensure excellent drainage. Cure garlic and onions under cover -- a shed or garage with good airflow. Even a few hours of rain on curing bulbs can significantly reduce storage life.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Alliums that experience drought stress during bulb development produce small, tight bulbs. Irregular watering is a common cause of disappointing allium harvests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently during bulb formation -- from spring until leaves begin to yellow. Stop watering completely once leaves start to die back naturally.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Alliums need full sun for good bulb development. The bulbing trigger in onions and garlic is day length -- both need long days combined with warmth to form bulbs. In shade or under trees, they often produce only small, undeveloped bulbs.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant alliums in your sunniest, most open bed. Weed competition also significantly reduces yield -- keep allium beds completely weed-free from early spring.

3.notes: Start indoors. Choose 90-day varieties. Frost improves flavor.

start_indoors.label: primary

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

pests.name: Cabbage worm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Large irregular holes in leaves. Green caterpillars (1-1.5 inches) blending into foliage. White cabbage butterfly flying nearby is a warning sign.
pests.cause_seasoned: Pieris rapae butterfly larvae. Lay eggs on leaf undersides.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick caterpillars and egg clusters. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) spray every 2 weeks. Row covers as barrier.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Row covers from planting. White butterfly decoys (territorial behavior). Plant nasturtiums as trap crop.

pests.name: Cabbage aphid
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Dense gray-green colonies on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl and pucker. Honeydew and sooty mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Brevicoryne brassicae. Populations explode rapidly in cool weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Strong water blast. Insecticidal soap spray directly on colonies. Remove and compost heavily infested leaves.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid excess nitrogen. Encourage parasitic wasps with flowering herbs nearby.

pests.name: Flea beetle
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Many tiny round shot-holes in leaves, especially on seedlings. Plants look peppered. Small shiny beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple flea beetle species. Worst in spring on young plants.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers on seedlings. Diatomaceous earth. Kaolin clay spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Delay planting. Use transplants. Interplant with aromatic herbs.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Clubroot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plants wilt in hot weather despite watering. Stunted growth. Yellowing leaves. Roots are swollen, club-shaped, and deformed when dug up.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Plasmodiophora brassicae soil pathogen. Survives in soil for up to 20 years. Thrives in acidic, wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove and destroy infected plants -- do not compost. Lime soil to raise pH to 7.0-7.2.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Minimum 7-year rotation away from brassicas in infected soil. Maintain soil pH above 6.5. Improve drainage.

diseases.name: Downy mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Yellow patches on upper leaf surface with gray-purple fuzzy mold on undersides. Affects seedlings and mature plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Peronospora brassicae fungus. Favored by cool moist conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected leaves. Improve air circulation. Copper-based fungicide as preventive.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Avoid overhead watering. Space plants generously. Choose resistant varieties.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Start 6-8 weeks before transplant date. Brussels need a long season -- in zones 3-5, start early indoors.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Kale, broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, Brussels sprouts, turnip, kohlrabi -- share clubroot and downy mildew
rotation.note_seasoned: Clubroot can persist 20 years -- in infected soil extend to 7-year rotation.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 3-5 days on the stalk -- much longer than off
storage.freezer_seasoned: Blanch 3-5 minutes depending on size, freeze -- excellent. Most commercial frozen sprouts are excellent quality.
storage.notes_seasoned: Leave on the stalk in the fridge for longest shelf life. Freeze surplus immediately -- frozen sprouts are genuinely excellent.

varieties.note_seasoned: Gustus is consistently rated for flavor -- less bitter than older varieties.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Possible in large containers. 5-gallon minimum, one plant per pot. Tall plants may need staking.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Round seed leaves pushing up cleanly. Brassicas germinate readily in cool, moist conditions.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep soil consistently moist at 60-70°F. Brassicas do not need heat -- they prefer cool germination.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- slightly waxy and blue-green in color.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch for damping off -- good airflow and not overwatering prevents it. Thin to one plant per cell.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Sturdy plants with multiple leaf sets, ready to go outside.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harden off well before transplanting. Net immediately after planting to protect from cabbage white butterflies -- do not delay on this.

growth_stages.name: Head Forming
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Central head beginning to form. On broccoli, a tight green dome. On cauliflower, a white curd appearing in the center.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: For cauliflower, tie the outer leaves over the developing curd to blanch it and keep it white. Do this as soon as the curd is visible.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Broccoli: tight green head before any yellow flowers open. Cauliflower: firm white curd at full size. Cabbage: firm, dense head that does not give when squeezed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest broccoli with a long stem cut -- side shoots will continue producing for weeks. Cauliflower and cabbage are once-and-done harvests.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Harvest time -- how did it look?

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to start your brassicas indoors
notifications.body_seasoned: Broccoli, cauliflower, and cabbage need 6-8 weeks indoors before transplanting. Start now -- they grow slowly at first but reward the patience. Cool temperatures suit them perfectly.

notifications.title_seasoned: Brassicas outside -- net them immediately
notifications.body_seasoned: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves within hours of planting. Cover with fine mesh netting immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Caterpillar damage can devastate an unprotected crop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Cauliflower curd forming -- time to blanch
notifications.body_seasoned: Tie a few outer leaves loosely over the developing curd now to protect it from light. This keeps the cauliflower white and tender. Check every few days -- once the curd is visible it develops quickly.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your broccoli heads
notifications.body_seasoned: Broccoli heads that are ready to harvest look like tight green domes with no yellow showing. Once you see any flower buds opening it is past its best. Cut with a long stem and watch for side shoots to develop.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start a fall brassica crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Brassicas do well as a fall crop and often taste better -- frost sweetens cabbage and broccoli. Start seeds now for a crop that matures in the cooler autumn months.

notifications.title_seasoned: How are your brassicas getting on?
notifications.body_seasoned: Check under the netting for caterpillar damage -- they can strip a plant surprisingly fast. Also look at the developing head for any signs of bolting or discoloration.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Heat stress -- brassicas may bolt
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Sustained high temperatures cause broccoli and cauliflower to bolt -- heads open into flowers before they are full size. Harvest anything that looks close to ready before the heat peaks.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for clubroot and downy mildew
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Humid conditions favor several brassica diseases. Ensure good spacing and airflow. Check leaves for yellowing or powdery patches and remove affected material promptly.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Late frost -- protect young brassicas
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Established brassicas handle frost well, but young transplants need protection for the first few weeks. Cover with fleece tonight.

germination.text_seasoned: Brassicas are reliable germinators in cool conditions -- 60-70°F is ideal. They do not need heat mats.
Sow into cells or modules rather than trays -- brassicas develop long tap roots and resent root disturbance.

seedling.text_seasoned: Grow brassica seedlings in the coolest, brightest spot you have. Warmth makes them soft and leggy.
Feed with a dilute liquid feed once the first true leaves appear. Brassicas are hungry plants from the start.

established.text_seasoned: Net immediately after transplanting. Cabbage white butterflies find brassicas within hours and lay clusters of yellow eggs on leaf undersides. Check the netting is secure all around -- one gap and caterpillars will find it.

Brussels sprouts are tall plants and the heaviest-laden brassica in the garden. Stake plants once they pass 18 inches; in exposed sites, hill soil up around the base to keep them upright through autumn winds.

head_forming.text_seasoned: Sprouts form in the leaf axils starting from the bottom of the stalk and progressing upward over weeks. Tiny green knobs appearing where each leaf meets the stem is the cue.

Some growers top the plant -- pinching out the growing tip -- once the lowest sprouts are pea-sized. This redirects the plant's energy into evening up sprout size on a single stalk. It is optional; ungtopped plants produce a longer harvest window.

harvest.text_seasoned: Harvest sprouts from the bottom of the stalk upward as each one reaches 1 to 1.5 inches across and is firm to the touch. Snap them off with a downward twist or cut with a knife. The plant continues maturing the upper sprouts for weeks.
Wait until after the first hard frost if you can -- frost converts starches to sugars and dramatically improves flavor. This is the single biggest variable in how good homegrown sprouts taste.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 50-100 sprouts per plant over the season
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are harvested from the bottom up over several months
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Brussels sprouts are a long-season crop that demands patience. The reward is months of harvesting from one plant through autumn and winter.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Established brassicas handle frost well -- it actually sweetens them. But young transplants in their first 2-3 weeks are more vulnerable. A hard freeze can damage or kill recently transplanted seedlings.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover new transplants with fleece for the first 2-3 weeks after planting if frost is possible. Once established they are among the hardiest vegetables you can grow.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cabbage white butterflies lay eggs on brassica leaves and the caterpillars can strip a plant in days. This is by far the most common reason brassicas fail. If you did not net, this is almost certainly what happened.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Net immediately after transplanting -- before you do anything else. Fine mesh netting secured all the way around is the single most important thing you can do for brassicas. Check netting for gaps weekly.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brassicas in waterlogged soil develop root problems. Clubroot -- a soil-borne disease -- causes swollen, distorted roots and wilting. Once present in soil it persists for many years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Improve drainage before planting. If clubroot is suspected, rotate brassicas to a new bed and do not grow them in the affected soil for 4-5 years. Liming to raise soil pH above 7 discourages clubroot.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brassicas need consistent moisture to develop good heads. Drought stress causes premature flowering in broccoli and cauliflower, and split heads in cabbage.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently and mulch around plants to retain moisture. A dry spell during head formation is the most damaging period.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Cauliflower is the most demanding -- it needs consistent temperatures and care to form a good curd. Broccoli heads opening into yellow flowers usually means the temperature swung too warm. Both benefit from 6+ hours of sun.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cauliflower in particular needs a consistent, cool growing environment. Autumn sowings often perform better than spring ones in warmer zones. Shade cloth can help in warm spells.
