fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Feed balanced fertilizer monthly. Switch to a lower-nitrogen, higher-potassium feed once plants start flowering for better pod production.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 10-10-10 -- switch to low N once flowering

pests.name: Corn earworm
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small round holes in pods, often near the tip. Inside the pod, a green, brown, or reddish striped caterpillar up to 1 3/4 inches long with scattered black spots. Frass (dark droppings) visible at entry holes.
pests.cause_seasoned: Helicoverpa zea moth larvae, the same species also called tomato fruitworm. Multiple generations per season, heaviest pressure in mid to late summer.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick affected pods and destroy. Apply Bt (Bacillus thuringiensis) to young pods at first sign of damage. Spinosad is effective on later instars.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Scout pods twice a week during peak bloom. Harvest every 2-3 days so larvae have less time to develop inside pods. Till garden residue in fall to expose overwintering pupae.

pests.name: Stink bugs & leaffooted bugs
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Pods curl, twist, or develop wart-like protrusions where bugs have fed. Small dimples or dark spots on pod surface. Shield-shaped stink bugs or narrow leaffooted bugs visible on plants, especially in morning.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several species, including brown and green stink bugs and the leaffooted bug (Leptoglossus spp.). They pierce pods with needle-like mouthparts and suck sap, deforming developing tissue.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and egg masses (look for barrel-shaped eggs in tight clusters on leaf undersides). Insecticidal soap knocks down nymphs but has little effect on hard-shelled adults.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Clean up weedy borders and overwintering sites near the garden. Encourage predatory wasps and assassin bugs by avoiding broad-spectrum sprays.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of small soft-bodied insects on new growth and undersides of leaves. Leaves may yellow or curl. Sticky honeydew followed by sooty black mold.
pests.cause_seasoned: Cotton aphid (Aphis gossypii) is the most common species on okra. Populations build quickly in warm weather, especially on plants pushed with excess nitrogen.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with a strong water spray. Insecticidal soap or neem oil applied to the underside of leaves. Ladybugs and lacewings provide effective natural control.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Avoid over-fertilizing with nitrogen, which produces soft growth that aphids favor. Interplant with flowering herbs to support beneficial insects.

pests.name: Flea beetles
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny round shot-holes in leaves, worst on seedlings and young plants. Small shiny black beetles jump when disturbed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Several flea beetle species feed on okra foliage. Most active in spring on young plants; mature okra tolerates damage well.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Row covers until plants are established and flowering. Diatomaceous earth applied to dry foliage. Neem oil if damage is heavy on seedlings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Set out transplants rather than direct-seeding so plants pass through the vulnerable seedling stage indoors. Keep garden weed-free to reduce overwintering habitat.

diseases.name: Root-knot nematodes
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Stunted, yellowing plants that wilt in afternoon heat despite adequate water. Poor pod set. Pulling a plant reveals knotty galls and swellings on the roots -- the signature sign.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Meloidogyne spp., microscopic soil-dwelling roundworms. UGA lists root-knot nematode as the most serious disease of okra. Sandy soils and warm climates favor the pest.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No effective in-season chemical treatment for home gardeners. Remove and destroy infested plants including roots at end of season.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate okra with non-host crops (corn, small grains, brassicas) for 2-3 years. Solarize infested beds in summer with clear plastic. Plant French marigolds (Tagetes patula) as a trap crop. Add compost to boost beneficial soil microbes.

diseases.name: Fusarium wilt
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Lower leaves yellow, wilt, and drop while upper foliage remains green initially. Vascular tissue inside stem shows brown streaking when cut. Whole plant collapse over 1-2 weeks.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fusarium oxysporum f. sp. vasinfectum, a soil-borne fungus. UGA reports wilt pressure is much worse where root-knot nematodes are also present, since nematode feeding creates entry wounds.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure once a plant is infected. Remove and destroy affected plants; do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Long rotation (4+ years) out of okra and cotton. Control root-knot nematodes, which open the door for Fusarium. Keep soil pH above 6.0.

diseases.name: Southern stem blight
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sudden wilting of an otherwise healthy plant. White cottony fungal growth at the soil line, often with small tan mustard-seed-shaped sclerotia. Lower stem becomes bleached and shredded.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Sclerotium rolfsii, a soil fungus most active in hot humid weather. Overwinters as sclerotia in soil and crop debris for several years.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove infected plants with a trowel-deep perimeter of soil. Bag and discard; do not compost. No effective organic rescue treatment.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Rotate with grass crops for 3-4 years. Bury crop residue deeply or remove it. Avoid piling mulch against plant stems where the fungus thrives.

diseases.name: Anthracnose
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Sunken, water-soaked lesions on pods that turn dark and may show pinkish spore masses in humid weather. Pods become unmarketable. Leaf spots with tan centers and dark borders may also appear.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Colletotrichum spp. fungus. Spreads by rain splash in warm wet weather. Overwinters on crop debris and seed.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected pods as soon as spots appear. Copper-based fungicide (labeled for okra) applied preventively during wet periods.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use certified disease-free seed. Rotate out of okra for 2-3 years. Space plants for airflow and stake or thin if canopy becomes dense.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Direct sow after last frost when soil is very warm (70°F+). Soak seeds 24 hours first. In zones 3-6, start indoors 3-4 weeks before in biodegradable pots.

storage.fridge_seasoned: 3-5 days -- okra is sensitive to cold, ideal 45-50°F
storage.freezer_seasoned: Slice or leave whole, blanch 3 minutes, freeze -- excellent
storage.notes_seasoned: Okra stored too cold (below 45°F) develops brown spots. Use the warmest part of the fridge.

varieties.note_seasoned: Clemson Spineless is the standard -- spineless pods are much easier to harvest than spiny types.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. This claim's nematode component aligns with the extension-documented mechanism, but the 'concurrent companion' application pattern reflects popular gardening practice rather than extension protocol.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Can be grown in containers. 5-gallon minimum. Compact varieties like Baby Bubba work best.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other malva family plants
rotation.note_seasoned: Few specific rotation concerns -- general 2-year rotation is sufficient.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Large seed leaves emerging. Okra germinates well in warm soil.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Nick or soak seeds overnight to speed germination. Soil must be 65°F+ -- okra refuses to germinate in cold soil.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Distinctive lobed leaves developing. Okra grows fast once warm.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to 18 inches -- okra gets large. Water consistently.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tall plants 2-3 feet, woody stems. Beautiful hibiscus-like flowers forming.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a balanced fertilizer. Okra is a hungry plant that keeps producing if well-fed.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pods at 2-4 inches -- tender and snap-crisp when broken.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick every 2-3 days. Okra pods left past their prime become tough and woody in days. Wear gloves -- okra irritates skin.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Slowing pod production, woody stalks, nights cooling below 55°F.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Harvest any tender pods before first frost -- larger pods turn fibrous quickly. Cut down the woody stalks and chop or shred before composting; whole stalks can take a long time to break down.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your okra season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your okra
notifications.body_seasoned: Get your okra in the ground now. Prepare the soil well and water in after planting.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your okra for harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Your okra should be approaching harvest readiness now. Check the crop-specific signals and harvest at the right moment for best flavor.

notifications.title_seasoned: How is your okra doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a while -- how is it looking?

germination.text_seasoned: Okra needs warm soil to germinate -- 70 to 95 degrees, ideally 80+. Direct-sow after soil is reliably 70 degrees and last frost is 2 to 3 weeks past. Okra is one of the most heat-loving common vegetables.
Soak seeds in water for 12 to 24 hours before sowing to soften the hard seed coat. Sow 1/2 to 1 inch deep, 4 to 6 inches apart in rows 3 feet apart. Germination takes 7 to 14 days in warm soil.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin seedlings to 12 to 18 inches apart once they have 2 to 3 true leaves. Crowded okra produces fewer pods.
Okra seedlings tolerate heat that would stress most vegetables. They do not, however, tolerate cool weather -- nights below 60 degrees substantially slow growth.

established.text_seasoned: Okra grows rapidly in heat -- plants reach 4 to 8 feet tall by midsummer in warm climates. The taller varieties may benefit from staking in windy sites.
Water deeply once a week and mulch to retain soil moisture. Side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer at first flowering. Okra is moderately heavy-feeding but not as demanding as cucurbits.

harvest.text_seasoned: Pick okra pods at 2 to 4 inches long -- larger pods become woody and tough almost overnight. Daily picking during peak production is essential; pods left to mature signal the plant to stop producing.

Wear long sleeves and gloves -- okra leaves and stems carry fine spines that cause skin irritation in some people. Cut pods cleanly with a knife or pruners; the stems are tough and pulling damages the plant.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: Okra production drops as nights cool below 60 degrees. Plants are killed by light frost. Harvest all usable pods before first expected frost.
Pull and compost spent plants. Rotate to a new bed each year -- okra has fewer rotation concerns than most crops because it shares few pests with common vegetables.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 30-50 pods per plant over the season
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Mid-to-late summer is the heavy run -- pods size up fast in heat, and a productive plant gives a handful every 1 to 2 days at peak.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Okra is easy and prolific in warm climates. In cooler zones, choose the shortest-season varieties.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Okra is a tropical-origin heat lover -- damaged at any stage by cold and killed by light frost. Cold soil at sowing (below 70 degrees) rots seed before germination. Cool nights below 60 degrees stunt growth severely; okra is a rare crop where cool weather, not frost, is often the limiting factor in marginal zones.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to direct-sow until soil reaches 70 degrees minimum and night temperatures stay above 60. In cooler zones, start transplants indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost (use peat pots to minimize root disturbance) and use black plastic mulch outdoors. Choose short-season varieties (Clemson Spineless at 55 days) for cool-summer regions.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Okra has fewer serious pests than most vegetables. Flea beetles, aphids, and stink bugs are the headline pests; corn earworm occasionally bores into pods. Root-knot nematodes damage roots in sandy southern soils. Southern stem blight, anthracnose, and powdery mildew are the main diseases.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off aphids; tolerate moderate flea beetle damage on established plants. For root-knot nematodes, rotate okra with crops that do not host the pest (most legumes, brassicas). Choose disease-resistant varieties for southern gardens. Okra's relatively short pest list is one of its appeals.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Persistent waterlogging causes root rot -- rare in established okra because the deep taproot tolerates moderate drought, but young plants in heavy clay can drown. Wet foliage drives powdery mildew and bacterial blight in humid summers.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Water at the base, not overhead, and water early in the day so foliage dries before evening. In heavy clay or wet sites, plant in raised beds. Established okra tolerates dry conditions well; do not overwater.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Okra is more drought-tolerant than most warm-season vegetables but produces smaller, tougher pods under severe drought stress. Yields drop substantially when plants are water-stressed during flowering and pod development.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply once a week -- 1 inch minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture and reduce evaporation. Okra's deep taproot makes it more drought-tolerant than shallow-rooted crops, but consistent water still produces best yields.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Tall thin plants with few pods
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Okra needs full sun -- 8 hours minimum -- and serious heat to flower and fruit well. In partial shade plants grow tall and leafy but produce few flowers and pods. Okra is a hot-sun, hot-soil, hot-air crop; cool partial-shade conditions are the wrong environment.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in the sunniest, hottest spot available. South-facing exposure or near a heat-reflecting wall is ideal in marginal zones. In cool-summer climates, accept that okra is not the right crop and grow cool-season vegetables instead.

crops.description_seasoned: Heat-lover that thrives where others struggle. Harvest pods at 3-4 inches -- left longer, they become woody. A Southern staple that belongs in more gardens.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick at 3-4 inches, every 2 days. Larger pods become tough and fibrous very quickly. Thumbnail should pierce skin easily.

crops.name: Nectarine

3.notes: Challenging. Choose cold-hardy varieties like Reliance. Protect blossoms from late spring frosts.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. (UMN Extension 'Growing apples in the home garden'; UMN Extension 'Growing stone fruits in the home garden')

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Stone fruit harvest runs June through August for most varieties. Peaches and nectarines ripen mid-to-late summer; apricots earliest (June-July); sweet cherries June-July; sour cherries July; plums July-September depending on type (Japanese types earlier, European types later). This month-by-month synthesis of stone fruit harvest windows follows Iowa State University Extension's commercial-orchard reference material on peach, plum, and cherry harvest timing. UMN Extension is cited for complementary climate-zone guidance on northern-Midwest stone fruit cultivation.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

storage.room_temp_seasoned: Ripen on counter, then use immediately
storage.freezer_seasoned: Peel, slice, freeze flat then bag -- excellent
storage.notes_seasoned: Same as peach -- ripen at room temperature, refrigerate only when fully soft.

varieties.note_seasoned: Mericrest is the most cold-hardy nectarine -- reliable in zones where most nectarines struggle.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text_seasoned: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text_seasoned: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 120-150 lbs from a mature standard tree (peach-equivalent yield -- same species)
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors_seasoned: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: Canadian-bred cold-hardy nectarine from Ontario, hardy to -30°F. Disease-resistant to brown rot and bacterial spot -- the top choice for humid eastern zones where other nectarines fail. Medium-sized freestone yellow fruit. Self-pollinating. Ripens August.
Cold-hardy New Hampshire-bred nectarine. Large red-skinned freestone fruit with yellow flesh. Self-pollinating. One of the more reliable nectarines for zones 5-6 growers.

Large freestone with deep red skin and yellow flesh. Crack-resistant with good shelf life. Cold-hardy buds reduce spring frost crop losses. Self-pollinating. Widely available and popular for home orchards.

The flavor benchmark among nectarines -- classic high-acid, high-sugar profile. Large yellow freestone with red blush. Self-pollinating. Adaptable across a wide range of conditions. Best mid-range choice for zones 6-8.

Low-chill white-fleshed nectarine for warm climates. Large fruit with dark red skin and crisp, sweet white flesh. Self-pollinating. Early ripening. Makes nectarines possible in zones 8-9 where standard varieties fail.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Plant bare root fruit trees in early spring while they are still dormant, as soon as the soil can be worked. In Minnesota, this is April or May. Bare root plants suffer severely from transplanting shock -- plant as soon as soil is workable and before bud break. harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Stone fruit harvest runs June through August for most varieties. Peaches and nectarines ripen mid-to-late summer; apricots earliest (June-July); sweet cherries June-July; sour cherries July; plums July-September depending on type (Japanese types earlier, European types later). This month-by-month synthesis of stone fruit harvest windows follows Iowa State University Extension's commercial-orchard reference material on peach, plum, and cherry harvest timing. UMN Extension is cited for complementary climate-zone guidance on northern-Midwest stone fruit cultivation.

crops.description_seasoned: Smooth-skinned peach relative. Very similar growing requirements but slightly more disease-resistant. Same chill hour requirements as peaches.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Background yellow, slight give at stem end, easy detachment. Similar to peach but firmer at pick.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Nectarines are genetically identical to peaches -- the difference is a single recessive gene that produces smooth skin instead of fuzzy skin. Hardiness and chill hour requirements are essentially the same as peach (generally zones 5-9). However, nectarines are notably more disease-prone than peaches because the smooth skin lacks the protective fuzz that deters fungal pathogens and insects. Brown rot, bacterial spot, and peach leaf curl are all more severe on nectarines, which makes reliable fruit production in humid eastern zones harder than for peaches. The same early-spring bloom risks apply -- fruit buds suffer damage at -13°F and meaningful loss at -18°F. In warm climates (zones 8b+), low-chill varieties (Arctic Star, Desert Delight, Sunraycer) under 300 chill hours are required. Miniature varieties (Stark HoneyGlo, Garden Delight) stay under 6 feet, making nectarines practical for containers or small gardens. Self-fertile; no pollinator required.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Low-chill varieties available -- check variety before purchasing for warm zones
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. Identical care to peach.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Remove fruit in year one. Identical first-year care to peach.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Light feeder. Balanced feed in spring, potassium-rich feed after harvest. Sour cherries are more tolerant of average soil than sweet.

tasks.description_seasoned: Prune after harvest in summer. Sour cherries fruit on 1-year-old wood -- leave plenty of new shoots.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Pollinator category is mechanistically grounded. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Soil-category claim has a mechanistic basis. Specific claim not matched by pattern.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Allium sulfur-based volatile organic compounds have documented aphid-repellent effects (Durenne and Gosset, 'Companion Plants for Aphid Pest Management,' Insects 2018, 9(4):112). The companion application is described by several extensions at home-gardening rigor: Mississippi State University Extension ('Companion planting improves gardens,' Snyder via Reeves) explicitly states 'Chives tend to repel aphids'; Utah State University Extension ('Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting,' Mohr et al.) lists onions, garlic, and chives as repelling common garden pests; UC Cooperative Extension Master Gardener publications (Butte County 'Best Friends in the Garden' and Fresno County 'Winter companion planting to repel insects') likewise list allium VOCs among aphid-repellent companions. These extension sources describe the pairing at tradition-plus-plausible-mechanism rigor rather than validated protocol -- the Kansas State Extension / Johnson County 'Companion Planting' page caveats that allium sulfur repellency is 'centralized to the garlic itself -- and only with certain pests.' The earlier catalog attribution to 'UC IPM' does not match UC IPM's Pest Notes on aphids (pn7404), which focus on reflective mulches, water sprays, soaps, and natural enemies rather than allium interplanting.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Bad companion claim, no pattern match. Default to traditional pending review.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Peachtree borer
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Gummy, amber-colored sap mixed with sawdust at base of trunk near soil line. Weakened, declining tree.
pests.cause_seasoned: Synanthedon exitiosa clear-wing moth larvae. Bore into trunk near soil.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Dig out larvae by hand in autumn. Apply beneficial nematodes around trunk base in autumn.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Keep base of trunk clear of mulch and debris. Apply pyrethrin spray to trunk base in early September.

diseases.name: Brown rot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Brown soft spots on ripening fruit, rapidly expanding. Fuzzy gray-brown spore masses develop. Fruit mummifies on tree.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Monilinia fructicola/laxa fungus. Spreads rapidly in warm humid conditions near harvest.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove and destroy all affected fruit immediately -- do not compost. Apply sulfur fungicide preventively near harvest.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove mummified fruit from tree and ground. Improve air circulation with pruning. Avoid fruit injury.

diseases.name: Black knot
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Hard black galls/swellings on branches and twigs. Galls enlarge each year. Severe infection kills branches.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Apiosporina morbosa fungus. Affects plum, cherry, and related stone fruits.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Prune out knots 4 inches below visible growth in winter. Destroy -- do not compost.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Remove wild plum/cherry trees nearby. Annual inspection and removal of small knots.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze on a tray then bag -- excellent, and essential since crop comes all at once
storage.notes_seasoned: Sour cherries are almost never eaten fresh -- freeze or process immediately after picking.

varieties.note_seasoned: Meteor and North Star are genetic dwarfs -- 8-10 feet, fully self-fertile, and very cold-hardy. Perfect for small gardens.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Plant bare-root trees in late winter/early spring while dormant. Container trees can go in spring through early autumn. Stake against wind for the first 2 years.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Fruit trees need to be grown in the ground. Dwarf varieties on very dwarfing rootstocks can be tried in very large (30+ gallon) containers but are challenging and rarely as productive.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Fruit trees and perennial shrubs are permanent plantings -- crop rotation does not apply. Choose the planting site carefully as it is permanent.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Planting
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree planted correctly -- crown at soil level, roots spread, stake in place.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Dig twice as wide as the root ball, same depth. Spread roots over a mound in the planting hole. Stake firmly. No fertilizer in the planting hole.

growth_stages_year_one.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: New leaf buds breaking, early shoot growth. The tree is putting energy into roots.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week. Remove all flowers -- every flower removed in year one is energy that goes into root development.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension, healthy leaf color, scaffold branches developing.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Choose 3-4 main scaffold branches evenly spaced around the trunk. Remove everything else to the trunk. Train scaffold branches outward with spreaders or weights.

growth_stages_year_one.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages_year_one.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fallen, buds tight and dormant.
growth_stages_year_one.user_action_seasoned: Winter is the time to prune. Cut back scaffold branches by a third, remove crossing or inward-facing growth. Apply a thick mulch around the base before frost.

growth_stages_annual.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare branches before bud break -- the ideal pruning window.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Prune before buds swell. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Open up the center to light and air.

growth_stages_annual.name: Bud Break
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Buds swelling and beginning to open. Green tips showing.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer now. Check stakes and ties -- loosen any that have become tight. Watch for late frost forecasts.

growth_stages_annual.name: Blossom
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- the most frost-sensitive moment of the year.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Watch the forecast vigilantly. A single frost night during blossom can take the entire crop. Cover with fleece if frost threatens.

growth_stages_annual.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Small fruitlets forming after successful pollination.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Thin fruitlets when they are marble-sized. Leave one fruit every 6 inches on apples and pears. Thinning feels wasteful but produces fewer, larger, better-quality fruit.

growth_stages_annual.name: Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Fruit at full color and size, comes away easily when lifted and twisted.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Harvest in stages -- not all fruit on a tree ripens at once. Early fruit on the sunny south side ripens first. Pick at the right time and handle gently.

growth_stages_annual.name: Post Harvest
growth_stages_annual.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves beginning to turn, crop harvested.
growth_stages_annual.user_action_seasoned: Apply a balanced fertilizer after harvest to support next year's bud development. Clear fallen fruit promptly -- it harbors pests and disease.

growth_stages.name: Planting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Bare-root or potted tree just planted. Base of the trunk right at soil level, and the graft union -- the knobby joint where the variety was grafted onto the rootstock -- sits 2 to 4 inches above the ground.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Dig the hole twice as wide as the roots and the same depth. Spread the roots over a small mound in the bottom of the hole. Stake firmly against wind. Don't add fertilizer to the planting hole. Water in deeply.

growth_stages.name: Root Establishment
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First leaves breaking from the dormant branches. New shoot tips extending. The tree is putting almost everything into root growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first summer. Pinch off any flowers that form -- year-one fruit costs the tree more strength than it returns. Keep weeds and grass cleared 2 to 3 feet around the trunk.

growth_stages.name: First Season Growth
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong shoot extension from the trunk. The first major side branches are starting to take shape.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Stone fruit trees are trained to an open-vase form: 3 to 5 main branches angled outward at roughly 45 degrees, evenly spaced around the trunk, with no central leader. Pick those 3 to 5 main branches and remove everything else cleanly back to the trunk. Use branch spreaders (small props that hold a branch at a wider angle) or hanging weights so the chosen branches stay angled outward as they grow.

growth_stages.name: First Dormancy
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Leaves fully dropped, buds tight on the stems. The tree is in true winter dormancy.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: First-year dormancy is a holding period -- the work happens later. Mulch heavily around the base before hard freeze. Wrap the trunk in young-tree wrap to prevent sunscald and rodent damage. Major pruning waits until late winter (the next stage).
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Tree wrapped and mulched for winter?

growth_stages.name: Dormant Pruning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tree fully dormant; buds tight; late winter into early spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Maintain an open-center (vase) form: 3 to 5 main scaffold branches angled outward from a short trunk, with no central leader. Stone fruit needs sun and air movement through the canopy. Remove dead, diseased, damaged wood, then anything growing inward.

growth_stages.name: Blossom
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Pink or white bloom opening. Apricot is earliest and most frost-exposed.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Watch overnight temperatures closely -- stone fruit blooms ahead of apple. Cover smaller trees with fleece on frost nights. Avoid sprays while pollinators are active.

growth_stages.name: Fruit Set and Thinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Petal fall complete; small green fruitlets visible. A natural drop reduces the load in late spring.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches on the branch (peach and nectarine especially). Stone fruit overload makes the fruit small and breaks branches.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Background color shift complete (yellow on peach/nectarine; full color on plum/cherry); fruit gives slightly to gentle pressure.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pick when fruit lifts and twists free with a gentle motion -- forced fruit is not yet ripe. Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window; check daily during peak.

growth_stages.name: Post-Harvest Sanitation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mummified fruit hanging on tree or fallen below; leaves yellowing.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit from the tree and the ground -- these are the brown rot spore source for next year. Apply a potassium feed after harvest while leaves are still working.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your fruit tree
notifications.body_seasoned: Bare root fruit trees are planted in winter while dormant -- now is the window. Prepare your hole in advance, plant with the graft union above soil level, stake firmly, and water in well. The time and care you put into planting directly determines the next 30 years of performance.

notifications.title_seasoned: Remove all blossom in year one
notifications.body_seasoned: Every flower you see on a newly planted tree should be removed. It sounds wrong, but the energy that would go into making fruit goes instead into root development. You will get far more fruit in year three because of this decision in year one.

notifications.title_seasoned: Dormant pruning window -- prune before buds break
notifications.body_seasoned: Late winter before buds swell is the best time to prune fruit trees. Cut to just above an outward-facing bud. Open up the center for light and air. Remove dead, diseased, crossing, and inward-facing wood. Sharp, clean cuts only.

notifications.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- protect your fruit crop
notifications.body_seasoned: Your tree is in blossom -- the most vulnerable moment of the year. A frost tonight could take the entire crop. Cover with horticultural fleece if you can reach the branches, or light a candle in a lantern underneath if the tree is too large to cover.

notifications.title_seasoned: Thin your fruitlets now
notifications.body_seasoned: When fruitlets are marble-sized, thin to one per 6 inches on apples and pears, two per cluster on peaches and nectarines. Thinning feels heartbreaking but produces larger, better-quality fruit and prevents branch breakage under the weight of a heavy crop.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost during blossom -- critical protection needed
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Blossom frost is the most damaging weather event for fruit trees. Even a brief frost at -1°C can destroy the entire year's crop. Cover with fleece tonight.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Drought stress during fruit development
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Water deeply around the drip line of the tree. Drought during fruit development causes premature drop, bitter flavor, and poor size. A deep weekly watering is better than light daily watering.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- fungal disease risk for fruit
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Brown rot, powdery mildew, and scab all thrive in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow through the canopy -- pruning for an open center pays dividends here. Remove any infected fruit immediately.

planting.text_seasoned: Set the graft union a few inches above final soil level. Burying it lets the scion root and you lose the dwarfing rootstock effect.
Stake securely for the first two seasons. Drive the stake into the hole before the tree goes in to avoid root damage later.

establishment.text_seasoned: Water deeply once a week through the first growing season. Roots are still inside the original root ball and dry out quickly.
Mulch a 3-foot circle around the trunk to hold moisture. Keep mulch a few inches clear of the trunk to prevent collar rot.

first_growth.text_seasoned: Stone fruit trains to an open-center form, not a central leader. Choose 3 to 5 scaffolds angled outward from a short trunk and remove the central leader once the scaffolds are set.
Wide-angled scaffolds are stronger and let light into the interior. Use spreaders or weights to set the angle in the first two seasons.

dormancy.text_seasoned: First dormancy is when you commit to the open-center form. Stand back and look at the structure before you cut.
Make clean cuts just above an outward-facing bud. Ragged stubs invite disease, especially Cytospora canker on stone fruit.

dormant_prune.text_seasoned: Maintain the open-center vase: no central leader, 3 to 5 scaffolds, an open interior. Light and air through the canopy is the main brown rot control you have.
Work the three Ds first -- dead, diseased, damaged -- then thin to keep the open form. Stone fruit tolerates and rewards heavier annual pruning than pome fruit.

blossom.text_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms ahead of apple, so spring frost risk is higher. Watch overnight forecasts and cover small trees with fleece on frost nights. Apricot is the earliest bloomer and the most frost-exposed.
Do not spray during bloom. Pollinators are working and the flower window is short.

fruit_set.text_seasoned: Thin peach and nectarine to one fruit every 4 to 6 inches along the branch. Unthinned stone fruit stays small and the weight breaks limbs.
Plum and cherry usually self-thin reasonably well, but a heavy set is still worth thinning by hand to improve fruit size.

harvest.text_seasoned: Stone fruit ripens fast and over a short window -- check daily during peak. Fruit should lift and twist free with a gentle motion; if it resists, leave it another day.
Pick into shallow containers to avoid bruising the fruit underneath. Stone fruit does not finish ripening off the tree the way pears do.

post_harvest.text_seasoned: Remove every mummified fruit -- those leathery brown remnants on branches and ground are the spore source for next year's brown rot. This is the single most important post-harvest task on stone fruit.
Apply a potassium feed while leaves are still working. The feed goes into next year's flower buds, not this year's growth.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 20-40 lbs from a mature semi-standard tree -- lower than sweet cherry but reliably self-fertile
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Full production hits around year 4 to 6 on standard rootstocks, year 3 to 4 on dwarfing stocks. A well-thinned mature stone-fruit tree produces a heavy crop over a 1 to 2 week harvest window.
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: No fruit in year one. The tree puts everything into roots and scaffold structure. Remove any flowers that form -- they cost more in tree vigor than they return in fruit.
factors_seasoned: open-vase pruning for sun and air
consistent water from pit-hardening through harvest

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

varieties_detail.notes_seasoned: The gold standard sour cherry -- accounts for 95% of US commercial tart cherry production. Bright red fruit with yellow flesh and clear juice. Self-fertile. Medium-sized tree (15-20 feet). Named for the Montmorency Valley in France where it originated in the 1600s.
Dwarf sour cherry (8-10 feet) bred by University of Minnesota. Self-fertile, extremely cold-hardy, disease-resistant. Dark red fruit with red flesh. Best choice for small gardens in cold zones.

Dwarf sour cherry (under 10 feet) also from University of Minnesota. Self-fertile. Large bright red fruit. Blooms late, reducing spring frost risk. Similar to North Star but with larger fruit and slightly later harvest.
Hungarian tart cherry, sweeter than Montmorency with darker fruit and juice. Good for fresh eating in addition to pies and preserves. Self-fertile. Ripens slightly later than Montmorency.

Canadian-bred dwarf hybrid (Prunus fruticosa x cerasus) -- extremely cold-hardy, staying under 8 feet. Self-fertile but cross-pollination between Romeo and Juliet increases yield. Fruit is tart-sweet, good for both fresh eating and preserves. The hardiest cherry option for zones 2-3.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit blooms before apple, often when frost is still common. A single hard frost during the brief bloom window can eliminate the year's crop. Apricot is the earliest-blooming and most frost-exposed -- in colder zones it can lose the crop most years.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Watch overnight forecasts through bloom and cover smaller trees with horticultural fleece on frost nights. In frost-prone sites, choose later-blooming varieties on your next planting -- apricot in particular has varieties selected for late bloom that ride out spring frost better.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Brown rot (Monilinia) is the headline disease on stone fruit -- it turns ripening fruit into soft brown lesions, then leathery mummies. Plum curculio leaves crescent-shaped scars on young fruit. Peach leaf curl distorts new leaves in spring. Cherry fruit fly maggots ruin cherries near harvest.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sanitation drives brown rot control: remove every mummified fruit from tree and ground at the end of the season. For peach leaf curl, a single dormant copper spray before bud-swell prevents the season's infection. Open-center pruning helps everything by drying the canopy faster after rain.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Flowers appeared but no fruit set
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Pollination needs vary by stone fruit type. Peach, nectarine, and sour cherry are usually self-fertile and set fruit alone. Sweet cherry and many plums and apricots need a compatible second variety with overlapping bloom. A self-sterile tree alone will bloom heavily and set nothing.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check the pollination requirement of your variety before assuming poor weather. If a partner is needed, plant a compatible second variety within 100 feet -- a neighbor's tree counts if it is close enough. Bloom-time charts from extension publications help match pollinators.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit is unusually intolerant of wet feet. Trees in saturated soil show yellowing leaves, weak shoots, and gummy bark splits at the base (Phytophthora collar rot). Decline can be rapid -- a stone-fruit tree can fail in a single wet spring.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Drainage is set at planting. On a wet site, plant the next tree on a 12-inch raised mound or move sites entirely. Stone fruit on its own roots tolerates wet less than pome fruit -- choose a Phytophthora-resistant rootstock if available.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Poor fruit quality or low yield
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Stone fruit needs 6 to 8 hours of direct sun to color, sweeten, and ripen evenly. In shade or in a crowded canopy, fruit stays small and pale and brown rot pressure increases because the canopy stays wet longer.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Maintain the open-center form with annual pruning -- this is more important on stone fruit than on any other tree fruit. Light and air through the canopy is both a yield driver and a disease control. Site new trees in full sun, away from buildings or larger trees that will shade them as they mature.

crops.description_seasoned: Self-fertile, more cold-hardy than sweet cherry, and produces abundantly. Montmorency is the classic variety. Perfect for pies, preserves, and syrups.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Bright red, tart flavor when tasted. Good indicator is color -- leave longer for less acidity.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Sour cherries (also called tart or pie cherries) are dramatically more forgiving than sweet cherries. They are genuinely cold-hardy to zone 4, self-fertile, bloom late enough to escape most spring frosts, and tolerate a wider range of soils. Sour cherries are the practical choice for home growers in challenging climates where sweet cherries struggle. The tradeoff is that the fruit is too acidic for most fresh eating -- sour cherries shine in pies, preserves, juice, and dried applications. In warm climates (zones 8+), sour cherries have the same chill hour limits as sweet cherries (700-1,200 hours) and fail to break dormancy. Dwarf varieties (North Star, Meteor, Romeo, Juliet) stay under 10 feet tall, making sour cherries genuinely practical for small gardens where sweet cherries would overwhelm the space. Trees begin bearing in year 3-4 and can produce 30-50 quarts at maturity.
crops.chill_hours_note_seasoned: Highest chill requirement of common fruits. Zones 4-6 ideal
crops.pollinator_notes_seasoned: Self-fertile. One tree is sufficient. Montmorency is the most widely grown variety.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: No harvest years 1-2. Allow to establish before first light harvest in year 3.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Microgreens are harvested within 2 weeks of germination -- no fertilizer needed. Good seed-starting mix is sufficient.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small flies around growing trays. Larvae in growing medium.
pests.cause_seasoned: Bradysia species.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Yellow sticky traps. Let medium dry between waterings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Good airflow. Avoid overwatering.

diseases.name: Damping off
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seedlings collapse at soil level shortly after germination. Stems appear pinched.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Various Pythium and Fusarium fungi in overly wet conditions.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove affected trays. Improve air circulation.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use sterile growing medium. Do not overwater. Good airflow.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist twice daily during germination, once daily after
watering.amount_seasoned: Keep growing medium moist but not waterlogged
watering.method_seasoned: Bottom watering preferred -- prevents damping off and mold
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Gray mold, damping off, foul smell

storage.fridge_seasoned: 5-7 days in sealed container lined with paper towel -- keep dry
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not suitable
storage.notes_seasoned: Harvest and refrigerate immediately. Do not wash until ready to eat. Paper towel absorbs condensation.

varieties.note_seasoned: Sunflower microgreens are the most satisfying for beginners -- large seeds germinate reliably and the flavor is excellent.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow seeds densely on damp growing medium (coco coir, hemp mat, or potting mix). No soil preparation needed -- use trays specifically for microgreens.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Microgreens are always grown in shallow trays indoors -- a 10×20 inch propagation tray is standard. No minimum gallon requirement.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A
rotation.note_seasoned: Indoor tray crop -- no rotation needed.

growth_stages.name: Sowing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds evenly distributed on moist growing medium.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly. Mist thoroughly, cover with a blackout lid or second tray, and press down firmly to ensure seed contact with the medium.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprouting -- white roots and pale shoots pushing up under the blackout cover.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave covered and check moisture daily. The weight of the tray on top helps seeds develop straight, strong stems.

growth_stages.name: Blackout Phase
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shoots pushing against the lid -- they should be pale yellow and reaching upward.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: When shoots are pressing against the blackout cover, move to light. The stretch in darkness builds stem length.

growth_stages.name: Growing in Light
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Greening up fast as chlorophyll develops. Cotyledons (seed leaves) opening fully.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water from below by setting the tray in water and allowing it to absorb upward -- this avoids mold on the surface. Harvest when seed leaves are fully open.

notifications.title_seasoned: Move your microgreens to light
notifications.body_seasoned: Your microgreens should be ready to move from blackout to light -- check that shoots are pressing against the cover. Move to a bright windowsill or under grow lights now. They will green up within hours.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your microgreens for harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Microgreens are ready when the seed leaves are fully open and the first true leaves are just beginning to show. Harvest with scissors just above the soil line. Rinse and use immediately for the best flavor.

sow.text_seasoned: Sow densely -- microgreens are one of the few crops where crowding is desirable. Even coverage without gaps gives the best harvest.
Soak large seeds (sunflower, peas) overnight before sowing. They germinate more evenly and quickly.

germination.text_seasoned: The weight of a tray or board on top helps seeds press into the medium and develop straight, strong stems in the dark.
Check moisture once a day -- the medium should be moist but not waterlogged. If it feels wet on top, wait before misting again.

blackout.text_seasoned: Darkness forces upward growth and builds stem length. The stretch is intentional and desirable.
If shoots are very pale or yellow after 5+ days, they have been in blackout too long. Move to light immediately.

light.text_seasoned: Bottom watering prevents mold, which is the main challenge with microgreens. Set the tray in water for 10-15 minutes rather than misting the surface.
Harvest in the morning when the plants are full of water. Cut, rinse immediately, and use within a day or two.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One tray yields 50-200g depending on variety and tray size
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Ready in 7-14 days -- the fastest crop you can grow
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Microgreens are instant gratification -- from seed to harvest in under two weeks. Perfect for getting children interested in growing.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White fuzzy mold on the surface
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Surface mold is caused by overwatering or poor airflow. It is different from the white root hairs that are completely normal and healthy -- root hairs are orderly and attached to stems, mold is fuzzy and appears on the soil surface.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water from below by setting the tray in water -- never mist the surface once seeds have germinated. Ensure good airflow around the tray.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings fell over at the base
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Damping off is a fungal condition that rots the stem at soil level. It is caused by overwet, poorly ventilated conditions -- especially in the blackout phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Do not overwater during germination. Ensure the growing medium is moist but not wet before sowing. Improve airflow once seedlings emerge.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Patchy germination is usually caused by uneven seed contact with the growing medium, or the surface drying out during germination. Larger seeds like sunflower and peas benefit from pre-soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Press seeds firmly into the surface after sowing. Soak larger seeds for 8 hours before sowing. Ensure the medium is thoroughly moist before you start.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Microgreens kept in blackout for too long become etiolated -- pale, stretched, and weak. Once moved to light they should green up within hours. If they do not, they have been in darkness too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Move to light as soon as shoots are pressing against the blackout cover -- usually day 3-5. They green up fast once in light. Do not wait until they look fully grown under the dome.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Wilted or crispy after moving to light
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: Start new trays weekly for continuous harvest. Rinse and drain seeds before sowing for even germination. Harvest at first true leaf stage -- clip above the soil line with clean scissors.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow a new tray every 1-2 weeks year-round indoors. Microgreens are harvested once -- cut the whole tray at the soil line when the first true leaves appear. This is pure succession growing: sow, harvest in 7-14 days, start the next tray. Keep 2-3 trays at different stages so you're never waiting. Used potting mix can go straight into the compost or outdoor beds.

recommended: Black Oil Sunflower (standard, most widely used)
varieties.note_seasoned: Black oil sunflower seed is the standard for sprouts -- small seed, high germination, classic flavor.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow seeds densely on damp growing medium (coco coir, hemp mat, or potting mix). No soil preparation needed -- use trays specifically for microgreens.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Microgreens are always grown in shallow trays indoors -- a 10×20 inch propagation tray is standard. No minimum gallon requirement.
