pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small flies hovering around substrate. Larvae damage mycelium and fruit bodies.
pests.cause_seasoned: Bradysia species. Attracted to damp organic substrate.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Yellow sticky traps. Reduce surface moisture. Apply beneficial nematodes to substrate.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Maintain good air exchange. Avoid overwatering substrate.

diseases.name: Green mold (Trichoderma)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Green patches on substrate or growing medium. Indicates contamination.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Trichoderma fungal contamination. Outcompetes mushroom mycelium.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Remove contaminated blocks. Sterilize equipment.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Proper substrate sterilization. Clean inoculation technique. Adequate air circulation.

watering.amount_seasoned: Keep casing moist but not wet -- a light white sheen on surface
watering.method_seasoned: Fine mist on casing layer surface only -- never soak through to mycelium
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Bacterial blotch, wet rot at base of pins
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: No pinning, dried cracked casing layer

storage.freezer_seasoned: Sauté first, then freeze -- good for cooking
storage.notes_seasoned: Never store in plastic. The supermarket plastic packaging is poor -- transfer to paper immediately.

varieties.note_seasoned: White button, crimini, and portobello are all the same species (Agaricus bisporus) at different stages of maturity.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Mushrooms are not grown from seed -- purchase grain spawn or a ready-to-fruit kit. Kits are the easiest starting point for beginners.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Mushrooms are grown indoors in substrate bags, buckets, or logs -- not in conventional containers. A 5-gallon bucket with drainage holes works well as a fruiting vessel.

rotation.family: Fungi (not a plant crop -- rotation does not apply)
rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A
rotation.note_seasoned: Mushroom cultivation is substrate-based and does not follow crop rotation rules.

growth_stages.name: Inoculation
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Kit or substrate set up. Nothing visible yet.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Keep at the temperature specified for your variety -- this is the most critical variable. Keep away from direct sunlight and drafts.

growth_stages.name: Colonization
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: White fuzzy mycelium spreading through the substrate. Healthy mycelium smells earthy and mushroomy -- not sour, not sweet.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Do not disturb. Maintain temperature and humidity. Contamination (green or black patches) means mold -- remove the affected area or start again.

growth_stages.name: Pinning
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Tiny pinheads forming -- small bumps or pin-sized mushrooms appearing at the surface.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Introduce fresh air exchange -- open the bag or kit twice daily. Maintain humidity at 85-95%. Pinning is triggered by the combination of high humidity and fresh air.

growth_stages.name: Fruiting
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Mushrooms growing fast -- oysters can double in size overnight at peak growth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Mist the growing surface 2-3 times daily to maintain humidity. Harvest before the caps fully flatten -- the edges should still be slightly curled under.

growth_stages.name: Second Flush
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: After harvesting the first flush, the substrate rests before a second flush of pins appears.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: After first harvest, soak the substrate in cold water for 12-24 hours to rehydrate, then return to fruiting conditions. A second and sometimes third flush follows.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: Rest period done -- seeing new pins?

notifications.title_seasoned: Mushroom kit set up -- now wait
notifications.body_seasoned: The mycelium is doing its work in the dark. Keep at the right temperature and resist the urge to open or disturb the kit. You should see white fuzzy growth spreading within a week. If you smell anything unpleasant or see colored patches, something has gone wrong.

notifications.title_seasoned: Introduce fresh air to trigger pinning
notifications.body_seasoned: Mushrooms pin when they sense high humidity and fresh air together. Open the kit or bag twice daily for fresh air exchange. Mist the surface to keep humidity high. The contrast between CO2 buildup and the fresh air burst triggers pin formation.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your mushrooms for harvest readiness
notifications.body_seasoned: Harvest just before the caps fully flatten -- the edges should still be slightly curled under. Oysters especially go from perfect to overripe fast. Twist and pull, or cut at the base. Do not leave overripe mushrooms -- they signal the substrate to stop producing.

notifications.title_seasoned: Soak substrate for second flush
notifications.body_seasoned: After your first harvest, soak the substrate in cold water for 12-24 hours to rehydrate it. Wring out excess moisture, return to fruiting conditions, and watch for a second flush within 1-2 weeks. Most substrates give 2-3 flushes before exhausted.

inoculation.text_seasoned: Temperature is everything for mushrooms. Check your specific variety -- oysters like 65-75°F, shiitake 60-75°F, lion's mane 65-75°F. Even a few degrees outside the range slows or stops growth.
Contamination prevention starts at setup. Clean hands, clean surfaces, work quickly when the substrate is exposed.

colonization.text_seasoned: Healthy mycelium is always white and smells of fresh mushrooms. Any other color -- green, black, pink -- is contamination and needs to be addressed immediately.
Patience during colonization is hard but essential. Opening the kit repeatedly introduces contamination risk. Check once a day at most.

pinning.text_seasoned: Fresh air exchange is what triggers pinning. Twice daily is ideal -- open the kit, fan it briefly with your hand, mist the surface, close it again.
A humidity tent (a plastic bag with holes) over your kit helps maintain the humidity needed for pinning. Mist the inside of the tent rather than the substrate directly.

fruiting.text_seasoned: Oyster mushrooms especially grow remarkably fast at peak -- check daily and harvest promptly. They go from perfect to overripe in 24-48 hours.
Harvest by twisting at the base rather than cutting where possible -- it removes the stub that would otherwise rot and contaminate the next flush.

second_flush.text_seasoned: A good substrate gives 2-3 flushes. Second flushes are often smaller than the first but still worth having.
An exhausted substrate that grows no more mushrooms can be broken up and used as excellent garden compost -- it is rich in mycelium and nutrients.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: 200-400g per flush from a tray
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Button mushrooms require more precise conditions than oysters but are very productive when happy
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Button mushrooms need a casing layer of peat or coir after colonization -- an extra step that makes all the difference.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Green, black, or pink mold appeared
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Contamination -- usually Trichoderma (green mold) or Neurospora (pink) -- means competing fungi got established before the mushroom mycelium could colonize the substrate. This usually happens because of poor sterilization, exposure to air during inoculation, or too high a temperature.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Work cleanly and quickly when the substrate is exposed. Keep temperature in the right range -- too warm invites contamination. Start fresh with a new kit or properly sterilized substrate.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Mycelium grew but no mushrooms appeared
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Mushrooms pin in response to high humidity and fresh air. If the substrate was fully colonized but no pins appeared, the fruiting conditions were not right -- usually insufficient fresh air exchange or humidity too low.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Open the kit or bag twice daily for fresh air exchange and mist the surface to maintain 85-95% humidity. The contrast between CO2 buildup and fresh air is what triggers pinning.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Substrate was too wet or soggy
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Overwet substrate prevents oxygen reaching the mycelium and creates ideal conditions for bacterial contamination. It can look and smell unpleasant and the mycelium will not grow through it.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Field capacity is the target moisture level -- squeeze a handful of substrate and only a few drops should come out. Wetter than this is too wet.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: A dried-out substrate stalls colonization and prevents fruiting. Oyster mushrooms especially need consistent humidity -- if the substrate cracks or feels dry, production stops.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Mist the growing surface 2-3 times daily during fruiting. Between flushes, soak the substrate in cold water for 12-24 hours to rehydrate it.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Temperature outside the optimal range for your variety significantly slows or stops growth. Too warm and contamination risk increases dramatically. Too cool and mycelium growth stalls.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Check the specific temperature requirement for your variety and monitor with a thermometer. A consistent environment is more important than the perfect temperature.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: Classic supermarket mushroom. Grown on composted manure substrate. Requires darkness and consistent humidity. Kit-based growing is most reliable for home growers.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Prepare new trays or beds every 3 weeks. Button mushrooms (Agaricus bisporus) produce 3-4 flushes over 6-8 weeks per tray. Each flush is smaller than the last. A new tray started every 3 weeks means you have one tray in peak production, one mid-cycle, and one just starting -- continuous harvests from a small setup. Button mushrooms need a casing layer (peat moss or coco coir) applied after colonization to trigger fruiting.

crops.description_seasoned: The world's most popular mushroom, and trickier than it looks. Button mushrooms need a specific composted manure substrate and a casing layer of peat moss. Rewarding once you get the setup right.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest at button stage (closed veil under cap) or slightly open. Twist and pull cleanly. Don't wait until fully open -- flavor peaks at the button stage.
crops.substrate_notes_seasoned: Most temperature-sensitive common mushroom -- needs consistent 55-65°F. Requires casing layer (peat moss + lime) over colonized substrate to trigger pinning.

crops.name: Marigold
crops.tip_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowers regularly to keep marigolds blooming all season. French marigolds (Tagetes patula) are more effective at deterring soil nematodes than African varieties.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Too much fertilizer produces lush foliage and fewer flowers. Plant in average to poor soil for best bloom.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Light feed time for your marigolds
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 10-10-10 -- avoid high N which reduces flowering

direct_sow.label: primary
direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Warm-season annual flowers are direct-sown or transplanted after last frost when soil has warmed. These are frost-tender and die at first hard freeze. Most bloom continuously through summer until frost; typical recommendation is to plant 7 to 14 days after last frost. (UMN Extension Annual Flowers; Cornell Extension; Iowa State Extension)

harvest_start.label: primary
harvest_start.synthesis_note_seasoned: Cut flowers or harvest edible petals as they open. For continuous bloom, deadhead spent flowers regularly. Perennial flowers should not be hard-harvested in their establishment year. (UMN Extension; Cornell Extension; UGA Vegetable Garden Calendar)

harvest_end.label: primary
harvest_end.synthesis_note_seasoned: Warm-season annual flowers are killed by first frost. Cut flowers before frost for last bouquets. (UMN Extension Annual Flowers; Iowa State Extension)

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 5-7 days -- drought tolerant once established
watering.method_seasoned: At soil level -- wet petals cause botrytis
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellow leaves, root rot, gray mold on flowers

storage.freezer_seasoned: N/A
storage.notes_seasoned: Dry petals on a screen for 1-2 weeks for use in teas, salads, and cooking. Dried petals store in an airtight jar.

recommended: Lemon Gem (signet type, edible, strongly scented)
varieties.note_seasoned: Lemon Gem is the best pest-deterrent marigold -- the strongest scent of all marigolds, edible flowers, and very prolific.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Tomatoes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Classic pairing -- marigolds deter whitefly and nematodes near tomatoes

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Iowa State University Extension's 'Growing Marigolds in the Home Garden' page documents that French marigolds release alpha-terthienyl which suppresses root-knot nematodes. Oklahoma State University Extension confirms the mechanism but notes that reduction occurs only in the marigold's immediate root zone. Extension consensus (ISU, UF/IFAS ENY-056, UH CTAHR PD-35, NC State, Mississippi State) is that marigolds work best as a dense cover crop for 2+ months BEFORE the vegetable crop, not as concurrent interplanting. The nematode component is extension-documented. The claim's additional assertions about deterring whiteflies are not supported in the extension literature on marigolds and should be read as traditional.

provenance.label: traditional
provenance.reason: Pest-deterrent claim without matching established pattern. Default to traditional pending review.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct sown after last frost. Many also benefit from indoor starting 6-8 weeks early for earlier blooms.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers grow well in containers. Use any pot with good drainage -- window boxes and hanging baskets work well.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: None -- marigolds improve soil wherever they grow
rotation.good_after: Excellent before any vegetable crop -- their roots suppress nematodes in soil for the following season
rotation.note_seasoned: Marigolds are beneficial anywhere in the garden. The nematode-suppressing effect of French marigolds (Tagetes patula) persists in the soil after plants are dug in at season end.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct-sown after the last frost when soil is reliably above 60 degrees, or started indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for an earlier display. Calendula, nasturtium, and sweet alyssum tolerate cooler soil and can go in earlier.

Sow shallowly -- twice the seed's diameter is the standard rule. Annual flower seeds are mostly small to medium and a 1/4 inch covering is plenty. Keep soil surface consistently moist for the 5 to 14 day germination window.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves. Crowded annual flowers grow leggy and bloom poorly. Many of these (calendula, nasturtium, borage) self-seed for next year if you let some flowers go to seed.
Pinch growing tips on cosmos, marigold, and zinnia at 4 to 6 inches tall to encourage branching. Pinched plants produce more flowers on stronger stems than unpinched plants.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently through establishment. Once flowering begins, most annual flowers are moderately drought-tolerant -- nasturtium especially flowers more in lean conditions and stops flowering when over-fertilized.
Side-dress lightly with compost mid-season for the heaviest bloomers (zinnia, cosmos). Skip fertilizer entirely for nasturtium and borage, which produce more leaves than flowers when fed.

budding.text_seasoned: Buds form fast on warm-season annuals once plants are established -- expect first buds 4 to 8 weeks after sowing depending on variety. The bud stage is short.
Watch for early signs of aphids on flower buds (especially calendula and nasturtium). Hose them off or wait for ladybugs; rarely worth spraying.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom. Annual flowers that go to seed stop producing new flowers -- the plant's job is done once seed is set. Regular deadheading can extend bloom by weeks or months.
Cut flowers for the vase regularly -- it counts as deadheading and most of these annuals (zinnia, cosmos, calendula) make excellent cut flowers. Cut in the morning when stems are turgid.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To save seed, let some flowers go fully to seed at the end of the season -- the petals fall and the seed head dries on the plant. Collect seed when fully dry and brown; store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place.

Many annual flowers (especially calendula, nasturtium, borage, cosmos) self-seed enthusiastically. Letting a few mature seed heads scatter naturally often gives you a free crop next year -- though hybrid varieties may not come true from saved seed.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous blooms all season with regular deadheading
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Marigolds are among the most reliable and useful flowers in the garden -- beautiful and functional as pest deterrents.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, zinnias, and cosmos are tender-killed by even a light frost -- the plant collapses overnight and does not recover. Calendula, sweet alyssum, and borage tolerate light frost and will keep flowering through cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant after the last frost date for warm-season annuals; cover with frost cloth on unexpected late frost nights. For longer cool-weather color, choose calendula, sweet alyssum, and borage, which tolerate light frost at both ends of the season.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids cluster on tender new growth and flower buds (especially nasturtium, cosmos, calendula). Spider mites take hold in hot dry conditions. Powdery mildew shows up on cosmos, zinnia, and bee-balm in humid weather or where plants are crowded.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off aphids with a strong spray of water -- chemical control is rarely needed. Increase airflow with proper spacing and pinching to reduce mildew. For mites in dry weather, increase moisture and rinse foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Annual flowers stop producing new flowers once they set seed -- this is the natural endpoint of the annual life cycle. Without deadheading, plants devote all energy to ripening the existing seed heads rather than producing new flowers. Heat stress in midsummer also pauses bloom on cool-preferring annuals (calendula, sweet alyssum) until cooler weather returns.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Deadhead regularly through the season -- a few minutes every few days extends bloom by weeks or months. For cool-preferring annuals, allow a midsummer pause and expect renewed bloom in early fall as temperatures drop.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress causes most annual flowers to wilt during the heat of the day, with leaves recovering at night when first stressed but eventually staying wilted as drought deepens. Flowers fail to open or open small. Severe drought ends the bloom cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target for most annual flowers. Mulch to retain moisture. Nasturtium and calendula handle drier conditions than zinnia or cosmos; choose accordingly for low-water gardens.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most annual flowers need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to bloom heavily. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy, and produce fewer flowers. Some (calendula, sweet alyssum, nasturtium) tolerate part-day shade better than others.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site annual flowers in full sun. For partly shaded spots, choose shade-tolerant annuals (impatiens, begonias, coleus) rather than fighting nature with sun-loving zinnias or cosmos.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 3 weeks from last frost through midsummer for continuous bloom and continuous pest protection in the garden. Marigolds start blooming 8-10 weeks from seed and continue until frost -- so one sowing does go a long way. But succession plantings keep fresh, vigorous plants coming in alongside companion crops planted later in the season. Deadhead earlier sowings to extend their bloom while newer plants establish.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Staggered sowings extend bloom season and replace spent plants.

crops.description_seasoned: The ultimate companion flower. French and African varieties deter nematodes, whitefly, and aphids while attracting beneficial insects. Blooms continuously from summer through frost.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowers regularly by pinching off the entire flower head. For drying: harvest when fully open, dry face-down in a warm airy place. For pest deterrent purposes, keep blooming all season.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Pinch or snip spent flower heads off at the base. Do this every few days -- deadheading marigolds extends blooming by weeks. Allow a few flowers to go to seed at the end of the season to collect seeds for next year.

crops.name: Nasturtium
crops.tip_seasoned: Do not fertilize nasturtiums -- too much nitrogen produces all leaves and few flowers. Plant in poor soil for best blooms. The peppery leaves and flowers are excellent in salads.

fertilizer.example_product: Skip feeding or use compost only
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Nasturtiums thrive in poor soil. Fertilizing produces leafy growth with very few flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: nasturtiums flower best in poor soil -- fertilizer reduces blooms

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Brassicas
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Trap crop for aphids and caterpillars

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines; UConn IPM). Nasturtiums are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and USU Extension. Protocol caveats: UConn IPM notes that trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents.' Caterpillar deterrence (cabbage looper, imported cabbageworm) on brassicas is in secondary gardening literature but not specifically in the extension trap-cropping publications reviewed; the extension-recommended brassica trap crops for lepidopteran pests are collards (DBM) and radishes (flea beetles), not nasturtiums.

provenance.label: extension_backed
provenance.reason: Trap cropping is an extension-documented IPM tactic (Cornell Cooperative Extension 2022 and 2025 Integrated Crop and Pest Management Guidelines for Vegetable Crops; UConn IPM 'Perimeter Trap Cropping for Cole Crops'). Nasturtiums specifically are named as an aphid and flea-beetle trap crop by WSU Skagit County Extension Master Gardeners (Wolfe, 2020) and Utah State University Extension (Mohr et al., 'Creating Sustainable School and Home Gardens: Companion Planting'). Protocol caveat: UConn IPM explicitly notes trap cropping 'works best for insects of intermediate mobility rather than those, like aphids, passively dispersed by air currents' -- so the aphid application here has a protocol-mismatch concern even though the companion is extension-named. The Cornell-IPM-specific attribution in earlier catalog reason text was not located in Cornell's published IPM material; actual backing is WSU/USU/UConn.

provenance.reason: 'Fennel suppresses neighbors' is a common gardening-book claim. Limited research; allelopathy is real but specific claim pattern is traditional.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 7-10 days -- nasturtiums actually flower better in lean, dry conditions
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Yellow leaves, fewer flowers, more foliage

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze flowers in ice cubes for drinks -- decorative
storage.notes_seasoned: Best eaten fresh. Flowers and seeds can be pickled in vinegar (capers substitute).

recommended: Empress of India (dark foliage, scarlet flowers)
varieties.note_seasoned: Alaska has stunning variegated foliage -- attractive even when not in bloom. Equally useful as pest trap crop.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct sown after last frost. Many also benefit from indoor starting 6-8 weeks early for earlier blooms.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers grow well in containers. Use any pot with good drainage -- window boxes and hanging baskets work well.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: None
rotation.good_after: Anywhere -- nasturtiums self-seed and improve wherever they grow
rotation.note_seasoned: Nasturtiums self-seed freely -- allow them to find their own spot. They work as trap crops for aphids in any location.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct-sown after the last frost when soil is reliably above 60 degrees, or started indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for an earlier display. Calendula, nasturtium, and sweet alyssum tolerate cooler soil and can go in earlier.

Sow shallowly -- twice the seed's diameter is the standard rule. Annual flower seeds are mostly small to medium and a 1/4 inch covering is plenty. Keep soil surface consistently moist for the 5 to 14 day germination window.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves. Crowded annual flowers grow leggy and bloom poorly. Many of these (calendula, nasturtium, borage) self-seed for next year if you let some flowers go to seed.
Pinch growing tips on cosmos, marigold, and zinnia at 4 to 6 inches tall to encourage branching. Pinched plants produce more flowers on stronger stems than unpinched plants.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently through establishment. Once flowering begins, most annual flowers are moderately drought-tolerant -- nasturtium especially flowers more in lean conditions and stops flowering when over-fertilized.
Side-dress lightly with compost mid-season for the heaviest bloomers (zinnia, cosmos). Skip fertilizer entirely for nasturtium and borage, which produce more leaves than flowers when fed.

budding.text_seasoned: Buds form fast on warm-season annuals once plants are established -- expect first buds 4 to 8 weeks after sowing depending on variety. The bud stage is short.
Watch for early signs of aphids on flower buds (especially calendula and nasturtium). Hose them off or wait for ladybugs; rarely worth spraying.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom. Annual flowers that go to seed stop producing new flowers -- the plant's job is done once seed is set. Regular deadheading can extend bloom by weeks or months.
Cut flowers for the vase regularly -- it counts as deadheading and most of these annuals (zinnia, cosmos, calendula) make excellent cut flowers. Cut in the morning when stems are turgid.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To save seed, let some flowers go fully to seed at the end of the season -- the petals fall and the seed head dries on the plant. Collect seed when fully dry and brown; store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place.

Many annual flowers (especially calendula, nasturtium, borage, cosmos) self-seed enthusiastically. Letting a few mature seed heads scatter naturally often gives you a free crop next year -- though hybrid varieties may not come true from saved seed.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Hundreds of flowers and leaves throughout the season
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Every part of the nasturtium is edible -- flowers, leaves, and the green seeds pickled as capers. One of the most useful garden plants.
factors_seasoned: poor soil produces more flowers than rich soil

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, zinnias, and cosmos are tender-killed by even a light frost -- the plant collapses overnight and does not recover. Calendula, sweet alyssum, and borage tolerate light frost and will keep flowering through cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant after the last frost date for warm-season annuals; cover with frost cloth on unexpected late frost nights. For longer cool-weather color, choose calendula, sweet alyssum, and borage, which tolerate light frost at both ends of the season.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids cluster on tender new growth and flower buds (especially nasturtium, cosmos, calendula). Spider mites take hold in hot dry conditions. Powdery mildew shows up on cosmos, zinnia, and bee-balm in humid weather or where plants are crowded.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off aphids with a strong spray of water -- chemical control is rarely needed. Increase airflow with proper spacing and pinching to reduce mildew. For mites in dry weather, increase moisture and rinse foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Annual flowers stop producing new flowers once they set seed -- this is the natural endpoint of the annual life cycle. Without deadheading, plants devote all energy to ripening the existing seed heads rather than producing new flowers. Heat stress in midsummer also pauses bloom on cool-preferring annuals (calendula, sweet alyssum) until cooler weather returns.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Deadhead regularly through the season -- a few minutes every few days extends bloom by weeks or months. For cool-preferring annuals, allow a midsummer pause and expect renewed bloom in early fall as temperatures drop.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress causes most annual flowers to wilt during the heat of the day, with leaves recovering at night when first stressed but eventually staying wilted as drought deepens. Flowers fail to open or open small. Severe drought ends the bloom cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target for most annual flowers. Mulch to retain moisture. Nasturtium and calendula handle drier conditions than zinnia or cosmos; choose accordingly for low-water gardens.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most annual flowers need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to bloom heavily. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy, and produce fewer flowers. Some (calendula, sweet alyssum, nasturtium) tolerate part-day shade better than others.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site annual flowers in full sun. For partly shaded spots, choose shade-tolerant annuals (impatiens, begonias, coleus) rather than fighting nature with sun-loving zinnias or cosmos.

harvest_end.label: primary

crops.description_seasoned: Fully edible -- flowers, leaves, and seeds. Acts as a trap crop for aphids, drawing them away from vegetables. Self-seeds prolifically and thrives on neglect.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick flowers and young leaves at any time -- the more you pick, the more they produce. Flowers are best in the morning. Young round leaves are mildest; older leaves are more peppery.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadheading is optional -- nasturtiums self-seed prolifically if allowed to set seed. If you want continuous flowers rather than seeds, remove spent blooms. Edible seed pods can be pickled as a caper substitute.

crops.name: Lavender
crops.tip_seasoned: Harvest lavender when about one-third of the buds on a spike have opened -- this is when fragrance and oil content are highest. Cut stems back by about one-third after bloom to encourage a second flush.

fertilizer.example_product: Espoma Rose-Tone (half rate) or skip entirely
fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Lavender is a Mediterranean plant that prefers lean soil. Over-feeding produces lush, disease-prone growth with fewer flowers.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: low N -- poor soil improves oil content and fragrance

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Hardy perennial flowers (Lavender, Echinacea, Bee Balm) are established by planting nursery transplants or divisions in spring. Once established, they return each year from the crown. Lavender is hardy in Z5-Z9; Echinacea and Bee Balm in Z3-Z9. (UMN, Cornell)

pests.symptoms_seasoned: Metallic green-and-purple striped beetles eating foliage and flowers. Larvae and adults both feed.
pests.cause_seasoned: Chrysolina americana. Affects lavender, rosemary, sage, thyme.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Hand-pick adults and larvae. Shake plants over a sheet and collect. Pyrethrum spray.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Check plants regularly autumn to spring. Remove in winter.

diseases.name: Root rot / Phytophthora
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Plant wilts and dies despite dry conditions. Stems turn brown at base. Common in heavy clay soils or overwatered plants.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phytophthora root rot from waterlogged conditions. Lavender is drought-tolerant and cannot tolerate wet roots.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: No cure. Remove plant.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Well-drained soil is essential. Never overwater. Add grit if soil is heavy. Raise beds if necessary.

diseases.name: Shab (Phomopsis)
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Gray-brown die-back of shoots from tips. Spreading dieback into woody stems. Worst after wet winters.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Phomopsis fungus. Enters through wounds or cold damage.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Cut out all dead wood to healthy green growth. Sterilize tools between cuts.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Annual pruning prevents old woody growth that is more susceptible. Good drainage.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Every 10-14 days once established -- very drought tolerant
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Root rot -- the most common lavender killer

start_method.notes_seasoned: Buy established plants -- lavender from seed is very slow and variable. Harden off over 7 days. Plant in final position -- hates being moved.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Excellent container plant -- terracotta pots ideal as they breathe and drain. 5-gallon minimum. Good drainage is critical; never let roots sit in water. Overwinter indoors in zones below 6. Repot every 2-3 years.

varieties.note_seasoned: Phenomenal is the best choice for humid climates -- more disease tolerant than English lavenders.

storage.freezer_seasoned: N/A
storage.notes_seasoned: Dry cut stems by hanging upside down in a warm airy place for 2-3 weeks. Dried lavender keeps its fragrance for 1-2 years.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Lavender is a permanent planting. Choose the site carefully -- it dislikes being moved. Replace with a new plant after 5-7 years when it becomes woody.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Most perennial flowers can be started from seed but establish slowly -- expect to plant in year one and bloom in year two. Many gardeners buy young plants instead of starting from seed.

If sowing from seed, several of these crops benefit from cold stratification (4 to 6 weeks of cold moist treatment in the refrigerator) before sowing -- echinacea and lavender especially. Direct-sown seed in late fall accomplishes the same thing naturally.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or transplant seedlings to recommended spacing once they have 4 to 6 true leaves. Perennials need their permanent home from the start -- moving them later disrupts establishment.
Mulch around young transplants to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the plant for the first season.

established.text_seasoned: Year one is mostly about root development -- many perennials produce minimal foliage and few flowers in the first season. This is normal; resist the urge to give up on a slow-establishing perennial.

By year two most of these perennials hit their stride and begin producing the heavy bloom you planted them for. Echinacea and bee-balm especially become more impressive each year for the first 4 to 5 seasons.

budding.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single annual bloom window -- echinacea midsummer, lavender early-to-mid summer, bee-balm midsummer, viola spring and fall, chamomile early summer. Buds form weeks before bloom.
Watch lavender for spittlebug at bud stage -- the white foam on stems is unsightly but harmless and rarely needs intervention.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadheading extends bloom marginally on most perennials but does not transform their cycle the way it does for annuals -- a perennial generally has one main bloom window per year regardless of deadheading. Deadhead for tidiness rather than to chase a second bloom.

Many perennials attract specific pollinators -- echinacea and bee-balm are bumblebee and hummingbird favorites; lavender draws honey bees in numbers; viola attracts solitary bees. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials self-seed if you leave seed heads to mature. Echinacea seed heads are particularly attractive to goldfinches and other birds -- leaving them standing through fall is good wildlife support.

To save seed deliberately, collect dried seed heads on a dry day, separate seeds from chaff, and store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place. Most perennial flower seeds need cold stratification before they will germinate; a winter outdoors or in the refrigerator does this.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Generous harvest of flower spikes from established plants
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Lavender takes 2-3 years to reach its potential but rewards patience with decades of fragrant blooms.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These perennials are hardy through their respective USDA zones -- echinacea zones 3-8, bee-balm zones 4-9, lavender zones 5-9 (varies by species; English lavender is hardier than Spanish), viola zones 3-8, chamomile (Roman) zones 3-7. Hard winter cold below the variety's range causes crown damage and may kill the plant entirely.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range before relying on it as a perennial -- some plants sold as perennials are actually annuals or short-lived perennials in cold zones. Mulch crowns in the colder end of the variety's range. For lavender in zones 5-6, choose hardy English lavender (L. angustifolia) and plant on the south side of a wall.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew is the most common problem on bee-balm and to a lesser extent echinacea -- both develop white powdery patches on leaves in humid summers or where plants are crowded. Aster yellows is a viral disease that distorts echinacea flowers. Lavender suffers root rot in poorly-drained soil rather than insect pests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose mildew-resistant bee-balm varieties (Marshall's Delight, Jacob Cline) and space generously for airflow. Remove and destroy plants showing aster yellows -- it spreads via leafhoppers and infected plants do not recover. For lavender, drainage prevention is better than disease cure.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single bloom window per year and then move on -- this is not a failure but the plant's normal cycle. After the main bloom, leaves stay green for the rest of the season but no new flowers come. Deadheading extends bloom marginally; in some cases (viola) it can produce a second smaller bloom in fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plan plantings with succession in mind so something different is blooming each month rather than expecting any single perennial to bloom continuously. Allow some seed heads to remain for wildlife and self-seeding.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lavender prefers dry conditions and is harmed by frequent watering -- drought is rarely lavender's problem. Bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile prefer consistent moisture and stress under drought, with leaf wilting and reduced bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile during dry spells -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Lavender needs water only during establishment and prolonged drought; once established it actively resents regular watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials prefer full sun. Lavender requires 6 to 8 hours of direct sun and grows poorly in any shade. Echinacea and bee-balm tolerate light afternoon shade. Viola actively prefers part shade in hot summers and may stop blooming in full sun once temperatures climb.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match the variety to the available light. For shaded perennial-flower spots, viola is the most cooperative; for full sun, lavender, echinacea, and bee-balm all thrive.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Perennial -- plant once and enjoy for many years. Divide every 3-4 years to maintain vigor.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Perennial herb that returns each year. No succession planting needed.

crops.description_seasoned: Drought-tolerant perennial that earns its place in any food garden. Attracts pollinators, deters deer, and produces fragrant flowers for cooking, tea, sachets, and more.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: For fresh use, cut just as flowers open. For drying, cut when 1/4 of flowers on spike are open.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: English lavender (Lavandula angustifolia) reliably perennial Z5-Z9. French (L. stoechas) and Spanish (L. dentata) lavenders are Z7-Z9. Needs excellent drainage; wet winter soil kills lavender faster than cold.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: Cut back lightly after first bloom. Do not expect a full harvest until year two when the plant is established.
crops.soil_prep_seasoned: Lavender demands extremely well-drained, low-fertility soil. Do not add compost or manure before planting -- lavender flowers best in lean, dry conditions. Add horticultural grit (20-30% by volume) if soil is heavy or clay. Raised beds or a slope are ideal. pH 6.5-7.5.

crops.name: Sunflower
crops.tip_seasoned: To harvest seeds, let the head dry on the plant until the back turns yellow-brown. Cut with 12 inches of stem and hang upside down in a paper bag to catch falling seeds. Cover with netting if birds are a problem.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Sunflowers are light feeders. Too much nitrogen produces leafy plants with small heads. One feeding at planting is usually sufficient.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: 10-10-10 -- avoid high N which delays flowering

direct_sow.synthesis_note_seasoned: Warm-season annual flowers are direct-sown or transplanted after last frost when soil has warmed. These are frost-tender and die at first hard freeze. Most bloom continuously through summer until frost; typical recommendation is to plant 7 to 14 days after last frost. (UMN Extension Annual Flowers; Cornell Extension; Iowa State Extension)

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

watering.method_seasoned: At soil level -- avoid wetting flowers

storage.room_temp_seasoned: 7-10 days in water as cut flower. Seeds: months in cool dry place
storage.freezer_seasoned: Seeds: freeze for longer storage
storage.notes_seasoned: Cut when 1-2 outer petals have opened. For seeds: dry the head fully on the plant, then hang in paper bag to finish drying.

varieties.note_seasoned: Lemon Queen is the best for pollinators -- multi-branching, produces dozens of flowers per plant over a long season.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct sown after last frost. Many also benefit from indoor starting 6-8 weeks early for earlier blooms.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers grow well in containers. Use any pot with good drainage -- window boxes and hanging baskets work well.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Potatoes -- sunflowers inhibit potato growth
rotation.good_after: Most crops -- sunflowers are light-feeding and leave soil in good condition
rotation.note_seasoned: Sunflowers have mild allelopathic effects on potatoes and some beans. Otherwise broadly compatible and beneficial anywhere.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Harvest
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: First disc florets opening on the outer edge of the head -- the window for cut flowers begins.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: For cut flowers, harvest when 1/2 to 3/4 of the disc florets are open. Cut in the morning with a long stem and place in water immediately for best vase life. If you're growing for seeds rather than cut flowers, leave the heads on the plant and see the Seed Saving stage.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

growth_stages.name: End of Season
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Stalks brown and brittle, heads drooping with seeds dispersed or harvested, frost imminent.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Cut down spent stalks and chop or shred before composting -- whole stalks take a long time to break down. Consider leaving a few standing through fall and winter as wildlife habitat; goldfinches and other birds will work through any remaining seed heads.
growth_stages.log_prompt_seasoned: How was your sunflower season? Worth logging what worked.

notifications.title_seasoned: Time to plant your sunflower
notifications.body_seasoned: Get your sunflower in the ground now. Prepare the soil well and water in after planting.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your sunflower for harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Your sunflower should be approaching harvest readiness now. Check the crop-specific signals and harvest at the right moment for best flavor.

notifications.title_seasoned: How is your sunflower doing?
notifications.body_seasoned: You have not logged anything in a while -- how is it looking?

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Sunflower is direct-sown after last frost when soil reaches 50 degrees minimum (60 is better). Sow 1 inch deep, 6 to 12 inches apart for small varieties or 18 to 24 inches apart for giant types.
Seedlings emerge in 7 to 14 days in warm soil. Sunflower seedlings are vulnerable to slugs, snails, and cutworms in their first weeks; check daily and protect with collars if needed.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves. Crowded sunflowers produce smaller heads and smaller seed; spacing matters even for ornamental plantings.
Stake tall varieties early -- once a sunflower is established, its taproot resents disturbance. A bamboo cane next to the seedling provides support that can be tied in as the plant grows.

established.text_seasoned: Sunflowers are heavy feeders. Side-dress with compost or balanced fertilizer mid-season for best growth. The plants tolerate moderate drought once established but produce best with consistent water.
Tall varieties (over 6 feet) need staking in windy sites -- a single strong storm can topple a mature sunflower. Tie loosely to allow some movement but prevent breakage.

budding.text_seasoned: Sunflowers form a single dominant bud at the top of the main stem (in single-bloom varieties) or multiple smaller buds along branching stems (in branching varieties). Most ornamental and seed-type sunflowers are single-bloom.
The bud-to-bloom transition is sensitive to water stress -- consistent water during this 2 to 3 week window produces fuller, more uniform heads.

flowering.text_seasoned: Sunflowers track the sun (heliotropism) when young, then fix east-facing once mature. The flowers attract pollinators heavily -- bees and butterflies in particular.
Bloom typically lasts 2 to 3 weeks per head. After bloom, the back of the head turns from green to yellow then brown as seeds ripen.

harvest.text_seasoned: For seed harvest, wait until the back of the head turns brown and dry -- usually 30 to 45 days after bloom. Cut the head with about 12 inches of stem and hang upside down in a dry place to finish curing.

Cover heads with paper bags or netting during ripening to protect from birds and squirrels -- both will strip a ripening head bare in days. Animal pressure is the leading cause of failed seed harvests.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Once heads are fully dry, rub the seed face to release seeds. Sort out empty hulls and debris. Properly dried sunflower seed stores in airtight containers for a year or more.

If saving seed for next year's planting, choose seeds from the most vigorous and best-formed heads. Most sunflower varieties are open-pollinated and come true from saved seed if isolated from other sunflower varieties during bloom.

end_of_season.text_seasoned: After harvest, cut spent stalks at ground level and chop into the compost. Sunflower stalks are large and woody; chopping speeds decomposition.

Sunflower roots are notably allelopathic -- they release chemicals into the soil that suppress some other plants. Do not follow sunflower with delicate seedlings; rotation to nitrogen-fixing legumes restores the bed well.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One large bloom per stem for most varieties; branching types produce multiple smaller blooms
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sunflowers are reliable and beginner-friendly. A single 8-foot Mammoth or a row of branching varieties both look spectacular.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sunflower seedlings are damaged by frost; established plants tolerate light frost but are killed by hard frost. Cold soil at sowing (below 50 degrees) significantly slows germination and may rot seeds.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Wait to direct-sow until soil reaches 50 degrees minimum (60 is better) and last frost has passed. For early bloom, start transplants indoors 3 to 4 weeks before last frost (use peat pots to minimize root disturbance -- sunflower has a sensitive taproot). In short-season zones, choose shorter-season varieties to ensure seed harvest before fall frost.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Birds and squirrels strip ripening seed heads -- the leading cause of failed seed harvests. Slugs and cutworms damage seedlings. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Sunflower head moth larvae feed on developing seeds. Powdery mildew, downy mildew, and rust appear in humid summers but rarely seriously affect mature plants.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Cover ripening heads with paper bags or fine netting from the moment the back of the head starts to yellow -- this is the critical window for animal damage. Hose off aphids; protect seedlings with collars against cutworms. For powdery mildew, choose resistant varieties and water at the base.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sunflower has a deep taproot and tolerates drought well, but cannot survive waterlogged soil. Persistent saturation causes root rot and stunted growth. Heavy rain on tall plants in soft soil can cause toppling even without disease.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant in well-drained soil. Stake tall varieties early to prevent toppling. Water deeply but infrequently; once established, sunflowers do well with weekly deep watering. Avoid overhead watering that can spread fungal disease.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress during budding and bloom produces smaller heads with fewer or smaller seeds. Sunflower tolerates drought better than most annuals once established but produces best with consistent water during the bud-to-bloom transition and seed-fill window.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water deeply once a week, more during the budding and flowering window. Mulch heavily to retain soil moisture. The deep taproot makes mature sunflowers more drought-tolerant than shallow-rooted crops, but seed production drops noticeably with severe water stress.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sunflower needs full sun -- the name is not a coincidence. In partial shade, stalks grow weak and tall (etiolated) trying to reach light, heads are smaller, and stems may topple. Sunflower in deep shade simply will not produce a meaningful head.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun -- 8 hours minimum, ideally more. South-facing exposure is ideal. Avoid planting where larger plants will shade sunflowers as the season progresses; sunflowers themselves shade out other plants nearby and should be sited with that in mind.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 2 weeks from last frost through midsummer for a continuous display and staggered seed harvest. Each planting blooms for 2-3 weeks -- a single sowing gives a brief moment. Succession turns that moment into months. For cut flowers, pick when petals are just opening. For edible seeds, wait until the back of the head turns yellow-brown and petals have dropped. A late sowing in midsummer will still produce fully before first frost in most zones.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Individual plants bloom briefly. Staggered sowings provide continuous color and seed harvest.

crops.description_seasoned: Annual powerhouses that attract pollinators at scale. Edible seeds, excellent windbreak, and a beacon for birds in the autumn garden. Dwarf varieties work well in smaller gardens.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: For seeds: harvest when back of head turns brown and seeds are plump -- usually 30-45 days after flowering. For cutting: harvest when just 1-2 rows of petals are open, early morning.

crops.name: Borage
crops.tip_seasoned: Borage self-seeds very freely. Allow a few plants to go to seed each year and you will always have borage. Use young leaves in cooking -- mature leaves are quite rough in texture.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Borage grows best in average to poor soil. Fertilizing is unnecessary and may reduce flower production.
fertilizer.npk_hint_seasoned: borage needs no feeding -- it thrives in ordinary soil

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze flowers in ice cubes for drinks -- traditional use
storage.notes_seasoned: Borage flowers are very delicate. Use the same day or freeze in ice for drinks.

recommended: Common Blue Borage (standard, one primary variety)
varieties.note_seasoned: Borage has minimal commercial breeding -- standard blue is the most productive and useful for companion planting.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Strong bee attractor during strawberry bloom
