start_method.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct sown after last frost. Many also benefit from indoor starting 6-8 weeks early for earlier blooms.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers grow well in containers. Use any pot with good drainage -- window boxes and hanging baskets work well.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: None
rotation.good_after: Anywhere -- particularly useful at bed edges and near brassicas
rotation.note_seasoned: Sweet alyssum self-seeds freely. Use as a living mulch or bed-edge plant anywhere in rotation.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct-sown after the last frost when soil is reliably above 60 degrees, or started indoors 4 to 6 weeks before last frost for an earlier display. Calendula, nasturtium, and sweet alyssum tolerate cooler soil and can go in earlier.

Sow shallowly -- twice the seed's diameter is the standard rule. Annual flower seeds are mostly small to medium and a 1/4 inch covering is plenty. Keep soil surface consistently moist for the 5 to 14 day germination window.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing once seedlings have 2 true leaves. Crowded annual flowers grow leggy and bloom poorly. Many of these (calendula, nasturtium, borage) self-seed for next year if you let some flowers go to seed.
Pinch growing tips on cosmos, marigold, and zinnia at 4 to 6 inches tall to encourage branching. Pinched plants produce more flowers on stronger stems than unpinched plants.

established.text_seasoned: Water consistently through establishment. Once flowering begins, most annual flowers are moderately drought-tolerant -- nasturtium especially flowers more in lean conditions and stops flowering when over-fertilized.
Side-dress lightly with compost mid-season for the heaviest bloomers (zinnia, cosmos). Skip fertilizer entirely for nasturtium and borage, which produce more leaves than flowers when fed.

budding.text_seasoned: Buds form fast on warm-season annuals once plants are established -- expect first buds 4 to 8 weeks after sowing depending on variety. The bud stage is short.
Watch for early signs of aphids on flower buds (especially calendula and nasturtium). Hose them off or wait for ladybugs; rarely worth spraying.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowers to extend bloom. Annual flowers that go to seed stop producing new flowers -- the plant's job is done once seed is set. Regular deadheading can extend bloom by weeks or months.
Cut flowers for the vase regularly -- it counts as deadheading and most of these annuals (zinnia, cosmos, calendula) make excellent cut flowers. Cut in the morning when stems are turgid.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: To save seed, let some flowers go fully to seed at the end of the season -- the petals fall and the seed head dries on the plant. Collect seed when fully dry and brown; store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place.

Many annual flowers (especially calendula, nasturtium, borage, cosmos) self-seed enthusiastically. Letting a few mature seed heads scatter naturally often gives you a free crop next year -- though hybrid varieties may not come true from saved seed.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous blooms throughout the season with regular deadheading
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Flowers in the vegetable garden are one of the most worthwhile additions -- beautiful, functional, and good for pollinators.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, zinnias, and cosmos are tender-killed by even a light frost -- the plant collapses overnight and does not recover. Calendula, sweet alyssum, and borage tolerate light frost and will keep flowering through cool weather.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plant after the last frost date for warm-season annuals; cover with frost cloth on unexpected late frost nights. For longer cool-weather color, choose calendula, sweet alyssum, and borage, which tolerate light frost at both ends of the season.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Aphids cluster on tender new growth and flower buds (especially nasturtium, cosmos, calendula). Spider mites take hold in hot dry conditions. Powdery mildew shows up on cosmos, zinnia, and bee-balm in humid weather or where plants are crowded.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Hose off aphids with a strong spray of water -- chemical control is rarely needed. Increase airflow with proper spacing and pinching to reduce mildew. For mites in dry weather, increase moisture and rinse foliage.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Annual flowers stop producing new flowers once they set seed -- this is the natural endpoint of the annual life cycle. Without deadheading, plants devote all energy to ripening the existing seed heads rather than producing new flowers. Heat stress in midsummer also pauses bloom on cool-preferring annuals (calendula, sweet alyssum) until cooler weather returns.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Deadhead regularly through the season -- a few minutes every few days extends bloom by weeks or months. For cool-preferring annuals, allow a midsummer pause and expect renewed bloom in early fall as temperatures drop.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Drought stress causes most annual flowers to wilt during the heat of the day, with leaves recovering at night when first stressed but eventually staying wilted as drought deepens. Flowers fail to open or open small. Severe drought ends the bloom cycle.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week is the rough target for most annual flowers. Mulch to retain moisture. Nasturtium and calendula handle drier conditions than zinnia or cosmos; choose accordingly for low-water gardens.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most annual flowers need full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to bloom heavily. In partial shade plants stretch toward the light, become leggy, and produce fewer flowers. Some (calendula, sweet alyssum, nasturtium) tolerate part-day shade better than others.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site annual flowers in full sun. For partly shaded spots, choose shade-tolerant annuals (impatiens, begonias, coleus) rather than fighting nature with sun-loving zinnias or cosmos.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Sow every 4 weeks through the season for continuous groundcover and pollinator attraction. Alyssum shears back well -- cutting it hard after the first flush triggers a second bloom within 2-3 weeks. Succession planting combined with periodic shearing gives near-constant bloom. Particularly useful to stagger alongside companion vegetables planted at different times.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Multiple sowings maintain continuous coverage throughout the season.

crops.description_seasoned: Low-growing annual that forms a carpet of honey-scented flowers. Significantly increases beneficial insect populations, particularly hoverflies whose larvae eat aphids. Excellent as a living mulch between vegetables.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: No harvest per se -- deadhead clusters of spent blooms to promote continuous flowering. Plants self-sow readily -- allow some to go to seed for next year.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Shear back by about one-third when flowering slows in midsummer heat -- plants will resprout and flower again in autumn. No need to deadhead individual flowers.

crops.name: Echinacea
crops.tip_seasoned: Leave the seed heads standing through winter -- goldfinches and other seed-eating birds rely on them. Cut back to the ground in early spring. Division every 3-4 years keeps plants vigorous.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Light feeder. Over-fertilizing produces lush, floppy growth and reduces flowering. Annual top-dressing with compost is usually sufficient.

plant_out.label: primary
plant_out.synthesis_note_seasoned: Hardy perennial flowers (Lavender, Echinacea, Bee Balm) are established by planting nursery transplants or divisions in spring. Once established, they return each year from the crown. Lavender is hardy in Z5-Z9; Echinacea and Bee Balm in Z3-Z9. (UMN, Cornell)

tasks.description_seasoned: Deadhead spent flowers through summer to encourage reblooming. Leave some seedheads in fall for birds and self-seeding.
Divide clumps every 3-4 years in early spring or fall to maintain vigor.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Weekly once established -- very drought tolerant

storage.freezer_seasoned: N/A
storage.notes_seasoned: Medicinal use: dry whole flower heads and leaves for tea. Dry at low heat (95°F) to preserve medicinal properties.

varieties.note_seasoned: Magnus is the benchmark -- large, bright, reliable, and extremely attractive to pollinators.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Echinacea can be grown in large containers. 5-gallon minimum. Taproots go deep -- tall containers work better than wide shallow ones. May not overwinter well in containers in zones 4-5; mulch heavily or bring indoors.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Echinacea is a long-lived perennial. Divide clumps every 3-4 years to maintain vigor. Self-seeds freely -- allow some seed heads to remain for naturalizing.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Most perennial flowers can be started from seed but establish slowly -- expect to plant in year one and bloom in year two. Many gardeners buy young plants instead of starting from seed.

If sowing from seed, several of these crops benefit from cold stratification (4 to 6 weeks of cold moist treatment in the refrigerator) before sowing -- echinacea and lavender especially. Direct-sown seed in late fall accomplishes the same thing naturally.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or transplant seedlings to recommended spacing once they have 4 to 6 true leaves. Perennials need their permanent home from the start -- moving them later disrupts establishment.
Mulch around young transplants to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the plant for the first season.

established.text_seasoned: Year one is mostly about root development -- many perennials produce minimal foliage and few flowers in the first season. This is normal; resist the urge to give up on a slow-establishing perennial.

By year two most of these perennials hit their stride and begin producing the heavy bloom you planted them for. Echinacea and bee-balm especially become more impressive each year for the first 4 to 5 seasons.

budding.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single annual bloom window -- echinacea midsummer, lavender early-to-mid summer, bee-balm midsummer, viola spring and fall, chamomile early summer. Buds form weeks before bloom.
Watch lavender for spittlebug at bud stage -- the white foam on stems is unsightly but harmless and rarely needs intervention.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadheading extends bloom marginally on most perennials but does not transform their cycle the way it does for annuals -- a perennial generally has one main bloom window per year regardless of deadheading. Deadhead for tidiness rather than to chase a second bloom.

Many perennials attract specific pollinators -- echinacea and bee-balm are bumblebee and hummingbird favorites; lavender draws honey bees in numbers; viola attracts solitary bees. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials self-seed if you leave seed heads to mature. Echinacea seed heads are particularly attractive to goldfinches and other birds -- leaving them standing through fall is good wildlife support.

To save seed deliberately, collect dried seed heads on a dry day, separate seeds from chaff, and store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place. Most perennial flower seeds need cold stratification before they will germinate; a winter outdoors or in the refrigerator does this.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous blooms throughout the season with regular deadheading
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Flowers in the vegetable garden are one of the most worthwhile additions -- beautiful, functional, and good for pollinators.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These perennials are hardy through their respective USDA zones -- echinacea zones 3-8, bee-balm zones 4-9, lavender zones 5-9 (varies by species; English lavender is hardier than Spanish), viola zones 3-8, chamomile (Roman) zones 3-7. Hard winter cold below the variety's range causes crown damage and may kill the plant entirely.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range before relying on it as a perennial -- some plants sold as perennials are actually annuals or short-lived perennials in cold zones. Mulch crowns in the colder end of the variety's range. For lavender in zones 5-6, choose hardy English lavender (L. angustifolia) and plant on the south side of a wall.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew is the most common problem on bee-balm and to a lesser extent echinacea -- both develop white powdery patches on leaves in humid summers or where plants are crowded. Aster yellows is a viral disease that distorts echinacea flowers. Lavender suffers root rot in poorly-drained soil rather than insect pests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose mildew-resistant bee-balm varieties (Marshall's Delight, Jacob Cline) and space generously for airflow. Remove and destroy plants showing aster yellows -- it spreads via leafhoppers and infected plants do not recover. For lavender, drainage prevention is better than disease cure.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single bloom window per year and then move on -- this is not a failure but the plant's normal cycle. After the main bloom, leaves stay green for the rest of the season but no new flowers come. Deadheading extends bloom marginally; in some cases (viola) it can produce a second smaller bloom in fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plan plantings with succession in mind so something different is blooming each month rather than expecting any single perennial to bloom continuously. Allow some seed heads to remain for wildlife and self-seeding.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lavender prefers dry conditions and is harmed by frequent watering -- drought is rarely lavender's problem. Bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile prefer consistent moisture and stress under drought, with leaf wilting and reduced bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile during dry spells -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Lavender needs water only during establishment and prolonged drought; once established it actively resents regular watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials prefer full sun. Lavender requires 6 to 8 hours of direct sun and grows poorly in any shade. Echinacea and bee-balm tolerate light afternoon shade. Viola actively prefers part shade in hot summers and may stop blooming in full sun once temperatures climb.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match the variety to the available light. For shaded perennial-flower spots, viola is the most cooperative; for full sun, lavender, echinacea, and bee-balm all thrive.

crops.description_seasoned: Native North American perennial that blooms for 6-8 weeks in summer, attracting bees, butterflies, and goldfinches. Roots, leaves, and flowers are the source of echinacea supplements. Extremely drought tolerant once established.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: For fresh cutting: harvest when petals are fully open and slightly reflexed. For seeds: leave spent flower heads on plant through winter -- birds feed on them and seeds self-sow.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Coneflower, very hardy native perennial Z3-Z9. Self-seeds and spreads in favorable conditions.
crops.year_one_notes_seasoned: May not bloom in year one from seed. Allow full establishment before heavy harvest.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Light deadheading extends the blooming season. However, leave seed heads standing through winter -- birds (especially goldfinches) feed heavily on echinacea seeds. The dried seed heads are also architectural and attractive in winter.

crops.name: Bee Balm
crops.tip_seasoned: Bee balm blooms 90-120 days from seed -- but if you're buying a plant from a garden center (most people do), expect flowers in the first season. Divide clumps every 2-3 years to keep plants vigorous and prevent powdery mildew.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Moderate feeder. Annual spring application of compost or balanced fertilizer is sufficient.

tasks.description_seasoned: Cut back to ground level after frost. Bee balm spreads aggressively -- divide every 2-3 years to control and rejuvenate.
Divide every 2-3 years in spring to maintain vigor and control spread. Discard woody center, replant vigorous outer sections.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

watering.method_seasoned: At soil level -- overhead watering spreads powdery mildew

storage.freezer_seasoned: N/A
storage.notes_seasoned: Dry leaves and flowers for tea -- bergamot-like flavor. Hang bunches upside down in a warm airy room.

varieties.note_seasoned: Marshall's Delight is the most mildew-resistant variety -- important since powdery mildew is bee balm's biggest challenge.

good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Plant bee balm near squash -- it draws in bees that are essential for squash pollination

start_method.notes_seasoned: Buy as plants or start indoors 8-10 weeks before last frost. Harden off over 7 days before planting out.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Bee balm can be grown in large containers -- actually helpful since it contains its aggressive rhizome spread. 5-gallon minimum per plant. Repot every 2 years as it becomes root-bound quickly. Not suitable for window boxes or hanging baskets. Divide every 2-3 years to keep it vigorous.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A -- permanent planting
rotation.note_seasoned: Bee balm spreads via rhizomes and becomes a permanent feature. Divide every 2-3 years to prevent it taking over and to reduce powdery mildew pressure.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Most perennial flowers can be started from seed but establish slowly -- expect to plant in year one and bloom in year two. Many gardeners buy young plants instead of starting from seed.

If sowing from seed, several of these crops benefit from cold stratification (4 to 6 weeks of cold moist treatment in the refrigerator) before sowing -- echinacea and lavender especially. Direct-sown seed in late fall accomplishes the same thing naturally.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or transplant seedlings to recommended spacing once they have 4 to 6 true leaves. Perennials need their permanent home from the start -- moving them later disrupts establishment.
Mulch around young transplants to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the plant for the first season.

established.text_seasoned: Year one is mostly about root development -- many perennials produce minimal foliage and few flowers in the first season. This is normal; resist the urge to give up on a slow-establishing perennial.

By year two most of these perennials hit their stride and begin producing the heavy bloom you planted them for. Echinacea and bee-balm especially become more impressive each year for the first 4 to 5 seasons.

budding.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single annual bloom window -- echinacea midsummer, lavender early-to-mid summer, bee-balm midsummer, viola spring and fall, chamomile early summer. Buds form weeks before bloom.
Watch lavender for spittlebug at bud stage -- the white foam on stems is unsightly but harmless and rarely needs intervention.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadheading extends bloom marginally on most perennials but does not transform their cycle the way it does for annuals -- a perennial generally has one main bloom window per year regardless of deadheading. Deadhead for tidiness rather than to chase a second bloom.

Many perennials attract specific pollinators -- echinacea and bee-balm are bumblebee and hummingbird favorites; lavender draws honey bees in numbers; viola attracts solitary bees. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials self-seed if you leave seed heads to mature. Echinacea seed heads are particularly attractive to goldfinches and other birds -- leaving them standing through fall is good wildlife support.

To save seed deliberately, collect dried seed heads on a dry day, separate seeds from chaff, and store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place. Most perennial flower seeds need cold stratification before they will germinate; a winter outdoors or in the refrigerator does this.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous blooms throughout the season with regular deadheading
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Flowers in the vegetable garden are one of the most worthwhile additions -- beautiful, functional, and good for pollinators.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These perennials are hardy through their respective USDA zones -- echinacea zones 3-8, bee-balm zones 4-9, lavender zones 5-9 (varies by species; English lavender is hardier than Spanish), viola zones 3-8, chamomile (Roman) zones 3-7. Hard winter cold below the variety's range causes crown damage and may kill the plant entirely.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range before relying on it as a perennial -- some plants sold as perennials are actually annuals or short-lived perennials in cold zones. Mulch crowns in the colder end of the variety's range. For lavender in zones 5-6, choose hardy English lavender (L. angustifolia) and plant on the south side of a wall.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew is the most common problem on bee-balm and to a lesser extent echinacea -- both develop white powdery patches on leaves in humid summers or where plants are crowded. Aster yellows is a viral disease that distorts echinacea flowers. Lavender suffers root rot in poorly-drained soil rather than insect pests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose mildew-resistant bee-balm varieties (Marshall's Delight, Jacob Cline) and space generously for airflow. Remove and destroy plants showing aster yellows -- it spreads via leafhoppers and infected plants do not recover. For lavender, drainage prevention is better than disease cure.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single bloom window per year and then move on -- this is not a failure but the plant's normal cycle. After the main bloom, leaves stay green for the rest of the season but no new flowers come. Deadheading extends bloom marginally; in some cases (viola) it can produce a second smaller bloom in fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plan plantings with succession in mind so something different is blooming each month rather than expecting any single perennial to bloom continuously. Allow some seed heads to remain for wildlife and self-seeding.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lavender prefers dry conditions and is harmed by frequent watering -- drought is rarely lavender's problem. Bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile prefer consistent moisture and stress under drought, with leaf wilting and reduced bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile during dry spells -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Lavender needs water only during establishment and prolonged drought; once established it actively resents regular watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials prefer full sun. Lavender requires 6 to 8 hours of direct sun and grows poorly in any shade. Echinacea and bee-balm tolerate light afternoon shade. Viola actively prefers part shade in hot summers and may stop blooming in full sun once temperatures climb.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match the variety to the available light. For shaded perennial-flower spots, viola is the most cooperative; for full sun, lavender, echinacea, and bee-balm all thrive.

crops.description_seasoned: Native North American perennial with edible flowers and oregano-flavored leaves. Attracts bees, butterflies, and hummingbirds in extraordinary numbers. Spreads by rhizomes to form large, long-lived clumps.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut flower stems just as the top whorls of flowers open. For fresh use in cooking/tea: pick young leaves before flowering when flavor is strongest. Deadhead to extend bloom.
crops.hardiness_notes_seasoned: Monarda, native North American perennial Z3-Z9. Attracts pollinators heavily. Prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead spent flower clusters promptly -- this encourages reblooming. Cut the stem back to a set of leaves with visible buds. Powdery mildew is common on bee balm; removing spent stems also helps airflow.

crops.name: Viola
crops.tip_seasoned: Violas decline in summer heat. Plant as a cool-season annual and replace with warm-season flowers when temperatures consistently exceed 80°F. In mild climates they can bloom for 6 months straight.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Moderate feeder during cool season. Regular feeding maintains continuous bloom.

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

storage.freezer_seasoned: Freeze flowers in ice cubes -- classic use for cocktails and drinks
storage.notes_seasoned: Edible flowers with a mild sweet-grassy flavor. Use fresh or freeze decoratively in ice.

recommended: Penny Lane Mix (small pansy type, very cold-hardy)
Johnny Jump Up (heirloom, tiny, extremely prolific)
Delta Pure Yellow (bold color, good for edging)
varieties.note_seasoned: Johnny Jump Up is virtually indestructible -- self-sows prolifically and blooms from late winter through summer.

provenance.label: mechanistic
provenance.reason: Flowering plants attracting predatory insects is a documented biological control mechanism (UC IPM, Cornell). Specific pairings vary in effectiveness.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct sown after last frost. Many also benefit from indoor starting 6-8 weeks early for earlier blooms.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers grow well in containers. Use any pot with good drainage -- window boxes and hanging baskets work well.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: None
rotation.good_after: Anywhere -- edible flowers and beneficial companion
rotation.note_seasoned: Violas self-seed freely and can be grown anywhere. Biennial types overwinter and bloom early spring.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Most perennial flowers can be started from seed but establish slowly -- expect to plant in year one and bloom in year two. Many gardeners buy young plants instead of starting from seed.

If sowing from seed, several of these crops benefit from cold stratification (4 to 6 weeks of cold moist treatment in the refrigerator) before sowing -- echinacea and lavender especially. Direct-sown seed in late fall accomplishes the same thing naturally.

seedling.text_seasoned: Thin or transplant seedlings to recommended spacing once they have 4 to 6 true leaves. Perennials need their permanent home from the start -- moving them later disrupts establishment.
Mulch around young transplants to retain moisture and suppress weeds. Hand-weed close to the plant for the first season.

established.text_seasoned: Year one is mostly about root development -- many perennials produce minimal foliage and few flowers in the first season. This is normal; resist the urge to give up on a slow-establishing perennial.

By year two most of these perennials hit their stride and begin producing the heavy bloom you planted them for. Echinacea and bee-balm especially become more impressive each year for the first 4 to 5 seasons.

budding.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single annual bloom window -- echinacea midsummer, lavender early-to-mid summer, bee-balm midsummer, viola spring and fall, chamomile early summer. Buds form weeks before bloom.
Watch lavender for spittlebug at bud stage -- the white foam on stems is unsightly but harmless and rarely needs intervention.

flowering.text_seasoned: Deadheading extends bloom marginally on most perennials but does not transform their cycle the way it does for annuals -- a perennial generally has one main bloom window per year regardless of deadheading. Deadhead for tidiness rather than to chase a second bloom.

Many perennials attract specific pollinators -- echinacea and bee-balm are bumblebee and hummingbird favorites; lavender draws honey bees in numbers; viola attracts solitary bees. Avoid spraying anything during bloom.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: Most of these perennials self-seed if you leave seed heads to mature. Echinacea seed heads are particularly attractive to goldfinches and other birds -- leaving them standing through fall is good wildlife support.

To save seed deliberately, collect dried seed heads on a dry day, separate seeds from chaff, and store in paper envelopes in a cool dry place. Most perennial flower seeds need cold stratification before they will germinate; a winter outdoors or in the refrigerator does this.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Continuous blooms throughout the season with regular deadheading
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Flowers in the vegetable garden are one of the most worthwhile additions -- beautiful, functional, and good for pollinators.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: These perennials are hardy through their respective USDA zones -- echinacea zones 3-8, bee-balm zones 4-9, lavender zones 5-9 (varies by species; English lavender is hardier than Spanish), viola zones 3-8, chamomile (Roman) zones 3-7. Hard winter cold below the variety's range causes crown damage and may kill the plant entirely.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Confirm your variety's hardiness range before relying on it as a perennial -- some plants sold as perennials are actually annuals or short-lived perennials in cold zones. Mulch crowns in the colder end of the variety's range. For lavender in zones 5-6, choose hardy English lavender (L. angustifolia) and plant on the south side of a wall.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew is the most common problem on bee-balm and to a lesser extent echinacea -- both develop white powdery patches on leaves in humid summers or where plants are crowded. Aster yellows is a viral disease that distorts echinacea flowers. Lavender suffers root rot in poorly-drained soil rather than insect pests.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Choose mildew-resistant bee-balm varieties (Marshall's Delight, Jacob Cline) and space generously for airflow. Remove and destroy plants showing aster yellows -- it spreads via leafhoppers and infected plants do not recover. For lavender, drainage prevention is better than disease cure.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials have a single bloom window per year and then move on -- this is not a failure but the plant's normal cycle. After the main bloom, leaves stay green for the rest of the season but no new flowers come. Deadheading extends bloom marginally; in some cases (viola) it can produce a second smaller bloom in fall.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Plan plantings with succession in mind so something different is blooming each month rather than expecting any single perennial to bloom continuously. Allow some seed heads to remain for wildlife and self-seeding.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Lavender prefers dry conditions and is harmed by frequent watering -- drought is rarely lavender's problem. Bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile prefer consistent moisture and stress under drought, with leaf wilting and reduced bloom.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water bee-balm, echinacea, viola, and chamomile during dry spells -- 1 inch per week is the rough target. Lavender needs water only during establishment and prolonged drought; once established it actively resents regular watering.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Most of these perennials prefer full sun. Lavender requires 6 to 8 hours of direct sun and grows poorly in any shade. Echinacea and bee-balm tolerate light afternoon shade. Viola actively prefers part shade in hot summers and may stop blooming in full sun once temperatures climb.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Match the variety to the available light. For shaded perennial-flower spots, viola is the most cooperative; for full sun, lavender, echinacea, and bee-balm all thrive.

succession_policy.tip_seasoned: Plant in autumn and again in early spring to maximize the cool-season windows. Violas thrive in cool weather and look shabby in summer heat. The autumn planting often overwinters and blooms in earliest spring before you can sow again. A fresh spring sowing then carries the season forward. In zones 8+, autumn plantings provide color through winter. Two well-timed plantings beat multiple summer sowings.
succession_policy.reason_seasoned: Two seasonal windows -- fall and spring -- allow successive plantings.

crops.description_seasoned: Cool-season flowers that bloom when almost nothing else does, filling the critical early-spring gap for pollinators. Completely edible with a mild, sweet flavor. Tolerates frost and even light snow.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Pick flowers as soon as they open for eating or cutting. For continuous bloom, deadhead every 2-3 days. Harvest in morning when petals are firm and flavor is most sweet.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Deadhead regularly by pinching off spent flowers. In summer heat, shear plants back by one-third and they will rebloom in cooler autumn weather.

crops.name: Sweet Pea
crops.tip_seasoned: Sow seeds outdoors in early spring as soon as soil can be worked -- sweet peas need cool weather to germinate and establish. Nick the seed coat with a nail file before planting to improve germination rate.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: As a nitrogen fixer, sweet peas need minimal nitrogen feeding. High potassium feed from bud set encourages flowering.
fertilizer.notify_message_seasoned: Time to feed your sweet peas

pests.name: Aphids
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Clusters of tiny soft insects on new growth and leaf undersides. Leaves curl, yellow, or become sticky with honeydew. Sooty black mold may follow.
pests.cause_seasoned: Multiple aphid species. Populations explode rapidly in warm weather.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Blast off with strong water jet. Apply insecticidal soap or neem oil directly to colonies. Introduce ladybugs or lacewings.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Plant marigolds and nasturtiums nearby. Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates soft, aphid-attractive growth. Encourage beneficial insects.

pests.name: Slugs & snails
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Irregular holes in leaves overnight. Slime trails visible in morning. Seedlings may be severed at soil level.
pests.cause_seasoned: Slugs and snails. Active in cool, moist conditions and at night.
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Set out beer traps at soil level. Apply diatomaceous earth around plant bases. Hand-pick at night with a torch. Iron phosphate slug pellets are organic-approved.
pests.prevention_seasoned: Reduce mulch depth near seedlings. Eliminate hiding spots. Encourage hedgehogs and ground beetles.

diseases.name: Powdery mildew
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: White powdery coating on leaf surfaces, stems, and sometimes fruit. Leaves may yellow and die. Worst in warm days with cool nights.
diseases.cause_seasoned: Fungal disease favored by humid conditions with poor air circulation.
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Spray with diluted neem oil or a baking soda solution (1 tsp per quart water). Apply potassium bicarbonate spray. Remove and destroy affected leaves.
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Space plants for good airflow. Water at soil level, not on foliage. Choose resistant varieties. Avoid overhead irrigation.

storage.freezer_seasoned: N/A
storage.notes_seasoned: Sweet peas are purely decorative -- do not eat seeds or pods, they are toxic. Excellent cut flower only.

recommended: Spencer Mix (large ruffled flowers, most fragrant)
varieties.note_seasoned: Spencer varieties have the largest, most ruffled flowers and strongest fragrance -- the classic sweet pea for cutting.

good_beginner_seasoned.name: Radishes
good_beginner_seasoned.why_seasoned: Mark rows and break up soil

provenance.reason: Root-zone partitioning is a real ecology concept. 'Carrots loosen soil for tomatoes' is a plausible mechanistic claim but not well-studied for specific pairs.

start_method.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers can be direct sown after last frost. Many also benefit from indoor starting 6-8 weeks early for earlier blooms.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Most annual flowers grow well in containers. Use any pot with good drainage -- window boxes and hanging baskets work well.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: Other legumes -- peas, beans -- share diseases
rotation.good_after: Brassicas, nightshades -- sweet peas fix nitrogen like other legumes
rotation.note_seasoned: Sweet peas are in the legume family and fix small amounts of nitrogen. Rotate away from edible peas and beans in the same family.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seedlings emerging. Most flowers germinate readily in spring warmth.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Most flowers can be sown directly or started indoors. Annuals started indoors get a head start on the season.

growth_stages.name: Seedling
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: True leaves developing -- often very different in appearance from the seed leaves.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Thin to recommended spacing. Crowded flowers bloom less and are more prone to disease.

growth_stages.name: Established
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Strong plants with multiple sets of leaves, approaching budding.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Pinch out growing tips on many annual flowers to encourage bushy, multi-stem plants with more blooms.

growth_stages.name: Budding
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flower buds forming. The anticipation before the first bloom.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Feed with a high-potassium fertilizer to support bud development and continuous blooming.

growth_stages.name: Flowering
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Flowers open -- pollinators arriving.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Deadhead regularly on most annuals to keep production going. Leaving spent flowers to seed tells the plant its job is done.

growth_stages.name: Seed Saving
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seed heads forming and drying on the plant.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Let the last flowers of the season set seed. Collect when seed heads are dry and papery. Store in paper envelopes in a cool, dry place.

notifications.title_seasoned: Last frost passed -- sow your flowers
notifications.body_seasoned: Most annual flowers go directly in the ground after last frost. Prepare the bed, sow thinly, and water in. They will establish quickly as the weather warms.

notifications.title_seasoned: Start deadheading to keep flowers coming
notifications.body_seasoned: Remove spent flowers regularly -- every few days at peak season. This prevents seed setting and keeps the plant producing new blooms. Five minutes of deadheading extends the flowering season by weeks.

notifications.title_seasoned: Let the last flowers set seed
notifications.body_seasoned: Stop deadheading now and let the last blooms set seed. Collect seed heads when they are fully dry -- shake into a paper bag or clip the whole head. Label and store in a cool dry place for next year.

notifications.title_seasoned: Plant flowers near your vegetables for pest control
notifications.body_seasoned: Marigolds, nasturtiums, and calendula planted among vegetables deter pests and attract beneficial insects. Get them in now alongside your tomatoes, cucumbers, and brassicas before pest season begins.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: Frost warning -- protect tender annual flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Tender annual flowers like marigolds, nasturtiums, and zinnias are frost-sensitive. Cover with fleece tonight or bring containers inside. Hardy annuals like calendula and sweet peas handle light frost well.

weather_triggers.title_seasoned: High humidity -- watch for powdery mildew on flowers
weather_triggers.body_seasoned: Many flowers are prone to powdery mildew in humid conditions. Ensure good airflow between plants and avoid watering the foliage. Remove affected leaves promptly.

germination.text_seasoned: Sweet pea (Lathyrus odoratus) is a cool-season climbing legume, not a true pea. Sow seeds outdoors 4 to 6 weeks before the last frost, or start indoors in mid-winter and transplant out in early spring. Sweet pea is one of the few flowers that wants cold soil, not warm.
Soak seeds in water overnight before sowing to soften the hard coat -- some growers nick the seed coat with a file as well. Germination takes 10 to 21 days; do not give up early.

seedling.text_seasoned: Pinch the growing tip when seedlings are 4 inches tall to encourage branching. This is the single most useful technique for boosting sweet pea yield.
Provide trellising before transplanting or as soon as direct-sown seedlings emerge. Sweet pea needs to climb from day one and resents being moved or having a trellis added later.

established.text_seasoned: Train tendrils onto netting, twine, or wire support as plants climb. Some varieties grow 6 to 8 feet tall and need substantial support; bush varieties top out at 3 feet.
Water consistently and feed every 2 weeks with a balanced fertilizer -- sweet pea is one of the few flowers that responds well to regular feeding. Mulch heavily to keep roots cool.

budding.text_seasoned: Buds form 8 to 10 weeks after sowing in spring-sown plants. The budding-to-flowering transition is fast in cool weather; faster than for most annual flowers.
Watch for powdery mildew at the bud stage, especially in still humid weather. Spacing and trellising for airflow are the main preventive measures.

flowering.text_seasoned: Pick flowers regularly -- sweet pea is one of the all-time great cut flowers and the more you cut, the more it produces. A plant that goes to seed stops flowering completely; deadheading is essential here.

Heat ends the sweet pea bloom cycle -- when daytime temperatures consistently exceed 80 degrees, plants stop flowering and decline rapidly. In hot zones, sweet pea is over by early summer; cool zones may extend the bloom into July.

seed_saving.text_seasoned: If saving seed, allow a few late flowers to set pods. The pods turn from green to brown and dry on the vine; collect when fully dry. Many sweet pea varieties are open-pollinated and come true from saved seed.

Plan to replace plants entirely each year -- sweet pea is a cool-season annual and does not repeat-perform from the same root system the way perennial vines do. Save seed or buy fresh seed each fall for next spring's sowing.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: Generous early-season bloom flush; reduces sharply in summer heat
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Sweet peas are a cool-season crop -- early spring through early summer -- not a continuous summer flower. Plan for a flush rather than a season.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sweet pea is unusual among flowers in tolerating cool weather and dying off in heat. Young plants tolerate light frost; mature plants flower through cool spring weather but stop and decline once daytime temperatures consistently exceed 80 degrees. The end of sweet pea is heat, not cold.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Sow as early as possible -- 4 to 6 weeks before last frost in most zones, or even in fall in mild-winter zones for spring bloom. Choose heat-tolerant varieties (Old Spice series, Cuthbertson types) for warmer zones, and accept that sweet pea is a spring crop only in hot regions.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Powdery mildew is the headline sweet pea disease, especially in still humid conditions or on crowded plantings. Aphids cluster on tender new growth. Slugs damage young seedlings. Sweet pea root rot can take hold in poorly-drained soil.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Space plants for airflow and trellis to keep foliage off the ground. Water at the base rather than overhead to keep foliage dry. For aphids, hose off or wait for predators. For slugs, set traps or use a barrier method around seedlings.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Two main causes: heat stress (the most common, when daytime temperatures exceed 80 degrees consistently) and seed set (the plant's signal that its job is done). A sweet pea that has set even a few seed pods stops producing new flowers; consistent deadheading or harvest prevents this.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Deadhead religiously -- check daily during peak bloom. In hot climates, accept that sweet pea has a 6 to 8 week window in spring and plan succession plantings of warm-season flowers to follow.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sweet pea has shallow roots and needs consistent moisture, especially during bloom. Drought stress shortens the bloom cycle and produces small flowers on short stems. Heat amplifies drought damage substantially.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water consistently -- 1 inch per week minimum, more in heat. Mulch heavily to keep roots cool and conserve moisture. Drip irrigation outperforms overhead watering for sweet pea by both providing consistent water and keeping foliage dry.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Sweet pea needs full sun -- 6 to 8 hours minimum -- to flower well. In partial shade plants grow tall and leafy with sparse bloom. In hot climates, light afternoon shade can extend the bloom cycle by reducing heat stress without compromising flower production.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Site in full sun in cool climates, full morning sun with afternoon shade in hot climates. South or southeast exposure is ideal.

crops.description_seasoned: Climbing annual with intensely fragrant flowers and nitrogen-fixing roots. Attracts early-season pollinators and improves soil for neighboring vegetables. Requires a trellis. NOTE: flowers and seeds are toxic -- do not eat.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Cut stems with 2-3 flowers open, 2-3 in bud. Pick every 2-3 days without fail -- any pods that form signal the plant to stop flowering. Morning harvest extends vase life.
crops.deadheading_seasoned: Remove spent flowers immediately -- any pods forming signal the plant to stop flowering. Check every 2-3 days. Never let pods develop if you want continuous blooms.

crops.name: Radish Microgreens
crops.tip_seasoned: Radish microgreens are the best crop to start with -- they germinate in 24 hours and are ready in less than a week. Sow densely and keep the blackout lid on until you see the seed hulls rising.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist 2-3 times daily during germination; once or twice daily once in light
watering.amount_seasoned: Keep growing medium moist but never waterlogged
watering.method_seasoned: Bottom watering or fine mist -- top watering can cause damping off
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: Gray mold, foul smell, stems rotting at base
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Dry crispy sprouts, slow germination, wilting seedlings

storage.fridge_seasoned: 5-7 days in a sealed container lined with paper towel
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not suitable
storage.notes_seasoned: Harvest and refrigerate immediately. Do not wash until ready to eat. The paper towel absorbs moisture and prevents rapid deterioration.

varieties.note_seasoned: China Rose is the most widely grown radish microgreen -- reliable germination, consistent pink color, and excellent spicy flavor.

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Microgreens draw all their nutrition from the seed and growing medium. No fertilization needed for 5-7 day crops.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Tiny flies around trays; larvae damage roots and stems at soil level
pests.cause_seasoned: Overwatering creating wet growing medium
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Allow medium to dry slightly between waterings; yellow sticky traps
pests.prevention_seasoned: Don't overwater; use clean growing medium; bottom-water where possible

diseases.name: Damping off
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Seedlings collapse at soil line, stems thin and water-soaked
diseases.cause_seasoned: Overwatering, poor airflow, contaminated medium
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Improve airflow; reduce watering; discard affected tray and start fresh
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Use clean trays; don't overwater; sow at correct density; ensure airflow

start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow seeds densely (cover tray surface) on damp growing medium. No soaking needed. Cover with second tray for 2-3 day blackout phase, then move to light.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Grown in shallow 10×20 inch trays -- standard propagation trays work perfectly. No minimum gallon requirement.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A
rotation.note_seasoned: Indoor tray crop -- no rotation needed. Clean trays between batches.

growth_stages.name: Sowing
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds evenly distributed on moist growing medium.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Sow densely and evenly. Mist thoroughly, cover with a blackout lid or second tray, and press down firmly to ensure seed contact with the medium.

growth_stages.name: Germination
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Seeds sprouting -- white roots and pale shoots pushing up under the blackout cover.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Leave covered and check moisture daily. The weight of the tray on top helps seeds develop straight, strong stems.

growth_stages.name: Blackout Phase
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Shoots pushing against the lid -- they should be pale yellow and reaching upward.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: When shoots are pressing against the blackout cover, move to light. The stretch in darkness builds stem length.

growth_stages.name: Growing in Light
growth_stages.what_to_look_for_seasoned: Greening up fast as chlorophyll develops. Cotyledons (seed leaves) opening fully.
growth_stages.user_action_seasoned: Water from below by setting the tray in water and allowing it to absorb upward -- this avoids mold on the surface. Harvest when seed leaves are fully open.

notifications.title_seasoned: Move your microgreens to light
notifications.body_seasoned: Your microgreens should be ready to move from blackout to light -- check that shoots are pressing against the cover. Move to a bright windowsill or under grow lights now. They will green up within hours.

notifications.title_seasoned: Check your microgreens for harvest
notifications.body_seasoned: Microgreens are ready when the seed leaves are fully open and the first true leaves are just beginning to show. Harvest with scissors just above the soil line. Rinse and use immediately for the best flavor.

sow.text_seasoned: Sow densely -- microgreens are one of the few crops where crowding is desirable. Even coverage without gaps gives the best harvest.
Soak large seeds (sunflower, peas) overnight before sowing. They germinate more evenly and quickly.

germination.text_seasoned: The weight of a tray or board on top helps seeds press into the medium and develop straight, strong stems in the dark.
Check moisture once a day -- the medium should be moist but not waterlogged. If it feels wet on top, wait before misting again.

blackout.text_seasoned: Darkness forces upward growth and builds stem length. The stretch is intentional and desirable.
If shoots are very pale or yellow after 5+ days, they have been in blackout too long. Move to light immediately.

light.text_seasoned: Bottom watering prevents mold, which is the main challenge with microgreens. Set the tray in water for 10-15 minutes rather than misting the surface.
Harvest in the morning when the plants are full of water. Cut, rinse immediately, and use within a day or two.

yield_expectations.per_plant_seasoned: One tray yields 50-200g depending on variety and tray size
yield_expectations.peak_production_seasoned: Ready in 7-14 days -- the fastest crop you can grow
yield_expectations.first_year_note_seasoned: Microgreens are instant gratification -- from seed to harvest in under two weeks. Perfect for getting children interested in growing.

moon_phase_preference.source_note_seasoned: Traditional moon-phase planting guidance, not extension-backed.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: White fuzzy mold on the surface
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Surface mold is caused by overwatering or poor airflow. It is different from the white root hairs that are completely normal and healthy -- root hairs are orderly and attached to stems, mold is fuzzy and appears on the soil surface.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water from below by setting the tray in water -- never mist the surface once seeds have germinated. Ensure good airflow around the tray.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Seedlings fell over at the base
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Damping off is a fungal condition that rots the stem at soil level. It is caused by overwet, poorly ventilated conditions -- especially in the blackout phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Do not overwater during germination. Ensure the growing medium is moist but not wet before sowing. Improve airflow once seedlings emerge.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Patchy germination is usually caused by uneven seed contact with the growing medium, or the surface drying out during germination. Larger seeds like sunflower and peas benefit from pre-soaking.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Press seeds firmly into the surface after sowing. Soak larger seeds for 8 hours before sowing. Ensure the medium is thoroughly moist before you start.

failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Microgreens kept in blackout for too long become etiolated -- pale, stretched, and weak. Once moved to light they should green up within hours. If they do not, they have been in darkness too long.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Move to light as soon as shoots are pressing against the blackout cover -- usually day 3-5. They green up fast once in light. Do not wait until they look fully grown under the dome.

failure_diagnostics.label_seasoned: Wilted or crispy after moving to light
failure_diagnostics.what_happened_seasoned: Microgreens dry out fast under grow lights or in a sunny window. They need consistent moisture from below during the light phase.
failure_diagnostics.next_season_tip_seasoned: Water from below once a day during the light phase -- set the tray in a shallow dish of water for 10-15 minutes and let it absorb upward.

indoor_cycle.tip_seasoned: The fastest microgreen. Mild peppery flavor. Sow thickly for a dense mat. No pre-soaking needed.

crops.description_seasoned: The fastest microgreen -- bold, peppery flavor ready in 5-7 days. One of the easiest crops to grow and a great entry point for microgreen beginners.
crops.harvest_ready_seasoned: Harvest at 5-7 days when cotyledons are fully open and bright purple-pink. Don't wait -- radish microgreens turn bitter and tough quickly. Cut at soil level with scissors.

crops.name: Broccoli Microgreens
crops.tip_seasoned: Broccoli microgreens are worth growing for the nutrition alone -- the sulforaphane content is highest when harvested young (8-10 days). Mist evenly and keep good airflow to prevent mold on the dense canopy.

watering.frequency_seasoned: Mist twice daily -- morning and evening
watering.amount_seasoned: Keep medium moist throughout -- broccoli doesn't tolerate drying out
watering.method_seasoned: Bottom watering after the blackout phase; mist lightly from above to maintain humidity
watering.signs_overwater_seasoned: White fuzzy mold on stems (different from root hairs -- mold is fuzzy, root hairs are straight)
watering.signs_underwater_seasoned: Slow growth, wilting despite watered medium, pale yellow leaves

storage.fridge_seasoned: 5-7 days in a sealed container with paper towel
storage.freezer_seasoned: Not suitable
storage.notes_seasoned: Broccoli microgreens are more perishable than radish. Refrigerate immediately and consume within a week.

recommended: Red Acre Cabbage blend (adds color to mix)
varieties.note_seasoned: Standard broccoli seed works well -- no special microgreen variety needed. Buy untreated seeds only (fungicide-treated seeds are not safe for eating as microgreens).

fertilizer.notes_seasoned: Seed nutrients are sufficient for the 8-12 day growing period.

pests.name: Fungus gnats
pests.symptoms_seasoned: Small flies near trays; larvae in growing medium
pests.cause_seasoned: Overwatering
pests.organic_treatment_seasoned: Reduce watering; bottom-water only; yellow sticky traps
pests.prevention_seasoned: Good airflow; clean growing medium; don't overwater

diseases.name: Mold / damping off
diseases.symptoms_seasoned: Fuzzy white or gray mold on stems or growing medium surface
diseases.cause_seasoned: Overwatering, high humidity, poor airflow, sowing too densely
diseases.organic_treatment_seasoned: Increase airflow with a small fan; reduce watering; harvest immediately if mold appears
diseases.prevention_seasoned: Good airflow; correct sowing density; don't overwater; clean trays between batches

start_method.notes_seasoned: Sow densely on damp medium. Blackout for 3 days, then move to light. A small fan for airflow dramatically reduces mold risk on dense brassica canopies.

container_notes.notes_seasoned: Standard 10×20 propagation trays. Good airflow around the tray is important to prevent mold.

rotation.avoid_after_seasoned: N/A
rotation.note_seasoned: Clean and sanitize trays between batches to prevent disease carryover.
